screen that wrote keys the resolver did not read would look exactly like a working one and do nothing,
and that failure is invisible from either side alone.

**One shared registry change.** `SettingKind` gains `number` — a bounded integer field for the
assistant's daily question ceiling — and its bounds are **required** rather than optional, checked by
`apps/web/test/settings-mode-purity.test.ts`: a numeric field with no stated ceiling renders as one
that will take anything and be refused by the server, which teaches the wrong thing about what a firm
may choose. `SettingValue` widens to carry a number rather than stringly typing one, so no staging
boundary compares `"500"` against `500`.
- **Three notification settings were read on every pass and writable by nothing.** The preference
subsystem stores two tiers of one key, and only one of them had a route. A member could set their own
per-category matrix; the FIRM tier — the in-app floor that stops somebody silencing a category their
firm insists on — was composed into `resolveCategoryPreference` on every fan-out and could not be set
by anybody. The same held for the two firm settings beside it: `notifications.retentionDays`, read by
the nightly sweep that deletes notification rows, and `notifications.digestLocalHour`, asked of every
firm by the hourly digest pass. All three write statements existed, were correct, and had exactly one
non-test reference in the repository: their own definition. Nothing failed, because the read side
returned the default forever and the tests that covered the floor inserted the row themselves.

**`GET` and `PATCH /api/v1/firm/notifications/policy`** close it, under a new
`firm:manageNotificationPolicy` seeded to Owner/Admin only. **The permission is the decision here, not
a detail.** The member preference route rides `notifications:read`, which is deliberately seeded to
every default role including Read-only, because reading one's own feed is not a privilege. Reusing it
for the firm tier would have meant any member of any firm could raise the floor for all their
colleagues and shorten the whole firm's retention window — `apps/api-worker/test/firm-notification-policy-routes.test.ts`
seeds exactly that member and asserts 403 on both verbs, and swapping the route's permission back to
the member key was watched to turn both red with `expected 200 to be 403`.

**Two more properties were pinned by breaking them.** Writing the firm tier must not write the
administrator's own preferences: the test reads the `scoped_setting` rows directly and asserts a
firm-tier row with the value and zero user-tier rows for the actor, and pointing the write at
`writeMemberNotificationPreferencesStatement` instead turned four tests red. And the floor has to
actually bind, which is only observable from the other side — a member silences a category through
their own route, the firm raises the floor through this one, and the member's own read comes back
`inApp: on`, `inAppLockedBy: firm-policy`, with their own choice still on the row so lowering the floor
returns them to `off` rather than to the default.

**The window and the hour are refused outside their bounds, never clamped.** Thirty to three hundred
and sixty-five days, and an hour from 0 to 23; anything else is a 422 with nothing written. A firm that
asked for five years and silently got one would believe it had the first. Removing the bound was
watched to turn that test red.

**The sparse merge is now one function for both tiers.** `mergeNotificationPreferences` moved out of
the member route into `@magna-carta/notifications`, so "clear this channel" means the same thing
whichever tier is patching. Two copies of that is two subtly different notions of what an absent
preference is.

**A fitness function for the shape this was found by.** `pnpm run lint:unwired-writes` fails any
exported write-shaped function in `apps/` or `packages/` that nothing outside a test calls. It was
measured against the whole tree before it was kept, in both variants: the strict form reports four
today, every one a written allowlist entry with its reason (a test logger, an unused port factory over
a function production calls directly, and two control-plane tables that are seeded by hand because the
platform has no self-service grant surface for them). Replayed against the tree as it stood one commit
earlier it reports ten, including the three auto-file writers whose absence made the auto-file engine
evaluate an empty set. The looser variant — "no reference outside the defining file" — was measured at
nine against four and rejected: all five extra hits are the same correct idiom, a statement composed
into an ordered batch by a helper beside it, which is how every write whose ordering is the invariant
is written here. An allowlist entry with a blank reason, an entry naming a function that no longer
exists, and an entry whose function has since gained a caller are each failures of their own, so the
gate cannot go quiet without somebody deciding it should.

**Not built, and named rather than left implicit:** the firm's email DETAIL-LEVEL ceiling
(`notifications.emailDetailLevel`) has no write statement in either tier, so it is invisible to a scan
that looks for writers with no callers. Building only the firm half would let a firm raise what its
members' mail carries with no member lever to lower it again, which is the asymmetry the subsystem is
built to prevent; it wants both halves in one change. Recorded on the `notifications.firm-policy`
ledger node.
- **A firm can now record a client's telephone number.** It could not before. `directory_phone` and
`directory_address` were real tables with no domain module at all — not one statement in the
repository inserted a phone number or an address — and email had a write path reachable only from
inbound mail capture. All three are reachable now, through fourteen operations under the firm-scoped
chokepoint, with a combined read that answers all three channels at once.

**Permission and preference are separate facts.** A contact point records whether it may be used and
whether it is preferred, because someone can be reachable by a method that is not their preference.
At most one point is preferred across all three channels, since "write to me" is one answer about
every channel rather than one answer per channel. Withdrawing permission is what the surface offers
instead of deletion — deleting the value loses the instruction that came with it.

**A date of birth is a date again.** It was filed as an encrypted identifier, which is matched only by
exact blind index, and a date of birth carries too few plausible values to index safely — so the code
deliberately refused, and the date could not be searched or range-queried. It is now a plain date on
the person, with date of death and a separate deceased flag beside it, registered in the PII registry.
The birth-year compromise was withdrawn on the way: a year cannot fill in a court form.

**Addresses take the international field set** — no hardcoded state or ZIP, no required field — and the
seam a validation provider would land in ships without the provider. Sending a client's address to a
third party is a disclosure only the firm can authorise, so the recommendation is recorded and nothing
is adopted.
- **The three contact tables are reachable.** `directory_email`, `directory_phone` and
`directory_address` had been in the per-firm schema since the baseline migration with nothing able to
write to them: phone and address had no domain module at all, and `contact-email.ts` was a write path
built for and reachable only from inbound mail capture. Twenty-five directory routes touched none of
the three, and `entity-sections.ts` listed seven panes, none of them Contact. A firm could not record a
client's telephone number.

This change adds `contact-phone.ts`, `contact-address.ts`, `contact-points.ts`, `contact-preference.ts`,
`phone-number.ts` and `postal-address.ts` to `packages/directory`, lifts `contact-email.ts` to a general
write path, mounts thirteen routes on `apps/api-worker/src/routes/directory.ts`, and adds the Contact
and Dates panes to the record screen. One additive migration
(`20260830T120000_directory-contact-points.sql`) carries every column: the plan had been to reach the
tables first and add columns after, and that was reversed deliberately, because each of the owner's
rulings on this pass is a column the ENTRY SURFACE has to be able to take and building the pane twice
was the alternative.

The columns: `contact_permitted` / `contact_preferred` / `contact_note` on all three tables, with at
most one preferred contact point per entity ACROSS the three (three UPDATEs in the write batch, since
"write to me" is one answer about every channel and `is_primary` is a different fact — the channel's
default row); `contact_system` / `contact_use` / `country_calling_code` / `national_number` /
`extension` / `country_region_code` on phone, with `number` keeping its meaning as the number AS
ENTERED; the international address field set (`recipient`, `organization_name`, `street_two`,
`dependent_locality`, `sorting_code`) plus `address_use`, `address_type` and a `normalized_key` that is
a duplicate key and deliberately not a canonical postal form; the four verification columns on all
three; and `date_of_birth` / `date_of_death` / `deceased` on `directory_person`, in the clear and
registered for erasure. `structurePhoneNumber` implements the E.164 assignment rule rather than
carrying a metadata library, so a national-form number yields a null calling code rather than a guessed
one.

Eight of the design's open questions were answered by the owner and every section they touched was
rewritten in
[`docs/specs/2026-08-30-directory-entity-model-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-08-30-directory-entity-model-design.md):
the date of birth is the full date in plaintext (the `birth_year` compromise is withdrawn), citizenship
is dropped, the organization taxonomy is deferred whole, a failed verification never gates a send, and
the point person on an organization is an edge type rather than a flag because the point person is
frequently not an employee. Three decision fragments are new — the permission-and-preference split, the
point-of-contact edge, and the address-provider recommendation — and four existing ones were amended to
what was built. `point_of_contact_for` is decided and NOT built: a new `EDGE_TYPES` value must be
classed in `packages/conflicts/src/edge-classes.ts` in the same change, which was outside this stream's
file ownership.
- **`custom_field.target` widens to `matterAsset`, and the widening needed no migration.**
`CUSTOM_FIELD_TARGETS` in `packages/custom-fields/src/types.ts` is the one home for the vocabulary;
the drizzle column, the route's request enum, and the asset scope read all derive from it, and
`packages/custom-fields/test/schema-name-sync.test.ts` pins the column's `enumValues` to the constant
so a fourth target cannot be added in one place only. The column is a bare `text NOT NULL` with no
CHECK and drizzle's `enum` option emits no SQL, so nothing at the database had to change —
`readCustomFieldValuesForScope` and the merge catalogue's target filter are the readers that did.
- **A firm-supplied fillable PDF is now a template KIND rather than a second subsystem.**
`document_template_version.kind` is `wordProcessing | pdfForm`, defaulting to the existing value, and
the two kinds share the catalogue, the immutable version ladder, the ingest gate, the field-manifest
shape, the binding index, the per-firm dictionary, the formatters, the absence model, the provenance
row, and the telemetry — while sharing no engine. `prepareFormTemplateVersion`
(`packages/document-assembly/src/pdf-form.ts`) reads the AcroForm field set through an injected reader
over `crates/pdf-core`, scrubs the upload, and builds the manifest from the bytes that will be STORED;
`fillFormTemplate` (`src/fill-form.ts`) plans the fill and hands it to the same engine. The assembly job
branches on the kind in exactly one place, with the version read, the byte cache, the batched
merge-context resolution, and the protected-field chokepoint on one side of it and the absence
accounting, the ingest chokepoint, the provenance row, and the telemetry on the other.

**A box binds only what a human confirmed, and the exact name match is refused as well as the near one.**
Mappings come from the registration request or from the firm's existing
`document_template_field_mapping` library — the same store the Word `MERGEFIELD` conversion writes to. A
field whose name IS a merge key character for character is reported as `proposedMergeKey` and nothing
applies it: a proposal built on exactness becomes one built on normalization and then on resemblance,
and the line has to sit where it fits in one sentence. Every terminal field the form declares comes out
either bound or on a fourth manifest list (`unboundFormFields`) with its reason —
`no-confirmed-mapping`, `not-fillable`, or `unclassified`. An unclassifiable field is never filled as
text (a text fill writes an appearance stream, and an appearance stream prints), and a form binding
nothing warns that every document from it is the blank form — the failure `FORMTEXT` and the
placeholder-showing content control each produced before their lists existed.

The absence model is unchanged, with one divergence stated rather than smuggled: a tick box and a
set-answer box have nowhere to print a marker, so an unanswerable one is left unanswered with a reason
recorded, and a non-boolean value bound to a tick box or a value outside a drop-down's option set is a
reported absence rather than a guess.

**Flatten-or-not is left open as a typed seam.** `FormFillFinish` is a required parameter on the fill;
the platform's one answer is a named constant in `apps/api-worker/src/assemblies/pdf-form-engine.ts`, set to
`interactive` while the owner decision stands open, because flattening is irreversible.

Also: `crates/pdf-core`'s `FormField` gains `required` (`/Ff` bit 2, inherited down the field tree), which
the manifest records; and the per-firm lineage gains
`20260816T170000_document-template-kind`.
- The download register: a per-member shelf at `/downloads` of what the platform produced for that
member, held for seven days and downloadable again until it expires. It exists because the platform
had no durable record of a generated file at all — a bulk bundle is addressed by the content hash of
its selection and a conversion by its job id, both held only in a Durable Object and an R2 object, so
a member who closed the tab lost the artifact while its bytes sat in the bucket until the lifecycle
rule reaped them.

Routing completions through the notification feed was considered and **rejected on the owner's
ruling: notifications carry matter work, and a generated file is platform mechanics.** The two
surfaces stay separate in both directions — no producer raises a notification to say an artifact is
ready.

Two row kinds share one table because the member asks one question. A kept **artifact** points at
bytes that cannot be re-derived and re-downloads as a freshly minted presigned GET, so the browser's
own download manager keeps pause and resume; the register never proxies bytes. A kept **snapshot** is
an export, and stores the tabular DOCUMENT rather than a rendered file — one row serves every format,
and cells keep their number face so a re-rendered workbook still sums. New: `download_item` (per-firm,
member-scoped, journaled with its `downloads:shelf` seed to every default role), four routes under
`/api/v1/downloads`, and a retention sweep on the daily per-firm cron that takes the stored document
before the row. The export menu keeps every download it takes, in all six formats, including the three
the browser renders and the printer never sees.
- `icon-sm` — the Button's square at the small control height.

The icon size is a square at the medium height, which is right for a toolbar and four points too tall for a band that already holds one line at the small scale: a table's counts strip, a card's own header. A glyph control joining such a band had to either grow it or be styled off the recipe. This is the size that lets it join without doing either.
- **A raised hand and six reactions, relayed by the room and stored nowhere.** `RosterParticipant`
gains `hand` and `handRaisedAt` — two wire fields over ONE stored fact, projected in
`room/room-roster.ts` and nowhere else — and the client `presence` frame gains an optional `hand`.
The browser decides the boolean and the room stamps the instant, for the reason a chat message's
instant is the server's: a queue ordered by what each person's machine said is not one ordering. A
host lowers one hand or all of them with `lower-hands { participantId | null }`, authorized from the
STORED participant record like every other host frame and refused `not-host` otherwise; nobody is
spared by "lower all", including the host who pressed it. A lowered or raised hand travels on a
ROSTER change rather than a frame of its own, which is what keeps a host's queue right for the
browser that joined a minute after the hand went up.

**`MEETING_REACTIONS` is a closed vocabulary of six** — `thumbs-up`, `thumbs-down`, `heart`, `laugh`,
`applause`, `celebrate` — named by meaning rather than by the glyph that draws them, so upgrading the
icon package is not a change to the meeting protocol. A `reaction` naming anything else does not
parse.

**The room coalesces above `ROSTER_DELTA_THRESHOLD`, which is the whole design.** Three hundred
people applauding one sentence is three hundred inbound frames and, relayed one by one, ninety
thousand outbound inside a second. At or below the threshold the room sends `reaction
{ participantId, name, at }` and leaves the sender out; above it, reactions accumulate into a
per-name count flushed as ONE `reactions { counts, at }` frame per second for the whole room, driven
by the next frame with the room's own alarm as the backstop. The branch is counted over the WELCOMED
SOCKETS rather than over the roster: it is choosing a fan-out, and a roster read there would spend
three hundred keys on every reaction in exactly the room the coalescing exists for. The load harness
now drives a second of applause and measures it at **one frame per socket and zero roster reads per
reaction**.

**A new refusal reason, `rate-limited`, and it is the first throttle here that refuses rather than
drops.** Every other one discards a frame inside its window, which is safe because those frames
restate themselves. A hand may be the last thing somebody does for ten minutes and a reaction is a
single act with no later frame to carry it, so both answer to `SIGNAL_INTERVAL_MILLISECONDS` —
exported from the protocol package, because a client that paced itself by a different number would be
refused for behaving correctly — and the frame inside the window is refused with the socket kept
open.

**Nothing reaches the record.** No table, no migration, no audit row and no personal-data
registration: a hand and a reaction are transient room state on the terms the roster already is,
deleted when the stay ends and when the meeting does. One event,
`meetings.room.reactionsRelayed`, carrying the count and whether it was coalesced, and no field for
which reaction it was.
- `docs/handover/2026-08-24-matter-screens.md` — a handover an instance can start from cold. Three parts: what eight rounds of file-manager review taught about building UI here (the owner's standing rulings, the browser harness, and the failure mode where a check tests a property adjacent to the complaint and passes forever), where sign-in actually stands (email and password with two-factor genuinely work; passkeys, magic links, SSO, workspace selection and the rest are declared in one place, and the real blocker is two account-side steps only the owner can perform), and the brief for the matter screens still to build.
- **A hit carries what the firm already said about the same party — as context, and nothing more.**
The sixth and last read of the conflicts read surface, built under the owner's ruling of 2026-09-02.

`readPriorConclusions` matches on the ENTITY alone, across every check but the one in hand, and the
check response carries the result as `previouslyAnswered` — a field deliberately separate from
`disposition`, so a hit with an earlier answer about the same party is still **unanswered**.

The case that settled the rule, and the reason a narrower key would not be safer: a company cleared
in March under Rule 1.9 as a FORMER client re-surfaces in September through the graph, as the
subsidiary of a CURRENT client. That is a Rule 1.7 question on a materially higher bar. Same entity,
different question. Matching on the entity and presenting the March clearance as the September hit's
answer would carry a judgment across two conflicts that are not the same conflict.

Both narrower keys were rejected on that same case rather than a different one. Adding the source
class would hide the September hit precisely BECAUSE it arrived through the graph; adding the
evidence tier would make a firm turning on the over-inclusive band look like a new conflict. Neither
makes the judgment safer — they only move where it is wrong.

It needed a second index. `conflicts_hit` carried only `(check_id)`, so matching a party across
earlier checks scanned a table that is append-only and only grows;
`conflicts_hit_entity_created_index` on `(entity_id, created_at)` holds it, with a plan probe beside
the two check-history probes.

`conflicts-gaps.ts` is now down to one entry — the assembled report document, which is its own work.
- **A conflicts hit shows every answer recorded against it, not just the last one.** The conflicts log
is append-only precisely so that a reviewer who clears a hit and later reverses leaves both acts
standing — a reversal is a second row, never an edit — and until now nothing read that back. The hit
window showed the reviewer's latest word and a line saying the earlier ones were on the record and
unreadable.

`GET /api/v1/conflicts/hits/{hitId}/dispositions` serves the trail on `conflicts:read`, oldest
first, each entry carrying its own rationale, its reviewer, and for a waiver its own waiver record
and what that record is short of. `readDispositionTrail` uses the same `created_at`/`rowid`
tie-break `readCurrentDisposition` does, so the two reads can never disagree about which answer is
the latest — the pair that most needs a stable order is an answer and its reversal.

The hit's existence IS checked, unlike the matter posture read and for the opposite reason: "no such
hit" is not a state with a meaning of its own, so an empty trail must mean "nobody has answered this
hit" and nothing else. Conflating them would let a mistyped handle read as an unanswered candidate.

**The conformance gate caught a real contract bug on the first emit.** Reusing `DispositionDetail`
in the new response registered one component name under two schema shapes — the check response uses
it as `.nullable()`, and zod-to-openapi carries the component name onto the nullable schema, which
that library resolves first-write-wins. A trail entry is now its own component, which is also the
honest reading: on the check response `disposition` is the latest word and null means unanswered; on
the trail every entry is an act that happened and there is no null to express.
- **File Unlock & Password Recovery is a real, working tool, and a locked PDF leads straight to it.** The Tools catalog has named this capability for a while over a backend that was fully built and unreachable from any screen; it now has one. Dropping an encrypted PDF, ZIP, or Word/Excel/PowerPoint document onto the File Workbench and choosing Unlock offers exactly the two things the tool has always promised: unlock it with a password you have, or start a search for one you have lost.

Recovering an unknown password is a search that can run for hours, so starting one hands off to its own screen, addressed by the search rather than by the file that started it — leave it, close the tab, come back tomorrow, and the same link finds the same search exactly where it was left. It can be cancelled at any time, and a password it finds is shown once, to the person who started the search.

**Opening a password-protected PDF from a matter no longer just fails.** The reader now asks for the password right there, checks it in the browser without a round trip to the server, and opens the document the moment it is right. A wrong guess says so and lets the reader try again; a reader who does not have the password at all is pointed straight at the recovery tool.
- **A party could be put on a matter through the API and never read back.** Fifteen directory
endpoints, and the only matter-party operation among them was create. `readMatterParties` was not
missing: it is production code the conflicts checker calls on every run, exported from the package
and covered by tests, and no route mounted it. Whatever a client wrote, it could not ask for.

Two more holes came out of the same seam. Nothing anywhere set `matter_party.deleted_at`, and five
separate readers filter on that column, so a party linked by mistake was permanent and the only
remedy was a hand-written statement against the firm's database. And the shared row type omitted
`capacity` even though the link write has always stored it, so callers reading a party through the
package saw an absence that was not real.

The matter Parties section is built on the repaired seam. It lists who is on the matter with the
role, the directory name resolved in the same read rather than a query per row, and the capacity
where one was recorded, and it can sever a link with a confirmation that says what severing does.
Severing is a soft delete on purpose: a conflicts report that named a party has to stay reproducible,
so the row is retained and marked rather than removed. The sever publishes no bus message where the
link publishes one, because removing a party can only ever retract a conflicts hit, never create a
new one, and a retracted hit still showing is the safe direction to be wrong in.

Adding a party from the screen waits on the directory picker, so that action renders disabled with
the one line saying what it waits on. The route behind it has always worked.
- **The matter Calendar section reads the firm's own record.** Thirty-three calendar endpoints have
been built since early August and no screen called any of them; the section rendered a stub. It now
reads two things a matter's calendar is actually made of: every deadline recorded against the matter,
soonest first, and every event, furthest ahead first. Neither list is narrowed — a deadline already
satisfied or vacated is part of the record, and a cancelled setting is shown as cancelled rather
than hidden, because a setting that was called off and one that never existed are different facts.

Overdue leads. A deadline that is open and past its moment is the only thing on the screen anyone
still has to act on, so it is the only thing that alarms; the count is stated at the top. Past due is
the server's own read-time derivation in each deadline's own time zone, not a stored flag — there is
no column anywhere that says a firm missed something, and this screen adds none.

**The event listing answered with a type identifier and no name.** A screen handed
`eventTypeId` has nothing to render, which is the same hole the cost listing had for its vendor and
the time listing had for its timekeeper. The listing and the single-event read now resolve the type's
name through a display projection that joins the type catalog; the join is LEFT, so an event
classified under nothing stays in the list rather than falling out of it. The lean single-event read
the six lifecycle services use is untouched — resolving whether a change is allowed does not need a
type name, and widening six reads to serve one is the wrong trade.

Recording a date from this screen still waits on the participant picker, so those actions render
disabled and say why. Where a page shows only the first page of a longer record, it now says so
rather than presenting a truncated list as the whole thing.
- **The matter's paper file is kept at one of the firm's offices, and the status window states which.**
`matter.physical_file_location_id` is a new nullable per-firm column pointing at `location`, set
through `PATCH /api/v1/matters/{id}` (`matters:edit`) and answered by the matter detail read as
`physicalFileLocationId` plus a resolved `physicalFileLocationName` — `selectMatterDetailStatement`
now joins `location` twice under two aliases, because a matter names two different offices.

It is deliberately not `matter.location_id`. That column says which office RUNS the matter and is the
citation on the matter header; this one says where its folder is KEPT, and a folder travels. One word
("Location") on two screens was hiding two facts.

The status window's Physical File renders the row through `$lib/offices`' `OfficeLink` and sets it
through `OfficePicker`, reading the matter itself when the window opens so a file moved elsewhere
between two openings does not leave the window stating where it used to be. Held In and Destroy After
keep the Soon mark: what a folder sits inside is a record that does not exist yet, and there is no
retention clock anywhere to derive a destruction date from. `MATTER_PHYSICAL_FILE_FACTS` carries a
`served` flag so which rows are real is one list with one test.

The New Matter dialog's Location moved from `vocabulary-picker.svelte` to the same `OfficePicker`,
which reads the firm's offices through the shared store; the dialog's `locations` prop is accepted and
no longer read, and nothing imports `VocabularyPicker` now.
- **The matter status seal is the control that changes it, and the program answers what closing requires.** Pressing the seal on a matter's masthead opens the status window; the lifecycle action left the overflow menu, which held nothing else and is gone with it. The window is short by design: the status, what closing requires with each requirement already answered, where the firm's paper file is kept, and the one step the status allows. One step per status, never a status picker, because none of the three operations takes a status on the wire.

`GET /api/v1/matters/{id}/close-readiness` is new. The close hook's rules are pure reads with a separate commit guard, so running them read-only is the same question the close asks and none of the write — which means the window can list what closing requires with each one marked met or unmet, rather than handing somebody boxes to tick or a button to press to find out. One reply answers every requirement, because the route runs every rule and reports every failure, so a rule it does not name is a rule that passed; a refusal naming a rule this build has never heard of becomes its own unmet row rather than disappearing. An unmet requirement disables the press, per the rule that a control does not offer a press whose refusal is predictable — but an unanswered one never does, because nothing has been predicted there and the close is the authority either way. The route reports an already-closed matter as not closable with that as its blocker, so one definition of the word survives. A close refused at the last moment answers in the same shape and re-answers the requirements already on screen rather than arriving beside them. Those sentences reach the screen through a new `errors` array on the shared problem envelope, which until now dropped everything a refusal said beyond its one summary line.

**The step is seated on the status, not at the foot of the window.** Somebody may open this window to read where the file is kept, and one whose bottom-right corner offers Close Matter puts the act they did not come for exactly where a hand goes by habit. The corner offers only Done; the step is a quiet secondary control beside the fact it changes, with the requirements that gate it directly beneath, where they read as the reason it is disabled.

**The window is the firm's wide working window, and it has two sides.** The left is bounded and always will be: a status and the one step it offers. The right is a panel that grows into a real physical-file register, so it is sized for the work it will hold rather than for today's three empty rows — the structure that will hold results renders at rest. The division is the point. Left: the status and the step it offers. Right: the firm's own paper file. They are apart because the paper file is a STANDING fact and not a consequence of the step — a firm keeps a matter's folder in a box, commonly with other matters' folders and commonly at a remote store, and closing the matter moves none of that. Laid out under the requirements it would read as what closing does to the file, which is the one thing it must not say, so the panel says the opposite in as many words.

**Location**, **Held in** and **Destroy after** render, each holding nothing and marked Soon. There is deliberately no sentence under them naming the dependency: a row that reads "Not recorded" beside the Soon mark has said it is not built, and a paragraph repeating that under three rows was the loudest copy on a window whose whole point is to be short. The middle row deliberately does not say "Box": firms keep files in boxes, in cabinet drawers, in safes, on shelves, and a row that named one of them would decide the medium for every firm. What holds a file will be a record carrying its own kind, which a matter points at — for the same reason it is not part of the location, since one container holds several matters' folders. That system needs its own design work and the ledger node says so. None of it is modelled: the platform has no register of the firm's OWN paper files, and no retention policy anywhere to derive a destruction date from — the custody register is explicit that it runs no timer at all, destroying an original on a written basis by two people rather than because a date arrived. Custodian is client property left with the firm to guard, which outlives the matter that brought it in, and is not the firm's file for a matter; conflating them would put a client's will where a paper file belongs. The gap is now a ledger node (`matters.physical-file`) rather than an absence.

**`StatusMark` is a new design-system component** (`@magna-carta/design-system/status-mark`): the affirmative mark, a disc filled in the success tone with the check knocked out of it. It existed as a recipe class three surfaces reached for with their own icon import, and they had already drifted onto two different Lucide glyphs — `circle-check` in the file manager, the larger-tick `circle-check-big` in the catalog and the record-window gallery. One mark that reads the same everywhere is the whole point of a register, so the glyph is decided in one place now and `statusMarkClasses()` is retired; a met requirement in the status window looks exactly like a clean file in the file manager, because it is the same component. It carries an accessible name by default and takes `decorative` where words beside it already say the word.

The masthead also gained the way back, as a bare arrow at the head of the ledger line — the labelled `BackLink` rule earns its label above a masthead, where "back" is ambiguous; on a matter's own ledger line the docket is the only place up.
- **The browser is asked for a treated microphone, and the room says what it got.** `publish()` in
`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/client/meeting-client.svelte.ts` captures through the constraint builder
in `client/media-effects.ts`: noise suppression, echo cancellation and gain control asked for as
plain booleans, never `{ exact: true }`, because an exact constraint a device cannot meet rejects
the whole capture and a member with no microphone is worse than one with an untreated microphone.
`readAudioTreatment` reads back from the track what the browser actually applied, three-valued
(true, false, or not reported), and `readBlurCapability` probes the platform's own background blur
and answers controllable, platform-controlled or unavailable. The `MediaEffects` seam sits between
capture and publish with a pass-through stage, so the picture and sound slices swap in one place.
The preference is remembered per member. The Effects popover in the control bar draws no control
that cannot act: where the browser offers no blur, one sentence says so.
- **Polls and a question queue, on the record on chat's own terms.** Six per-firm tables by one
additive migration — `meeting_poll`, `meeting_poll_option`, `meeting_poll_respondent`,
`meeting_poll_answer`, `meeting_question`, `meeting_question_upvote` — the poll and question trios in
`@magna-carta/meetings`, and twelve routes in `routes/meeting-polls.ts` and
`routes/meeting-questions.ts`. Every act is a route with an audit row of identifiers and instants;
opening, closing, reading who answered what and marking a question answered are host acts that ask
the GRANT on the meeting through `requireHostGrant`, so an Attorney holding `meetings:host` and no
grant is `403 meeting-not-host`. Answering, asking and upvoting need an open stay, as posting a chat
message does.

**Anonymity is two tables that cannot answer each other's question.** `meeting_poll_answer` holds what
was chosen and, on a poll that shows no names, a participant pair of literal NULLs written by a
statement that has no argument for them; `meeting_poll_respondent` holds that a stay answered, the one
instant, and nothing about what. The answer names its option as the pair `(poll_id, option_id)`
against the option table's own unique pair, so an answer to another poll's option fails at the
foreign key. One participation per member per poll — the respondent insert refuses a later stay of the
same member, not only the same stay — and no audit row ever carries the question, a label or which
option was chosen.

**Six room frames and no client frame.** `poll-opened` and `question-asked` carry the row whole so
three hundred browsers are not sent to the read at once; `poll-closed` carries the final tally;
`question-updated` the new state, with an empty body for a redaction; `poll-tally` and
`question-tally` go through the reactions' per-second bucket, extracted to
`room/room-coalescing.ts` and now shared, holding the latest count the route read rather than a sum.
A guest's socket receives every frame with its user identifiers nulled. Two telemetry events,
`meetings.room.pollRelayed` and `meetings.room.questionRelayed`, carry socket counts and nothing a
person typed. Every participant CHECK accepts `attendee` beside `member` and `guest`, and a poll and a
question carry a nullable `breakout_id` by value, both while the migration is unlanded.
- **A meeting can now be asked about after it has ended.** The room holds no rows, deletes its own
state as it goes and hibernates between frames, so a three-hundred-person meeting that went wrong
left attendance and an Error ID on whichever refusal a member happened to see. `meetings.room.*` in
`@magna-carta/telemetry`'s catalog is now the durable trace: one allowlist builder per act — joined,
welcomed, published, subscribed, layer changed, presence relayed, refused, socket lost, swept,
superseded, admitted, denied, muted, removed, locked, ended, the alarm and what it found due, a
frame's storage spend, and a browser's own report — each correlated by firm, meeting and, where the
act is about a person, stay. `apps/api-worker/src/meetings/room/room-diagnostics.ts` is the room's
one emitter and nothing may throw out of it; every other module reaches it with one call.

**The redaction is structural, not a rule at the call sites.** There is no declared field for a
display name, a track name, a session description or a chat line, so an edit cannot add one without
adding it to the catalog first, where it would have to be argued for. A test reads the whole emitted
set back as text and fails on any of them. What is left is identifiers the platform minted, counts,
closed enums and instants — the posture the custody and asset registers take, for a sharper reason:
the metadata of a law firm's meetings is a disclosure with no transcript attached.

**A refusal is sent and recorded in one call**, because a refusal recorded and not sent — or sent and
not recorded — is exactly the drift the Error ID exists to close: the member ends up holding a handle
the record does not know, and the support search the field exists for finds nothing.

**Two things are deliberately not recorded per occurrence**, because they are the frames a large room
sends most. Presence is one event per coalesced flush carrying the count it covered. What a frame
spends in storage is sampled, one frame in twenty, and is approximate under concurrency — a budget,
never a ledger, and the catalog says so.

**A browser now tells the room what its connection is doing.** `diagnostic-report` is an additive
client frame carrying quality, round trip, loss fraction, jitter, the outbound layer and the count of
inbound streams. Every field is optional — an absent measurement is "not taken", never "none" — and
every one is bounded in the schema, because it is the one frame whose whole content is an
unverifiable claim about the sender and telemetry aggregates these. The room takes one per
participant per five seconds and drops the rest in silence, keeps the last sample on the participant
record for the inspect call, and acknowledges nothing.

**`GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/inspect` reads one live room**, behind the platform-operator
guard. It is the only meeting route that names the firm in the query rather than addressing the room
by the session firm, and the reason is structural rather than convenient: its caller belongs to no
firm, so there is no session firm to read. A firm permission was rejected — a member who could read
the room's internals could read a colleague's connection quality and their place in the meeting. It
answers with the roster (role, presence, track and subscription counts, last sample), the door, the
open sockets and which stay each carries, the alarm and which of its deadlines are pending, the
storage key count and approximate size, the routing sessions and the ended marker, and it changes
nothing. A room nobody has ever addressed answers with empty lists, because that is itself the
finding.

**The room's fan-out cost is a number now.** `apps/api-worker/test/support/meeting-room-load.ts`
drives real socket pairs against the real object: everybody arrives, everybody publishes, everybody
talks at once, the gallery turns a page, a tenth of the room reconnects, the host ends it. Forty
clients run in the ordinary suite as an assertion on the two bounds; three hundred run by hand
(`VITE_MEETING_ROOM_LOAD_PARTICIPANTS=300`). At three hundred: one frame per join per socket exactly,
0.4 storage lists per frame, 414,180 frames delivered, 1,500 on the busiest socket, in twenty
seconds.

**It falsified a design claim on its first run, and found a bug.** Every deferred presence transition
armed the alarm through the full reconciliation, which reads the whole roster AND the whole door to
find the nearest deadline — two roster-wide reads on the frame a room of three hundred sends most,
measured at 1.2 storage lists per frame against a design that claims one. The deadline is already
known where the transition is deferred, so `relayPresence` now answers with it and the caller arms
for that instant; the same pass fell to 0.4. Separately, the room's direct replies to one socket
called `send` unguarded, and `send` on a closed socket throws — and a throw out of `webSocketMessage`
resets the Durable Object, dropping every socket in the meeting. A supersede, a leave or the end of a
meeting racing a queued frame would have ended the meeting for everybody in it. The room-wide
broadcast had swallowed that since it was written; every direct reply now goes through the same
`trySend`.

**A member given a grant mid-meeting is now told who is already at the door.** Every other `waiting`
frame goes out because the queue moved; this one goes out because the audience did. A co-host
appointed at the twentieth minute learned the roster had changed and nothing at all about the people
standing outside, so their lobby panel stayed empty until the next knock — which, in the case that
matters, is a meeting where the person who could let somebody in has just been appointed. An empty
door is stated rather than left silent.

**The event form can open a meeting with its lobby on.** `CalendarEventMeetingInput` takes an
optional `lobby`, read on the create path exactly as the medium beside it is. Omitted means off,
which is what every meeting scheduled before the door existed was — a form that did not ask must not
quietly put a firm's own colleagues in a queue.

**Twenty import cycles left the API worker.** Every one of them ran through `authForEnv` living in
`app.ts`, which imports every route module — so a route-specific guard that has to resolve a session
for itself (the platform-operator lane, which the per-firm chokepoint cannot serve because its caller
belongs to no firm) closed a cycle, and a second route in that lane added two more findings. It moved
to `src/auth-instance.ts`, which takes only the `Bindings` type from `app.ts`. The `import/no-cycle`
ratchet drops from 36 to 16.
- **A meeting can have a guest from outside the firm, on a signed link.** Two additive per-firm tables
join the lineage (`meeting_guest_invitation`, `meeting_guest_stay`, migration
`20260924T090000_a-guest-holds-a-signed-link-and-a-stay-of-its-own`). An invitation is one row per
Directory person or organization per meeting, holding only the SHA-256 of the link's secret; a stay
is the guest's own presence in the room, beside `meeting_attendance` rather than a nullable column on
it. The in-the-room and waiting predicates are now unions over both tables, composed in one place
(`MEETING_STAY_TABLES`), so a guest counts against the room's and the door's ceilings exactly as a
member does.

**The chokepoint has a guest lane.** A route declaring `guestLane: "invitation" | "grant"` is
admitted by a signed credential in the `x-meeting-guest` header — or, on the socket upgrade alone,
the `guest` query parameter — in place of the session, member-active and permission steps. The
handler gets a firm and the credential's names and never a user id. Registration refuses a guest
route that names a permission or is authenticated, and a guest credential sent to any other route is
answered the reserved 404. The credential shares the support session's signed format
(`src/signed-token.ts`) under its own `typ`.

**Ten routes.** A host (`meetings:host` and a grant on the meeting) invites, lists, rotates and
withdraws links under `/api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/guests`; the invitation is mailed after its batch
commits and the token is never returned, stored or logged. A guest reads a reduced summary
(`GuestMeetingSummary`, a schema of its own with no matter or event field), arrives at the door,
opens the socket, reads and sends chat once admitted, and leaves, under `/api/v1/guest/*` with no
meeting identifier in any path. Opening the link spends nothing; an arrival does, up to twenty.

**The room redacts per viewer.** `welcome`, `roster`, `roster-delta` and `message` frames are built
for the socket they go to: a guest's copy carries `userId: null` for everybody. Roster entries and
the hosts' `waiting` list gain `kind` (`member` | `guest`), and a waiting guest's entry carries the
name the link was minted for (`invitedName`) beside the name typed at the door.
- Host controls for meetings, as far as the server goes: who is running a room is a grant on the
meeting rather than a permission key half the firm holds.

`meetings:host` says a firm lets a member convene meetings. It could never say who is running THIS
room, because that changes while the meeting runs — hosting is handed over, co-hosts are named and
withdrawn, and the member who opened the room may have been called away an hour ago. So the meeting
record carries the answer in a new `meeting_host` table: the starter gets a grant in the same batch
as the room, a co-host is another under the same meeting, and a hand-over closes one and opens
another at one instant. A grant is CLOSED and never deleted, because the question a firm asks months
later is who was hosting when something happened, which is a question about an interval.

**Hosting does not pass on its own.** A host whose tunnel drops for ninety seconds has not stopped
hosting, and a room reassigned on a socket loss would hand a client meeting to whoever happened to
be next in the roster. What replaces it is a claim: a key-holder may take a room nobody is running,
refused the moment anybody else holding a grant is in it and audited as a claim rather than as a
hand-over, because nobody gave it.

**Ending a meeting narrows.** It was gated on the key alone, so any Attorney in the firm could close
any meeting they could see the event for, from anywhere, without being in it. It now needs a grant
like every other act here; the ordinary case is unchanged because the starter holds one, and a
key-holder closing an abandoned room claims it first, which leaves a record of exactly that.

The acts split by whether somebody could later ask who did it. Removing a participant, locking the
room and changing who is hosting are routes with audit rows; muting one person, muting the room,
asking somebody to unmute and spotlighting a participant are frames on the signaling socket, because
each is about this moment and an audit row for each would fill a matter's log with the mechanics of a
conversation. A mute closes the target's audio at the routing service rather than asking their
browser nicely — a mute the browser could decline is not a mute — and asking somebody to unmute is a
request their screen answers, never a microphone opened for them.

The room authorizes every host frame from the STORED participant record rather than from the socket's
attachment, so a co-host whose grant was withdrawn ten minutes ago stops on their next frame instead
of when their socket happens to close. No new permission key: the authority is in the grant, and the
key is narrower than it was.
- **Scheduling a meeting is recording a calendar event with a medium on it.** The event form — the one
form, for a matter's event, the firm's, or one member's — gains a **Meeting** choice on its Where
tab: None, Video meeting, Audio call. Answering it writes the meeting row at save time through
`createMeeting`, so the entry window offers **Join** from the moment the event exists rather than
from the moment somebody presses Start. There is no second record and no second form: a meeting has
never carried a title, a time or a participant list of its own, and a scheduling feature that minted
its own invitation record would have been minting a second answer to when the meeting is and who is
at it.

**The room opens after the event commits, and that ordering is forced rather than chosen.**
`createMeeting` reads the event through the visibility predicate before it writes, so a meeting
composed into the batch still inserting the event it hangs on would be refused by its own gate. What
makes the second write safe is the property the create path already had: one meeting per event, held
by a partial unique index rather than by anything the caller passes — so the step carries no
idempotency key of its own, a retried save finds the room the first attempt opened and writes
nothing, and the response carries the same identifier on a replay as on the first commit.
`POST /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/events` and `POST /api/v1/firm-events` take
`meeting: { medium: "video" | "audio" } | null` and answer `{ id, meetingId }`; the two `PATCH`
routes take the same field and answer `{ ok: true, meetingId }`.

**An edit keeps the meeting; a cancellation settles it.** Moving an event's day or hour touches
nothing on the meeting, which carries no time of its own — and `meeting` on a correction can only
ADD a room, never take one away, because ending a gathering is an act with its own route and its own
audit row. Cancelling an event ends a **scheduled** meeting in the same batch as the cancel, so a
room nobody entered cannot outlive the setting it was for. Cancelling an event whose meeting is
**live** is refused, `409` with the new `meeting-in-progress` problem type naming the remedy: ending
a live meeting as a side effect of a calendar edit would take a room away from the people in it on
somebody else's click, and cancelling while leaving it running would have the record say the setting
is off while the product says it is happening.

**The colleagues on the event are told, through the notifications subsystem and nothing else.**
`calendar.event.meetingScheduled` is an outbox row in the same atomic batch as the room it announces
— so a batch that rolls back leaves no message, and a message that exists is proof the room was
opened. It carries identifiers, the medium, and the member handles named on the event at the write,
and no title, description, location or participant name. The new `named-members` audience is the
plural of `named-recipient` and resolves on its reasoning: the people to invite are the people who
were on the event when it was recorded, not whoever happens to be on it when the queue drains.
Directory-entity participants get nothing, and the form says so under the choice rather than leaving
a member to discover it from a client who never arrived. Firm events do not raise the invitation
yet: `notification_event.subject_kind` is a SQLite `CHECK` with no `firmEvent` value, and widening
one rebuilds a table `notification_recipient` points at — the firm meeting is scheduled, created and
joinable, and it is the notification alone that waits on that migration.

**Who is already busy is read, never refused.** Where the form lists colleagues, each one's own
calendar is read for the day being booked — the member filter the server already resolves in SQL —
and what it finds at the chosen hour is stated beside their name. It states and never blocks: two
things at once is routinely correct, and a scheduling form that would not let a member book over a
colleague is a form people stop using. What it prints is what the grid paints and never a title: the
federated read declares non-privileged labels by contract, so a matter event reads as its type, and
printing one matter's content on another matter's form would be a disclosure.

**The Meetings page schedules.** It gains the product's one create control, which opens the same
event form with the meeting choice preset to Video meeting, over the same `calendarContext` every
other calendar surface reads — a second assembly of the roster, the type catalog and the firm's
rooms would be a second answer to what the form is offering.
- **A meeting now says why a tile is poor, from the browser's own connection.**
`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/client/connection-quality.ts` is a pure module that reads one
`RTCStatsReport` against the reading before it — packets lost, jitter, bytes, frames and the
outbound camera's resolution and simulcast layer, with the round trip taken from the candidate pair
actually carrying the media — and turns the connection's climbing counters into rates over the
interval. `qualityOf` judges three dimensions against stated thresholds and lets the worst one
decide; nothing measured is `unknown`, which is deliberately not `good`.
`client/diagnostics.svelte.ts` samples every five seconds through an injectable timer while a
meeting is live, keeps five minutes of samples and the last sixty wire events, and answers the
quality of the local uplink and of each other participant — traced from a media section back to its
owner through the mapping the subscriptions module already keeps.

**Nothing it holds is recorded.** The samples live in the tab, go when the meeting does, and never
reach the meeting's record, which stays who was in the room and for how long. `report()` assembles
the redacted snapshot a periodic post will one day carry — participant handles, qualities, the
uplink's numbers, the event ring — and a test reads it as text to hold that no session description,
display name or track name is in it. `sendReport` is a no-op until the room has a frame to receive
it on.

**The events come through a seam, not a reference.** Signaling and subscriptions emit through a
small `DiagnosticsSink` that defaults to a no-op, so neither has to know diagnostics exist and both
still run under a test with nothing listening.

**Three room-facing fixes found in review, each with a case that fails without it.** A `subscribe`
and a `close` are now chunked at the protocol's `MAX_SUBSCRIBE_TRACKS` / `MAX_CLOSE_MIDS` the way
`layer` already was — the room refuses an over-large frame whole, so every track it named would have
stayed black. A simulcast layer is recorded as settled only when the room's `layered` names the
media section, with what the plan wants held separately, so a `layer` frame the room's window drops
is asked for again rather than leaving a tile at the wrong size. And a `sync` the room never
answered no longer latches the socket shut for the rest of the meeting: the latch lets go after two
seconds, so a later gap can ask again.

**A roster row is authoritative the moment it arrives.** The presence map is kept beside the roster
and used to be never overwritten by one, so a rejoin delta saying "not speaking" — which is what the
room sends, because it resets deferred presence on a rejoin — was ignored, and a stale speaking mark
held that person at the front of everybody's gallery with their microphone pulled. Rows a frame
actually carried now overwrite the map; rows merely carried forward in a delta's merged list do not.
- **The room now relays a chat message as it is said.** `MeetingRoom` gains two RPCs the chat routes
call AFTER their own writes commit, on the `participantLeft` / `end` precedent: `messageSent`
broadcasts a `message` frame carrying the whole record the list route returns, and `messageRedacted`
broadcasts `message-redacted { messageId, redactedAt }`. The route is still the record and stays the
record — the frame is a copy of a row that is already committed, the write never goes through the
socket, and a browser that misses one is caught up by the read. Both frames reach every WELCOMED
socket and never the lobby, which is structural rather than filtered: a waiting socket is never
welcomed and the broadcast skips everything that is not. **The room stores nothing about a
message** — no key, no count — and a room nobody holds a socket on is a no-op.

**And the read converges what the relay cannot.** A poller walks forward on `(sent_at, id)`, and a
redaction moves no row's position in that ordering — so a message already handed to a browser could
be taken back somewhere the poll would never look again, which the frame closes for a socket that is
open and nothing closed for one that reconnected. `GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` now
carries a second array beside the page, **`redacted: [{ id, redactedAt }]`**: the messages taken back
since the caller's own `since` instant. It is populated only for a caller that says where it read to,
because a first page already carries whatever the record holds.

**One event, `meetings.room.messageRelayed`**, carrying the socket count and which of the two acts it
was. There is no declared field for the message handle and none for its body: what was said is the
transcript's to hold, under the matter's own retention, and the telemetry stream has different
readers.
- Every migration batch now leaves behind the instant before it ran.

The lineage runs only forwards, so a migration that succeeds and turns out to be wrong had no way back at all. A migration that FAILS never needed one — workerd rolls the whole context back and the database is exactly as it was, which is why a day of failed migrations damaged nothing — but the successful-and-wrong case is unrecoverable without a point to return to.

Before applying a pending batch, the firm's database takes a Cloudflare bookmark: an opaque handle naming that instant, which the platform can restore the object to. It is written beside the ledger with the timestamp and the tags the batch applied, so a reader knows which deploy it precedes rather than having to work it out. The diagnostics read carries it, which means the restore point is visible on the same panel that reports a stuck lineage.

Taking it is best-effort, and recording it never fails the migration that succeeded: a firm on the right schema with no restore point is a worse diagnostic, not a worse database. One row, replaced each batch — Cloudflare's retention window bounds how far back an object can go, and a list of bookmarks older than that window would be a list of restore points that no longer restore anything.
- A migration that rebuilds a table other tables point at is now refused at authoring time.

`REVIEWED_REBUILDS` asks whether a human audited the copy. That is the wrong question for this shape, because no amount of care makes it applicable: a rebuild drops the table it replaces, and in a durable object foreign keys are enforced at the statement and at the commit, with `PRAGMA foreign_keys=OFF` a no-op inside the single execution context a migration runs in. Four ways around it were tried against real durable-object storage and all four fail. So a drop with children cannot complete against any firm database that holds data — it completes only against the empty ones the suite used to build.

The migration-integrity sentinel now reads the schema **as it stood at that migration** — a table gains references over time, and the head's answer is not the one that decides whether the drop could have completed — and refuses any rebuild of a table anything references. Pointed at the migration that caused the outage, it names it and the thirty-five tables that reference `matter`.

The six that predate the finding are listed as debt rather than permission. Each is unappliable to a firm whose rebuilt table has children, and the list must not grow; widening a CHECK or dropping a column on a parent table needs a different answer.
- A time entry filed on the wrong matter can be moved to the right one.

Time gets recorded against the wrong matter — a person is on two of them in one afternoon, the picker was left where it was, the timer was bound before anybody had decided. Until now the only remedy was to strike the entry and type it again, which loses its number, its internal memo, its codes, its attached files and its whole history, and leaves a struck row standing on a matter the work was never really on.

**`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/refile` moves it instead.** Its own route rather than a `matterId` on the update, and deliberately: this is a cross-matter write. Two ledgers change, two matters' totals move, and the rate the entry froze was resolved against the matter it is leaving. A patch field would let anything that can edit a narrative also move money between matters without meaning to.

**What carries, and what is re-asked.** The entry number carries — a reference that changes is a reference that lies, and anything that cited it has to keep resolving. The consequence is stated rather than hidden: the number's own shape names the matter the entry was FIRST written on, so after a move that prefix is provenance and not a claim about where the entry lives now. The description, the memo, the codes, the attachments and the history all carry untouched.

The **rate and the rounding increment are re-resolved** against the destination, on the entry's own work date. Both are matter-scoped — the rate chain reads matter, then client, then timekeeper; the increment resolves matter, then client, then user — so carrying one client's answers to another is how a firm bills at the wrong rate. This is not the rate-snapshot invariant bending: that rule says a rate card edited later never re-rates a standing entry, and it still holds. What changed here is the question, not somebody's later edit to the answer. The acknowledgement reports what the entry now carries, so a screen that assumed only the matter moved is not left showing the wrong money.

**What it refuses, and why.** Anything past draft, anything on a bill, anything a draft invoice has claimed, a matter this firm does not have, and the matter the entry is already on. Past draft the entry is evidence somebody is relying on — an approved entry is a reviewer's decision about a matter, a billed one a line on a finalized invoice — and the answer to both is a void and a fresh record, never a move nobody can see. Refusing the no-op move rather than reporting success keeps the act's meaning.

**Every move is on the record**, as one audit event naming both matters, so a reader of the entry's history can see where it came from and when it moved.

On screen, the Matter field is now settable on every draft — in the Time Sheet's Matter cell and in the record window. On a row not yet written it is still the choice that lets the row be written at all; on one the firm holds, picking another matter moves the entry. The one thing a move cannot do is take a written entry off a matter altogether: the record has to be somewhere.
- `lint:one-ui` now recognizes a modal panel built outside the shells.

The expensive shape was never the crude one. A raw `<dialog>` and a scrim in a `<style>` block were already caught; what passed every gate was a screen importing the design system's own `Dialog.Root` and `Dialog.Content` and composing a panel by hand. It renders correctly, it typechecks, it lints, and it reads fine in review — it simply does not share the answers the shells settle.

Three source signals, because a modal built outside the system arrives as any of them: a composed `Dialog`/`AlertDialog`/`Sheet` panel outside a declared shell's home, a scrim written as utilities (`fixed inset-0` at the modal layer, which the style-block rule cannot see and which is the shape this repository actually writes), and a reach for the platform's own modal. Both shells also stamp `data-modal-shell` on the panel they render, which is the half that reads behaviour rather than source — a marker a rendered-DOM check can require of anything carrying the `dialog` or `alertdialog` role, and the only thing that catches a panel whose parts were aliased on import or chosen at runtime.

Which homes may compose a panel is **declared**, in `registry.json` beside the component register, rather than listed inside the rule — so adding a shell is a reviewed edit to the file that already answers "what is in the system". Being a registered component is deliberately not enough on its own: `RecordAttachments` is registered and still holds a confirmation that should be an `ActionDialog`, so it carries an allowance rather than an exemption.

A second rule, `footer-set`, asserts the action bar the way the header set has always been asserted against the record window: exactly the dismissal then the commit, in that order. A reader who has learned where the commit sits has learned it in every panel in the product, and a third control would un-learn that everywhere in one edit.

The thirty-seven panels that predate all this are carried as printed allowances with a reason each. They are debt, not exemptions: an allowance that outlives its violation is itself a failure, so the list can only shrink.
- **`pnpm run lint:modal-headers` — the scan that reads a panel's two lines.** The sibling of `lint:screen-headers`, built the same way: pure rules in `modal-headers.mjs`, the filesystem in `index.mjs`, fixtures beside both.

Every rule it asserts was already written down — in the shells' own prop documentation, and in the owner's rulings of 2026-09-08 — and none of it held. A rule recorded in a ledger binds the people who read the ledger; a rule with a gate binds the diff.

- **`heading-act`** — an acting panel's heading names the act in the imperative. A panel that makes a record says "New &lt;Noun&gt;"; a reading panel and a record window name the thing they show, and are asked nothing. The verb vocabulary is a closed set, so a new act is one reviewed line rather than a noun quietly becoming a heading.
- **`heading-question`** — no heading ends in a question mark. The panel is what makes it a question: a destructive kind already takes the `alertdialog` role and traps the decision.
- **`heading-case`** — interior articles and short prepositions stay lower case.
- **`subject-not-prose`** — no fact, and no subtitle snippet, is sentence-shaped.
- **`reference-shown`** — a panel handed a record's number as a prop names it in its heading or its subtitle. The registry of what counts as a record number is read out of the schema's own `*_number` columns, so a record kind that grows a number is asked this question the day its column lands; the eleven columns that are numbers of something else — a telephone, a vehicle, a parcel of land, a row in an import — are recorded with the reason each is not a record's own name. The scan exits non-zero if it can no longer parse the schema, because a rule that finds nothing passes vacuously.
- **`allowance`** — every recorded allowance still describes a real violation, on `lint:one-ui`'s discipline. The list is empty today, which is the honest state: the nine violations the first run found were fixed rather than recorded.
- **A hard-coded model identifier goes wrong on a schedule this repository cannot see, so the inference
catalog now records when each pin was last checked and against what — and the gate says so.**

No model changed. The reasoning default resolves to the same model it did yesterday, the embedding
model is the same, and the gate is green.

**The reasoning half.** The firm default was the literal string `anthropic/claude-opus-4-8` written into
`settings.ts`. It is now derived from a **reasoning tier** — `most-capable` / `balanced` — that the
catalog assigns an occupant to and validates at module load, so moving the platform forward is a data
edit rather than a hunt for every literal. `reasoning-tier.ts` additionally lets deploy configuration
re-point a tier with no build at all. **That override can only ever select a model already curated in
the catalog**, which is the design and not a gap: a deploy-time string cannot carry a human's finding
that a model is zero-data-retention eligible, so adding a model still costs a code change and a
verification while choosing among verified ones does not. A rejected override falls back to the catalog
occupant and is reported rather than swallowed. A firm that has explicitly chosen a model keeps it —
re-pointing a firm's own selection because the platform default moved would override a decision it made
about its own confidential content.

**The staleness half, which is the part that stops this recurring.** Every entry now carries two
verification dates instead of one: `verifiedOn` for the confidentiality facts and
`availabilityVerifiedOn` for the lifecycle facts. They are separate because they live on different
provider pages and go stale independently, and a single date would let the cheap lifecycle check
silently refresh the confidentiality claim nobody re-read. Beside them sit the provider's own published
facts — `retirementNotBefore` and `supersededBy`. `model-pin-freshness.ts` reads those dates against a
calendar (never a network, never prose) and grades findings two ways: **`expired`** — past a published
retirement, or unread past the hard interval — fails the gate, because a model past its retirement may
return an error rather than an answer; **`due`** — a successor exists, a retirement approaches, a fact
is overdue — is reported and does not, because a decision that belongs to a person should not arrive as
a broken build.

Read against the provider's deprecation reference on 2026-08-14, the pass reports three findings and no
failures: `claude-opus-4-8` and `claude-sonnet-4-6` each have a published successor, and
`claude-haiku-4-5` reaches its earliest published retirement date in 62 days. All three were true before
this change and nothing in the repository could say so.

**What it cannot see, stated rather than implied:** a successor released since the last time somebody
looked. Supersession is not derivable from in-repo data, and a gate-time call to the provider's models
endpoint would need a network and credentials in CI and would fail for reasons unrelated to the change
under test. The gap is _bounded_ by the re-read interval, not closed.

**The embedding half is a different problem and gets a different answer.** Every stored vector is a
function of the model that produced it, so the pin is free to move only while no index exists and costs
a full re-embedding of every corpus afterwards. **No mechanism makes a frozen pin cheaply changeable and
none is claimed here.** What is built instead protects the window: the embedding entry records
`pinState: "open"`, and a fitness scan refuses to let that window close by accident — while the pin reads
open, no source file may reach a vector index. Comments are stripped before the scan, so the deferred
semantic-search module's descriptions of the adapter nobody has written do not count as writing one. The
first code that writes a vector fails that test, and clearing it means recording `frozen` — a line whose
only honest author is whoever has decided which model the index is built with. Verified by construction:
the scan was run against a deliberate vector write and reported exactly it.
- Matter notes: the Notes section on a matter is real, and a note is a record rather than a text field.

Until now the platform had no note anywhere. What it had were scalar `note` columns on a dozen individual records, each one nullable free text on one row, attributable to nobody, editable in place, with no history and no reader but that row's own detail view. The matter's Notes section had promised "dated, attributed, and searchable" since the shell was built.

A note is dated and attributed when it is written, and those never move. Correcting one appends a version and keeps the old one, so the history is every body the note has ever had, each with its own author and instant; a colleague correcting a partner's note is recorded as having corrected it. Nothing is edited in place, because what makes a note worth having is that it was written then, by that person, saying that.

Withdrawing is the answer to text that should never have been typed: another client's privileged material, somebody's medical information, a note filed against the wrong matter. The words stop being shown everywhere, including the matter's activity history and search, while the record that the note existed, who wrote it and who withdrew it stays, with a required reason standing where the text was. There is no delete anywhere in the feature: no button, no route, no capability. The one case where bytes must genuinely leave is a legal question that reaches a person through the erasure report.

Reading, writing and withdrawing are three separate permissions, seeded to the seats that work matters and not to Billing or Read-only. A note joins the matter's activity history as one more entry carrying its author and its date and never a word of its text, on the same discipline that keeps an email's subject line off that read. No merge field can resolve to a note, so work product cannot be assembled into a letter under the firm's letterhead, and notes stay outside discovery collection: producing one means exporting it as a document first, which gives it a version, a hash and a custodian of record.

Search finds notes on the matter you are on, and matches the current text only. A note corrected to take out a name stops being findable by that name, which is usually why somebody corrected it.
- **A PDF opens and is drawn locally, by the engine the platform already had.** Opening a portable
document from the file manager now takes it to `/documents/{fileId}/view`, where its pages are
rasterized in the browser by `crates/pdf-core` compiled to WebAssembly and run in a Web Worker
(`apps/web/src/lib/documents/pdf-render.worker.ts`). The engine was built, tested and used by three
workers; nothing in the web application had ever loaded it. Only pixels leave the worker, so the
standing rule that an active format is never handed to a parser that could execute it is kept by
construction rather than by policy, and the reader needs no container, no deploy activation and no
round trip per page. Loading it in the worker is also what keeps its several megabytes off every
other screen: nothing is fetched until a document is opened. Pages are drawn as they come into
view, at a resolution that follows the zoom and is capped so a bitmap cannot outgrow the tab.

**And the text editor no longer opens what it would corrupt.** `readTextDocument` decoded with a
non-fatal `TextDecoder`, so a document in a legacy single-byte encoding, ordinary among older files
carrying curly quotes or accented names, opened with every such character replaced. Saving would
then have written that loss into a new current version. It now decodes with `fatal: true` and
refuses, offering the download instead. The shared byte read both surfaces use is now one module
(`document-bytes.ts`).
- **A sixteenth repo-wide lint, `pnpm run lint:ungranted-permissions`,** fails any permission that
gates a member-facing surface and that no committed seed grants to any role. It is the sibling of
`lint:unwired-writes` for a defect that gate is structurally unable to see: these are permissions
rather than writes, so nothing is exported, nothing is uncalled, and the route the permission gates
has a caller, a test and a correct chokepoint check. The only symptom is a 403.

**Two demand sources, both surfaces a member reaches.** A chokepoint-enforced route, read out of the
committed OpenAPI snapshot (`defineOpenAPIRoute` writes `x-mc-permission` and `x-mc-surface` onto
every operation, and a byte-exact test fails if the snapshot drifts from the code — so the fact is
already committed in a shape with no parsing ambiguity); and a Tools catalogue manifest, since
`toolsByGroup` renders only the tools whose permission the member holds. Grants come from every
`role_permission` and `direct_grant` seed in both migration lineages, read by column name rather than
by position so a seed written with its columns reordered still counts.

**Measured in four variants against `main` at the commit this branched from — 102 declared
permissions, 90 seeded — and the two wider ones were rejected:**

| Variant                                         | Hits | Real | False |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ---- | ---- | ----- |
| Every declared permission with no seed          | 12   | 9    | 3     |
| Every permission named by **any** route meta    | 7    | 4    | 3     |
| Named by a `surface: "app"` route meta          | 5    | 4    | 1     |
| **Kept:** that, plus a Tools catalogue manifest | 10   | 9    | 1     |

The middle form is the worst of the four and worth naming: it drops the five real Tools cases and
keeps all three false ones. Excluding `surface: "public"` is what removes two of the three, and it is
grounded rather than fitted — the chokepoint skips its session, authn and RBAC steps entirely for a
public surface, so a role holding `firm:provision` would gain nothing. The single remaining exception,
`diagnostics:overview`, is on the allowlist with the reason: a diagnostic support session carries the
