whole `diagnostics` namespace through `resolveSupportPermissions`, and a role that held it would give
every member of the firm the help-desk view the tier exists to keep separate.

**Replayed against 2026-06-22, it names the defect on the commit that shipped it.** At `0185ce46`,
the commit immediately before the editor-launch route landed, the rule reports seven and no
`documents:*` — correct, the routes did not exist. At `507d9f9b`, the commit that added the route, it
reports eight, and the new one is `documents:edit`. At `0f4d53fa` it picks up `documents:checkout`.
Fifty-eight days before the gap was found by reading. Every hit in that replay was real: besides the
editing keys and the five Tools manifests still ungranted today, it names `customFields:purge` and
`tools:speedTest`, both of which were genuinely unheld then and were seeded later.

Same shape as its two siblings — pure rules beside an impure runner, fixtures the gate self-tests
against on every invocation and that the suite drives through the same entry point, two vacuity
guards (no demand collected, no seed collected), and a per-permission allowlist whose entries each
carry a required reason. A blank reason, an entry no surface demands any more, and an entry whose
permission a seed now grants are each failures of their own, so the gate cannot go quiet by accident.

What it does **not** catch, and no rule here pretends otherwise: a permission granted to a role no
member holds, and a capability with no permission at all.
- `POST /api/v1/directory/persons` takes the whole draft (other names, pronouns, dates, emails, phones, addresses, identifiers, organizations) and `createPersonRecord` writes it in one effect batch, each part composed by the module that owns it (`compose*` functions on person, name-history, contact-email/phone/address, edges, identifiers). The sections under `apps/web/src/lib/directory/sections/` are data-blind components used by the dialog to draft and by the Contact and Identifiers panes to persist. The organization keeps a one-section dialog beside the same duplicate gate.
- **`reset-platform.mts` — the pre-launch clean slate, ordered so it cannot strand a resource.**

Destroying a firm's resources is not a fan-out, it is a sequence, because nothing outside the control
plane can enumerate what a firm owns: there is no API that lists Durable Object instances, and
`ai_search_instance` is deliberately the only index of the managed search instances
(control-plane-schema.ts: "Nothing ever calls the service's list operation"). Empty the control plane
first and every bucket and every search instance survives with nothing able to name it — still
running, still billed, against an account ceiling of 5,000 for the instances. So the control plane
goes last, and the script refuses to touch it while any search instance is still live, or if any
bucket failed to delete.

Three details worth keeping: the table list is read from `sqlite_master` rather than written down, so
a table added later cannot silently survive the wipe; each firm's key is crypto-shredded first,
because it is the one step whose value survives a later failure; and the firm databases themselves
are left unaddressed rather than wiped, since clearing Durable Object storage needs a route that
would outlive its one use. Dry run unless `--destroy` is passed AND the account id is typed out.
- **A pull request now opens with the questions its review asks.** `.github/pull_request_template.md` pre-fills every new pull request with the sections the conventions already require and previously left to memory: what and why, the Conventional Commits type, what reaches production at merge (migration, contract, binding), the documentation lanes with the exact fragment path each one takes, the local `pnpm test` result the 2026-09-03 ruling asks every description to state, and the golden rules a review most often catches late. The template links to `docs/conventions/documentation.md` and `documentation-style.md` for the standards rather than restating them, so it stays a layout and those files stay the home.
- **Raw control characters in tracked source and Markdown now fail the gate; write the escape.**
`pnpm run lint:control-characters` (`tooling/lint-control-characters.mjs`) rejects every C0 byte and
DEL that is not tab, newline, or carriage return, prints the exact escape to write in its place, and
runs in the governance job beside the process-reference scan and in the pre-push hook.

The reason is legibility rather than correctness: a raw NUL is invisible in a file read, in
`git diff`, in a review pane, and in most editors, so the source reads as one thing and means
another. A separator written as a literal NUL read as `.join("")` to two separate readers on the same
day and produced a wrong diagnosis of a real defect. The escape is the same value at runtime and says
what the byte is.

Ten source files carried eighteen raw bytes and all were converted: the hash-domain separators in
`joining-secrets.ts`, four composite map keys (`scoped-setting-statements.ts`, `normalize.ts`,
`matter-suggestion.ts`, `fusion.ts`), the three in `metering-statements.ts` including the `split()`
that had to agree with them, the C0 range in the assembled-document-name regular expression, and two
tests whose subject IS the byte — the expression fuzz alphabet, the denied-construct corpus, and the
zip local-file-header magic in the JPEG appended-data test. None needed the escape hatch; the escape
is clearer in the tests too, which is where the argument for the raw byte would have been strongest.

The scan covers Markdown, which the process-reference scan deliberately exempts. That is not
symmetry for its own sake: a code sample in a document gets copied into source, one spec already
carried a NUL inside a cache-key sample, and the first draft of this rule's own convention entry was
written with a raw escape byte in its prose. It self-tests on every run, on the ledger-staleness
idiom — over invisible bytes, a check that has quietly stopped firing is indistinguishable from a
clean tree.
- **A discovery review set is now its own search corpus, and a matter query is structurally unable to
name its splits.** The index scope key had been widened from a matter to a corpus everywhere except
the half that decides disclosure: the split CATALOG was still keyed by matter, so a review set indexed
under its own matter would have put material an opposing party produced into the result set of an
ordinary matter search. Under a protective order that is not a cache miss. `index_split` gains
`corpus_kind` and `corpus_id`, every scope read moves onto them, and `matter_id` stays as provenance
that nothing enumerates by — which is what the split's R2 prefix, the compaction backstop's candidate
set, and the query path's own key resolution all now agree on.

**A review document reaches the index through the same coordinator and the same consumer as a
committed file version. What differs is only where the passages come from.** Its text was already
extracted, certified in a manifest and written to R2, so indexing reads that object rather than
handing an opposing party's bytes to a second parser — a second parse is a second answer to what the
document says, produced by whatever engines happen to be deployed that day, with nothing comparing it
to the one the firm stands behind. The text object gains a form-feed page separator so the pages come
back as the passages they were; a form feed cannot occur inside one, because normalization drops every
control character before anything is derived. Where the text and its page metadata disagree the index
job REFUSES rather than pairing them positionally, because a search hit that names the wrong page of a
production is worse than no hit: somebody cites it. Only the primary of a duplicate group is indexed,
which is the entire economic argument for deduplicating at all.

**A document the index has not taken is recorded on its own row, and deliberately not as an
exception.** The exception vocabulary is a closed list held by a database constraint, every code in it
is a sentence about what could not be READ, and every one is rendered into a report a firm hands to
another party — so "our own search index has not caught up" is not one of them, and a later deploy
would silently change the number. `review_document.index_state` gives the property that was actually
wanted: the backlog is countable and pageable from the corpus rather than only from a Durable Object
somebody has to know to open. The one index-stage failure that IS about the document — its derived
text gone from the bucket — files `source-bytes-missing`, which the vocabulary already has.

**The reads the review surface will sit on exist and are measured.** The review-document list page
filtered by Custodian of Record, load, family, processing state and exception code; the live exception
surface with its counts by reason; the occurrences a suppressed copy stays reachable through; and what
the corpus still owes the index. The list is keyset-paged over `(sort_date, id)` in two segments
rather than one predicate — a production routinely arrives with documents nothing can date, a
descending sort puts those after every dated one, and a single keyset clause over a nullable column
either drops the whole undated tail or becomes an OR the planner cannot turn into a range.

**Found and closed while building on it: none of the discovery surface was access-scoped except
coding.** The review-set list was not, and a name is enough — "Plaintiff's production, Ridgeway
settlement" on a matter tells a reader that a production was received. Neither were the review set,
its loads, its Custodians of Record, or any of the write routes: a member holding every discovery
permission and on no access list could rename or CLOSE a walled review set, which releases its derived
artifacts irreversibly. All of them now go through the access list and answer ABSENT rather than
refused, and the visibility fitness sweep grew a second registry so the new reads are held to the same
wall from the same table-driven pass.

**The load profile found a real defect on its first run, which is what it is for.** The list page —
the read every reviewer makes hundreds of times a day — cost 10.3 ms per page mid-corpus at the
250,000-document ceiling, because SQLite turns `a < ? OR (a = ? AND b < ?)` into a scan from the end
of the index down to the cursor rather than a seek. The same predicate written as a row value is
0.26 ms and flat with corpus size: a 39-fold difference on the hottest read in the subsystem, and
invisible at any volume small enough to demo. Two further reads sorted through a temporary b-tree
because their indexes stopped one column short of the order they are served in.

**Two numbers that were asserted are now derived.** The per-review-set ceiling rests on 633 MiB
measured at 250,000 documents against 66 MiB at 25,000 — at the exact size rather than extrapolated
from a tenth of it — which leaves room for roughly a dozen ceiling-sized review sets inside a firm's
database. The allocation batch size stays at 100 because one batch costs 0.62 ms and the parameter and
query walls are what cap it, not its cost.

**Semantic indexing is deliberately not built.** The owner flag is open on evidence rather than
neglect: the cost is now priced at roughly 490 times the keyword half's for a ceiling-sized review
set, and the recall gain that would justify it has never been measured on legal prose with relevance
judgements. The per-review-set flag stays a column nothing reads, because turning it on would embed a
corpus on a guess and the embedding model pin is unchangeable once one vector exists.
- **`MAX_MEETING_PARTICIPANTS` moves from twelve to three hundred**, and the guarded insert that
actually holds the ceiling is unchanged — it binds the number as data, so the cap moved by moving one
constant. What had to be built is on the two ends of the connection rather than in the routing
service, which forwards whatever it is asked for.

**The room sends what changed.** Above `ROSTER_DELTA_THRESHOLD` (sixteen participants) every
broadcast is a new `roster-delta` frame — `{ joined, left, updated }`, with `left` carrying handles
rather than whole entries — because a full roster to three hundred sockets on every one of three
hundred arrivals is ninety thousand frames of the whole list for three hundred facts. At or below the
threshold the full `roster` frame is still sent, where the list is smaller than the bookkeeping a
difference costs. `welcome` always carries the whole roster, since a socket that has just arrived
holds nothing to apply a difference to, and a new `sync` frame is the way back to the truth for a
client that suspects a gap: the room answers that one socket with one full `roster`. Every path that
changes the roster knows who it changed, so the difference is built at the call site rather than by
comparing two lists — and a frame costs **at most one** `storage.list`, asserted in the room suite
against a three-hundred-participant roster seeded directly into the object.

**Cameras publish three layers and subscribers choose between them.** `subscribe` tracks take an
optional `preferredRid` (`f`, `h`, `q`) and a new `layer` frame changes the choice for tracks that
are already flowing — `PUT tracks/update` upstream, answered with `layered`. It is deliberately not a
second `subscribe`: the media is already arriving, and asking for it again would build a second media
section and renegotiate the connection, so a gallery page turning would cost every tile on the page a
renegotiation. Both fallbacks are `asciibetical` because the layer names sort in size order, so "the
next one along" means "the next size down" without the service being told what the names mean. A
`layer` naming a pair this room is not carrying is `refused` with `unknown-track` through the same
check a `subscribe` answers to — one function, so the two cannot drift.

**Who is talking is relayed, not measured by everybody.** A browser measures its own microphone and
sends `presence { speaking, muted }` on transitions; the room stores both on the participant, relays
a `presence` delta `{ participantId, speaking, muted, at }` to everybody else at most once per second
per participant, and carries the two booleans on `RosterParticipant` so an arriving browser sees who
is talking immediately. A transition inside the window is **dropped rather than deferred** — the
stored state stays current either way, and a presence frame carries the whole of what it is about, so
an unsent frame loses nothing a later one does not restate. Deferring would mean arming this object's
one alarm at sub-second range on a room that otherwise sleeps between a minute-long grace and a
day-long marker.
- **The meeting screen pages a large room rather than drawing all of it.** What a browser pulls is now
decided by one pure function over the roster, the presence facts, the pins and the gallery page
(`apps/web/src/lib/meetings/subscription-policy.ts`): at most sixteen cameras, at most one screen
share, at most twenty-four microphones, ordered pinned first, then whoever is sharing, then the most
recent speakers, then roster order. It is a function rather than a method on the client for one
reason — the case that matters is three hundred participants, and three hundred browsers cannot be
stood up in a test.

**The client makes the plan true and nothing more.** `reconcile()` asks for what the plan names and
is not already coming in, closes what the plan no longer names by its media section, and moves a
simulcast layer where the plan changed it; a burst of `roster-delta` frames costs one pass rather
than one pass each, because reconciliation acts on the first change and folds everything inside the
next quarter second into one. Cameras publish three layers (`f`, `h`, `q`) and a subscriber asks for
the full picture on a page of four tiles, half on a page of nine and a quarter beyond — a screen
share still publishes one layer, because a quarter-size document is unreadable. A `roster-delta`
naming somebody this browser has never heard of is a gap, and the answer is one `sync`, not a guess.

**Every voice is played once, apart from the tiles.** The people a browser hears and the people it
shows are different sets, ranked differently on purpose, so playback moved out of the tile into one
component over the pulled streams. Sound coming through the tiles is how a room goes quiet the
moment somebody turns a page.
- **The matter file manager's rulings are written down and checked by a browser. Three settled
decisions were silently reverted in one round of mockup review, and nothing caught any of them.**

Design review on this surface runs in rounds: it is built, the owner walks it, corrections come
back. Each round was rebuilding the page from scratch, so anything decided two rounds earlier and
not restated in the newest message came back as whatever the model would have produced unprompted.
In one round that cost the forward button, the breadcrumb's home icon (back to the word "Files"),
and the matter search's position (back into the file-manager toolbar) — none of them mentioned in
the instructions that undid them, all of them already settled.

`docs/conventions/file-manager-rulings.md` is the cumulative ledger: every ruling, numbered, each
marked `settled`, `regressed`, `open` or `superseded`. A ruling in it is not re-proposed. It is
linked from `design-corrections.md`, which already carried the same lesson from the sign-in flow's
fifteen revisions.

`tooling/file-manager-rulings/` is the half that does not rely on anyone reading. It opens the
surface in headless Chromium and asserts each mechanically-checkable ruling — that Back, Forward and
Up all exist and that Forward enables once Back is used; that the breadcrumb root is an icon; that
the inspector carries five named tabs and offers no action buttons; that every column but Name
drags; that clicking a row does not open the inspector. It found two real defects while it was being
written: an "already removed" line that was still on the page because the script that removed it had
aborted before writing, and a hover-only `visibility` rule that made every version-row button
untargetable while a presence-only assertion passed.

The harness is also what keeps the ledger honest. A status is a claim about the built screen, and
it goes stale the moment a round builds something without returning to the table — twenty-six rows
were stale on the first reconciliation, all of them understating what had been built. That direction
of staleness costs the same as the other one: it sends the next round to rebuild what already
exists, which is exactly how the forward button was lost. The ledger now opens with the rule that
the harness runs first and any row it contradicts is corrected in the same commit. Standing at
reconciliation: 99 settled, 21 open, 1 regressed (renaming still selects the extension), 1
superseded.

Only mechanically-checkable rulings are in the tool. Taste stays a person's job.
- `ScreenSearch` — the product's one control for searching within a screen, distinct from the top bar's command palette.

Eleven list surfaces answered "search this screen" four different ways, sharing no code: matters and the file manager each hand-rolled an expand-from-icon search, the directory and custodian carried an always-present labelled field, the Time Sheet had the shape specified but only in a mockup, and matter parties, matter costs, notifications, user administration and tools had nothing at all. The design system's own `DataTable.Search` was built for the job and had zero consumers — because it bound straight to a table's global filter and so could only narrow rows already in the browser, which is exactly why the screens that search on a server went and built their own.

The component carries the shape the standing list-screen rule already decided. It rests as an icon, so a screen nobody is searching pays no vertical space for it; it expands on use and collapses when left empty; a live query keeps it open behind a single accent hairline, so a narrowed list carries its reason on screen. There is no clear button — Escape clears the query, a second Escape closes the control and hands focus back to the icon that opened it.

It is one component by construction: registered in the one-implementation registry, so a second file claiming the name fails the gate. And it serves either transport without the calling screen writing anything different — the screen hands over `onsearch` and says whether to run it on every keystroke, for data already here, or after a pause in typing, for a request that leaves the machine. The control owns the query, the debounce and the in-flight flag; it owns no results. `DataTable.Search` is now a thin preset over it that supplies `onsearch` from a table, so the common case stays one line.

Three things ship as seams, built and exercised in the catalog but wired to no screen: a scope control at the field's leading edge, an in-field match count, and a shortcut key. Each says in the code what will use it. The scope names the surface it searches and will never offer "everywhere" — searching everything is the top bar's job.

Adopting it on the screens is separate work, and one of those adoptions removes a defect: in a right-aligned action row the search has to sit to the leading side of the primary action, or the primary action slides sideways on the first keystroke.
- **Natural-language document search, built whole and switched off — every gate closed, no instance in
existence, and the one part that could answer a question deliberately absent.**

A firm can now be given a search that takes an ordinary question against a matter and returns
passages of its own documents. None can yet, and that is the shape of the work rather than a
shortfall: everything the feature needs exists except the adapter that calls the managed index, which
waits on evidence rather than on effort.

**The gate is a gate on a gate.** `search.naturalLanguageEnabled` defaults off, and the write path
refuses to open it unless the firm has accepted the **current version** of a written disclosure —
recorded firm-level, with who accepted it and when. When the feature ever changes what it copies or
what it can do, the version moves, every firm's acceptance stops matching, and they are asked again
without anybody remembering to ask. The setting change, its audit row, and the message that
provisions the instance ride one transaction, so there is no state where a firm's gate is open with
no provisioning in flight.

**The disclosure refuses two things rather than hedging them.** Data residency for the managed store
is not something the platform can specify or verify, so it offers no guarantee and tells a firm with
a residency obligation not to enable the feature. Deletion of the managed index is a request whose
completeness the platform cannot demonstrate, so the statement says exactly that — the platform
deletes the extracted text it wrote, from storage it owns, and can enumerate the catalog to show it,
and stops there. Neither sentence is a caveat on a promise; they are the absence of a promise.

**What can reach the index is an allow-list with one entry.** The instance is pointed at a derived
text feed, never at a firm's bucket — a bucket holds received productions, mid-edit working copies,
conversion artifacts and index splits, and pointing an index at it would put an opposing party's
production into a search of the firm's own working files. The feed writer runs from one place, the
existing search index job, as a **second consumer of the extraction already computed there**: the
bytes are read once and parsed once, and the keyword split and the feed both read that one result.
A test asserts the extraction runs exactly once.

**A matter left out has its copies deleted, not merely stopped.** Once a firm opts in every matter is
fed — a search covering only the matters somebody remembered to tick has invisible gaps, and a lawyer
who finds nothing concludes there is nothing. The escape hatch enqueues deletion of that matter's
feed objects, because an exclusion that only stopped new writes would leave the material that
prompted it sitting in the index.

**Deletion is planned from the catalog and never from a bucket listing**, so an object the catalog
does not know about is a reported inconsistency rather than a silent miss; reconciliation runs as
part of every teardown and its result is recorded.

**The meter keeps measurement and estimate in different objects**, structurally, so a renderer cannot
show them alike: query counts and fed bytes are exact because the platform makes every call and
writes every byte, the ingestion figure is derived from fed bytes at a ratio stored on the row, and
managed storage is a **named gap** rather than a zero, because no per-firm figure is published and a
guess presented as a meter is a future billing dispute.

**Not built: the retrieval adapter and its route.** The design's central claim is that the metadata
filter is a recall optimization and read-time re-authorization is the boundary — but the route still
must not ship until the filter's semantics have been observed against a real instance, because a
filter that fails open, or that is accepted and silently ignored, cannot bear even the optimization's
weight. Both ports resolve, through the production resolvers, to typed unavailable outcomes; an
absent binding reports `instance-not-provisioned` rather than an empty success, which would be
indistinguishable from a corpus in which nothing matched.

Fitness tests assert what a later edit could quietly undo: no generation call anywhere, no
public-endpoint enablement anywhere, the port's input has no slot a caller-supplied filter could
arrive in, the feed writer emits exactly one object class and cannot emit a reserved one, and the
instance configuration constant is the only place the metadata schema is spelled — because changing
that schema re-indexes every document in every firm's instance.
- **You can sign out — and sign out of your other devices.**

`Sign out` in the profile menu was the last control left over from before accounts existed: a session could be started and never ended. It ends the real session now, and it leaves by loading a fresh page rather than navigating within the application, so nothing the session had read stays behind in the tab for the next person at that computer. A sign-out that does not go through says so and keeps you where you are — the one thing worse than not signing out is believing you did.

**Account → Active Sessions** is a new section beside Profile and Security: every computer and phone signed in as you, one row each — the device, when it signed in, the address it signed in from, and when it expires — with the one you are reading on marked and left alone. Sign out of any of them, or **Sign out everywhere else** in one go, which is the right move when you cannot tell which row is the intruder. The screen states the one thing that would otherwise be discovered the hard way: a device signed out here can take up to five minutes to be turned away, so somebody who thinks their account is compromised is told to change their password as well.

Two facts the screen deliberately refuses to state. It shows no "last used" time — the record knows when a session STARTED and not when it was last active, and a stamp that read as the second while meaning the first would have people clearing rows that were in use. And a browser it cannot identify is listed as unrecognised rather than guessed at.

Under it: `logout` and `session.revoked` join the control-plane audit trail, decided by the endpoint the session was deleted under rather than by the deletion itself — sweeping an expired session and the rotation that happens when a second factor is enabled both delete a session row, and neither is somebody leaving. And Better Auth's session-freshness dial is turned off, because in the pinned version it gates the listing and none of the writes: left at its default it would have hidden the signed-in-devices screen from anybody signed in longer than a day, which is exactly the long-lived session the screen exists to let somebody find and end.
- **The foundation for a setting that repeats, and for saying what one would collide with.** The owner: "start recurrence… check conflicts."

**The rule and its expansion** (`apps/web/src/lib/calendar/recurrence.ts`). A repeating setting is ONE row with a rule, expanded across the window a read asks for — the alternative multiplies a firm's calendar by the length of its longest series before anybody looks at it, and turns "move the series" into fifty-two writes. The stored form is an RFC 5545 `RRULE`, because it is what every calendar product reads and writes and a firm exporting its calendar should not find this product's dialect in it. What the form offers is narrower than the standard allows, and `parseRecurrence` returns null for a rule it cannot present rather than half-showing one it would silently rewrite.

Two decisions worth stating because they are the ones a reader would argue about. **The expansion walks civil days, never instants** — so a weekly nine o'clock setting is nine o'clock on both sides of a daylight-saving change, where an instant-based walk would move half a firm's Tuesdays by an hour twice a year. And **a month with no such date is skipped, not pulled back**: a firm that said the 31st did not mean the end of the month, and February gets no occurrence rather than an invented one on the 28th.

**The schema** gains `recurrence_rule`, `recurrence_parent_id` and `recurrence_occurrence_on` on both event tables. An exception — one occurrence moved, renamed or called off — is a REAL event that knows which date of which series it replaces, so every read that already understands an event understands it, including the rule that a cancelled setting stays visible and struck. An exclusion list would have needed a second mechanism to say "and this one was cancelled". The added columns carry their own CHECK rather than the table being rebuilt, on the mechanism the task-rungs migration proved against real durable-object storage: a rebuild drops the table it replaces, and `matter_event` is a parent three tables reference.

**What a setting would collide with** (`schedule-conflicts.ts`). Recurrence is why it exists: one hearing at a bad hour is visible in the day schedule the form already draws, but a weekly setting for a year is fifty-two chances to collide and nobody scrolls a year to check. A double booking is never refused, only stated — two things at once is not something the platform knows to be wrong. Civil days and wall clocks, never instants; back-to-back is not a collision; a vacated hearing competes for nobody's Tuesday; and a series reports DAYS rather than collisions, because "three of the twelve dates" is the question a person asks.

**Not yet wired.** No service reads or writes a rule, no route carries one, no form offers one, and no read expands one — so nothing in the product repeats yet. The arithmetic and the storage are in place and asserted; the service, the contract and the form are the next slice.

Also withdrawn in the same round, before anything was built: the separate zone for a setting's END. The owner: "only have one field for time zone. always the same for start and stop." The forms already ask once, and no `end_time_zone` column exists or should.
- **A calendar setting can carry a repeat rule.** A new `recurrence_rule` column on `matter_event` and `firm_event` (migration `20260916T000000_event-recurrence`), threaded through both statement modules, both services, the shared `event-shape` asserts, and the create/update/detail contracts on both scopes. The record forms and the entry window edit it through one `recurrence-field.svelte`, over the rule the draft holds.

**One row carries the series; nothing writes an occurrence.** A weekly status conference is one record with a rule on it, not fifty-two records. A row per date would multiply a firm's calendar by the length of its longest series before anybody looked at it, make "move the series" fifty-two writes, and make a correction a reconciliation. The dates are read back from the rule, inside the window somebody asked for — a year at most, which is the platform's own cap — so the work is bounded by what is on screen rather than by how far the rule runs.

**The grammar lives in `@magna-carta/civil-time/recurrence`, which both sides depend on.** The form writes a rule and the calendar service has to refuse one it could not itself have written; the web app does not depend on `@magna-carta/calendar` (a backend package carrying SQL), so a grammar held in either would have been copied into the other, and two readings of "what is a valid rule" disagree the first time one of them is corrected. A rule this platform cannot read back is a series nobody could edit again, so it is refused at the write (`calendar-invalid-recurrence`) rather than stored.

**RFC 5545 is the storage, and it is deliberately read narrowly.** `FREQ`, `INTERVAL`, `BYDAY`, `COUNT`, `UNTIL`, and `BYSETPOS` only in the one spelling this product writes. `parseRecurrence` answers null for anything else — a real answer the surfaces treat as one: the event still reads and still paints, and the form states that the rule was recorded elsewhere rather than half-showing a simplified version that saving would make true. The standard is stored rather than a private shape because a firm exporting its calendar should not find this product's dialect in it.

**Expansion walks civil days, never instants.** A weekly nine o'clock setting is nine o'clock on both sides of a daylight-saving change, which is true only because the walk counts days and the wall clock rides along untouched. A month with no such date — the 31st in February — is skipped rather than pulled back to the 28th: a firm that said the 31st did not mean the end of the month, and inventing a date it did not choose is worse than a month with no occurrence in it. A `COUNT` is counted from the series' own beginning, so occurrences before the window still count against it.

**A continuance does not inherit the series.** Continuing a hearing moves one setting to a new date; carrying the rule across would make the replacement repeat, which nobody asked for.

Nothing here generates deadlines. A recurring event is not a docketing rule, and the no-arithmetic position on deadlines is untouched. The occurrences are not painted on the grid yet — that is the next slice, along with the this-occurrence-or-series question an edit has to ask.
- **Shipping's `matterContext` moves from `none` to `optional`, and the buy flow gained a matter picker.** Until now the wizard never sent a `matterRef`, so every shipment was created with a null matter — and `chargeToCaptureInputs` treats a null matter as a firm-administrative charge with nowhere to disburse and emits nothing. The whole cost-recovery path was built, tested and structurally unable to fire: `packages/costs`, the outbox event, the adapter and the per-line idempotent capture, all correct, and nothing ever gave them a matter.

`optional` rather than `required` because the schema already says so — `shipment.matter_ref` is nullable, and a firm posts plenty of mail to a bank or an insurer with nothing to bill. The picker offers "No matter" as a real answer rather than treating an unfiled shipment as an omission, and the step says what the choice decides.

The consumer's own suite already covered the null-matter case; what had no test was a matter reaching a shipment at all, so the round trip — draft, register row, shipment read — is now asserted, along with the no-matter case beside it.

Unchanged and deliberately so: whether the platform's service fee is billed on to the client. That is already a per-firm setting defaulting to off (`cost.recover_platform_fee.shipping_service_fee`), and postage as a pass-through is always recovered regardless.
- **The fourth surface: a shipment opens in a record window over the register.** `/shipping/[id]` survives as its address and redirects into it, the same shape as a directory record's former address and for the same reason — a record opened in place needs no way back. The route is registered in `STANDING_EXEMPTIONS` as declining a back affordance, beside the directory's, because nothing ever renders there.

`RecordWindow` rather than the modal design's `reading` kind, settling **D4**: a shipment has a history and two acts, and one of them voids a bought label, which is destructive and about money. Tracking is asked for rather than fetched on open — the tracking route is a live carrier call, so a reader clicking through ten rows would otherwise be ten calls nobody asked for — and the tab states when it was last asked, because an event list with no timestamp beside it reads as current forever.

The label is fetched through the generated client and opened as an object URL rather than linked to by address: the contract's paths live in the client, and the bytes are behind the session anyway, so a blob the browser already holds beats a second authenticated navigation a pop-up blocker could lose. Which shipment is open comes from the URL rather than a local variable, so the browser's own back button closes the window — the gesture a reader reaches for whether or not the window offers one.
- **Notification preferences, the firm policy floor, and the one property that makes them safe: a
suppressed notification is counted, never merely absent.**

A member now sets, per category, whether it reaches their in-app feed and how often it is mailed —
one `notifications.preferences` key on the shipped `user → firm → default` scope chain, defaulting to
on in app everywhere and a daily mail except `jobs` and `system`. The two channels compose in
**opposite directions**, and that asymmetry is the decision rather than an implementation detail. In
app, the firm's tier is a **floor**: a firm may insist a category reaches its members and a member
cannot switch it back off. By email, the **member's tier wins**: a firm may never raise somebody's
cadence, because forcing email is forcing privileged-adjacent metadata into a mailbox the firm may not
administer, beyond both the audit log and the visibility filter. `security` and `trust` are
non-silenceable in app from either tier; a member may still set their email cadence to `off`.

**The part worth reading.** A category set `inApp: off` writes **no feed row** — not a hidden one, not
one somebody later discovers. Which produces the failure mode every preference system has: silence.
Afterwards, "nobody was told" and "this person asked not to be told" look identical, so a member
cannot be reassured and a real fan-out fault cannot be found. So the fan-out writes a
`notification_in_app_suppression` tally beside the rows it did write — member, category, civil day,
whose choice it was, and a count — and reports a `notifications.suppressed_by_preference` counter with
both closed labels. No event, no subject, no matter, no kind: a per-item record of what somebody
declined to hear would be a second feed holding exactly the pointers they asked not to be given. The
tally ages out on the firm's own retention window, and a member's preference read reports their own
back to them, so they can see that their choice and not a fault is why nothing arrived. An audience
everybody silenced is counted apart from an audience that resolved to nobody — only the second is a
bug.

**A firm may also designate trust-compliance recipients** — a firm-tier list, written under
`trust:manage` and audited by count and never by name, whose members join the recipient set of every
trust-category notification on top of whatever the kind's audience already resolves. **A designation
is not a grant of access:** the designated member gets an ordinary recipient row and the shipped
visibility filter still decides at read, so a notification about a matter they may not see leaves
their feed and their unread count byte-identical to a firm where it was never raised — no placeholder,
which would be an existence oracle.

**API, no screen:** `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/notifications/preferences` (the member's own, scoped to the
session and never a path parameter; the `PATCH` audited with the categories touched and never a
subject, a matter, or a recipient) and `GET`/`PUT
/api/v1/firm/notifications/trust-compliance-recipients`. The notification centre and the preference
screen remain unbuilt, so `docs/user/` gains nothing here — there is no surface a member can reach yet.

**Also repaired in passing:** the per-firm drizzle snapshot had fallen a migration behind the schema,
so the next `generate` would have re-emitted a full `review_document` table rebuild against firms that
already have the columns. The snapshot is refreshed to the lineage head; the new migration adds one
table and nothing else.
- A voided time entry can be put back.

Voiding is how a mistaken entry is retired, and it has always been one-way. That is right for the act and wrong for the accident: people void the wrong row, void on a colleague's say-so that turns out to be mistaken, and void an afternoon's work when they meant to void one line of it. Until now the only repair was to type the whole entry again, which loses its number, its internal memo, its codes, its attached documents and its history — exactly the loss that made a misfiled entry worth moving rather than re-typing.

**`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/unvoid` returns it to draft** with all of that intact. It restores to DRAFT and never to submitted or approved: those were somebody's judgement about an entry that has since been withdrawn, and they have to be given again. The restore is recorded as its own event, so a reader of the entry's history sees both acts.

**It is not a lifecycle transition, deliberately.** The state machine still says nothing leaves a terminal state, because every other record kind in the product reads that same table and none of them has been designed for a backward move. This is its own guarded act with its own refusals, the way refiling a misfiled entry is its own statement rather than a field on the update.

**The one void that must stay a void is an entry converted into a cost.** That conversion moves the entry's value onto a cost record and voids the time in the same batch, precisely so the firm cannot count the work twice; restoring the time afterwards would undo the half of that act that was protecting the client. The conversion is recorded in the audit trail and nowhere else — no column on either row names the other — so that is what the route asks before it will restore anything.

On screen it is the verb in the place the opposite verb lives: the ledger's own menu turns Void into Unvoid on a voided row, and the record window offers it on the action bar, which is where somebody lands when they open an entry to find out what happened to it.
- **Members come out of a zip and onto the matter.** The file manager could browse an archive and
never open one: the controls existed and were disabled, each naming the archive-extraction engine as
what it waited on. `packages/file-manager/src/zip-member-extract.ts` is that engine, and
`POST /api/v1/files/{id}/archive-extractions` is the route over it.

Extraction is selective by construction. A member is located from its own local header offset and
only its compressed bytes are read, so pulling one document out of a multi-gigabyte archive costs
that document rather than the archive; nothing ever holds the container. The inflate is the
runtime's own `DecompressionStream("deflate-raw")`, which was available all along and which nothing
in this repository used, so there is no compression library and no C or C++ near an attacker's
bytes.

A zip is a format designed to be lied to, so every length in it is treated as a claim. Size and
ratio are checked against the firm's caps before anything is read, the inflate is capped as it
streams rather than after it has been held, and the inflated bytes are checked against both claims
the archive made about them, its recorded length and its CRC-32. A member whose bytes do not match
its container is refused rather than filed, which is the case that matters: a member somebody
swapped is exactly a member that inflates cleanly. The firm's `archiveCaps` have existed with only
`maxEntries` ever read; `maxUncompressedBytes` and `maxExpansionRatio` now govern what they were
written for.

Every extracted member re-enters through the ordinary ingest gate, sniffed and scanned fresh, with
`declaredContentType: null` because a name inside an archive is the other party's claim about its
contents. The verdict-inheriting duplicate path is deliberately not used: the archive passed the
gate and its members never did.
- **Every archive the platform recognises can be opened and looked inside — without unpacking it.** A zip, a tar, a 7z and a rar all browse the same way: open one in the file manager and it shows what it holds, folder by folder, on the matter it sits on. Nothing is extracted, nothing is downloaded first, and a soft-deleted archive browses exactly like a live one.

Which format an object is comes from the object's own first bytes, never from its name, so an archive somebody sent under the wrong extension still opens and a text file named `.zip` is refused as what it is.

Each format is read from its headers alone — the zip's central directory, a tar's chain of 512-byte member headers, a rar's block chain in either generation, and a 7z's header at the end of the file — which costs two or three small ranged reads whatever the archive weighs. A multi-gigabyte production lists as quickly as a small bundle.

Two archives cannot have their lists shown, and each is named rather than reported as damaged: a 7z whose file list is itself encrypted (the members are there; the names need the password), and one packed by a coder no reader here covers. Both still download.

Taking members OUT remains zip-only, and the refusal now says so by name instead of claiming the other formats have nothing inside them — which a person looking at the listing can see is false.
- **The auto-file engine stops evaluating an empty set.** The guardrail function, the port on the
capture core and the evidence gatherer all shipped without the one thing that makes a delegation a
delegation: something that delegates. Nothing in the product created a rule — `createEmailAutoFileRule`
had exactly one caller in the repository and it was a test — so every unrouted capture paid two
indexed lookups, matched nothing, and returned `NO_AUTO_FILE_RULE_MATCHED`. Eight routes in
`apps/api-worker/src/routes/auto-file-rules.ts` close that: create from a filing, set the promotion
posture, suspend, resume, revoke, the matter's rules, one message's decision history, and the firm's
thirty-day review.

**Three refusals carry the weight, and each is pinned by a test that was watched to fail with the
refusal removed.** A rule may not be **stored** asking to file while the firm's ceiling is down —
accepting the posture and quietly staging would tell the member who set it that their firm had opted
into unattended filing, which is precisely the act no individual member may perform. A
`threadContinuation` rule is refused unless the conversation is already filed to the named matter,
because its entire claim is "your firm already decided this" and without a filed link that claim is
false. And a rule reached through a different matter's path is absent, so access to one matter can
never act on another's delegation.

**The review read narrows before it hydrates, and carries no cursor.** The matter set goes through
`filterAccessibleMatters` before a single rule row is read, so a rule on a matter the caller cannot
open contributes no entry, no count and no suspension line — it never enters the answer rather than
being filtered out of one. The window is fixed at thirty days and unpaged on purpose: a cursor over a
set a wall can shrink hands out short pages and calls them the end of the list. Counts come from the
links themselves rather than the ledger, so a filing somebody has since removed reads as removed —
the same signal the circuit breaker's undo input is derived from, which keeps the two from telling a
firm different stories about one rule.

**A partial index on `email_matter_link.auto_file_rule_id`,** over the automatic links only. The
shipped undo derivation subqueries that column with nothing behind it, which is a scan of every link
the firm holds, issued on the capture path the moment a rule matches. Partial so a firm with no rules
carries an empty index and the index grows with rule activity rather than with mail volume.

**A closed-set fitness sweep over four homes.** A rule kind, a suppression reason and a demotion
reason each live in the domain package's unions, the per-firm schema's column enums and CHECK
constraints, the data-access layer's structurally-identical declarations, and the API's zod enums —
four homes, which is the price of those layers not depending on each other.
`packages/email-filing/test/auto-file-closed-set-fitness.test.ts` reads all four out of the real source
and fails when one moves alone; adding a third kind to the API enum only was watched to turn it red.
It also asserts that no phrasing table interpolates anything, which is what makes "the explanation
carries no message content" a property of the code rather than of the caller's care.

**The load profile, and one claim that came back narrower than it was written.** Ten thousand rules
across a thousand matters cost no more per capture than ten (0.331 ms against 0.374 ms on this
machine) — the lookup is by match value, so the flat-cost claim holds. Two hundred firings inside the
breaker's window report as the cap rather than as two hundred, and the cap still sits above the
threshold, so a runaway rule neither drags its whole history onto every later capture nor escapes the
breaker. The thread claim is the narrow one: the rule lookup for a conversation really is by
identifier and really is flat, but the read beside it — the thread's already-filed matters — joins
over every message in the conversation and grew thirty-one fold from eight messages to two thousand
(0.06 ms to 1.888 ms). That is inside a queue consumer's budget and is the same read the suggestion
endpoint already issues inside a request budget, so nothing was changed for it; the measurement
reports it rather than restating a sentence its own numbers contradict.
- **A discovery load now produces the two records a firm hands to another party: a manifest of what
arrived, and an exception report naming every document that could not be read and why. Duplicate
copies are suppressed from extraction without being suppressed from the corpus, and an archive
becomes a family instead of a file that mysteriously held no words.**

This is the remainder of the processing sub-slice: deduplication with occurrence rows, container
families over the guarded archive expansion the engine already had, and the load manifest and
exception report written at load completion.

**The exception report is the piece worth having.** A production is a claim — _we produced everything
we could read_ — and without a document the claim is an assertion. The report names every item the
claim excludes and gives the reason for each, from a closed vocabulary in which every code is a
different sentence: `encrypted` and `password-protected` stay apart because a password can be asked
for and a key cannot, and `no-text-extracted` exists precisely so a document that yields nothing is
listed rather than indexed as empty. It is written per load, in a machine-readable and a printable
form, only once the load reconciles — a report that does not add up is not one — and it is
**reproducible**: the generation reads the instant the corpus stopped moving off the load row rather
than taking a clock, every walk is ordered by identifier, and nothing is derived from the
environment, so the same load reported twice is byte-identical.

**Deduplication keeps the duplicate.** The identity is the content hash the ingest gate already
recorded, or the email record model's own dedup key for a message — never the near-duplicate
fingerprint on the same row, which collides by design and would be suppressing a document from review
on a heuristic. The copy is marked non-primary, keeps its own Custodian of Record and its own load,
reaches its own terminal state (mirroring the primary's, including inheriting its named reasons when
the primary is one nothing could read), and is named by an occurrence row. "Which custodians held
this document" is one indexed read. Primacy is taken by a single guarded statement and held by a
partial unique index, so a group can never have two primaries and the copies can never be extracted
twice or attributed to neither.

**A container family is a chain-of-custody claim.** An archive that reaches the extractor is expanded
by the engine under its five existing guards, and every entry re-enters the ordinary ingest gate —
presigned session, magic-byte sniff, hash, malware scan — by the same path an email attachment takes.
The entries become `container-child` documents of the archive, sorted by path so a re-processing
numbers them the same way; the archive becomes the family head, processed with no text object of its
own and an entry listing in its sidecar. Entries the engine described rather than opened become a
named exception on the archive carrying a **count and a kind, never a path**. One level of expansion
per document, absolutely: a child that is itself a container is one the engine already declined to
open, and it says so.

**Found and fixed along the way.** A document waiting on the scan gate parked and was acked, which
meant nothing would ever look again — it now re-reads the row and throws so the queue redelivers,
which is what a container's children need since their bytes cross the gate after their message
exists. A `quarantined` verdict is deliberately never re-read, because the two failure directions are
not symmetrical.

Also: the extraction facts gain the digest set the engine already computed in the same pass, so the
manifest's MD5 and SHA-1 — which load-file specifications still ask for and which nothing else in the
platform would ever compute — reach the row; a legacy binary keeps the digests of the bytes that
arrived rather than of the conversion made to read them; the exception row gains its load, so the
report walks its own index instead of joining the corpus; and the record artifacts carry a
`review-load-record` object class, stamped apart from the derived text and sidecars so a collection
rule cannot delete the evidence and keep the cache.

Not built: the review-document index enqueue, opt-in semantic indexing, the review-document list read
and the shared discovery load-profile volume, which are the next sub-slice. No review surface.
- `$lib/export` — the common tabular export seam: one document shape (title, second-stamped instant,
table sections) built from exactly what a screen shows, with plain-text and CSV renderers over it
(byte-order mark, CRLF, RFC 4180 quoting). Firm Usage is the first consumer; its Download Report is
now a format menu, and its filenames carry a timestamp to the second. Native .xlsx waits on a
deliberate library adoption; Word and PDF belong to document assembly's one rendering path
(docs/decisions/pending/a-data-export-is-one-document-and-a-format-is-a-renderer.md).
- Billing — the invoice delivery record: `invoice_delivery`, one append-only row per attempt at getting
a bill to its client, so **"has this bill been given to the client" is finally a question the
platform can answer.** It was specified, its identifier prefix was registered, and the table did not
exist.

**"Sent" is deliberately not an invoice status, and this is why.** A bill goes out possibly several
times and possibly by several channels, and a re-send is not a change to the financial record.
Modelling delivery as a status would force the finalized invoice row to stay mutable for its least
load-bearing field, which is the one concession that stops an append-only table being one. So a
second delivery is a second row: channel, recipient reference, the firm-supplied delivery date, an
optional external reference, the outcome, and who recorded it. Three triggers hold append-only
unconditionally — including the BEFORE INSERT guard that catches `INSERT OR REPLACE`, which fires
neither of the other two because SQLite runs `recursive_triggers` off by default. Two more hold what
a row may describe: a delivery names a **finalized** bill (a draft is still being written; a voided
draft was never issued to anybody), and it cannot predate the bill's own issue date, which is the one
thing about a firm-supplied date the platform can check.

**It records a delivery; it does not perform one — and that is the design rather than a shortfall.**
Nothing here renders an invoice and nothing carries one to a client. Every row is a delivery the firm
made and is reporting: handed over at a meeting, put in the post, emailed from the firm's own mailbox,
submitted to the client's own e-billing portal. Out-of-band delivery is the common case, so a table
that could only hold deliveries the platform itself performed would leave the question unanswerable
for exactly the firms that most need to answer it.

**Surfaced, never a gate.** `readInvoiceDeliveryState` rides the invoice detail read rather than
waiting to be asked for separately, because the surface that has to show it is the one where a firm
decides to take fees out of a client's trust ledger — several jurisdictions expect the client to have
been given a bill first — and a fact that must be fetched on purpose is a fact a surface forgets to
show. Finalization alone still gates. The reasoning is uncomfortable and worth keeping written down:
a hard delivery gate would be satisfied by firms recording deliveries that never happened, which
converts a compliance record into a checkbox and makes the record worse than not having one.

**The state read is built to answer the two questions that look like one.** A bill with no rows has
never been sent; a bill with three failed attempts has been chased and has not landed. Both are "not
delivered", and the attempt counts are what tell them apart — a surface showing one message for both
would tell a firm nothing it needs. The recorded date is the **first** success, not the most recent
one, because when the client was first given the bill is the question a jurisdiction asks and a
courtesy re-send weeks later does not move it. A batched form answers a whole set of open receivables
in one query, since a reminder pass asking per invoice would be an N+1 against the table that grows
with a firm's whole billing history.

`billing.invoice.delivered` is emitted in the same batch as the write, carrying identifiers, the
channel, and the outcome — and never the recipient reference. A client's address is the client's own
fact and a topic payload fans out to every subscriber's notification record; it resolves behind the
deep link, through billing's own access-checked read.

Migration idx 68 (`20260817T000000_billing-invoice-delivery`); two new chokepoint routes on the
existing `billing:draft` and `billing:read` keys, so no permission inventory moved. A PII registry
entry for the recipient reference, on the footing the contact a firm records reaching a client it
holds unclaimed money for sits on.

**Two owner questions this raised and did not answer.** Whether a delivery recorded in error may be
superseded by a correcting row — the table is append-only and the design names no correction shape,
unlike a credit note, whose answer is a further credit note. And the `outcome` vocabulary, which the
design names as a column without enumerating: `delivered` and `failed` are the built floor rather
than an answered set.
- **One item's chain of custody is now readable.** The ledger has always recorded item-scoped rows — `custody_movement.item_id` is nullable precisely so that withdrawing one instrument, superseding it, or holding it alone is recordable against the item rather than the envelope — and nothing could read them back at that scope. A packet's history was the only history, and an item's rows sat inside it unmarked, so a `withdrawn` entry did not say which of a packet's five instruments left.

`GET /api/v1/custody/packets/{packetId}/movements` takes an optional `itemId`. **The filter is deliberately not `item_id = ?`**: an item inside a packet goes wherever the packet goes, so the scope is the item's own rows PLUS the packet-wide ones. A read that returned only the rows naming the item would answer "Contents described" over a decade of moves and check-outs and present that as a chain of custody, which is the failure worth guarding — `apps/api-worker/test/custody-routes.test.ts` pins it, including that the OTHER item's rows stay out.

Every row already carried `itemId`, so which of the two kinds an entry is never has to be inferred. `movementDetailLines` takes a scope: reading a packet's history an item row names its item ("About Item 1: Original will"), and reading one item's history the packet-wide rows say "The whole packet". Neither says anything in the list where it is the ordinary case, so no history repeats itself on every line.

In the packet window each item in Contents opens onto its own rail, and opening is what reads the ledger — a packet with nine items draws a list rather than nine histories nobody asked for.
- **The deploy gate requires the Cloudflare provisioning credentials, and a firm's upload path can be checked from the server.** `wrangler.jsonc` adds `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN_FIRM_PROVISIONER` and `CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID` to `secrets.required`, so a deployment can no longer run the development provisioner (which records a bucket name and creates no bucket) or the development presigner against real firms. `apps/api-worker/src/files/upload-readiness.ts` verifies the six preconditions of the browser's direct-to-storage write in order — bucket recorded, bucket exists, ingest notification, expiry rules and CORS policy (each re-applied as a whole-set PUT), and a signed HEAD proving the S3 credential is honoured by the bucket (a 403 names the token scoped to one bucket and the re-mint) — and `POST /api/v1/firm/upload-readiness` runs it for the session's firm, audited, on `firm:manageScanPolicy`; the version panel runs it with its other reads for a member holding that key and shows the report as its fourth foldable section, on the Database section's own rows and heading (model in `versions/upload-readiness-model.ts`). The provider interface carries `kind` and `bucketExists` so the report states which adapter ran rather than inferring it. The first real run of the check also exposed that `configureBucketNotifications` was never idempotent — R2 refuses a rule that overlaps one already configured (11020), so a resumed provisioning, and the check, failed on a bucket whose rule was in place; a refused overlap is now read back from the bucket's configuration and passes when the rule it meant to add is already there for the same queue — and when it is not, the failure names what the bucket holds (each queue and the prefixes sent to it), so a bucket configured for a queue the deployment no longer names is told apart from an API refusing something else. A queue id is compared without its hyphens, because the API accepts the bare UUID on a path and answers with the hyphenated one. `GET /api/v1/meta/database-health` gains a `fileStorage` block — the upload path, the provisioning adapter, and the last readiness check read back from its audit row, never run — and the version overlay's Database section shows it as a fifth row. The first draft's deployment-mode object, startup refusal, daily sweep and firm-row cache were cut on the owner's ruling that best means easy to diagnose and not overcomplicated.
- **A meeting can hold arrivals at a door.** `meeting.lobby` is `'off' | 'on'`, chosen at Start beside the medium and — unlike the medium — changeable by a host afterwards: a medium is what the people already in the room agreed to, and a lobby is a standing decision about who may come in. One lobby per MEETING and never one per firm, on the owner's ruling of 2026-09-20: a firm runs several meetings at once, so a firm-level door would queue the people arriving at a partner's deposition behind the people arriving at a staff briefing, in front of a host who is in neither.

**A waiting arrival is a stay from the moment it reaches the door.** `meeting_attendance.waiting_from` and `admitted_at` are additive on the existing row rather than a second table: the socket upgrade's ticket is an open stay and a waiter needs a socket, the signaling room's own storage is transient and is deleted when the last socket closes, and the record has to be able to say who waited and was never let in. `joined_at` therefore widens to mean "when this stay began", at the door or in the room, and the read carries all three instants so nothing downstream has to infer anything.

**"In the room" and "has an open stay" stopped being the same sentence, so both are single exported fragments.** `IN_THE_ROOM_PREDICATE` and `WAITING_PREDICATE` in `packages/meetings/src/meeting-statements.ts` are composed by the live count, the capacity guard, the roster and the lobby list, so the four cannot drift into disagreeing about who is present.

**The capacity guard moved from the door to the ADMISSION.** `MAX_MEETING_PARTICIPANTS` counts admitted open stays only, which is what the room actually holds, so the arrival insert cannot be the statement that holds it. `admitAttendanceUnderCapStatement` carries the count in its own `WHERE` and is `guarded()`, and the door gets its own much smaller ceiling — `MAX_MEETING_LOBBY` (100), refused as `meeting-lobby-full`, because a queue is not somewhere a firm should be able to accumulate ten thousand rows and the guest door lands on this path next.

`POST /api/v1/meetings` takes `lobby`; `POST .../join` answers `{ waiting, participantId, displayName, iceServers }` and mints the relay credentials either way — they last an hour, which covers any wait anybody will sit through, and minting at admission would need a second round trip at the exact moment somebody is being let into a meeting that has started without them. Four new routes on `apps/api-worker/src/routes/meeting-lobby.ts`, all of them host acts including the read: `POST/GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/lobby`, `POST .../lobby/admissions`, `POST .../lobby/denials`. The read is the one in this family that the people inside the room may not make — it is a list of people a host has not decided about yet.

**There is no server-side "admit everyone".** Admit all sends the identifiers the host's panel was showing, because a server-side "all" would admit whoever arrived in the millisecond after the host looked at the list — precisely the person the host did not decide about. The response reports one outcome per identifier (`admitted`, `not-waiting`, `room-full`), so a host admitting five people into two free seats learns which three did not get in.

**On the wire:** a waiting socket is stored under `waiting:<attendanceId>` and never under `participant:`, so `storedParticipants()` — the one read every roster, delta, subscription check and broadcast is built from — cannot include them; a waiter is not omitted from the roster by a filter somebody has to remember. It receives `lobby { position, waiting, at }` instead of a welcome, `admitted { at }` followed by the ordinary welcome, `refused: denied` with a 4000 close, and `ended`. Every other frame from it is refused `not-admitted` with the socket kept open, decided before the routing client is even resolved. Hosts receive `waiting { participants }`, whole, and nobody else does. `room-state` gains `lobby`, and `welcome` gains the lobby list — empty for everybody who is not running the meeting.

**Barred entry is one rule with two labels.** A stay closed `removed` or `denied` bars that member from this meeting while it runs; only the sentence differs (`meeting-removed`, `meeting-not-admitted`). A denial that did not bar would be a button that does nothing.

**Turning the lobby off admits nobody**, and the lock beats the lobby. A setting is not a decision about a named person, and somebody may be waiting precisely because the host intends to deny them; a locked room is shut to everybody, so there is nothing to queue for. A host or co-host of the meeting never waits, and holding `meetings:host` is deliberately not enough — a paralegal with the key walking past the door of a confidential matter discussion is what a host turns the lobby on to prevent.

**The lobby's one deadlock has an exit.** A lobby-on meeting whose host has gone leaves everybody queued for somebody who will never admit them; a key-holder claims the hostless room from inside the lobby, and a grant written for a member whose stay is waiting admits that stay in the same batch — so there is no instant in which somebody is hosting a room they are not in. That admission carries no capacity count, deliberately: refusing the claimer for a full room would restore exactly the deadlock the claim exists to end.

The screen is the web half and is not built: the waiting state, the host's lobby sheet with its badge, and the lobby switch at Start.
- Email auto-file — the rule circuit breaker's thresholds are now a per-firm setting, on the settings
idiom the scan policy and the direct-filing ceiling already use.

The breaker's two numbers were fixed in code: twenty-five firings per rule per rolling hour, and
three undos within a rule's last ten firings. Both remain the platform defaults, so a firm that never
touches the setting sees exactly the behaviour that shipped. What changes is that the numbers are
resolved per firm — `emails.auto_file_circuit_breaker` on the existing `setting` table, so there is no
schema change and no migration — and read through one helper by both the settings route
(`GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/email-auto-file-policy`, which now carries `circuitBreaker` beside
`directFilingPermitted`) and the capture consumer. The queue path and the API cannot disagree about
what a firm chose.

**The thresholds are settable; the breaker is not optional.** The design that raised the question
named the numbers and said nothing about a floor, so one is enforced rather than assumed. Every
threshold is a whole number inside a fixed range — one to five hundred firings per hour, one to a
hundred for the recent-fire window and the undo count — and `maxUndosInRecentFires` may not exceed the
`recentFireWindow` it is counted over, because a threshold above the window it is measured against
could never be reached and the breaker would read as configured while never tripping. The fire
ceiling is finite for a second reason as well: the activity read walks up to the threshold plus one
row per candidate rule per captured message, so an unbounded threshold is an unbounded read on the
capture path.

One definition of what a firm may set: the bounds live in `@magna-carta/email-filing` beside the
guardrail that applies them, the zod schema that refuses a bad write is built from those bounds, and
the pure decision function re-checks them — thresholds it cannot act on are unevaluable evidence, so
the capture stages rather than filing past a guardrail nothing can reach. Absent thresholds are
treated the same way, on the rule the module already holds for every other field: a gatherer that did
not answer the question has not given permission.
- **Beta Access is live, and it needed no new endpoint.** The firm's release channel was always in the session bootstrap — every session resolves it to evaluate the feature flags it carries — and `PUT /api/v1/firm/release-channel` has existed behind `firm:manageReleaseChannel` since release channels landed. The page was two seams over a working subsystem, and its two rows ("release channel" and "beta opt-in") were one fact asked twice. `SessionBootstrap` in apps/web now declares the `channel` and `flags` the contract already returned and nothing read.

**Instant with a consent, not the draft footer.** Entering beta requires an explicit acknowledgement that the firm accepts pre-release behavior on live client data — the route refuses it otherwise — and the shared commit footer's recap is a generic list of staged changes, which is exactly not that. So the one act that needs saying carries its own dialog, and stepping back to stable is immediate, because the server asks nothing to go back and neither should the screen. The asymmetry is the server's and the page mirrors it rather than inventing symmetry.

**A firm on alpha is told and offered nothing.** Alpha is a platform channel a firm can neither enter nor leave from inside the product; the write's vocabulary is the narrower `{stable, beta}`. A switch there would be a control whose only outcome is a 422 for a reason the firm cannot act on.

The channel is re-read from the session after a change rather than taken from the write's own answer: what actually changes the product is the flag set the new channel resolves to, and that arrives with the next bootstrap.
- **`/billing` and `/costs` — the firm's own money surfaces, and one component set behind both scopes.**

Billing's sidebar row was a Soon stub over a read that already worked: `GET /api/v1/billing/invoices` takes `clientEntityId` as an _optional_ filter, so an unnarrowed call has always answered for the whole firm, and `GET /api/v1/billing/receivables/aging` was a shipped route with no consumer anywhere outside the generated client. Costs was worse — no row at all, because `GET /api/v1/costs` answered one matter entire and returned an empty list for anything else, exactly the shape the time listing was in before its own span. It gains `from`/`to` across every matter, cursor-paged over the same statement the per-matter shape walks, with each row's matter and vendor resolved in that statement rather than a lookup per disbursement, over a new leading-date index (`cost_entry_incurred_date_index`) — the counterpart of the one `time_entry` took a day earlier. The span is gated by `costs:track` alone and not by a second capability: the per-matter listing already answers for any matter that permission names, so a span reveals nothing iterating matters would not. Time's is gated because time is personal; a disbursement is the firm's own money.

Two gaps from the matter Billing tab's screen design close with them. The invoice listing takes a **matter** — predicate over `invoice_line` rather than the balance row, because a balance row exists only after finalization and filtering on it would drop every draft — and carries that matter's share as three figures, since a draft's share is its lines and a finalized bill's is its balance, and null there means "not owed yet" rather than zero. And the **client's name** is resolved in the listing and the detail. The matter's register had been listing the CLIENT's whole billing history and then reading every one of those bills' details to work out this matter's share: the client's account under the matter's heading, at a request per bill.

`bill-columns.ts`, `invoice-window.svelte`, `invoice-print-sheet.ts` and `bill-actions.ts` now take a matter or take none; the cost columns gain a Matter column hidden inside a matter and brought forward across the firm. Both money-column pairs are declared in both scopes with one of each hidden, so a stored layout means the same thing on both screens. The matter-anchored acts are refused on the firm's register with a scope refusal — a third kind beside the state and permission refusals the verb set already carried.

Seams: `cost_entry.invoice_id` reaches the wire, and one **Open The Bill** verb in the shared ledger catalogue (`opensTheBill`, on the terms `reclassify` and `canRestoreVoid` already follow) lands a billed cost OR time entry on the matter's Billing section with that bill open — `time_entry.invoice_id` had been on the entry contract since it was written and nothing on the time surfaces read it, so that gap was a verb rather than a read; `?invoice=` opens a named bill on either register; the money toolbar's sibling row ends with the way out to the firm-wide twin, read from the sidebar's own registry so the two cannot call one place two things. Design: [`docs/specs/2026-09-07-firm-money-surfaces-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-09-07-firm-money-surfaces-design.md). The invoice detail resolves each matter's number and title beside every line AND every balance — the lines because a draft has no balance rows, so reading the balances alone would say a draft charges nobody — and the window offers one link per matter.

A cost's own record answers with what `cost_entry` already held. `created_at` and `created_by` were
in the table from the baseline schema and were never projected, so Date Entered and Entered By said
"not served" about facts the firm's database was holding; both reach the wire now, with the
recorder's name resolved by a `member` outer join in the same statement the vendor's and the
matter's already were — outer, and `created_by` deliberately not a foreign key, because who wrote a
disbursement down has to survive that person leaving. It is **not** a permission fact: the costs
design rules that a cost belongs to the matter and not to its recorder, so no read or write on a
cost is scoped per person. The two surfaces had been carrying byte-identical copies of
`canWorkDraft` whose comment promised a recorder gate that ruling refuses; they now share one
function that states the real rule — a draft is editable, and everything past it is evidence.

`kick_back_reason` was the same story with more at stake. The kick-back transition returns a cost
to **draft** and writes the reviewer's reason on the row, and the next submission clears it — so a
non-null value means exactly "this draft came back and has not been sent again", and it is the only
thing telling a returned draft from one nobody submitted. It never reached the wire, so the person
who had to fix the cost was told nothing, anywhere. It now leads the record window's Details pane
and sits above the chain on the details panel, with a hidden **Returned** column on the ledger. The
surface reads it as a draft fact even though the server already guarantees that, so no later
transition that forgets to clear it can print "returned because…" over an approved cost; and it
shows whether or not the firm runs review, because a reason already written on a record is a fact
about that cost rather than an invitation to a workflow. It stays off the printed sheet — a
reviewer's rejection note is the firm's own business.

`GET /api/v1/costs/{id}` stopped being a third shape: it was a hand-written column list that
resolved none of the three names, so opening a cost answered with less than the row it was opened
from. And `invoiceId`, which this same change put on the wire, is now read where it is served — the
details panel, the record window and the print sheet each still said "not served" over it. The
address they open goes through one `billHref` in the money surface, which three files had been
spelling by hand and one of them without encoding the identifier.
- Billing — corrections after finalization: credit notes, client credits, write-offs, and reversals,
plus the contingency shrunk-basis residual the fee-models review left open.
