one outbound call has switched the gate off. A refusal is `403`. A live verifier that will not
answer, or that rejects our own secret, is a retryable `503` carrying a retry window — never a `500`
with an Error ID for a fault the caller cannot act on.

**It ships dormant, and dormant is loud.** No Turnstile widget exists, so no secret is provisioned,
so every environment resolves the not-configured verifier and the protected endpoints behave exactly
as they did before. The absence is not silent: every decision — including every unprotected pass —
records one `human_verification.decided` point carrying the route, the outcome and a closed-set
reason. An unprotected anonymous endpoint that says nothing is how this became a runbook checkbox in
the first place, so the dormant state is the one that is counted hardest. The missing credential is
reported, never thrown: a throw at composition-root construction is what makes a not-configured path
unreachable, which is the bug the credential-store seam was reworked to avoid.

**The posture when no verifier is provisioned is fail-open, and it is one deployment variable away
from fail-closed.** These endpoints include the platform's only self-serve way in; defaulting to
refusal would have made the act of adding abuse protection its own outage. Both branches are tested.
Recorded for ratification as a pending decision.

The challenge solution is a bearer credential and reaches no log, no counter dimension, no error
message and no URL — structurally, since the telemetry catalogs have no field it could occupy.
Activation is queued for the owner in `docs/deploy-queue.md`; the runbook no longer claims this is a
manual checkbox.
- **The assistant's interface is designed, and the list endpoint can finally be asked for one matter's
conversations.**

Two places were reserved for Magnus and both were stubs: an announced sidebar destination at
`/magnus`, and a `soon` section on the matter strip. The reservation said where, and never what makes
them two places rather than the same page rendered twice. That is now written down in
[`docs/specs/2026-09-07-magnus-interface-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-09-07-magnus-interface-design.md),
and the answer is short: **the sidebar destination is a place, the matter section is a section of a
record.** The first is the member's own workspace across everything, where a new conversation starts
on no matter; the second is one matter's file of transcripts, where a new conversation starts on that
matter and the screen offers no picker. Both compose one conversation surface, on the Tasks precedent
— one component, two routes, neither knowing the other exists.

The difference is deliberately **not** a difference in what the assistant can see. The matter link
scopes the record and not the prompt, so a conversation filed on a matter puts none of that matter's
content into anything the assistant is sent. Standing inside a matter is exactly the context that
makes a reader assume the opposite, so the section states it in one line above the composer, and that
line goes away when context grants ship and not before.

`GET /api/v1/magnus/conversations` takes an optional `matterId`. Without it the matter's own surface
could not ask for its own conversations — the column has been there, indexed and populated, since the
record was built, and nothing could filter on it. It narrows; it never becomes a default, and absent
still means every conversation the other conditions allow rather than the ones on no matter.
- **Magnus has an interface, in both of the homes it was always going to need.**

The assistant's backend has been complete and unreachable since it landed: the conversation record,
both fail-closed consent gates, the queue-dispatched path to an answer, the audit and the metering.
There was no way in. There are now two, and they are two on purpose.

**The sidebar's Magnus is a place** — the member's own workspace, every conversation they have had
across everything, newest first, each citing the matter its transcript is kept on when it is kept on
one. A conversation started here belongs to no matter.

**A matter's Magnus is a section of that record** — the conversations kept on that matter's file and
no others, where a new one is filed on the matter without the screen asking. It draws no header and
no way back, because the matter's own masthead and section strip are already on screen.

Both are one component read through two routes, on the Tasks precedent: a conversation looks and
behaves the same wherever it is opened, and neither screen knows the other exists. What differs is
what the place IS, not what it can do.

**The one thing the matter section says that the workspace does not** sits above its composer:
_Magnus reads only what you type in this conversation. Keeping the conversation on this matter's file
does not let Magnus read the matter: not its documents, not its calendar, not its parties._ Standing
inside a matter is exactly the context that makes a reader assume the opposite, and the matter link
scopes the record rather than the request. That line goes away when the assistant can genuinely be
given a matter to read, and not a day before.

**A member accepts a disclosure before their first question**, and it says the things a member — not
an administrator — needs told: what leaves the platform, that the assistant sees only what they type,
that it can do nothing but answer, that the transcript is a firm record readable inside the firm and
never by a client, and that it can be wrong, is not legal advice, and is theirs to verify. The
version accepted is recorded, so a change to what the assistant can see or do asks everybody again.

**Every state the record can actually reach is on screen.** The two firm-closed screens name which
consent is missing and who can change it, rather than offering a control the reader cannot use. A
question in flight shows its pending answer. Each of the five ways an answer can fail is said in
words a member can act on — the model was unavailable, the firm switched the assistant off while the
question waited, the day's allowance is spent, the message was too long, it was cancelled — and none
of them reads "something went wrong". An answer built from a shortened conversation says so, because
only the member can tell whether the dropped part mattered.

**The transcript reads as a record, not a chat window.** The new `Conversation` component in the
design system draws a speaker label over a body, hairline-separated, in the register the rest of the
platform reads its records in — no bubbles, no avatars, no coloured alignment, no motion. It holds
no copy of its own.

Magnus stays **off until a firm turns it on**, and turning it on still takes the settings write path:
the firm-administrator enablement screen is the next piece. Until then every firm's Magnus renders
its closed state and names the gate.
- **Magnus sorts its rail, keeps a conversation on a matter, attaches a matter's files, and the firm
chooses its model.** The conversation listing (`GET /api/v1/magnus/conversations`) takes a `sort`
of `date`, `name` or `matter`, honoured over the whole record with a cursor that pages within that
order; the rail carries the control in its empty state too. A conversation is renamed where its
name is read (Enter commits, Escape cancels, blur commits; a refused rename keeps the old name and
says so). `PATCH .../conversations/{id}/matter` keeps a conversation on another matter or on none,
refusing a closed matter and auditing both matters, because which matter a transcript is kept on
decides who may read it. `POST .../conversations/{id}/attachments` attaches one of the matter's
files BY REFERENCE (`magnus_conversation_attachment`, a new per-firm table); on each later question
the file's current version is read, its text taken through the platform's own extraction port, and
sent ahead of the question under a heading naming the file within a 64 KiB budget, and the row
records whether the model saw it whole, cut, or not at all. Nothing of a file is copied. The
disclosure moved to version 2 (what Magnus can see changed), so every member is re-prompted.
Settings · AI and the Assistant gains the model control: `inference.primaryReasoningModel` is
chosen from the catalog's verified reasoning entries through the product's combobox, or returned to
"the platform's current model" (which DELETES the firm's row rather than pinning today's default);
the page states each entry's retention posture and verification dates and the catalog's version and
effective date. `magnus-surface.svelte` is split into the rail, the transcript and the composer, and
the composer names the model that answers.
- **A matter's documents now have a working screen.** Open a matter, go to Files, and the whole
loop is there on real records: what the firm holds for that matter, adding something new to it,
saving the next version of it, and reading the history of every version kept.

**Two ways to add one.** From a file you already have — drag it in, and it goes straight to storage
without passing through the application, is checked, and appears. Or from one of the firm's
templates: pick one, and the document is built against this matter and filed onto it like any other.
If the merge could not fill something in, the screen says which fields were left blank and which
ones are printing text left over from the template, because a document that reads as finished and is
not is exactly the failure worth catching before it goes out.

**Nothing on the screen is decoration.** A document still being checked says so; one the scanner
rejected is listed with its reason rather than silently never appearing; a document with no cleared
version cannot be opened, and the controls that would open it say why. Saving never overwrites — the
returning bytes are checked and kept as the next version, and the previous one stays exactly as it
was, with its size and content hash.

**Editing in the browser is honest about where it is.** Opening the editor is a real operation: the
document moves to co-editing, the open is recorded, and a signed token scoped to that one version is
minted. The editor itself is served by a separate per-document container that exists only in a
deployed environment, so on a developer's machine the frame stays empty and the screen says that
plainly rather than looking broken.

**Matters can now be reached by their own address.** Until now the matter screens resolved only the
three built-in samples, so a firm's actual matter could not be opened at its own URL at all. It reads
the firm's record first now and falls back to the samples, and the two are never confused: a sample
matter says it is one and offers nothing that would write to a firm.
- **Matter plans — `matter_plan_template`, `matter_plan_task_template`, eleven routes, and the two
provenance columns `matter_task` was deliberately left without.**

A plan is firm-authored configuration, never a record: rows come only from the createPlan route
behind `tasks:managePlans`, which is why both list reads are claimed bounded-by-construction rather
than paged. The platform seeds none, and the migration inserts none.

`proposeMatterPlan` is a PURE read — it computes the dates and resolves the roles and commits
nothing. `acceptMatterPlan` writes the kept subset in one batch, because a matter carrying six of
eleven steps after a half-failed batch is worse than one carrying none. The proposal is a GET and
acceptance is the POST, which is how the surface says out loud which one writes.

The anchor vocabulary is `matter_opened` and `none`, held by a CHECK so a third value is a reviewed
migration; every candidate beyond it is the front half of a docketing rule. `addCalendarDays` is the
one piece of date arithmetic in the package, and `test/no-arithmetic.test.ts` now pins that function's
uniqueness rather than the absence of arithmetic — an exception has to be visible to stay one.

Provenance is not a live link: a test edits every field of a template and asserts the accepted task
comes back byte-identical. Three more pin what the review exists to catch — an offset landing on a
Sunday, a role resolving to nobody and arriving NAMED rather than blank, and a kept step whose
predecessor was dropped waiting on nothing rather than on a task never created.

`opened_at` holds a civil date on some paths and an instant on others, so the anchor read cuts ten
characters rather than parsing — the same cut the note ordering already makes.

The offer is rendered on the matter's Tasks section rather than the new-matter screen: a matter
opened before its plan existed can still take it, and somebody who declined can come back.
- **Meetings, slice 1: a members-only video meeting started from a calendar event.** Media goes from the browser to the Cloudflare Realtime selective forwarding unit and never through a Worker; a `MeetingRoom` Durable Object per meeting brokers each browser's session with the unit over hibernating WebSockets, keeps the roster and writes attendance. `@magna-carta/meetings` holds the domain half on the communications package's shape, two tables join the per-firm lineage, and the routes sit under the chokepoint behind `meetings:host` and `meetings:join`.

A meeting belongs to exactly one calendar event and carries no title, time or participant list of its own — those are the event's, read through a join — so authorization, visibility and the walled-matter question are answered once, by the event, rather than a second time by a free-standing meeting object. One meeting per event by unique index, created on demand by the first member who presses Start. The record keeps who was in the room and when, and nothing that was said: no recording, no transcript, no chat, which is what lets the feature ship before the jurisdiction consent machinery exists. Without `REALTIME_SFU_APP_ID` and `REALTIME_SFU_APP_SECRET` the create and join routes answer 503 and the calendar shows no Start control, so an unprovisioned account sees the feature dormant rather than broken. Design: [`docs/specs/2026-09-18-meetings-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-09-18-meetings-design.md).

External guests, recording, dial-in by telephone and rooms larger than the slice-1 cap of twelve are each their own node in the feature ledger, sequenced after this one.

**The sidebar gains a Communications group** (owner ruling, 2026-09-18) between Workspace and Money, holding Messaging and the new Meetings row; the `/meetings` screen behind that row lists what is live, ahead and recently ended, over a cursor-paged `GET /api/v1/meetings`. Messaging keeps its stored id so a member's stars survive the move.

**The browser's half of an audio call.** The client takes the room's medium at `join` and captures the microphone ALONE in a call — a camera captured and muted still lights the device's own indicator, and the room would refuse the picture anyway — so it offers one track, declines a screen share before the picker is ever opened, and draws each participant as their initials over an audio element instead of a dark video one. The control bar drops the two controls a call cannot honour rather than grey them, the entry window offers **Start Meeting** and **Start Call** side by side under the one host key, and Join, the Meetings page's row glyphs and the header all read the medium off the record.
- **`pnpm run lint:money-arithmetic` — the money gate.** `@magna-carta/money` has been the one place an amount is added, rounded and split since it was built, and nothing enforced it. The scan looks for three things outside that package: arithmetic on a money-shaped name (`*Minor`, `*_minor`, `*E4`), a hard-coded minor-unit conversion (`/ 100`, which floats a currency value and fixes the exponent at two digits for every currency that will ever register), and a float escape (`toFixed`, `parseFloat`, `Number`) on a money expression. Comments, strings and template text are blanked by a state machine before any rule runs, with offsets preserved, so a reported line is the real line.

It landed against **152 findings across 73 files**, in a debt register that may only shrink. The classification is the useful part:

- **26 are display**, and one signature causes all of them: `formatMoney` takes a major-unit amount, so every surface divides on the way in — the same line copy-pasted into twelve Svelte surfaces. A minor-unit entry point that reads the exponent off the currency retires them mechanically.
- **69 are real arithmetic**, worst first: `document-assembly`'s expression evaluator is a **second money engine** — add, multiply, remainder, divide, an exact-division refusal and its own safe-integer guard, with an oracle test deriving the answer a third way in BigInt. `billing/contingency.ts` derives entitlement and residual in bare numbers. `trust/three-way-proof.ts` derives the whole reconciliation in raw numbers, which is the one place in the product where a cent of drift is a bar-compliance event. Twenty-seven findings are a hand-written `reduce` that is exactly `sum`, and "unpaid" is written out as `totalMinor - appliedMinor` in eight files.
- **The rest are tests and fixtures**, where the test re-computes the formula it is testing — and twelve conversions that look like display and are not: five feed a data-table column accessor whose totals row then **sums the divided floats**, so the conversion became arithmetic one layer down where the call site cannot see it.

**One finding the scan cannot see, recorded in `invariants.md` instead:** `billing/fitness.ts` computes the contingency entitlement in SQL as a float divide with hand-rolled half-up rounding, while `contingency.ts` computes it in TypeScript. Two answers that can round apart — and the fitness check meant to catch a divergence is one of the two.
- **The Nevada starter court-form library is designed, with the sources researched to primary and the terms recorded per publisher.** [`docs/specs/2026-08-14-nevada-court-form-library-design.md`](docs/specs/2026-08-14-nevada-court-form-library-design.md) and its implementation plan settle what a shipped form is; [`docs/research/2026-08-14-nevada-court-form-sources-and-terms.md`](docs/research/2026-08-14-nevada-court-form-sources-and-terms.md) records what each of Nevada's six publishers actually publishes, in what format, and what each says about reuse — every claim sourced to a direct retrieval, with the two sources whose terms could not be established labelled as not established rather than assumed.

A shipped form is **compiled reference data in a pure package**, on the `@magna-carta/trust-jurisdictions` model, and a firm **adopts** one — which registers an ordinary template through the existing pipeline and ingest chokepoint. Nothing is seeded at provisioning, a correction is a package release rather than a migration against every tenant, and after adoption the copy is the firm's and the platform never edits it. The platform **authors its own template from prescribed statutory or rule text and cites the authority** rather than redistributing a court's published document: the two Nevada corpora a firm most wants both assert copyright expressly (one of them a private nonprofit), while the Nevada Revised Statutes assert nothing and prescribe several forms' operative words verbatim.

**An unreviewed form cannot be adopted at all**, and the whole Nevada set ships NOT REVIEWED — the trust jurisdiction posture, per form rather than per library, with the review bound to a content-derived revision so an amendment re-closes the gate. Staleness is a build-time obligation expressed as a CI check that fails, because no Nevada source emits a currency signal. **A form declares its forum as values** and a wrong-court assembly is one of three distinct refusals, the middle of which (a court whose forum is not typed) refuses rather than passes.

Three decisions ship as fragments at `Proposed`. **Eleven owner flags open in a new `N` series, of which N1 through N5 gate the build** — whether the platform authors rather than redistributes, what the starter set contains, who reviews, whether fillable-PDF templates get built at all, and whether permission is sought from the two copyright-asserting publishers. The plan does not start until those five are answered.

Three findings about the shipped document-automation subsystem came out of the audit and are recorded in the design. A **fillable PDF cannot be a template** today, so the entire statewide Supreme-Court-approved corpus is unreachable whatever the licensing answer is. A **legacy Word form field binds nothing and nothing says so**: the normalizer matches `MERGEFIELD` and leaves every other field instruction as authored, so a Nevada appellate `.docx` registers cleanly, declares no keys, reports no absence, and files a document carrying the form's frozen help text — the `unconvertedMergeFields` safety net does not cover `FORMTEXT`. And **four caption facts have no merge key**: the court's county and address, and any party's address, telephone or email address.

No product code in this change.
- **The note primitive and the tasks subsystem are designed, in that order, and the first finding is that
the activity stream everyone was about to build has been shipped since the case-calendar slice.**

**Both reported gaps are real, and were verified rather than inherited.** All 175 per-firm tables were
enumerated: there is no `note`, `comment`, `annotation`, `activity` or `timeline` table. What exists
are scalar `note` / `notes` columns on a dozen individual records — custody movements, trust movements
and reconciliations, invoices, matter assets, resource bookings — each one nullable free text on one
row, attributable to nobody, editable in place, with no history and no reader beyond that row's own
detail view. They are not a primitive; they are the symptom of one being absent. Corroborated three
more ways: no `NoteId` among the 166 identifier types (this platform reserves handles before it builds
things — `PortalGrantId` is reserved with no portal); no node describing a note anywhere in
`roadmap.d/`; and `apps/web/src/lib/matters/sections.ts` already promising a Notes section at maturity
stage `soon`, "dated, attributed, and searchable," over nothing. The `matter` table carries `closed_at`
and no reason column of any kind, and the only later `ALTER TABLE matter` in the tree adds
`system_key`.

**Activity is the calendar's federated read with one more source on it, and building a second timeline
was the failure to avoid.** `packages/calendar` already reads one page across fourteen declared sources
under one comparable sort key, the platform's own cursor, and one required visible-matter predicate
composed in SQL before the `LIMIT`. Its registry states that a source is "a read-side declaration and
NEVER a write-side obligation," and its package invariant states why that matters: nothing is
projected, copied or backfilled, which is what makes the bug where the timeline disagrees with the
register unwritable, because the timeline IS the register. A note joins for one registry row, one
statement builder, one projection and one label decision — and the label decision is `declaresLabel:
false`, on the precedent that the filed-email source refuses a subject line and the time-entry source
projects a duration rather than a narrative. One thing does not come free and is stated rather than
discovered: a note on a **Directory entity** has neither anchor the registry expresses, and reaching
for the `firm` anchor — a reviewed one-entry allowlist — would be a silent loosening of the exemption
that package guards most carefully. So matter notes join the timeline first and entity notes wait for a
third anchor with its own predicate.

**An internal note and a client-visible comment are two entities, decided while the portal is still
unbuilt.** No visibility boolean, and no path by which one becomes the other. A boolean makes
publishing work product to the opposing party a one-character diff and an irreversible one — flipping
it back does not unsend what the portal rendered. Beyond that: a note's author is a member and a
comment's may be an external principal the portal places in the control-plane database as a distinct
principal type; a grant's scope vocabulary is matter, folder and file, so a comment is reachable
through a grant and a note is reachable through **nothing**, which is a structural protection a `WHERE`
clause would replace; and the tree already separates them, with `notes` and `messaging` as two matter
sections. Sharing a note is therefore a new comment authored by the member at the instant they authored
it, because a publication decision made in June must not alter a record made in January.

**A note is corrected by revision and retracted, never deleted — and it is neither the ledger nor the
calendar.** The ledger is append-only because a third party relies on it and the firm demonstrably
could not have changed it; nobody audits a firm's notes. The calendar edits in place because it records
a plan, and "a firm made to record a compensating row to fix a typo stops recording"; but a note is a
contemporaneous record whose weight is that it was written then, by that person. So: an identity row
plus revision rows, an edit appends and moves the head, every prior body retained. Retraction is a
state with its own actor, instant and reason — the body stops rendering and drops off the timeline
while the rows remain — and it exists so the case that would otherwise force a delete has an answer.
There is no hard-delete route; the one case where bytes must genuinely leave routes through the PII
registry's `report-manual` action, which is defined for exactly this and neither auto-erases free text
nor silently refuses. Authorship survives a departure: the author reference never nulls and never
repoints, because every sibling subsystem already made that choice and an unattributed contemporaneous
record is worth a fraction of an attributed one; the former-member signal is a read-time join on
`member.status`, never a column.

**Two containment rules, because both failures would look reasonable to whoever wrote them.** The
PDF scrub removes document-level surfaces and is structurally blind to merge-filled text, which is page
content — so a merge field resolving to a note body would put internal work product into a letter under
the firm's letterhead and the one machine built to stop privileged text escaping in a PDF would not see
it. **No merge field ever resolves to a note or a comment**, guarded by a source scan landing in the
same slice as the table. And `review_document.source_kind` is a three-value CHECK over file versions,
email messages and attachments, so a note is uncollectable into a review set today; that default is
**defended** rather than inherited, with export-as-document as the route if production is ever ordered,
because widening the enum puts every candid internal assessment one bulk load away from a production
set.

**Then tasks, and the date finding is bigger than the modelling.** The brief assumed the calendar ships
rules-based docketing and a task due "14 days after service" reaches the same computation a deadline
does. **It does not exist.** The calendar states as a capital-letter invariant that nothing computes a
deadline date, its time-zone module says it never derives a date from another date, a test scans the
sources for date-arithmetic identifiers, and `roadmap.d/calendar.md` records the absence as "a
deliberate position, not a gap." So a task reaches what does exist and adds nothing: the deadline's
three columns (civil date, optional wall-clock time, required zone — never midnight-local-as-UTC), the
calendar's own civil-date resolver with a dateless task due at the **end** of its civil day, and
read-time overdue with no column and no sweep, which is a stronger argument for tasks than for
deadlines because tasks are numerous. A matter plan's "14 days after" is the same forbidden arithmetic
wearing a template, so a template carries an **anchor and an offset**, instantiation renders a
**proposed** date, and a member's acceptance is the write — the propose-and-confirm interaction the
calendar already reserved for the statutory catalog it has not built, reused rather than reinvented,
with the anchor vocabulary held to one real value behind a CHECK constraint so growing it costs a
reviewed migration.

**The platform ships no matter plans**, for the calendar's reason about computed dates: a plan asserts
how a firm practises in a jurisdiction, and a shipped plan with a missing step is a malpractice vector
carrying the platform's name, trusted precisely because it shipped. Instantiation is a one-time copy
with provenance columns and no live link; nothing reconciles, because a drift report is the live link
with an approval step. Sequencing is one `blocked_by` predecessor that renders and sorts and gates
nothing. Open tasks register a close **advisory** and never a precondition — the advisory file's own
reasoning is this exact case — and nothing happens to the tasks at close, because closed is
archived-but-additive; they drop out of the default read through a filter, so reopening restores them
with no backfill. Task assignment **subscribes** to the notifications registry on its existing
outbox-row-is-the-emission discipline; the comparison-shaped due-soon and overdue points are declared
and wired to nothing, beside the calendar's identical declarations, so one sweep eventually serves both.

**A stale comment worth reporting, and it is not this design's to fix.**
`packages/notifications/src/recipients.ts` resolves the `matter-team` audience with "DECLARED AND
UNRESOLVABLE TODAY: there is no per-matter team table." `matter_assignment` **is** one — matter,
member, role, and a validity interval — and it shipped two merges later (`45003814` is the
notifications slice, `8d98eca0` the assignment table). Three registered notification types today
declare `audience: "matter-team"` and quietly deliver only to the responsible member, reporting
`substituted: true` to nobody. The substitution field was built so this would be a one-resolver change
when the table landed, and it landed. Task notifications use `designated` and do not depend on it.

**Ledger corrected, and one node deliberately not added.** All four `roadmap.d/tasks.md` nodes asserted
no spec exists; their evidence now names the spec and records it as Proposed pending owner flags, with
no status moved and no `spec:` key set — the precedent `roadmap.d/intake.md` set the same day.
`tasks.workflow-model` was `researching`, which the vocabulary defines as "a named open research
workstream," and the white paper's research list names exactly two, neither of them this; corrected to
`not-started`. **No node is added for the note primitive**: there is none anywhere in `roadmap.d/`,
which is a real finding and an owner decision about whether the register grows, not a gap for a branch
to fill. The matter close-reason gap is confirmed and placed: it belongs to `packages/matters`, not
here, because a close reason is a closed vocabulary reporting, conflicts and retention all need to read
programmatically, and answering "why did it close" with a free-text note answers it for humans and for
nobody else.

No feature code, no schema, no migration, no route. Fifteen owner flags in a new **W** series: eleven
decide what gets built, two decide how, and two are professional-conduct questions the design analyses
and answers neither. Two of the eleven — whether notes may ever enter the discovery collection
vocabulary, and whether a search result may carry a snippet of privileged text — are confidentiality
questions that additionally decide a build, so they sit with the build-gating set rather than beside
the two the design refuses to answer: what it means that the platform is about to acquire its first
durable, attributable, discoverable place to criticise a colleague, and what the matter close-reason
vocabulary contains, given that "declined" and "completed" attach different obligations under Model
Rule 1.18.
- **The notifications settings surface ships, both tiers.** The backend was complete on both and the pages were the only thing missing — the Notifications nav group rendered empty.

`/settings/notifications` (My Settings, instant, `notifications:read`) is the member's per-category matrix over `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/notifications/preferences`. `/settings/notification-policy` (Firm Settings, instant, `firm:manageNotificationPolicy`) is the firm's three levers over `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/notifications/policy`.

A MATRIX, not a page of rows: one subject with two independent answers per category, so both pages are tables rather than the settings row anatomy. Both are instant, the departure Users already makes — twelve rows times two channels plus two scalars is twenty-six independently meaningful, separately audited choices, and staging them behind one Save would make the pending count meaningless.

**Neither page computes what applies.** `resolveCategoryPreference` is the one place the two tiers compose, and it stays there: every member row arrives resolved with `inAppLockedBy` saying whether it may be moved and who decided, so a locked switch renders as a locked badge with the reason on hover rather than as a control that silently refuses. The asymmetry is what the firm page's wording carries — in app, `on` is a floor nobody may lower while `off` is only a default a member may raise; by email nothing is a ceiling at all, because forcing a copy into a mailbox that may be personal is not a thing a firm may do to somebody.

The member page shows what a choice COST: the server's per-category suppression tallies, said where the switch is, so switching a category off is a decision rather than a disappearance.

`apps/web/src/lib/notifications/category-vocabulary.ts` mirrors the wire enums by hand and says why in its header: reaching for `@magna-carta/notifications` for twelve words pulls most of the backend's dependency closure into the web app and trips `tooling/affected-lint/scope-fitness.mjs`, which caps fan-out sinks. `apps/web/test/notification-category-vocabulary.test.ts` checks the mirrored categories and cadences against the emitted contract, so a category added to the platform fails there rather than reaching a member as a raw key.
- **Settings · Offices, the firm's brand images on Firm Profile, and the office family under `apps/web/src/lib/offices/`.**

The whole locations backend had no screen. It now has one: a `DataTable.Grid` register over `GET /api/v1/locations` (which now joins each office's addresses, its staffing count, whether it prints its own logo and whether it is the firm's default), and one `RecordWindow` for entering, reading and correcting an office, with the entry segmented into Office, Addresses and Letterhead tabs on the left and the acts that commit on their own (members, the letterhead logo) in tabs on the right. `?office=<id>` opens a record on arrival, which is what `OfficeLink` links to.

The contract grows `location.email` (one per office; a telephone belongs to each address), the four international address lines and the country on `location_address` so the design system's `AddressFields` writes an office's address the way it writes anybody's, `PUT|DELETE /api/v1/locations/{id}/members/{userId}` composed onto the per-member replace-set, `PUT /api/v1/locations/{id}/firm-default` (without which the close refusal on the default office was unrecoverable), and `GET /api/v1/locations/{id}/letterhead-logo`, which streams the office's own mark or the firm's primary brand image. `firm_brand_image` is a new per-firm table, content-addressed by the bytes' SHA-256, behind `GET|PUT /api/v1/firm/profile/brand-images`, `PATCH|DELETE .../{sha256}` and `GET .../{sha256}/content`, all under `firm:manageProfile`. The office picker (`OfficePicker`), the link (`OfficeLink`) and the shared `firmOffices` read are the modular pieces the matter status window's Location consumes next.
- **Members come out of a tar and a 7z, and every extraction goes through one module.** `packages/file-manager/src/archive-members.ts` is the single door into an archive's contents: the format dispatch for listing AND extraction, one refusal vocabulary across every format, the firm's caps applied before any format-specific code runs, the budget a request shares across the members it takes, and the record of what each attempt cost and why it ended as it did.

The three questions an archive raises — what is in it, may this member be taken out, and what did taking it cost — were previously answered in three places, in zip's vocabulary, with the caps applied by whichever reader happened to run. A second format made that untenable and a third would have made it wrong.

A tar is the cheapest extraction on the platform: its members are stored whole, so taking one is a ranged read of its own bytes with no decoder involved. A 7z needs a real one — `crates/seven-zip-core` decodes the single block the member sits in, and because a solid block is one compressed stream over several members, reaching a later member costs the members ahead of it. That is why extraction carries a block ceiling of its own: a small member can sit at the end of a block that unpacks to gigabytes, and bounding only what the caller keeps would bound the wrong number.

A format whose reader needs a compiled engine arrives as an injected port, on the `MalwareScanPort` seam, so the domain package still carries no WebAssembly binding and a deployment that wired no engine refuses by name instead of crashing.

**rar lists and does not unpack, and that is the honest boundary.** Listing one walks its block headers and needs no decoder, which is what made it buildable. Decoding a rar member's packed data has no memory-safe implementation to build against and the reference implementation's licence forbids reusing its code. The Extract control says that rather than being offered and then refusing.

Also new: an entry that is a symbolic link, a hard link, a device node or a pipe is refused as `not-a-file` rather than filed as an empty document under a name that promises something else.
- **`Smith & Jones LLP` and `Smith and Jones, L.L.P.` are now one name to a conflicts check. The name
half of conflicts search depth ships two derived match keys, the nickname catalogue registered and
empty, and the name roles a check compares against turned into a firm setting recorded on the row.
Beider-Morse does not ship, and the reason is a measurement rather than an opinion.**

The shipped matcher compared names four ways — blind-index identifier equality, an exact
`normalized_display` probe, Double Metaphone, and trigram overlap — and `normalizeName` is a frozen
contract stored across every firm, so what it misses has to close beside it rather than in it.

**Spelling.** `normalized_match_key` and `normalized_match_key_bare` are nullable columns on
`directory_name`, derived inside `insertNameStatement` from the row's own normalized display so none
of the eight name-writing paths can omit one. The first canonicalizes connector words and
legal-entity spellings and **keeps** the legal form, so an equality means one name written two ways —
**tier 2**, the same rung as an exact name. The second removes the legal form, so `Smith & Jones LLP`
and `Smith & Jones LLC` meet — **tier 3**, because one firm re-formed and two unrelated legal persons
look identical from there. No tier is widened and no CHECK is rebuilt; the signals name themselves in
`matched_fields_json`. Existing corpora are filled by a resumable, budgeted sweep on the daily cron —
no stored cursor, because the selection predicate is the outstanding work — with a fitness probe
reporting what is left.

**Which names a check compared is now a setting, not a word.** The resolved name-role set is
firm-configurable, recorded verbatim on the check row beside the name keys compared and the phonetic
schemes that ran, and its shipped default searches former, maiden and alias names at the balanced
band — so the party who married and changed surname is no longer invisible at the setting nearly every
firm runs. Over-inclusive still searches every role and is deliberately not configurable, which is
what keeps the superset invariant structural. The owner flag behind the default stays open; answering
it is now a settings edit rather than a release.

**Nicknames are registered and empty.** `Bob`/`Robert` is not a phonetic relationship and no algorithm
derives it. The table ships with no rows, and every check records `nickname_equivalence` as a source
it could not search — read from the catalogue rather than asserted, so the day a firm curates one the
log stops saying otherwise without anybody editing code.

**Beider-Morse was built, measured, and taken back out.** The recall is real: over a thirty-pair
cross-origin surname corpus it reaches seven pairs Double Metaphone structurally cannot
(`Nowak`/`Novak`, `Kowalczyk`/`Kovalchik`, `Wojcik`/`Voychik` among them). The only maintained
pure-TypeScript implementation is MIT with zero runtime dependencies, so golden rule 14 never came
into it. What stopped it is workerd: the library compiles its rule tables into regular expressions at
module load, which Node does in 16 ms and **workerd does in 20,377 ms** — measured on the first person
create with the channel wired up. That is past the CPU limit, the request never completes, and a lazy
dynamic import is worse (Workers forbid runtime module loading, and it hangs). So the channel is not
shipped, the table is not created, the dependency is not taken, and the follow-on now carries a
numeric flip condition instead of a hopeful one: an encoder whose tables cost workerd single-digit
milliseconds, which is the Rust/WASM port the design already nominated.

**A schema claim in the design is corrected on the way past.** `directory_name_phonetic_code`'s open
`scheme` CHECK is real, but its PRIMARY KEY is `(name_id, scheme)` — one code per name per scheme,
which fits Double Metaphone's two and not an encoder returning tens. Whenever a variable-output
encoder lands it needs a table keyed by the code; the rule is now written beside the table so the next
reader does not rediscover it.
- **One layout for a screen with a navigational column beside its content — `NavigationLayout` in
the design system.**

Settings drew a two-column canvas by hand (a nav at the popover measure plus its gutters, inside a
negative-margin full-height row with its own scrollbar) and Magnus drew the same shape a second way
(a rail at an off-token container width, a different scroll treatment). The owner's ruling is that
this is one shape, so it is now one component: `@magna-carta/design-system/navigation-layout`
provides the `<nav>` landmark with a required accessible name, two token-derived widths (`standard`
— the settings measure — and `narrow`, which lands on the global sidebar's width), two independent
scroll regions wearing the house scrollbar with a reserved gutter so nothing shifts when a scrollbar
arrives, and the canvas geometry (the full height under the top bar, the work canvas's inset
cancelled) that consumers stopped needing to repeat. What the navigation holds is the consumer's
snippet — grouped section links, a control over rows, a grouped list of tools — so the component
imposes no list structure and takes no `items` prop. Below the `lg` viewport the navigation stacks
above the content and the layout scrolls as one. Settings and Magnus adopt it in their own rounds;
Tools and Reports can take the same shape as list-left, chosen-thing-right.
- The **File Workbench** — one Tools screen where a file that belongs to no matter is dropped once and read every way at once, instead of ten screens each asking for the same bytes.

Type, Hash, Malware Scan, Metadata, Email, Convert, Repair, Text Recognition, Unlock and AI Text are all capabilities of one surface. Two of them are real in the browser today with no backend at all: what the file actually is, read from its leading bytes against what its name claims, and its SHA-256 and SHA-1. The other eight render their own control, disabled, naming what they wait on.

A flagged file still gets everything. The scan verdict is reported on the file's row and in its Overview and gates nothing, because a file somebody does not trust is precisely what this surface is for and the readings a gate would withhold are the ones that answer whether to trust it. A fitness test holds it: every capability is evaluated against the same file under each verdict, and the answers have to be identical.

Conversion acts on the whole selection, and offers only the formats every selected file can reach — a production of sixty scans is one gesture, and a target half the selection cannot become is not offered at all rather than failing partway.

The file list is the product's one grid, so it sorts by name, type, size and arrival, filters per column, hides and reorders columns, and carries the count and the selection in its own footer — the same behaviours the matter's ledgers have. The list itself takes a drop, with nothing drawn for it until a drag is over it; each row has its own menu; and one control shows or hides the file beside its readings, whichever capability is open.

The capability set is a registry of self-contained modules: adding one is a module and a line in an array, and the Overview is contributed by the modules rather than written by hand, so the synthesis cannot fall behind the set. The modules carry no components — a panel reaches bits-ui through the design system, and golden rule 2 keeps that inside the design system strictly enough that a registry carrying one could not be loaded by a test at all.
- **A matter can be searched from one box, and the read layer behind it is a registry rather than a screen.** A matter is fourteen sections holding one case and nothing could ask that case a question: five sections had a hand-rolled search box, nine had nothing, and no query reached more than one of them.

`@magna-carta/matter-search` takes the federated timeline's architecture rather than inventing one, because it is the structurally identical problem — many subsystems, one federated read, one visibility seam, a bounded fan-out. A source declares where its rows live, which capability gates them, whether its answer is a listing or a ranked one, what it matches on, and whether it has a non-privileged snippet or declares that it has none. It is never a write-path obligation and there is no second copy of anything, so the answer cannot drift from the section a hit links into.

The shared statement builder is where the guarantees live rather than in anyone's diligence: it composes the matter binding itself, so a source cannot search across matters; it composes the visible-matter predicate before the `LIMIT`; it reads one row past the limit, so "there is more" is measured rather than estimated; and it names an `ESCAPE` on every `LIKE`. `test/source-fitness.test.ts` asserts all four over the SQL each source actually builds, plus the rule that is about disclosure rather than correctness — no registered source may name a discovery review table, because a review set is its own corpus precisely so a matter search cannot reach it.

`GET /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/search` carries two permission gates and the finer one runs first. `search:matter` gates the surface; then every source whose capability the member lacks is dropped **before a statement is built**, never post-filtered, and reported rather than returned empty. `in` narrows the registry before anything is built, which is what makes the default scope — the section the reader is standing on — the cheapest query rather than the most expensive.

`ScreenSearch` gains its first production consumer for the `scope` seam it shipped with, unchanged. The control renders from the matter **layout**, so every section inherits it and none can mount a second one; `sections.ts` now carries a required `searchSource` — a key, or `null` with the line saying what it waits on — and `pnpm run lint:matter-search-coverage` refuses a section that answers neither way, which is what makes the growth mechanical rather than remembered.

Eight sources ship — files and folders by name, time narratives, cost descriptions, billing lines, parties, calendar titles, notes and custody — and six sections decline with a reason. The matter-asset register has a written, reviewed query and is deliberately NOT registered: the section it would have landed a hit on no longer exists, so every one of its links would have been a 404. Notes composes `packages/notes`'s own model rather than restating it — one row, edited in place, ordered by the day the note is ABOUT rather than the day it was typed, so a hit sits where the Notes tab itself would put it. Two incidental fixes: the transport seam takes an `AbortSignal`, and the api-worker conformance suite was already red on this branch's base — the notes routes had landed without their six operation ids or a `notes` namespace binding.
- **The design system gains the undo and redo the product had twice and had never agreed on.**
`HistoryStack`, `UndoRedoControls` and `historyShortcuts` live at
`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/history/`, and all three are in `lint:one-ui`'s
one-implementation registry — so the third undo stack is now a gate failure rather than something
somebody notices a year later. There were two before this: the Time Sheet's snapshot stack and the
file manager's inverse-command stack, built weeks apart, bounded differently, labelled differently,
each carrying its own copy of the split-control markup.

**A step is a command with an inverse, never a snapshot.** A snapshot restores a screen; an inverse
restores the record, which is what a reader means by undo. The difference is not academic — a
snapshot cannot know which fields moved, which is why the Time Sheet's undo writes back **every** row
on the sheet rather than the ones the step changed, over rows the step never touched and over
whatever somebody changed in another window meanwhile.

**The outcome follows the inverse, never the pop.** `undo` answers once the writes have answered, and
a failure leaves the step where it was: on the stack, still offered, with the failing act named. The
Time Sheet announces "Undid {label}" the instant the stack pops while its write-through is unawaited,
so a reader is told the record went back before it has; the shared contract cannot do that. The
control hands the outcome back through `onOutcome` and says nothing itself, because the live region
belongs to the surface and a control that spoke would be a second voice on the same strip.

**And the sentence for what undo cannot reach.** `irreversibleAnnouncement` states both halves — that
undo does not reach this act, and where the repair that does reach it lives — because a surface that
offers a step and then announces a reversal that never ran is the worse failure, and "undo does not
reach this" is only half an answer when the other half exists.

**Building it found a live defect in what shipped: all four undo and redo dropdowns on the product
throw when they are opened.** Each renders `DropdownMenu.GroupHeading` with no `DropdownMenu.Group`
above it, and bits answers `Context "Menu.Group | Menu.RadioGroup" not found`. The throw happens on
the press rather than on render, so nothing showed it — two surfaces, built weeks apart, copied the
same markup. The shared control has the group, and the story that opens the menu is what pins it.

Also settled here: a walk in flight refuses the next one rather than interleaving two sequences of
inverses; only `push` grows the stack, so walking back and forth cannot drop the step at the far end;
and the keys are a handler the surface attaches to its own element rather than a window listener, so
two surfaces with stacks cannot receive each other's presses. They reach inside text fields by
default — on a rapid-entry grid the cell is not the surface — with yielding as the seam for a surface
that is one long field, which corrects the design document's stricter first claim.

Thirty-two unit tests and four story tests, the latter running as browser behaviour tests with their
own axe pass. The two ports are deliberately not in this change: those files belong to the streams
that own them, and each port picks up the missing group for free.
- **The directory-linking family, and the matter's parties built on it.** Three design-system
components: `EntityIdentity`, the one mark for a person or an organization wherever one is named;
`EntityPicker`, the one field one is chosen in, which takes a `search` and never fetches (the
settle, the floor, the abort of a superseded question and the three states live in
`picker-search.ts`, tested on their own); and `RecordParties`, the tab a record shows its people
in, the counterpart of `RecordAttachments`, with its confirmation on `ActionDialog` from the first
commit. `apps/web/src/lib/directory/directory-picker-source.ts` is the one adapter from the
directory's ranked search to the picker. The matter Parties page moves onto the tab and gains
`linkMatterParty`; its hand-composed removal dialog and its allowance go. The conflicts, custodian
and cost pickers still carry their own combobox over `searchDirectory` and fold onto `EntityPicker`
in a later slice; the one-implementation registry refuses a fourth copy meanwhile. The Directory's
route is renamed from `/contacts` to `/directory`.
- **The payments subsystem is designed, and the finding that matters most is not about payments: billing
shipped four fee models, credit notes, client credits, write-offs and the trust application, and a firm
still cannot record a client's cheque.**

`composeInvoiceApplication` refuses the `payment` application kind for **every** rail, not only the
electronic ones. A manual receipt needs no port, no adapter, no webhook, no merchant account and no PCI
posture — one composer, one ledger entry through the account-role map, and one application. It closes
the "a firm can produce an invoice and has no way to be paid for it" gap on its own, and it is the first
stage of the plan for that reason. Owner flag K1.

**Where the processor's fee lands for a trust-destined payment, which is the question the design lives
or dies on.** It lands on the firm's operating account, borne by the firm, always. A trust-destined
payment is two independent ledger entries — the gross deposit through `composeTrustEntry`, and
`Dr Merchant Fees / Cr Operating Bank` touching no trust account — and **they cannot be joined by a
ledger entry, because an entry joining them is exactly the commingling the guard refuses.** So they are
joined by a payment record instead, and that is the central move of the whole subsystem. The firm's
cushion inside the trust account may not bear it either: the second door's category is closed at
`firm_funds_deposit` and `bank_charge`, and a card processor's discount rate is not the institution's
service charge. The one shape that is dangerous because it _is_ expressible — a firm depositing its own
money onto a client's matter leaf through `composeTrustDeposit`'s free-text `source`, which the guard
cannot catch because the other leg is the trust bank — is refused by name.

**What could not be established, and is flagged rather than defaulted.** `processorFees` in
`@magna-carta/trust-jurisdictions` is exactly the field that would settle whether a fee may reduce
client principal, and Nevada — the only jurisdiction the platform ships — records it as `GAP`: four
sources searched for five terms with no hit, and the ethics-opinions index never worked through. The
corpus states the principle everywhere and verifies it almost nowhere, and the four jurisdictions that
address it expressly **disagree** — Arizona permits a merchant-fee cushion inside trust outright, Texas
and Maine instead permit a non-trust transit account with a two-business-day window and Texas adds a
three-business-day chargeback reimbursement duty. So the design implements only the arrangement that is
safe under every possible answer and refuses by name every arrangement that would need the field to
resolve. The `GAP` stands.

**A processor that debits the trust account is surfaced, never absorbed.** The fee arrives as a bank
statement line nothing can clear, the three-way proof reports a `bank-to-book` difference of exactly that
amount, and a close freezes the unbalanced answer. That is the existing posture applied to a condition
reconciliation exists to catch.

**The trust rail's hard requirement is a reconciliation requirement, not a compliance one.**
`composeTrustReconciliationMatch` ties one statement line to one ledger entry, so a batch-settling
processor leaves nine of ten deposits outstanding forever and one bank line unmatched, and a firm learns
that its trust reconciliation always disagrees. The gross-deposit rules want the same arrangement, but
the compliance reason is satisfied by arrangements that would destroy the reconciliation — so the
reconciliation reason is the one recorded, because it is the one that gets relaxed by somebody being
helpful.

Also settled: a payments-clearing account so one settlement entry matches one bank line; receipt recorded
before it is applied, because the `invoice_matter_balance` bounds CHECK aborts a whole batch and would
otherwise abort the record of money the firm already holds; no status column on a payment, with state
derived from an append-only event log; a partial refund as a full reversal plus a smaller re-application,
on the trust partial-release precedent; and a chargeback dated when it happened, never backdated into a
period whose reconciliation is already frozen.

**The platform's first inbound webhook** is specified here because there is none to copy: raw-byte
signature verification before parsing, the firm named by an unguessable path segment (the signing secret
is per-firm and the body is attacker-controlled until it verifies), idempotency keyed on the processor's
event id and settled by a UNIQUE at commit, and a scheduled settlement pull because webhooks are lost.
One concrete hazard is recorded rather than left to be rediscovered: `idempotencyMiddleware` reads the
body through `context.req.json()` and consumes the raw stream the signature is computed over, so mounting
the house idiom in front of a webhook route fails looking like a wrong secret.

Two documentation drifts found: the white paper's _Payments_ area still describes in-DOM hosted-fields
tokenization, which ADR-0181 rejected by name as SAQ A-EP; and `packages/trust-jurisdictions/CLAUDE.md`
together with the comment in `src/data/nevada.ts` still say the bank-charge carve-out is not wired and
that the composition guard refuses every posting to a firm-funds node, which stopped being true when
`composeTrustFirmFundsEntry` landed.

No feature code, no schema, no migration, no route. Twelve owner flags in a new `K` series; seven decide
what gets built and the plan does not start until they are answered.
- **The public changelog has a source, a contract, and a gate — the first of the community surfaces,
built alone.** A `changelog.d/` fragment now declares **`audience:`**, `public` or `internal`, and the
key is **required with no default in either direction**: assuming `public` would publish an internal
research note the first time somebody forgot, and assuming `internal` would let the public changelog
quietly stop being written, which is worse because nothing announces it. A `public` fragment carries
its customer-facing sentences in a **`## Public` block** below the developer entry — one file, one
commit, one review, two audiences, and no shared sentences to drift. `vp run changelog-build` folds
both halves in a **single pass**: the developer entry into `CHANGELOG.md` as before, the public entry
into the new **`docs/public-changelog.md`**, which it must, because folding deletes the fragment and
the public block lives nowhere else — a publish step deferred to later would have destroyed the prose
it deferred. Like `CHANGELOG.md` the new document is assembled and never hand-edited on a branch,
but unlike it the document is **curated on `main`**, where a dated section that arrives as one bullet
per fragment may be edited into the thematic roll-up a reader actually wants; what curation never
does is author a change with no fragment behind it. **`pnpm run lint:changelog-fragments`** (in the
gate's governance job, and re-run over the whole set inside the assembler before it folds anything)
refuses a fragment with no audience, a public one with no block, an internal one carrying a block
nothing would read, an unknown category, a non-kebab-case filename, or an emoji — golden rule 2's ban
is enforced here because bulleted highlights with emoji prefixes are the house style of every hosted
changelog product, and a published entry cannot be edited afterwards. New package
**`@magna-carta/product-updates`** holds the artifact schema and a **strict** parser from the
assembled document: it refuses a mistyped category heading, a bullet above the first dated heading,
an unparseable release heading, and a duplicate date, because the failure worth guarding is silent
omission — a shipped change dropping out of the published changelog with nothing raised. Entries are
**dated rather than versioned** since no release has been cut, with a `version` field carried and
null so the day one is cut is an edit to the document rather than a schema change. There is no
committed generated artifact and deliberately no drift gate: consumers build it from the document at
their own build time, so it cannot fall out of step. The five fragments then in `changelog.d/`
migrated to `audience: internal` mechanically. **No board, no votes, no database, no screen** — the
surface holds no firm data at all, which is why it sits outside the firm-scoped data-access rule by
having no business data in play rather than by taking an exception to it. 58 tests.
- **A matter can be re-checked on demand, and the firm's floor is readable.** Reads 3 and 4 of the
conflicts read surface, and both were routes the machinery was already waiting for.

`POST /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/conflicts-rechecks` on `conflicts:run` takes **no scope**, and that
is why it exists beside the general check route rather than being a call to it. "Re-check this
matter" has no scope for a caller to state, and a scope field would invite a screen to compose a
narrower search than the firm requires. It names no subjects either: `runConflictsCheck` reads the
matter's own live parties, so a party added since the last check is searched without anybody listing
them — which is the staleness a re-check exists to answer.

It is recorded as a MANUAL run naming the member who asked, and carries no cause. A cause is a
corpus change the platform noticed; a person asking now is not one. It also neither reads nor
satisfies the automatic re-check ledger — an open cause stays open, because the interval between a
cause and the check that answered it is evidence about the firm's procedure, and a manual run did
not answer it.

`GET /api/v1/firm/conflicts-policy` is `readConflictsPolicy` behind a route, on `conflicts:read` —
every member who can read a check is held to the floor, so a reviewer looking at a check that fell
short of it has to be able to see what it is. The check runner now states the floor instead of
marking it unreadable.

The route declares 409 among its responses because the shared conflicts error mapper can return the
idempotency chokepoint's refusal, and the typechecker caught the omission: a response a route can
produce but does not declare is a contract that lies about what a caller may receive.
- **The registration and invitation-redemption screens.** Joining is now something a visitor can do
from the app rather than only against the API: the **Register** link on the sign-in card opens the
three-way choice — a client at a law firm, someone who works at one, or someone starting a new one —
and the two invited doors both land on invitation redemption, because who belongs to a firm is that
firm's decision and never a stranger's. The founding door asks for the firm's name, then the
founder's own details, and sends one confirmation email; the screen that token is spent on reads it
out of the address bar as well as accepting it typed. The fork itself is settled in the browser: the
registration route answers the same constant for both invited doors, and spending a round trip and a
slice of the anonymous rate-limit budget to be told a constant would put the platform's front door
behind the API's availability.

**Redemption refuses as one.** The code, the last name and the date of birth are matched against a
single stored digest over all three, so the handler cannot know which was wrong — and the screen does
not pretend otherwise. One sentence, one alert, and all three fields carry the invalid mark together,
because the refusal belongs to the combination. The wording is a constant of the app's own rather
than an echo of the server's `detail`, so a change to the wording on the other side of the wire
cannot turn one answer into a per-field one, and a fitness test reads the screen and the page on
every run to keep it that way. What does vary is shown: the remaining attempts and the lockout
countdown render from the budget the server publishes, and stay absent when it publishes none.

**Every step says how far it carries.** A joining register sits beside the sign-in surface's register
of unbuilt capabilities, and the developer console's screen-state page renders both it and each new
screen in every state it can take. Two steps are marked as stopping short rather than shown as
working: the confirmation email carries a bare token and no link, so today the code has to be typed;
and neither the Terms of Service nor the Privacy Policy is published, so the two acknowledgements
gate the submit in the browser and are recorded nowhere. No credential is chosen while registering —
the password is set from the emailed link, which is the same act that proves the mailbox.

Dates on these screens are written out in full — `September 4, 2026, 14:03 PDT (UTC-07:00)`, never a
numeric date — because the one question a send time gets asked is whether the mail on screen is the
one this page just sent, and that should not need decoding.
- **The report screen, as two screens over one registry.** `/reports` lists every report the platform
declares, grouped by family, from `apps/web/src/lib/reports/report-registry.ts`; `/reports/<id>`
draws a report's controls from its declaration (a period on every report, a knowledge instant on a
bitemporal one, a trust account where the report is about one, the report's own options), reads
through the declaration's port when the scope is complete, and renders the answer as titled sections
of tables whose shape is the tabular export document's, so the export menu takes every report with
no per-report code. The scope rides the address. The trust-compliance pack is the first report wired;
the financial, productivity and operational families are declared at stage `soon`, visible and
disabled in the catalogue with what each waits on. A presenter computes nothing, and its test says
so. Adds `GET /api/v1/trust/accounts` (cursor-paged, `trust:read`), the one listing of a firm's
trust accounts, which the trust ledger's `account` gap has been waiting on; the ledger's wiring is
left to its own stream. Design: `docs/specs/2026-09-07-report-screen-design.md`. Sidebar row flipped
to shipped.

**The three questions the screen flagged, decided and built in the same stream.** The account
picker names `trust:read` in the refusal sentence when a member holding only the report key hits
it. The knowledge instant is the end of the chosen day in the zone of the office that holds the
account (the trust listing now carries `timeZone`, resolved through `timeZoneForLocation`), and
changing the account keeps the day and moves the instant. What the pack lists is a firm policy:
`firm:manageReportPolicy` (seeded to Owner/Admin), `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/reports/policy`
(audited), the pack route defaulting from it, Settings › Practice › Reports over the calendar
settings page's server-backed draft pattern, and the two selects gone from the run screen.
- **The calendar's third round: the room grid, bookings on an event, and the resource catalog.** `CalendarView` gains the `resource` scope: `/calendar/rooms` is the one component over `GET /api/v1/calendar/resources/{id}/availability`, a week at a time, with a picker that names the room and mirrors it into the address. A booking paints as the event it belongs to (the availability read carries a type name and never a title), takes the danger register with a "Double-booked" line where the read pre-paired it with another booking, and opens that event's window. Two small reads join the API, `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/bookings` and `GET /api/v1/firm-events/{firmEventId}/bookings`, over the package's existing `readBookingsForEvent`, so an event's window can list what it booked; the entry window gains a Rooms tab, a Book a Room verb (the booking takes the event's own window, lands even when it double-books, and says so) and Release per row. Settings › Practice › Rooms and Resources is the catalog: add, change, retire and restore, each an `ActionDialog` committing at once, gated on the session's `calendar:manage`.
- **`pnpm run lint:hard-rules` — the linter rules this repository can enforce now, in a pass that can fail.** The Oxlint ruleset is almost entirely advisory by design (`suspicious` and `perf` warn, `correctness` keeps its inherited severity), and the consequence nobody chose is that the gate's most expensive job — a whole-repo type-aware pass measured at about forty-five minutes — can fail on exactly one rule, `oxc/no-barrel-file`. Everything else it finds is a warning in a list of roughly eight hundred.

Three rules move out of that list and into a pass that fails:

- **`import/no-cycle`**, held at 36 and falling only. Nothing in the repository looked for a cycle before this: the project-reference check verifies that references exist, not that they form a directed acyclic graph, and a bundler resolves a cycle silently by handing one side a half-initialised module. The thirty-six sit in twenty-nine files, concentrated in the worker's route graph and the web app's calendar and directory screens.
- **`vitest/no-focused-tests`** and **`vitest/no-disabled-tests`**, held at zero, which is free because the tree is already clean. A stray `.only` is green, silent, and takes the rest of its file's coverage with it — and it can ride a whole review here, because the battery is asked for rather than automatic.

Six seconds over about 3,900 files, no type-aware pass, so it sits in the always-on governance tier. It **proves its own invocation**: every rule is run against a fixture written to trip it before its count on the repository is believed, because a wrapper whose plugin flag was renamed reports a clean tree forever.

The `import` and `vitest` plugins deliberately stay out of the shared ruleset. Enabling a plugin switches on everything it carries at its category severity, which adds warnings to the forty-five-minute pass and moves nothing from advisory to enforced.
- **Safe Website Viewer tool page.** The `web-domains` pair is complete on the screen side: a new
page at `/tools/safe-website-viewer` over the existing chokepoint route (`POST /api/v1/safe-browse`),
with the branching in a DOM-free seam (`apps/web/src/lib/tools/safe-browse/safe-browse.ts`) on the
WHOIS page's same-origin-fetch pattern. Everything the page renders is inert: the screenshot is an
`<img>` from base64, extracted text stays escaped text, and the suspect page's outbound links render
as plain text, never anchors. The catalog entry advances `soon` to `alpha`, so the listing tile,
list row, and command palette entry become launchable; palette synonyms ("phishing", "redirect")
widen its search net. A 502 from the remote renderer reads as a transient outage to retry, not a
fault to quote — the render engine is Cloudflare Browser Rendering, an account entitlement still
queued in `docs/deploy-queue.md`, so captures answer that outage state until it is enabled. Three
owner rulings issued against the WHOIS page in review land with it (recorded in
`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`): the query control sits at the reading edge rather than
the masthead's far-right actions slot, intro copy is one flowing paragraph, and orienting text
persists through result states.
- **Analysis: "Save New Version" is the only one of three version-cutting paths that does not know what
it is replacing, and the platform already contains the mechanism that does.**

The owner asked for this two rounds ago — the button felt confusing and worrying, and the request was
to identify the necessity, the improvement, and any replacement. `docs/specs/2026-08-24-save-new-version-analysis.md`
is the answer.

Three paths cut a version. `initiateCheckin`/`commitCheckinVersion` records the **base version** the
working copy was taken from and compares it on return: fast-forward if the base is still current,
otherwise the bytes still commit but as a `conflict_pending` conflicting copy, current is not
advanced, and a human reconciles. An unchanged round trip cuts no version at all.

`commitVersion` — the plain upload path, which "Save New Version" uses — has none of that. It reads
exactly one thing about the file it is replacing: whether the incoming hash equals the current hash,
and skips as a duplicate if so. There is no base and no divergence concept; `diverged` exists only on
the check-in result type.

So two people who both use Save New Version on the same document produce two versions, the second
silently becomes current, and nothing records that they collided. Neither person is told. The same
scenario through check-out / check-in is refused the current slot and flagged for reconciliation.
Same bytes stored either way — the difference is whether the system knows.

The recommendation is to retire the button and split the two jobs hiding inside it: editing outside
the platform becomes Check Out / Check In (both already built, neither surfaced), and a revision
arriving from elsewhere becomes "Add Revision" carrying its provenance. Neither refuses a write. One
question is left for the owner, on whether a checked-out file is read-only for everyone else.
- Discovery search — the keyword engine now reaches real per-firm R2. The `RangeReader` seam
`crates/search-core` was built against has a production implementation, and the worker and container
that hold it exist.

**The engine reads a firm's index without holding a key to it.** `containers/search` is a pure-Rust
service over `search-core`; its `HttpRangeReader` issues one HEAD for a split's size and then exactly
one closed-`Range` GET per read the engine makes, against `splits.magna-carta.internal` — a host that
resolves nowhere. `SearchIndexContainer.outboundByHost` intercepts it and forwards it over a service
binding into the app worker, where a new cookieless split-object host (`/search-objects/*`) verifies a
capability token, resolves the firm's bucket through `files/firm-bucket.ts`, and performs one R2
operation. `enableInternet` stays false and the container holds no credential — the same topology the
Collabora editor uses to reach the WOPI host.

**The token is a capability over one corpus.** HMAC-signed per firm from `AUTH_SECRET`, minted per
operation, read-only for a query and write-capable only for an index or compaction pass, and its allowed
key prefix is derived from its corpus rather than carried — so the request line chooses which split (a
query reads several) but cannot leave the corpus the token names.

**An unranged GET is refused rather than served whole.** `crates/search-eval` measures per-query ranged
reads, and every one is an R2 range GET in a deployment; that number only transfers if the adapter
issues exactly the reads the engine asked for. The host answers 416, the container's test double does
the same, and the container reports the ranged-read count it actually issued on every query response, so
the measured number and the billed number can be compared rather than assumed equal.

A published split is stamped `object_class: search-split` with its corpus as the matter dimension — a new
class in `@magna-carta/object-dimensions`, so a reader of the bucket can tell an index from a document.

`apps/search-worker` (`magna-carta-search`) shards by firm rather than by request, because an instance's
value is the splits it is already holding open. Its warm-poke cron handler is wired and the trigger is
deliberately off until a firm has indexing enabled.

**Still dormant, and unchanged:** `resolveSearchIndexPort` returns the deferred port until
`SEARCH_SERVICE` is bound, so every index job still parks in `deferred` and no query reaches an engine.
Activation is a deploy step — see `docs/deploy-queue.md`. The container keeps no split cache between
calls: a cached searcher would answer from bytes authorized on a previous call, and the residency sizing
is a measurement that needs a resident corpus.
- Search and discovery — a standardized, owner-readable performance benchmark for the read path, as the
new `crates/search-eval` harness beside the engine crate, on the `pdf-eval` pattern. One command
(`cargo run -p search-eval --profile benchmark -- benchmark`), and output written to be interpreted by
someone who did not build it: latency percentiles with the corpus size, index size, hit count, and
number of queries behind every figure, and the target stated beside it.

**It measures the real engine, and says plainly what it could not reach.** Queries run against
`crates/search-core` itself — Tantivy building splits and answering BM25 queries through the ranged-read
access pattern a split in R2 is designed for — so nothing is stubbed. What cannot run on a local machine
is named rather than approximated: the network, the search Worker and its Container, the warm cache,
Vectorize and the whole semantic half, reciprocal rank fusion, and the per-firm catalog read. That list
is printed before any number and is stored inside the baseline file, so a figure cannot be lifted out of
either without its caveats. Timing the deferred `SearchIndexPort` — which returns `engine-not-implemented`
anywhere off a deployment — is refused on purpose: an unlabelled number from a stub reads as the
system's speed and is worse than no number.

**Two axes, each varying one thing.** Corpus size, with the corpus compacted into one split at 250 /
5,000 / 25,000 documents, which is the shape compaction produces. And split fan-out, which is the shape
the pipeline publishes today — a split's object key is derived from one document version, and a query is
handed every live split key the catalog holds, so a matter of N indexed versions is N splits and one
query touches all of them. The axes meet at 5,000 documents so the comparison can be read directly.

**What the first run found.** Compacted, the engine holds up exactly as the split model claims: at
25,000 documents (200,000 passages, a 13.0 MiB index) an ordinary review query ran in 0.072 ms median /
0.163 ms p95, and per-query ranged reads stayed between 37 and 59 across a 97x growth in index size — the
round trips a query costs are set by what it asks for, not by how large the matter grew. Uncompacted, it
does not: the same 5,000 documents as 5,000 per-document splits cost **186,293 ranged reads for one
query** against 45 for the identical documents compacted, about 4,140x the round trips for the same
