answer. Every one of those is an R2 range GET in a deployment, so that shape cannot reach a sub-second
query however fast the engine is. Compaction is not an optimization for this read path; it is what makes
it viable, and there is now a number saying so.

**Two gaps in the engine the harness surfaced rather than papered over.** `search-core` exposes no way to
reuse an opened index across queries, so the warm steady-state latency the sub-second target rests on
cannot be measured through its public surface at all — the per-query index-open cost is broken out
instead. And it has no ranged multi-split query: the multi-split entry point takes in-memory slices only,
so the harness issues one ranged query per split and merges the results itself, which makes the fan-out
figures an explicit lower bound rather than a measurement of the deployed path.

A committed baseline (`crates/search-eval/search-benchmark-baseline.json`) carries its own timestamp,
machine label, build profile, corpus seed, and iteration counts, because none of those transfer between
machines. The benchmark is deliberately out of every gate — `pnpm test`, `pnpm check`, and
`vp run rust-check` never run it; the crate's own unit tests do, and finish in a fraction of a second. A
`benchmark` cargo profile is added because the workspace release profile optimizes for size, which
understates the engine and makes two runs incomparable.
- **Search split compaction — a corpus's live split count now tracks a threshold the platform chooses,
not the number of documents ever indexed into it.** The write pipeline publishes one split per document
version, and the standing read-path benchmark priced that shape: one query over 5,000 documents issued
**186,293 ranged reads** published as one split each, against **45** for the same documents compacted.
A ranged read is an R2 range GET in a deployment, so no engine speed reaches a sub-second query from
there. Compaction stops being a later optimization and becomes the thing that makes the read path
viable.

**The engine** (`crates/search-core`) gains `merge_splits_over_readers` — a segment-level merge, not a
re-index, because the schema indexes `body` without storing it and the documents cannot be read back out
of a split. Deletions are applied inside the merge: the superseded document ids are deleted by term and
the segment is repacked, so their postings leave the published bytes rather than being masked. It also
gains the two things the benchmark named as absences. `SplitSearcher` holds a split open across queries,
so a resident process pays the footer read, the index open, and the per-field setup once for the life of
the split — 2 warm reads against 40 cold, at the smoke tier — which is the state the sub-second target
is actually stated against and could not previously be measured at all. `query_splits_over_readers` is
the ranged multi-split query, so the fan-out shape production has now exists in the engine instead of
being assembled by the harness.

**The pass** is triggered by a live-split threshold the write path notices in one indexed count after
publishing, single-flighted per corpus by a `SearchCompactionJob` Durable Object, and run off a
dedicated queue. It is bounded by split count and by bytes and re-enqueues itself while the corpus is
still over threshold, so a matter holding thousands of splits converges over several bounded merges
rather than attempting one no Container could finish. The daily reconciliation cron is the backstop for
corpora that crossed the threshold through deletion or stopped being written to.

**The correctness is the publication order**, and it runs one way: the merged split is written to R2
first; one atomic batch then inserts its row, inserts its membership, and marks every source superseded;
and the source objects are left in place, retired by a later sweep after a grace period. A query that
resolved its split keys before the swap holds source keys whose objects still exist; one that resolved
after holds the merged key and none of the sources. No interleaving yields both, and none yields neither.
Deleting a source inside the pass that superseded it is the one ordering that could hand a live query a
key to bytes that are gone, which is why retirement is a separate sweep.

**Deletion and re-indexing** are handled by a new per-firm `index_split_member` table plus a per-split
exclusion on the query path. A merged split covers document versions and claims none on its own row, so
the membership is what says which versions are inside it. Re-indexing a document marks its membership
stale in the same atomic batch that publishes the replacement, and the query path carries those ids to
the engine per split — per split, because the same document is legitimately live at a newer version in a
different one. Marking is what makes a superseded version stop matching immediately; the next compaction
passes the same ids to the merge, which is what makes it stop costing anything.

Every threshold is a per-firm setting rather than a constant: compaction trades a query's Class B reads
against the merge's own reads and its write, and only a deployment can price that.

The benchmark reports it: a third axis merges every fan-out point through the engine and re-queries it,
so the saving is a subtraction inside one run over identical documents rather than a comparison across
two differently-built corpora.
- **Tasks — `@magna-carta/tasks`, the `matter_task` record, eleven routes, and two screens.**

`matter_task` holds what to do, whose it is, when it is due, whether it is still owed, the one task
it waits on, and the matter's files it points at; `matter_task_document` links those on the
`matter_note_document` model. Three permission keys (`tasks:read`, `tasks:write`, `tasks:assign`)
seeded to the seats that do firm work, Billing included.

**`matter_id` is nullable**, which is the opposite of the call `firm_event` made against
`matter_event`, and both table comments now say why. The calendar split its tables because a firm
event and a matter event are read on two different surfaces; tasks have one surface either way, so
splitting would mean unioning back together on the read every member makes most often. The
does-not-apply branch the calendar warned about is answered by confinement: `taskVisibilityFragment`
is the whole population of "may this member see this task", and every read composes it.

Nothing derives a date and no overdue column exists — the calendar's date-arithmetic source scan runs
over this package, and a schema scan asserts the absence. Cancellation and deletion are both real,
held apart by two CHECK constraints so each terminal state carries its own evidence.

Notifications raise four topics for two acts, split by whether the task is on a matter — the
`calendar.firmEvent.*` split, forced by the registry's two matter-anchoring fitness rules. The
assignee needed a sixth audience: the design routed assignment to `designated`, which is the firm's
trust-compliance designation and resolves to nobody when unconfigured, so as specified every task
assignment would have delivered to no one, silently. `named-recipient` reads the member from the
payload, so the person told is whoever was named at the write. `tasks` joins the category vocabulary
and `matterTask` the subject kinds — two CHECKs, so two table rebuilds.

Open tasks register a close advisory and never a precondition. The matter's Tasks section and My Work
at `/tasks` are one component reading two routes.
- The address form can now say a postal code reads wrong, and can offer a country's states, provinces or counties.

It could do neither before. The per-country table it renders from is a curated shape — which boxes a country uses, what they are called, what order they read in — and it carried no postal-code patterns and no administrative-area lists. The feature ledger has held that as the open question since the form shipped.

`@magna-carta/address-formats` is the missing half: 252 countries projected from the address-internationalization corpus into 182 postal-code formats and 62 administrative-area lists, 1,619 areas in all. The corpus is checked in and refreshed by a deliberate act rather than fetched at build time, so no build depends on a third party being up and no postal rule changes under a release nobody made. The generator validates as well as renders — every pattern must compile anchored and every published example must match its own pattern — so a bad corpus breaks the build rather than the address form.

The constraints reach the component as optional props, the way the country list already does. That is not ceremony: the design system links exactly one workspace package by design and `AddressFields` is domain-blind, so importing a corpus into it would end that for every consumer to serve two screens.

A malformed code renders as the field's hint and never its error, so the box is never marked invalid and nothing can refuse a commit — a code can match its country's published format perfectly and still reach nobody. "This country publishes no postal format" stays a different answer from "this is wrong"; seventy of the 252 fall in the first case. The region field takes a native datalist rather than a combobox, because it is not a closed choice: a combobox settles back onto a listed value on close, which would destroy an address in a place no published list carries.

Alongside it, `@magna-carta/address-lookup` adds the autocomplete port with no engine behind it yet — `suggest` and `resolve`, typed outcomes that never throw, and a deferred implementation that reports `engine-not-implemented`, the same wired-but-dormant shape the discovery search index takes. A surface written against it degrades to exactly today's behaviour with no branch and no flag to remove later.

No provider is adopted and nothing calls out. No address leaves the firm's tenancy.
- **A firm can now produce, from its own append-only records, the document a bar examiner asks for
about one trust account — and ask for the same period again in five years and get the same integers.**

The first shipped capability in the reporting area, which had eleven ledger nodes and nothing built.

**What the document is.** For one trust account over one period: the cover, every reconciliation whose
statement period ends inside it, each client's ledger with each matter under it, the
receipts-and-disbursements journal, the firm's own bank-charge cushion where it keeps one, the
exceptions, and the provenance. Served as JSON from
`GET /api/v1/reports/trust-compliance/{trustAccountId}` on a new `reports:trustCompliance` capability.

**Why it re-derives.** Every ledger-backed figure filters on **both** date axes the schema already
carries — `effective_date` for the period, `recorded_at` for what the platform knew. Give it a period
and a knowledge instant and the answer is a pure function of rows that can never change; omit the
instant and you get a live report, stamped and explicitly not claimed to reproduce. Five new select
builders in the trust package carry the second axis; the settled as-of statements are untouched,
because the three-way proof's contract does not move for a report. A reconciliation closed **after**
the knowledge instant reads as open and its attestation does not appear — printing it would be
printing knowledge from after the moment the document claims to be taken at.

**The test that is the point.** Produce a pack; post a correction with an effective date inside the
period and a `recorded_at` months later — the exact move that silently rewrites a signed month on any
single-axis report; re-run at the same instant. Every integer is identical. Re-run live and the
figures move, the attestation does not, and the difference is stated leg by leg.

**Nothing recomputes what another package owns.** The three-way proof, the client-ledger total, the
book balance, the outstanding-item list and the ledger's stored-balance check are all called through
the functions that own them. What this package adds is decomposition — a per-client, per-matter
breakdown of a total trust asserts, and a per-entry journal behind a bank balance it asserts — and
each decomposition ships with an agreement test proving it sums to its aggregate over rows written by
the real composers, not by the suite.

**Two blocks are labelled as outside the reproducibility claim, and that is a finding rather than an
omission.** The proof shown beside each attestation, and the outstanding items, unmatched statement
lines and balance checks in the exceptions section, are each read through an owner that takes no
knowledge instant. Bounding them here would have meant writing a second definition of the
reconciliation a firm attested to. They carry their own `computedAt` and an explicit
`boundedByKnowledgeInstant: false`, the document says which part may differ between two runs, and the
reproducibility test strips exactly those two blocks and holds everything else to byte-identical
figures. The first version of that test found the leak: the exceptions section was silently unbounded,
and it took a failing comparison rather than a review to notice.

**Read-only is checkable, at two layers.** `@magna-carta/reporting` composes nothing, holds no
binding, reads no clock and owns no table; a purity scan over its own sources rejects a write
statement, effect-batch machinery, a domain composer import, or an aggregate of its own over the
ledger, and asserts it has sources to check. At the route layer the conformance suite rejects any
mutating route gated on a `reports:` read key. Nothing is materialised.

**What it refuses, by name rather than by answering short.** A period holding more of an account's
activity than one document can carry — the remedy is a shorter period, and a report missing entries
with no way to tell would be worse than none. An account whose outstanding-item list is longer than
one reconciliation can account for — the trust package's own refusal, propagated unchanged. And it
prints no governing-rule citation for a jurisdiction nobody has had reviewed: every encoded
jurisdiction ships unreviewed today, so the cover states which of the four refusals applies, in the
corpus's own words, and produces the rest of the document — the figures are the firm's own records and
no rule elsewhere conditions them. Refusing the whole pack instead is a seam the owner can flip.

**Measured.** Over the load-profile trust volume, at one month and at twelve: the client-ledger read
0.6 to 1.4 ms, the journal 0.6 to 1.7 ms, and the whole document 63 to 106 ms. Nothing scans. The cost
is dominated by the per-reconciliation three-way proof, not by the per-row reads, so the
`ledger_line.effective_date` denormalization the design held in reserve is not warranted yet.

**Five capabilities seeded to Owner/Admin alone** — trust compliance, financial, productivity,
operational, and produce — deliberately narrower than the trust and billing reads a firm grants more
widely, because an aggregate across every matter and client is a different exposure from a per-matter
read, and a report about people is a different grant from a report about money.

**Not built, and named rather than half-built:** turning a pack into a filed, content-hashed firm
record. It needs a renderer that this repository cannot run — the conversion engines are not deployed
— and the two append-only tables that would record a production are deliberately left out of the
migration rather than shipped for nothing to write. The other three report families, delivery, and
every screen are also unbuilt. **Nine owner questions from the design remain open**; three of them
ship as defaults behind named seams and the pack records which it was produced with.
- **The matter's Billing tab carries the bill register and the fee ledger**, both ported from the
owner's own surfaces and both composed on the product's one grid — so sorting, in-header filters,
show and hide, reorder, pin, resize, selection, the totals row and the counts strip are inherited
rather than decided again.

Wired to the billing API that already existed: creating an invoice, claiming unbilled work, editing a
line, voiding a draft, finalizing, credit notes, write-offs, applying a client credit, recording
delivery, and reading invoices, credit notes, deliveries and client credits alongside the matter's
unbilled total and its fee arrangement.

**Money is integer minor units end to end, and the only division by one hundred is at the render
boundary.** Typed amounts are parsed digit by digit rather than through a float, because
`parseFloat("1.15") * 100` is `114.99999999999999` — pinned by a test.

Seven gaps between the design and what can be served are named on the screen rather than papered
over. There is no per-matter invoice listing, so the register is client-wide with This Matter as its
leading money column and the all-matters total beside it — which is the mockup's own distinction, now
load-bearing. Nothing serves a trust-account listing, so applying trust funds ships as the full
designed dialog with the act disabled and its dependency named, and the unreachable client call was
removed rather than shipped. Claiming works and releasing a claim does not. The matter read carries
no client, so the client is resolved from the party wearing that role, and a matter without one
refuses to draft a bill and says why.
- **The build register now says where we have been, reconstructed from version control rather than
remembered.** `docs/now.md` gains a _Where we have been_ section: the count at each of the nine
ledger statuses at every past commit that touched a `roadmap.d/` node file, what moved between one
commit and the next, and the movement per area since the series began.

**One parser, so the trend cannot disagree with the totals above it.** For each first-parent commit,
the ledger as it stood at that commit is read out of git and parsed by the same `parseArea` the live
render uses. The counts are persisted one record per commit — keyed by full commit hash — in
`docs/register-history.json`, so the expensive pass runs once: an ordinary `vp run register-build`
reads only the commits that file does not already hold, normally one.
`vp run register-build --rebuild-history` (or
`node tooling/doc-fragments/build-register-history.mjs --rebuild`) recomputes the whole series, which
is what to run after changing the ledger parser or the status vocabulary.

**A commit that does not parse is a hole, and stays one.** Nineteen of the forty commits in the
series are written in a ledger vocabulary today's parser rejects — one node carrying a `built` status
between 2026-08-04 and 2026-08-11 — and each is recorded with the parser's own reason and listed in
the document. Nothing is interpolated across them: the +27 shipped that spans that week is printed
beside the count of commits nobody read, rather than apportioned to the two rows on either side of
the gap.

**Rates, and no projected date.** The section states the change in shipped nodes since the ledger
began, the rate across the whole series, and the rate over the most recent stretch with no hole in
it. It projects no completion date, because the ledger puts no size on a node and a date derived
from node counts would treat a jurisdiction research corpus and a second authentication factor as
equal work.

Where the register used to say that no trend line could be drawn from the ledger without inventing
one, it now points at the section and names the two limits that survive: a snapshot shows when a
node's **status** changed and never when the work happened, and a capability added to the ledger
late arrives as a jump in the total rather than as work done. `pnpm run lint:roadmap` re-derives the
document from both committed inputs — the ledger and the reconstruction — so neither can drift.
- **The calendar's sixth round: many calendars in folders, a day of columns, and a form that asks where.** The owner walked the deployed calendar and issued eleven corrections; this is all of them, and the rulings are in [`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`](docs/conventions/design-corrections.md).

The firm calendar stops being one undifferentiated grid. A CATALOG of individual calendars (`apps/web/src/lib/calendar/calendar-sources.ts`) stands over what the calendar context already read: the firm's own two (matters and deadlines, firm events), a folder per role the firm handed out holding the members who hold it, the rooms, everything else that is booked, and the dates. Each row turns on and off on its own; each folder's own control carries the third state and completes a part-filled folder. The folders are the firm's own vocabulary — nothing here decides who counts as support staff — and a member holding two roles is filed under the first, because a calendar listed twice reads as two calendars and toggles as one. File-destruction dates are listed, marked Soon and refused, because a retention schedule is the one date calendar nothing serves yet.

**A calendar that is on is a read; a calendar that is off is no read at all.** The read plan is a plan per calendar (`readOneCalendar`) rather than one read narrowed afterwards: a member calendar is the member filter the server already resolves in SQL, a room calendar is the availability read, a date calendar is the federated read narrowed to that layer's own sources. The reads are made together, fail independently, and a failure now names WHOSE calendar it was. The same record arriving from two of them is merged into one row that knows it is on both.

**`CalendarGrid.Day`** is the fourth presentation and the only one with a time axis: an hour per row, a CALENDAR per column, which is what makes a Tuesday six attorneys spend in four places legible. A record on two calendars is drawn in both their columns on purpose. An entry with no hour sits in a band above the hours, where a filing belongs. The hours are the working day, widened without asking by anything outside it.

The firm-wide federated read carries **the hour**. `TimelineEntry` gains `timeOfDay` and `timeZone`, declared per source (`timeOfDayExpression` on the two select builders) and set on matter events, deadlines and firm events. It is the same class of fact as the sort key — when a thing happens, said in the record's own terms, never converted — and it is what lets a day grid put a hearing on the ten o'clock row without the projection ever naming it. Before this the firm calendar painted no times at all.

**One palette, one home.** The eleven colours the file manager's folders offer moved to `packages/design-system/src/lib/palette/`, with their fills as `--mc-palette-*` on `:root`; `FOLDER_COLORS` re-exports them unchanged and the folder recipe aliases the shared properties. A calendar offers the nine that read on a chip, and wears its colour as a rule down the chip's leading edge — the status register keeps the fill, so a cancelled setting on the blue calendar is still visibly cancelled. `PaletteSwatches` is the one control both surfaces pick from. An unchosen calendar is dealt a colour by position.

**Double-clicking an empty day or hour** starts a record on it, with the day and the hour as the form's opening answers. It is an accelerator, never the only path, and it never fires from a press on a chip.

The record forms change with the same round. **Where is Location**, and it is the product's dropdown-with-add over the firm's own offices and rooms, still keeping a courthouse nobody has a record of. **A conference link** is its own field and its own column — a nullable `conference_url` on `matter_event` and `firm_event` — because a deposition can be in a conference room and on a call at once. **The times are time fields** with the zone beside them as a shortcode, worked out on the record's own day (`formatTimeZoneAbbreviation`, in the design system's display vocabulary); a record has one zone, so the ends line states the same code rather than offering a second control. **The day being booked stands in the panel's context pane**, as the product's own calendar with a day view and no toolbar. And **the matter is no longer required**: no matter is a choice whose row says what it writes, and the form writes a firm event instead — which is the shape the data already had.

Two lines come off. "A matter is needed." is gone with the requirement. "Nothing recorded in September 2026." is gone from every grid: a month that is empty says so by being empty. The agenda keeps its sentence, because an empty list is a blank rectangle.
- **The calendar's fourth round: the event-type catalog and related links.** Settings › Practice › Event Types is the catalog on the Rooms and Resources pattern: a platform type is recategorized or retired (its name and code are the shared vocabulary), a firm type is added, renamed or retired; retiring asks first and is one way, as the contract is. Two reads join the API, `GET /api/v1/events/{eventId}/links` and `/firm-events/{firmEventId}/links`, over the package's existing `readLinksTouchingEvent`, recorded as bounded by construction; the entry window's Links tab lists the settings related by hand with the other end's title (read on that end's own path, under its own visibility), and gains Relate (a setting on the same matter, or a firm event within six months, with a note) and Remove. The plan's Timeline view on the Calendar section was not built: the matter's Activity section, which landed meanwhile, is that read's one screen.
- **The calendar's second round: layers, a colleague, a settled filter, and two cards.** The firm calendar can be widened to the timeline's date-bearing sources through a LAYER (`CALENDAR_LAYERS` in `apps/web/src/lib/calendar/calendar-vocabulary.ts`): custody dates first, the due-backs and review dates the safe custody register already federates, each painting its custody number and opening the register. Only sources whose rows fall due qualify; the timeline's history sources stay in the timeline rather than flooding a month. A colleague picker seats after Mine and Everyone and reads one colleague's calendar through the same member filter, under the reader's own visibility. The agenda gains "Hide settled", which leaves out cancelled settings and satisfied, vacated or superseded deadlines and says how many it left out; the month and the week always paint them struck (owner flag C5). Every refinement is mirrored into the address.

The firm-wide read now says a setting was called off: the `matterEvent` source emits `cancelledEvent` as its own kind (a closed word, never the reason a person typed), so the firm grid strikes a vacated hearing exactly as the matter section does, and the settled filter can leave it out. Before this the federated row carried no status and a cancelled hearing painted on the firm calendar as if it were still on.

`CalendarView` takes `agendaDays` and `limit`, and two hosts embed it: Home's Today card (the reader's own scope, today and tomorrow, six rows, a line to the rest) and the matter overview's Coming up card (the matter's next thirty days, six rows, a line to the Calendar section). Neither writes a read of its own.
- **The calendar is reachable, and it is one component.** Slices 6·1 and 6·2 had been the largest built-but-unreachable surface in the program: thirty-three routes, a federated read, firm events, resources, links and continuance, and one matter tab that read two tables. `docs/specs/2026-09-02-calendar-interface-design.md` plans the interface and this lands its first slice.

Two homes, on the EventRail division. `@magna-carta/design-system/calendar-grid` is the domain-free presentation: `CalendarGrid.Month`, `.Week` and `.Agenda` take entries with a civil day, a label, a detail line, a caller-formatted time, a subtle-register tone and a strike, and never learn what a hearing is. `apps/web/src/lib/calendar/` holds `CalendarView`, the one calendar every surface embeds with a scope (`firm`, `mine`, `matter`); it owns the window arithmetic on `CalendarDate` (a month is the full weeks it spans, never more than six, inside the read's cap), the read plan per scope, the projection through one vocabulary, the view state mirrored into the address, and the entry window. Both are registered in `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`, so a second month grid or a second calendar composition fails the gate.

The firm grid paints kinds and matter numbers, never titles: the federated read declares non-privileged labels by design, and the title is fetched for the one row somebody opened. Deadlines paint from their own access-gated read with titles and the read-time overdue flag; the federated read is narrowed to the event kind so nothing is painted twice; firm events paint from the firm's own listing. The three reads fail independently and the notice names which one did; each walk has a page ceiling and says when it hit it.

`/calendar` is the firm screen (Mine / Everyone, month / week / agenda, a Record menu); `/calendar/firm-events?entry=` is the deep link the federated read already emitted. The matter's Calendar section keeps its two tables as the List view and gains Month and Agenda over the same component, and its two record controls go live: the earlier deferral to a participant picker is answered by building the picker (a firm member, a directory entity, or somebody who is neither). The entry window is a `RecordWindow` with in-place editing and the verbs the record allows; every form is an `ActionDialog` over a pure draft model, asserted without a browser. The sidebar's Calendar row flips to shipped.
- **Two guards on the migration lineage, both closing gaps the audit found rather than suspected.**

`tooling/migration-integrity/` now diffs each lineage against the schema it claims to build: it applies the whole chain to node:sqlite and compares the result with `src/declared-tables.ts`, naming the table or column that disagrees. The package's own notes already prescribed exactly this comparison as something to do BY HAND when a divergence was suspected, which means it ran after the damage rather than before it.

The gap was wide open rather than theoretical. Hand-written migrations are the normal case here, so most of the lineage is authored beside the schema rather than derived from it — and the check that looks like it would catch a divergence does not, because `refresh-snapshot` re-derives the snapshot FROM the TypeScript, leaving snapshot and schema agreeing with each other and disagreeing with every database. Measured on the way in: 201 declared tables against 206 live, the five extras being the FTS5 virtual table and its shadow tables, and zero column drift. The discipline was holding; nothing was enforcing it. The FTS5 extras are enumerated by exact name in `UNDECLARED_BY_DESIGN`, not matched by prefix, so the next undeclared table is a finding rather than something the rule swallows.

`runPendingMigrations` now reports **out-of-order arrivals** — a pending migration whose tag sorts before a tag the database has already applied. Apply order is tag order, but the chain grows from parallel branches, and two merging can seat a migration behind one that already shipped: a database that woke in between applies the pair in the order it met them, while one provisioned afterwards applies them in tag order. Independent migrations reach the same schema either way; ones that touch the same objects do not, and that divergence is otherwise silent, because the ledger is a set of tags with nothing recording which arrived late.

It reports rather than refuses: the migration is genuinely pending and genuinely needed, and stranding a database over a usually-harmless condition would be worse. The report carries `outOfOrderTags` and `ledgerHead`, measured before the batch lands; a firm database holds it for its diagnostic read and the control-plane pass emits one `migration.arrivedOutOfOrder` event per tag.

The two migrations that prompted this were checked: they are independent, and both orders produce byte-identical schemas.
- **A firm can read the checks it has run.** `GET /api/v1/conflicts/checks` pages them newest first
over the uniform `{ data, nextCursor }` envelope, optionally narrowed to one matter. Each line names
what set the run going, who asked where anybody did, the strictness and depth it ran at, whether the
firm's floor raised the scope above what was requested, and how many candidates surfaced — never a
conclusion about them, which is a reviewer's act recorded as a disposition.

**The load-profile plan probe was right, and it was right in advance.** The design said the
unfiltered listing would plan a full table scan because `conflicts_check`'s only index leads with
`subject_matter_id` — which serves one matter's own history and cannot serve a listing across every
matter. The probe measured exactly that on the first run. `conflicts_check_created_id_index` on
`(created_at, id)` landed in the same change rather than as a note to revisit, and both shapes of the
read are now probed separately because they plan differently.

That index is not a micro-optimization. The conflicts log is append-only by design, with
`RAISE(ABORT)` triggers refusing UPDATE and DELETE, so a scan there is not a fixed cost — it rises
every week a firm operates.

The row is deliberately narrow: the whole check, its recorded scope, its statement and its hits are
one identifier away, and a listing carrying all of it would read every check's `inputs_json` for a
surface that shows none of it. The hit count comes from a correlated subquery served by the
`(check_id)` index rather than a `GROUP BY` join, which would have to de-duplicate the check row per
hit before the limit could apply.
- **The client is a party from the moment a matter exists.** `CreateMatterRequest` gains
`clientEntityId`; `packages/matters` `createMatter` writes the `client` `matter_party` row in the
same batch as the matter (`clientPartyStatements`), so billing, trust, document assembly and the
conflicts engine, which all derive the client from that link, find one from the first read.
`MatterDetail` and `MatterSummary` carry `clientEntityId` (one batched read per page, never per
row). The intake's client field is the design-system `EntityPicker` over the directory; the draft
refuses to create a matter of either status without a chosen client; `client-picker.svelte` and
`knownClientNames` are gone. "Open Client Record" is a real link, and "Run Conflict Check" runs a
preliminary check against the chosen client before the matter exists, reporting the hit count with
a link to the report. The overview's Client fact opens the directory record. The never-called
`client-migration.ts` backfill is deleted with the owner's ruling that there is nothing to back
fill; `client_display_name` keeps being written as the docket's caption, and the contract step that
drops it is not this change.
- Four new rules in `lint:one-ui`, so the consolidations cannot drift back one surface at a time.

A consolidation that is only a cleanup is a cleanup that gets undone: the next screen copies the nearest example, and the nearest example is whatever was written last. Each of these rules names one thing the platform has agreed to have once, and each was proved against a deliberately reintroduced violation before it landed.

- **`caps-register`** — the letterspaced small-caps voice built out of utilities, or finished by hand with an inline `letter-spacing`. The remedy is `FieldLabel`, or the `caps` option on the component being dressed.
- **`money-presentation`** — `style: "currency"` outside the two files allowed to print an amount. Date presentation is deliberately NOT gated and the runner says so: `Intl.DateTimeFormat` has twenty legitimate callers here doing time-zone arithmetic rather than display, and a rule that cried wolf over those is a rule somebody switches off.
- **`permission-refusal`** — the refusal sentence written out rather than taken from `permissionRefusal`. Both wordings are matched, and neither loosely: a dev-console note about somebody who "does not hold the address" is not a refusal, and the rule has a test saying so.
- **`details-panel`** — the panel's frame or scrolling body written out instead of composed from the shell.

Turning them on found four sites the hand migration had missed — an inline letter-spacing that had survived inside a converted component, two refusals written in full, and the false positive above, which is why the rule is now narrower than it started.

The last residuals went with them. The three `Card.Title`s in the invoice window that were field labels wearing a card title's name are `FieldLabel`s; the workbench's absence heading and the version chip's fleet label, both of which took their colour from `class:` directives and so slipped the first pass, are too. The app now writes the caps voice by hand nowhere and reaches for an inline `letter-spacing` nowhere.

One allowance is recorded rather than fixed: a Combobox group heading is a label, and the shared sentence is a sentence — ninety characters in a slot whose other branch reads "Add to the Firm's Practice Areas". It keeps the first clause of the shared wording verbatim so the two cannot disagree about the same permission.

`clockText` is gone. It was the last real second answer to "how long": a hand-derived `H:MM` beside the sheet, with a seconds mode the shared formatter lacked and no sign handling the shared one has. `formatClock(seconds, { toTheSecond })` is now the one clock, `formatDuration` reports it rather than deriving its own, and the equivalence was checked across 4001 quarter-minute probes before the old one was deleted. Its test moved to the formatter and gained the cases the sheet's copy never made.
- **The matter's Costs tab is the ledger that was designed for it**, ported from the owner's own
surface rather than approximated from a description of it. What stood there was a read-only
six-column table; what was designed is a working ledger, and the difference was never a smaller
version of the same thing.

Eleven columns with the grid's own sorting, filtering, hiding, reordering, pinning, resizing,
selection and totals. A four-figure footer — advanced, recoverable, billed, absorbed. A details panel
with three faces: the matter's own summary with its largest payees, a single cost with its standing,
its chain and its memo, and a multi-selection that counts what can be submitted or approved and
excludes voids from the amount it names. Recording and editing a cost, with the sentence that says
what the class and billing choice will mean. The review queue walker, kick-back, void, the print
sheet, and a problem report that reaches the real incidents endpoint.

It is wired to the costs API that already existed rather than to fixtures: listing, create, patch,
submit, approve, kick back and void, with the directory search behind the payee picker and the
expense-code catalogue behind the code labels.

**Where the screen cannot show something, it says which fact is missing rather than rendering an
empty cell.** The listing projection drops five columns the table already knows how to draw —
`receipt_file_id`, `kick_back_reason`, `invoice_id`, `created_at`, `created_by` — so entry number,
date entered, entered by, receipt, the kicked-back reason, and the invoice a billed cost rides are
each marked as not served. That is one projection change with no migration behind it, and it is the
single largest gap between this screen and the design it came from.
- The Firm Usage By Location table's Custodian Items column now reports: a bounded recursive walk in
`@magna-carta/custodian` (`selectCustodyItemCountsByFirmLocationStatement`, covered by the
schema-name-sync fitness test) rolls held items up to the office their container-tree root binds
to, with external roots collected on a Held Offsite row and checked-out items counted nowhere. The
export seam gains `$lib/export/export-menu.svelte`, the one Download menu every exporting surface
uses (a format is one added entry), and the pending export decision now carries the .xlsx library
evaluation: exceljs rejected on unfixed advisories and inactivity, write-excel-file recommended.
Also fixed on this branch: the test pool deadlocked on the new lazy entrypoint's request-time
dynamic import, hanging every SELF.fetch test — the worker test setup now warms the module cache.
- **The Custodian register gained its entry paths, and lost three tabs.** The whole `custody.*` write surface already existed and no screen reached any of it, so the register could be read and never begun: `apps/web/src/lib/custodian/custody-api.ts` had no POST at all and the primary action was a `SoonAffordance`.

Three modals over the existing endpoints, with `packet-draft.ts` holding the readiness and request assembly for all three so what is sent, and what stops a submit, is pure and tested rather than living in a component nobody can exercise without driving a dialog. An untouched optional field is absent from the body rather than sent empty, which is the difference between "nobody was asked" and "the firm was told the depositor is nobody" on an append-only record.

The screen is now one table: the By Owner, Holds and Due tab strip and its four panels are deleted, the status select above the rows is gone (Status is a column with its own filter, per the matters docket ruling), and the local search box is gone ahead of the centralized search component, with the server's `search` filter left plumbed for it. `packet-register.svelte` lends its grid back to the surface so the show/hide-columns and clear-filters controls sit in the screen's one action row.

Two shared-surface changes ride along. The data-table recipe's placeholder cell now sets `white-space: normal`: it inherited the grid's `nowrap`, so a wordy empty state was one unbreakable line that widened the table past its own frame and dragged the empty state off the inline end, on any surface, not only this one. And custody `out` renders as "On loan" rather than "Out": the two states in which property is off the shelf are `out` and `released`, they are opposites, and neither "Out" nor a first pass at "Checked out" separated them — both only say it left the building. "On loan" carries the return, and is the ledger's own noun for it (the row records a `borrower` and a `due_back_on`). `released`'s hover now states that custody has ended. The movement label is untouched: the act is still "Checked out" in a packet's history.
- **The directory record's remaining gaps close.** `EDGE_TYPES` gains the membership family
(`officer_of`, `director_of`, `partner_of`, `trustee_of`, `personal_representative_of`, `agent_of`,
`employment`, `member_of`, `shareholder_of`, `beneficiary_of`, `guardian_of`,
`point_of_contact_for`); `affiliation` stays for the rows already recorded and is no longer offered.
Every new type is classed in `packages/conflicts/src/edge-classes.ts` — the constituent types under
`control` for now, the over-inclusive direction, because the tighter fifth class waits for the
conflicts pass. `createDirectoryEdge` and `createDirectoryCategory` join the web client. The
relationships pane is one `edges-pane.svelte` registered three times: Relationships on both kinds,
People on an organization, Organizations on a person, each recording an edge through `EntityPicker`
with the type narrowed by the record's kind and the direction decided by the type
(`edge-draft.ts`, tested). `new-entity-dialog.svelte` and `merge-dialog.svelte` move onto
`ActionDialog` and their allowances go; the categories pane creates a category through the add row.
- **The matters list now names the responsible attorney**, and every screen that has to put a name to a colleague can.

`GET /api/v1/members` answers the firm's roster — display name, whether the member is still here, the roles they hold, and whether a professional profile has been written. No email address, no direct dial, no permission set: it answers who is on the firm, not how to reach them or what they may do. It rides its own capability, `firm:readMembers`, seeded to every default role including Read-only — adding a person to the firm is Owner/Admin's, and knowing who is already in it is not the same act. The read is un-paged, because a roster is bounded by the firm's headcount rather than by its activity, and a listing joining names against it has to have the whole lookup before any row renders honestly.

The docket's new **Responsible Attorney** column resolves that identifier the way Practice Area and Location already do — one roster read per screen, never a request per row. A matter whose responsible member the roster cannot name reads empty rather than printing a `user_…` handle, and a colleague who has left is still named on the matters they carried. The column had been left off the list entirely, with a note on the page saying why; the note is gone.

Two repairs travelled with it, both of the same kind — an account nobody can sign into:

- **Signing in worked only from the production origin.** Declaring the deployment's public URL had, as a side effect, made it the only origin the sign-in endpoint would accept a request from — so `wrangler dev` on localhost, a preview deployment, and every test that signs in were refused with "Invalid origin". The origin a request actually arrived at is trusted again, alongside the configured one; a genuine cross-site request still carries somebody else's origin and is still refused.
- **The development seed left a passwordless account.** Re-seeding against warm local state found the existing user and skipped its credential, then printed a password that did not work. The seed now converges every field it promises — firm attachment, verification, and the credential — so a re-seed repairs an unsignable account instead of reporting success for one.
- The download tray: a Download control in the top-bar actions cluster, seated beside the Time Keeper
on the owner's direction, whose panel gives the overview of what the platform has made for this
member and links to the full register at the bottom. The register shipped as a sidebar destination
only, which was the wrong reach for it — a download is something you look up for, not something you
go looking through the rail for.

It is deliberately NOT a transfer manager and must not become one: bytes move over a presigned URL
that the browser's own download manager drives
([`network-resilience.md`](docs/conventions/network-resilience.md) rules 1 and 2), so there is no
progress for this component to show and no transfer for it to own.

Its dot is real state rather than decoration — the shelf holds something that arrived since this
browser last opened the tray, kept per browser in `localStorage` and read defensively so a private
window degrades to "nothing is new" rather than throwing. One 16px corner holds one mark, so while
something is new the arrival dot takes the slot from the maturity dot; the stage stays stated on the
sidebar row. A shared revision signal (`download-shelf-signal.svelte.ts`) is what makes a download
appear in the tray at once instead of at the next page load — the export menu and the tray never
meet, since one is rendered by whichever screen is exporting and the other is seated once in the
shell. The Downloads destination moves to `alpha`.
- **The editor's About dialog names the platform's build.** `apps/edit-worker/src/editor-about.ts` appends a block to `#about-dialog-info-container` as the page streams through, after the editor's own version rows: the edit worker's baked-in build identity (`@magna-carta/build-identity`), which is the deploy's commit since every Worker in one deploy reports the same one; a development build says so. The stylesheet the worker already serves gives the block its spacing.
- The export menu gains the two document formats, rendered server-side through the platform's one
printer: `POST /api/v1/reports/exports` takes the tabular document the client already holds (wire
shape and bounds in the new `@magna-carta/export-document` package), composes a plain
word-processing package through document assembly's guarded writer (`compose/tabular.ts`, this
package's first table emitter — byte-reproducible, header rows repeating across pages, figure
columns right-aligned), and for PDF carries those bytes across the registry's one docx-to-pdf edge,
answering an honest 503 when the office-suite engine is unreachable rather than an Error ID. The
route rides the chokepoint under the new `reports:export` permission (seeded to Owner/Admin), and a
failed render surfaces as a toast carrying the server's own words — the design-system Toaster is
now mounted at the app root for it. Spec:
`docs/specs/2026-08-31-tabular-export-rendering-design.md`.
- `pnpm run lint:ledger-staleness` checks the `roadmap.d/` feature ledger against **the repository**.
Its twin, `pnpm run lint:roadmap`, holds `docs/now.md` to a fresh render of the ledger, and that pair
already made it impossible for a derived document to drift off its source. Neither could tell whether
the **source** was true. Two nodes proved it one day apart: `discovery.search` and
`discovery.search.keyword` read `designed` — "accepted design spec exists; no code" — after four
thousand lines of search engine had shipped, and the auto-file node's notes described a state that had
ended two slices earlier. A person found both, because nothing was watching.

**Six rules, all exact, none of them reading English.** A node whose status asserts there is no code
may not point at code that no shipped node accounts for; a line saying a named path is absent fails
the day the path appears; a parent may not claim less than its own children; every path named must
resolve; every `adrs` entry must be an `ADR-NNNN` with a file behind it; and `not-started` may not
carry a spec.

**Quiet on purpose, and measured rather than argued.** The ledger holds 702 nodes, so a rule firing on
two percent of them prints fourteen lines nobody reads twice. Every candidate was run against the whole
ledger before being kept, and three plausible ones were run and thrown away: keying off a node's slice
tag is 13 hits and 13 of them false, because a slice tag is shared by nodes at different maturities;
flagging build claims inside a pre-code node is 22 hits and 22 of them false, because "the engine it
reuses is shipped" is how a node correctly explains what it is waiting on; and coupling the diff to the
ledger needs a diff base and is satisfied by touching a node rather than by making it true. The kept
rules produce **zero** false positives on the ledger and on a checkout from before the search fix.

**It found four stale nodes nobody had noticed, all now corrected.** The jurisdiction-compliance engine
read `designed` with evidence saying `packages/trust-jurisdictions` did not exist yet, while the package
holds the typed profile model, the registry, overlay resolution, the review gate, Nevada encoded and
three test files — now `partial`. LEDES e-billing read `not-started` over a child that shipped early —
now `partial`. And four notification nodes cited two decisions by their pending fragment slug, long
after both were accepted as `ADR-0251` and `ADR-0258`.

The scan **self-tests before it scans**, on fixtures that include both original stale nodes. One of
those fixtures asserts that the scan finds nothing wrong with the auto-file node: its claim names no
path and no identifier, so catching it would need an English noun phrase resolved against the tree, and
that is the guessing this gate refuses. A node the tree genuinely cannot match carries
`ledger-staleness:allow — <reason>` in its `notes`, on the same marker-plus-reason terms as the
object-dimension scan.
- The matter's Files screen is now the file manager the mockup has been reviewed into, built against the firm's own records: a folder tree on the left, the files in the folder being shown in the middle, and the selected file's details on the right — three panes a person can resize by dragging either inner edge.

The list carries the columns a person chooses (File Type, Safety, Version, Size, Created, Date Modified), sorts by any of them, and holds a selection of more than one file. Right-click reaches Open, Download, Rename and Delete, and none of them is inert: Rename does not offer the extension for editing, Delete says plainly that the file moves out of the list and stays recoverable, and Download points the browser at each file's own short-lived signed URL.

A file that failed a scan is shown where its owner put it, marked, and stays selectable and downloadable. Nothing here blocks a file.

Two shapes came with it and are covered by their own tests: the folder tree survives a folder whose parent is missing (it becomes a root rather than vanishing with its files) and a cycle in the data (it terminates rather than recursing until the stack gives out); and the sort puts an unknown size below every known size rather than among the empty files, with Safety worst-first.
- **Three of the four shipping surfaces.** `/shipping` is the register (the product's grid over declared columns in `shipment-columns.ts`, so the reader chooses between the "where is my letter" columns and the "what have we spent" ones); `/shipping/new` is the stepped buy flow; `/settings/shipping` is the postage account, and the first occupant of the `integrations` settings group, which had been declared and empty since the group list was written. The tool's maturity stage moves from `soon` to `alpha`, which is what turns its dead rail row into a link. The shipment window that opens over the register — and the `/shipping/[id]` address that redirects into it — is the remaining surface.

Two seams were corrected mid-build rather than worked around. Writes carry their Idempotency-Key from a `WriteIntent`, because the generated mutation options have no notion of one and a second click is otherwise a second label. And `shipping-api.ts` calls the generated client's own functions rather than spelling `/api/v1/...` paths: `lint:screen-data` holds that count down and it only falls, so a new hand-written transport module would have been the wrong direction even though it compiled. Amounts print through `@magna-carta/money`; nothing divides minor units by a hundred, and a currency the package does not yet register is stated plainly rather than thrown over.
- **The Firm Usage screen ships at apps/web/src/routes/(app)/tools/firm-usage/** — the tables-only
quantitative snapshot over the extended `GET /api/v1/firm-usage`, computed on request, per
docs/decisions/pending/firm-usage-is-quantitative-tables-computed-on-request.md. Custodian holdings
render as a reserved column and per-firm compute as a Soon table, so both seams are visible on the
screen before their data exists.
- **A firm can set its own conflicts floor — the write path, and the screen over it.** The floor has
been a real setting since the matching engine shipped: `resolveScope` raises every narrower request
up to it, `readConflictsPolicy` serves it, and every check row records the value that was in force.
What it never had was a way to change it. `GET /api/v1/firm/conflicts-policy` served a value no route
could set, so a firm changed what its checks searched by writing the `conflicts.policy` row directly.

`PUT /api/v1/firm/conflicts-policy` closes it, on **`conflicts:configure`** — a new permission rather
than a reuse of `conflicts:run`, seeded to Owner and Admin alone. The three existing conflicts keys
all act on a check; this one does not. It decides what every LATER check searches, and no check row
records that a person chose it, which is why it is audited (`conflicts.policy.changed`, subject
`conflicts.policy`) and why the audit row is the only place the decision carries a name.

**What is stored is what runs.** The read has always repaired an unsound stored policy on its way out
— `party` unioned back into the floor, `current` back into the name roles, the candidate cap clamped
to what one atomic batch can carry. That is right for a value the platform did not write, and it
becomes a trap the moment a screen can write one: an administrator who deselected every source would
store `[]`, be shown `[]` on reload, and be reading a floor the platform would never run. So
`normalizeConflictsPolicy` was extracted from the read, the write normalizes through the same
function, and the **normalized value is what goes in the row**. `packages/conflicts/test/policy-write.test.ts`
asserts against the raw setting row rather than the read's answer, because a repairing read would
make a broken write look correct.

PUT rather than PATCH, for a reason that is about the domain rather than about REST: the floor is one
value, and a partial update would let two administrators saving different halves of one screen compose
a floor neither of them chose.

**Settings · Conflicts** is the surface. Draft mode throughout — instant apply would make a half-typed
cap ("5" on the way to "500") the firm's bound for as long as it took to finish the number. It renders
the response rather than its own request, and names each specific repair the platform made on the way
in instead of leaving an administrator to notice a control that moved on its own. Party and Current
render as locked controls carrying their reason rather than being hidden: a firm-wide invariant a
reader cannot see reads as an option somebody forgot to offer. `conflicts.matching-engine.strictness`
leaves `awaiting-screen`, and the depth node's traversal half does too.
- **File Safety & Scanning is live**, over `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/firm/scan-policy` — four settings where the page had two invented seam rows: the scan tier, the suspicious-score floor, the flagged treatment, and the step-up preference. The engine behind them was already there and unchanged; the ingest consumer reads the policy at queue-consume time and the download route at access time, so a save reaches both with no re-ingest, and the route audits it.

`apps/web/src/lib/settings/server-backed-draft.svelte.ts` is new and is why the page needed no machinery of its own. The calendar's week start was the first server-backed setting and carried a draft hardcoded to its one definition; the scan policy is four settings, two of which share one nested object on the wire. So the staging, counting, confirming and saving moved into one generic draft over a declared field list, and `calendar-settings-draft.svelte.ts` now maps fields through it instead of reimplementing it — two callers, one implementation.

The field mapping FOLDS rather than merging: `applyTo(patch, value, settings)` lets each staged field see what the ones before it already wrote, which is what makes the tier and the score floor arrive as one `policy` object carrying both instead of two patches overwriting each other. Either one alone still sends the other's current value, because the server takes the pair or neither.

`SettingsDraft` gains `saveRefusal`, and the shared commit footer disables Save and states it. The score floor is the first setting somebody can type an impossible value into; refusing at stage time would make the field untypable, and sending it would return a 422 the person never sees, so the draft says why the button is dead.
- **The day the week begins on is a firm setting.** The owner's ruling on the calendar's first slice: the week is the unit a firm plans in, so which day it begins on is the firm's decision, never a personal preference. `packages/calendar/src/settings.ts` holds it over the per-firm setting table (`calendar.weekStartsOn`, Sunday by default); `GET /api/v1/calendar/settings` reads it for every member who can read the calendar and `PATCH` moves it under `calendar:manage`, audited and idempotent, with the contract and the client regenerated. `CalendarView` reads it once with the rest of its context and hands it to every grid, so no surface picks a week start of its own.

Settings › Practice › Calendar is the page, and it is the first settings page with a server behind it: a draft that keeps the shape the shared rows and footer already understand but answers from the firm's own read and saves through the route, never through local storage. It shows no per-browser history, because a ledger in one browser would misstate a firm-wide fact; the record is the audit row. The standing rule is in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`.
- **`pnpm run lint:lints` — the gate over the gates.** Thirty-eight governance lints, and until now nothing asked whether any of them could still fail. The argument is `lint-control-characters.mjs`'s own, one level up: a check that never fires is indistinguishable from a clean tree, and that hazard applies hardest to the checks nothing checks.

Four rules, all deriving their subject from the `lint:*` scripts in the root `package.json` rather than a roster:

- **Every lint can fail** — it has a fixture test beside it, or a self-test that runs on every invocation. Twenty-five can today; thirteen are carried on a register in `tooling/lint-lints/rules.mjs` that may only shrink, and deleting a name is the whole procedure for tightening it. A name on the register that has since gained a test is reported too, so the debt cannot quietly outlive its payment.
- **Every lint is documented** — named somewhere a reader can find it, so a failing run leads somewhere. All thirty-eight are.
- **Every lint command the conventions cite exists** — the reverse direction, which nothing checked after a rename.
- **The fitness sweep's environment variable is pinned** — the gate's `MAGNA_CARTA_FITNESS_SCOPES` held identical to `FITNESS_SCOPES_ENV`, the way `lint:cache-keys` holds the two cache-key expressions identical. A rename on one side would leave the sweep on its default scope, covering half of what the step claims, and say nothing.

It states its own limits: it proves the machinery is present and wired, not that a fixture is meaningful, and one stale sentence naming a lint counts as documented.
- **The header chip now answers "can I reach my firm's records", not only "what version am I on" —
and both of its sections fold.**

A newly created firm produced screens that all refused with the same sentence — "Your role does not
grant this action in this firm" — for a reason that had nothing to do with roles: the owner's member
record had not yet been mirrored from the control plane into the firm's own database, so their
effective permission set was empty. That state was invisible from the interface, indistinguishable
from a role somebody had forgotten to grant, and self-clearing within minutes, which is the worst
combination a diagnosis can have.

- **A new read, `GET /api/v1/meta/database-health`.** It reports five facts separately: a timed
  round trip to the firm's own database, the control plane's answer and whether the firm's storage
  is allocated, the applied migration lineage against the one this build expects, the session's own
  member row with the roles on it and the permission count they resolve to, and any
  `member.provision` message for the firm still pending or dead-lettered. Every check reports a
  state rather than prose, a check that could not run says "unknown" instead of reporting health,
  and one failing check never fails the reply — the route has to be readable during the outage it
  is describing. It carries `permission: null` deliberately: a gated version of it would refuse
  exactly the session it exists to explain.
- **A Database section in the Build Versions panel** renders that read as four rows, each with the
  remedy its own state implies — a wait, an administrator's grant, a broken seeding, a connection
  fault — plus a Provisioning line when a member mirror is still on its way or has been given up on,
  and a Copy diagnosis control that puts the whole reading on the clipboard.
- **Deployment and Database each sit behind a caret now**, remembered per browser and open by
  default, with the fleet keeping its own fold inside Deployment. All three render through one
  disclosure snippet, and a shut heading carries what folding it hides: the count of Workers without
  a version, or the worst reading among the health rows.
- **Neither read fires until the panel is opened**, so the chip costs a page load nothing, and the
  panel's one Refresh control now re-asks both.
- **`pnpm check:scoped` now runs the repo-wide set — the checks a diff-scoped gate structurally cannot
find.** A repo-wide check does not live in the package whose code it governs, so the diff that breaks it
is routinely in a package that has never heard of it; three changes reached `main` red in one session that
way, while the whole-repo tier that would have caught all three was unavailable (Actions billing block,
and `pnpm check` OOM-killed at step one). Two new steps: `repo-wide lints` always (~0.7 s — twelve
whole-repo scans spawned concurrently as the commands their scripts name, rather than through twelve
`pnpm run` startups), and `repo-wide fitness sweep` whenever the diff touches first-party source (~2.5 s —
nine Vitest scans in one process under `tooling/check-scoped/vitest.repo-wide-fitness.config.ts`, which
costs 2.5 s against the root workspace's 8.5 s for the same files, plus a `schema` scope of ten more when
`packages/database` moves).

Membership is **derived, not listed** — a roster of repo-wide checks is the same drift one level up. The
lints are enumerated from the `lint:*` scripts in the root `package.json` (the CI `governance` job now
calls the same runner with `--all`, so the tiers cannot disagree); the fitness tests self-register with an
`@repo-wide-fitness` directive in their own header. Two lints are deferred with their numbers:
`lint:licenses` (1.6 s, dependency-set-only — runs when a manifest or lockfile changes) and
`lint:test-collection` (26 s — CI's own job). `apps/api-worker`'s route conformance is excluded outright at
26 s in the Miniflare pool.

Measured warm, before → after: a markdown-only diff 0.9 s → 1.6 s, one ordinary source file 2.3 s →
4.9 s, a `packages/database` schema file 4.7 s → 7.8 s. `lint:test-registration` learned about
**re-runner** configs (a Vitest config that owns no tests, only re-runs files belonging to other
projects) and refuses to let one be registered twice. Homes:
[`tooling/check-scoped/repo-wide.mjs`](tooling/check-scoped/repo-wide.mjs),
[`docs/conventions/build-performance.md`](docs/conventions/build-performance.md),
[`docs/conventions/testing.md`](docs/conventions/testing.md).
- **The matter lifecycle gains its first rung and a hold, and the intake desk stands on it.** A
matter now passes through `intake`, `consultation` (the status formerly stored as `prospective`,
renamed as spelled because no firm holds a matter yet; a reviewed rebuild of `matter` widens the
CHECK), `open`, `hold` and `closed`. A hold is an open matter the firm has stopped working without
closing it, for a recorded reason: `holdMatter` behind `POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/hold` (the reason
in the body) and `releaseMatter` behind `.../release`, guarded in the batch, drawing and surrendering
nothing, carrying `held_at` and `hold_reason` on the row (a second reviewed rebuild), and audited as
`matter.held` and `matter.released`, which the matter timeline, the activity section and the
responsible member's notifications all read. One permission, `matters:hold`, both ways, seeded to
Owner/Admin and Attorney. The docket keeps held matters under their own status; the conflicts corpus
and auto-file rules treat them as live; reopen returns a matter closed on hold to its hold. An intake draws no number of any kind; `graduateMatter` behind
`POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/graduate` (and its readiness read) runs the intake procedure as its gate
and draws the consultation number; `openMatter` requires a consultation and runs no intake gate;
reopen returns a matter to the rung it left. The docket excludes both unnumbered rungs. The sidebar's
Intake destination lists every intake and consultation in flight, starts one, completes it, and
schedules the consultation. The desk is a reading of the firm's matters rather than a register of its own: `readIntakeDesk`
in `@magna-carta/intake` behind `GET /api/v1/intake/consultations` (firm-wide, `intake:read`,
cursor-paged, capped at fifty because each row's standing is derived on read) joins the matters
listing to the client party, the member and matter-type names, the next scheduled event, and one
checklist read per row. The New Matter window gains an intake purpose (Intake, Start Intake,
no money block) and offers Intake among its statuses; the calendar's event window takes a seeded title and participants; the sidebar row
flips to alpha. The step-kind vocabulary gains `client-forms` and `payment` on the procedure's
own principle — a member's record ahead of the portal and the payments port — through a same-
transaction rebuild of `intake_procedure_step`. The design system's `EntityPicker` gains a
top-level New control and a per-kind add row (`onCreate` now carries the kind, and `createRefusal`
keeps the control present when the reader may not create); `directory-entity-picker.svelte` wraps
it with the Directory's own New Person and New Organization windows, seeded from what was typed,
and every surface that picks a person or an organization takes the wrapper.
- **The intake procedure: what a kind of matter must clear before it opens, as a firm-authored list
whose steps are answered by the subsystems that own the facts.** `@magna-carta/intake` adds
`intake_procedure` (bound to a matter type or every type), `intake_procedure_step` (eight kinds held
by a CHECK) and `matter_intake_step_record` (append-and-flip, one live record per step per matter),
four permissions seeded on the tasks split, twelve routes, and a reader seam per kind registered by
the composition root: the conflicts posture, the billing arrangement, document assembly, the trust
position and custom-field values answer today; identity verification and acknowledgement are a
member's record until a subsystem exists. `@magna-carta/matters` gained `openPreconditions`
mirroring the close hook, threaded through `openMatter` before the draw, and
`GET /api/v1/matters/{id}/open-readiness`. Surfaces: Settings · Intake Procedures, the matter's
Intake section, and Requirements To Open in the status window. The platform seeds no procedure.
- The matter's Activity section: fifteen subsystems' worth of history, in order, on one screen, each row named by the subsystem that owns it.

The federated timeline has been built, tested and served since the calendar slice — `GET /api/v1/matters/{matterId}/timeline`, fifteen declared sources read in place under one sort key, one cursor and one visibility contract, with nothing projected or copied. **Nothing in the web app called it.** The matter's story was scattered across the sections that each hold a piece of it, and the read that puts it back together answered to no screen.

**A consolidation view cannot know what its rows are, so it does not try.** Only the file manager knows what a file is; only the calendar knows what a hearing is called. The Activity section names no source and switches on none. Each subsystem declares its own half on both tiers:

- On the server, every timeline source now declares the read capability a description of its rows sits behind (`permission`), and a source whose rows have names declares a `describe` — one statement through `describeSelect`, which binds the matter, the page's row ids, the visibility predicate and the LIMIT, projecting a title, the subsystem's own word for what the row is, and that subsystem's own facts as one JSON object. The matter-scoped route asks for it after the merge, at most one statement per source present on the page, so the cost scales with the registry and never with the rows. The firm-wide read is never described, and a test asserts it: the no-label discipline on the projection is unchanged.
- On the client, an `ActivityContribution` per source lives beside the owning subsystem's own code (`$lib/file-manager/activity-contribution.ts`, `$lib/time/activity-contribution.ts`, and so on) and is registered once in `$lib/activity/contributions.ts`: the section word, the noun, the sentence for an undescribed row, the glyph, the Type word and the facts read out of the description in that subsystem's own vocabulary, how a row opens, and how one is made. `apps/web/test/activity-contributions.test.ts` scans the calendar package's own declarations and fails until every source has one; `pnpm run lint:matter-timeline-coverage` fails until every source is owned by a matter section's new `timelineSources` or declared ownerless in `sections.ts` with a reason.

**The permission gates the words, never the row.** A member who may not read notes still sees that a note was written on the matter, when and by whom — the entry carries no content — and does not see what it said. Six sources describe their rows today: a document by its name with its size, version and safety standing; a note by its opening line with when it happened and how many documents it points at; a time entry by its narrative with the hours; a cost by its description with the amount; an event by its title with its time and place; a deadline by its title with whether it is overdue, computed where the reader is. The rest keep the platform's own sentence, and adding one is a describe on the source and a contribution beside the subsystem.

**A file's type is what the file manager says it is.** The first cut took a name suffix for that. The new `$lib/file-manager/file-identity.ts` is the one place a file becomes words — the document type where the firm set one, else the label of the identification the design-system FileIcon resolves from the content type and the name ("PDF document", "Archive"), its size, and its safety standing out of the status register — and the Activity section draws the file manager's own glyph over the same inputs. Section and Type are two columns with two set filters: which part of the matter a row belongs to, and what it is in its own subsystem's words; one column doing both jobs had mixed "Deadline" with "pdf" in one list.

**It is the product's table, and its column controls are the column's own.** `DataTable.Grid` with Date (anchored), Time, Section, Type, Name, Details and Who; right-clicking a column heading opens the shared head menu for that column's filter, hide, pin and the roster of columns. There is no filter bar and no Columns button.

**It can make a record.** "+ New Note" opens the note window on the Activity section — the same window the Notes section opens, hosted by the new `NoteWindowHost` so the section knows nothing about notes beyond the fact that they have a window — and the row appears when it saves. A subsystem with a window of its own adds a create verb to its contribution and the control grows into a menu.

**Every section honours the entry an Activity row hands it.** Every deep link the timeline builds is `/matters/{id}/{section}?entry={rowId}`, and until now no section read it — a row opened onto a list. Now the Notes section opens the note in its window, read by its id through the new `GET /api/v1/notes/{noteId}` (so a note older than the first page opens all the same); the Time and Costs sections open the entry or cost in their windows, from the loaded page or by id; the Files section opens the file's folder, selects it and shows it in the inspector; the Calendar marks and scrolls to the row; the Custodian section opens the packet — the custody sources' deep links now carry the packet id through a `link_id` on the timeline projection, on matter-search's precedent, because the movement is the row and the packet is the door. A note row on Activity itself opens in the note window in place, through the same window host "+ New Note" uses.

**What happened to a document after it arrived is on the chronology.** A sixteenth source, `fileHistory`, admits the File History view's own events — renamed, moved, deleted, restored, a new version, an earlier version restored, the document type set, held by the safety check — through the one join that confines the audit log's polymorphic subject to a matter, exactly as the History view reads them. A first version's commit stays out, because a document's arrival is already the row that says it was added. Each row is named by the file as it is called now, typed by the History view's own action word through the same `historyActionLabel`, and opens onto the file.

**One register, two homes.** The Activity section's body is now `$lib/activity/activity-register.svelte`, and the Overview's "Recent activity" placeholder tile is that same register with a row budget of eight, the glance-level columns, and "See all activity" one step away — so what the Overview shows is what the Activity section shows, never a second summary of it. A firm-wide feed on the Home dashboard is the third home, and waits on the one design question it raises: whether a page spanning the member's matters may be described row by row, which the timeline's label discipline was written to refuse.

**Nothing says a document was "filed".** To a lawyer, filing means filing with a court, and this platform files nothing with a court: a document is added to the matter, an email is saved to it. The source keys stay `documentFiled` and `emailFiled` because they are wire contracts — which is exactly why the words a person reads are decided in the contributions and not taken from them.

Three deep links were repaired on the way. `emailFiled` pointed at a matter section spelled `email` and the three custody sources at `custody`; the app routes `emails` and `custodian`. A conflicts check has no matter section at all, so its rows state what happened and offer nowhere to go — the section registry says why, and the coverage lint keeps the answer current.
- **The matters list is a real docket, and a matter can be opened from it.** The screen was a hardcoded
empty state with a permanently disabled "New matter" button — no query, no rows, and a `disabled`
attribute written into the markup rather than derived from anything. The backend it was standing in
front of had been complete for months: create, cursor-paginated list, get, patch, and the whole
open/close/reopen/renumber lifecycle. Nothing was missing except the screen.

It now reads the firm's own matters through the listing and renders them on `DataTable.Grid`, the
platform's one table, so the docket inherits the settled machinery rather than reimplementing it:
type-aware sorting, the one-mechanism per-column filters, column show/hide, drag-reorder, pinning,
resize, and the counts footer. Columns are matter number, title, client, status, practice area,
Location (hidden until a firm asks for it) and created date. A scope control selects what the
listing is asked for, and the search box runs the server's own search over title, number and client
rather than narrowing the rows already on screen.

**"New matter" opens a real matter.** The dialog carries the contract's required set and nothing
invented: a title, whether the file starts as an opened matter or an unnumbered consultation, the
client, and the firm's own practice-area and Location vocabularies. The number is deliberately not a
field — it is drawn by the firm's counter at the moment the matter opens, atomically, and a field
for it would be a field for breaking that. Every submit carries an idempotency key, so a retry
cannot open a second matter.

Three gaps are on the screen rather than hidden, because a docket that quietly cannot answer a
question is worse than one that says so:

- **The responsible attorney is not a column.** The listing answers an identifier for it and nothing
