  on the server publishes the firm's members, so naming them would cost one request per row and
  printing the handle would be printing a handle at a person. The dialog's own responsible-attorney
  field renders for real, showing the person creating the matter, disabled and marked "Soon" with
  the dependency named.
- **The date column says "Created", not "Opened".** The listing serves the creation instant; a
  matter opened months after the consultation that started it has two dates and only the detail read
  carries the second.
- **Sorting and the column filters cover what has been loaded.** The listing is cursor-paged, so the
  footer counts the page rather than the firm until the record is fully read, and the line under
  "Load more" says exactly that.

A refused open now says where to fix it: opening a numbered matter needs the firm's numbering
scheme, and the refusal points at the settings page that configures one instead of leaving the
server's one-line reason to be interpreted.

The matter status register — prospective, open, closed, with their labels and their subtle badge
tones — moved out of the matter header into one shared module both surfaces read, so the header's
seal and the docket's status column cannot drift apart. Closed stays quiet neutral: a closed matter
is archived-but-additive, not a failure.
- **The notification centre and the live bell** — the two screens that were still `awaiting-screen`
over a read API that had shipped with no caller.

`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/notifications/+page.svelte` replaces the stub with the real feed: cursor
paged through the shared `PagedList`, narrowed by state and category as QUERY parameters so a
filtered read is cheaper rather than merely shorter, settling a row on follow and dismissing
separately, and reporting what the retention sweep took while unread. The top-bar bell became
`$lib/notifications/notification-tray.svelte` beside the download and upload trays, over a shared
count (`$lib/notifications/unread-count.svelte.ts`) polled slowly and on focus, paused while the page
is hidden, and never cleared by a failed read. The preference matrix at `settings/notifications` landed
from the settings stream while this was in flight and stands as it is; what this branch does there
is give its vocabulary and its transport one home each (`category-vocabulary.ts`,
`preferences-api.ts`) rather than the second copy this branch had grown independently.

A notification row carries no sentence, so the card is composed on the client from the kind and the
declared facts (`$lib/notifications/notification-presentation.ts`). A kind that module has no entry
for renders as its category's own noun rather than being dropped: a client that shipped before a type
did must not swallow a notification somebody was meant to see.
`apps/web/test/notification-presentation.test.ts` scans the server's registry as text — apps/web does
not depend on `@magna-carta/notifications` and should not start — and fails when a registered kind has
no words here.

**One contract gap closed.** `POST /api/v1/notifications/read-all` requires a `throughCursor` naming
the newest row the member saw, and no route handed one out: `nextCursor` names the page's OLDEST row
and is null exactly when a member's whole backlog fits on one page. The subsystem's own test minted
the cursor by hand, which is why nothing had noticed. The feed page now reports `readThroughCursor`
beside `nextCursor`, and that test uses it, so the encoding stays in the one module that owns it.
- **Notifications can now leave the platform, and a digest says only how much is waiting and in which
categories. A fixed subject carrying a count, a line of per-category counts, one link back in — and
nothing a person typed.**

This is the first time this subsystem hands anything to a mailbox. Every surface before it was a row
read inside the product, behind the session and the visible-matter predicate, where a row shown to
the wrong person is fixed by the next read. An email is a copy retained by a provider the firm did
not choose, forwarded, backed up, rendered on a lock screen — and it **cannot be re-filtered when
access changes**, which is the whole basis on which the wall here binds at read time. So the content
stops at what never depended on access in the first place.

**What a digest line may contain:** a category label from the closed vocabulary, and an integer.
**What it may not:** matter titles, matter numbers, client or party names, filenames, email subject
lines, deadline descriptions or dates, custody numbers, amounts, invoice numbers, platform handles.
The boundary is structural rather than remembered — the digest read selects a category, a kind, an
instant and two handles, and the renderer's only parameters are a closed label, integers, a cadence
and a configured origin, so there is no argument a title could arrive in. A golden test renders over
a fixture whose matter is named after its parties and numbered, and fails if any of it reaches the
output.

**The first reader of the per-category email cadence.** The preference slice stored a cadence and
nothing consumed it; the run now partitions each member's window by it. A category on the other
cadence is left to that cadence's own watermark; a category set `off` is **withheld and recorded**,
not dropped — every row a run did not mail gets a `suppressed` delivery row naming a closed reason,
so a member who chose not to be written to stays distinguishable from a member the platform silently
failed to write to. That is the same requirement the in-app suppression tally answers, met with the
mechanism the schema already had.

**Send first, mark second**, on a keyset watermark (an instant _and_ its event id — two events
sharing an instant must not straddle a boundary), per member per cadence, committed in one batch
after the send returns. A crash between them re-sends a summary; marking first would lose one. A
member with nothing visible in the window gets no email at all. Runs are anchored to the firm's own
morning, resolved from the default office the calendar already books against.

**Outbound mail is an unprovisioned seam.** The digest resolves its own send port rather than reusing
the shared adapter resolver, which falls back to the dev logging adapter when the Email Service
binding is absent — right for a password reset, catastrophic here, because the run would record
`sent` rows and advance watermarks for mail that was printed to a log. Absent a binding, a verified
sender, or a public origin, the port answers with a typed reason, the pass exits before reading a
firm, and the reason is counted every pass. Owner steps are in `docs/deploy-queue.md`.

Still deferred: the notification centre and the preference screens (no `apps/web` change here), and
the `matter-number` detail level, which stays declared and renders as `counts-only` so a firm's
stored ceiling is honoured at its most private reading rather than silently rewritten.
- **The numbering scheme has an editor, and a matter's number can be set by hand.** Settings ·
Matter Numbering replaces its Soon stub with two editors over the routes that already existed
(`GET`/`PUT /api/v1/numbering-scheme`, `POST /api/v1/numbering-scheme/preview`): one for the matter
number and one for the consultation sequence, each an ordered list of parts (text, the one counter,
year, date opened, office code, practice-area code, client code, attorney initials, client name)
with the scoping flag drawn as "restarts the count", starters for the common shapes, and a live
preview rendered by the server against a sample matter whose values are printed beside it. The
model lives in `apps/web/src/lib/matters/numbering-scheme.ts`; the editor in
`numbering-scheme-editor.svelte`. The matter's status window gains a Number block with Set Number
(Change Number where one stands) behind `matters:renumber`, over `POST /api/v1/matters/{id}/renumber`,
offered only where the matter has been active; `renumberMatter` now refuses an intake or a
consultation (`matter-not-open`), since no matter number exists before a matter is active.
- **`DataTable.Grid` — the platform's one table, as a design-system component.** The one-table ruling (`docs/conventions/time-tab-rulings.md`, TB2 — binding cross-surface) says any behavior gap between two matter tables is a defect by definition; until now the settled machinery lived only in the mockups. The design system's `data-table` now carries it as a composed component driven by a declarative column model: type-aware stable sorting (empties last in both directions), the one per-column filter mechanism living inside the header cell (flush at its end edge, one hover unit, space always reserved; contains-text, checkbox set with counts and select-all, numeric range, date range; active funnels unmistakable, clear affordances present only while a filter is in play), column show/hide with pinning at measured sticky offsets, drag-reorder with the anchored column immovable, resize grips with double-click fit, the Docket's selection model (click / Ctrl / Shift / Ctrl+A scoped to the table / arrows / click-empty-clears) with selection emitted as state — never presented, double-click activation as its own event with no select/deselect churn, the scope-honest totals row (voids excludable), zebra, and the "n of m · filtered" footer with one-click clear. Cells render through a consumer snippet, so status chips stay each surface's business.

The pure machinery (`grid-columns` / `grid-filters` / `grid-selection`) is unit-tested; the behaviors run as story play tests in the catalog. The owner's review surface is the developer console's new Table states page (`/developer-console/table-states`), which renders the real component over a litigation fixture in every state — the mockups' polish carried into the product, where it can no longer drift. Existing tanstack-adapter consumers are untouched; migrating the matter surfaces onto the grid is the pipeline's next slices.
- `pnpm run lint:one-ui` now holds the one-table ruling, which until today was a header comment on `DataTable.Grid` and a row in the port plan's table of rules nobody had built.

Two rules. `raw-table` fails a `<table>`, `<thead>`, `<tr>`, `<th>`, `<td>` or a table ARIA role written anywhere outside the design system's data-table home, on both sides of the app/design-system line, one problem per file at its first element. `table-machinery` fails the half that rule cannot see: a screen that composes the presentational primitives correctly and then writes what the Grid already carries — a sortable header (`aria-sort`, the `mc-table-sort` recipe), the headless engine composed by hand (`createSvelteTable`, a direct `@tanstack/table-core` import) or the adapter's toolbar parts. That is the shape the ruling calls a defect by definition: a second answer to "what does clicking a header do", with the recipe on it so it reads fine in review.

The audit that preceded the rule: twelve surfaces render through `DataTable.Grid`, eighteen compose the primitives for a plain grid of facts, one page wrote a raw `<table>` (the speed test's sample list, now on the primitives) and one wrote its own sort (the firm-usage By Location table, recorded as an allowance that names the port it needs). Every rule is proved against known-bad input in the tool's own test file, and the allowance fails the run the day its violation is gone.
- **`Sidebar.MenuTrigger` + `Sidebar.MenuSub` — the rail's second level**, and a general cluster
mechanism over them (`navigation/clusters.ts`). A destination names a `cluster`, the render tree
folds it there, and a cluster holding a single row is seated as a plain row instead. A cluster is a
fold and never a screen: it has no address, and pressing it opens the rows. The collapsed icon rail
draws every row flat, folds and all, because a rail with no labels has nothing to fold by.

**`navigation/favorites.svelte.ts` — the member's own shortcuts**, as the rail's first group. A
favorite is any pathname plus the title the screen had when it was saved; the glyph is resolved at
render time from the area the address sits under, so nothing has to be kept in step. The gesture
lives in `screen-header.svelte`, which is the one component every screen builds its title from, so it
reaches every page in the product without a screen opting in (`favoritable={false}` opts out).

**`Destination.permission`** — the gate a few destinations carry now that Firm Usage is one of them,
applied in the rail and in the palette alike. **`Sidebar.MenuButton`'s `trailing` snippet** — a grid
column sized to its contents that never shrinks, which is what stopped a long label clipping its own
maturity badge.
- **Attorney License Lookup has a screen** — the fourth tool page, and the first of the five the catalogue still owed. Pick a state, get that state's official attorney register, open it beside your work. It reads nothing back and stores nothing: the tool is a link generator (`backing: library`), and the registers are the authority, so a copy of one of their answers held here and going stale would be worse than no answer — a suspension is exactly the fact that changes after you look.

The branching lives in `$lib/tools/attorney-license/attorney-license.ts`, DOM-free and tested, the same split the WHOIS tool keeps. The state list comes from `@magna-carta/government-links`, whose licensing registry gained the state's own `name`: it was previously recoverable only by taking a suffix off the site's display label, and the alternative was a second hand-written list of the fifty states. The screen imports the `/licensing` entry point rather than `/registry`, so rendering a state picker does not ship fifty states of county assessor tables to the browser.

Two of the fifty-one registers are served over plain HTTP (Rhode Island's judiciary search and Washington's). That is a fact about US government portals rather than a transcription error, and the screen says so before the link instead of after it: on such a page the lawyer being asked about, and the answer, are readable by anything on the path. The link is still offered, because the register is the authority whatever it is served over.

The catalogue entry's description changed with it. It said the tool would "check a lawyer's bar standing and discipline history", which promised an answer this platform never sees.
- **`pnpm run lint:control-characters` now also rejects a raw U+FFFD.** The replacement character is
written `\uFFFD` or not at all.

It rides the existing scan rather than a new one, because the argument is the same one that scan was
already making: a character whose raw form a reader cannot recognise makes source that reads as one
thing and means another. U+FFFD is what a decoder emits for bytes it could **not** read, so a literal
one is indistinguishable from a file that was itself mangled in transit — nobody can tell a deliberate
one from damage. It has a second reason of its own: inside a `u`-flagged regular expression that is
actually used, it hangs the linter with no error and no file named.

The two findings are reported apart. The remedy is identical and the reasoning is not, and a reader
handed the wrong reason for their finding argues with the rule instead of fixing the line.

The scan's self-test gains the new cases, including the code points either side of U+FFFD — a botched
comparison that swallowed the whole range would otherwise pass as a tightened rule. It found a real
offender on its first run: a changelog entry that meant to quote the escape and contained the character
instead, written by someone who had spent that morning on this exact problem. Which is the argument.
- **The gilt scroll-edge rule is now the member's own choice.** `Settings · Accessibility` carries a Scroll Edge Markers switch, on the theme-preference seam beside contrast, motion and density: `magna-carta.scrollEdgeHints`, stamped on the document as `data-scroll-edge-hints="hidden"`, with "shown" removing the attribute exactly as a resolved "full" motion and a "comfortable" density do.

**Suppressed in the recipe, not threaded as a prop.** `ScrollEdgeHint` is drawn by the sidebar's nav list and by every register's grid, so a preference carried as a prop would have to be threaded through both and through everything after them. One rule in `scroll-edge-hint.css` keyed on the root attribute reaches all of it, and the component stays a component that knows about scrollports and nothing about members.

**Reduced motion is a different answer to a different question.** The recipe already shortens the rule's draw to instant under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and that stays: wanting less movement is not the same as wanting less information about where a list ends. So this axis has no OS signal to seed from and no "system" encoding — shown or hidden, and the seed-then-own contract contrast uses does not apply.

**It is the one appearance axis the no-FOUC boot script does not mirror**, and the mirror test now asserts that rather than leaving its absence to read as an oversight. The boot script exists to dress the first paint; nothing paints a scroll-edge rule before the application mounts, because the hint renders only once its scrollport reports there is more content that way.
- **Tasks gain the four things an outside system needs and none of the things a vendor does.**

The platform still integrates with nothing. It ships no adapter, schedules no sync, resolves no
conflict and maps no vocabulary — every one of those is a decision about somebody else's product and
belongs to the addon that knows it, on `@magna-carta/integrations` where the credential and
capability machinery already lives. What ships is the part the platform cannot delegate, and each
piece is here because it is impossible to add afterwards:

`matter_task_external_link` records that a task IS some object over there. `system` is open text with
a non-empty CHECK — the `directory_edge.edge_type` discipline — so a second system is an addon
rather than a reviewed migration, and nothing in the schema names a vendor. **Two uniqueness rules,
and they are different claims:** one remote object maps to at most one task, or two tasks fight over
one mirror and each wins half the time; one task holds at most one identity per system, or a change
here has two places to go and no way to choose. Both are INDEXES rather than service checks, because
a race between two syncs is exactly the case a pre-check loses — a test composes two colliding links
before committing either and asserts the loser aborts.

`matter_task_deletion` is the tombstone, written in the **same batch** as the delete. A row that is
gone cannot be enumerated afterwards, so a mirror learns of a deletion there or never, and one that
never learns keeps the work alive somewhere the firm has stopped looking. It carries identifiers and
nothing else: a tombstone preserving the title would defeat the delete it records. A deleted task's
external links go with it, so its remote object is free to be linked to a real task again.

`matter_task.updated_by` is echo suppression. A two-way sync must tell its own writes from a
person's, or it pushes back everything it just pulled and the two sides oscillate. Every write path
stamps it — including the cascade that clears a successor's blocker, because that successor really
did change. It is required rather than optional in the statement signatures, which is what made the
compiler name all six call sites.

`readTaskChanges` answers "what moved since I last looked" as two keyset streams with
**INDEPENDENT POSITIONS**. One shared cursor looks sufficient and is wrong in a way that would never
surface in testing: the cursor's id half comes from whichever stream produced the last row, and a
`matterTaskDeletion_` handle applied as the tie-break against `matter_task.id` silently excludes
every live task sorting below it at that same instant — a change lost permanently, at a page
boundary, under a clock collision nobody can reproduce on demand. A test walks five tasks written at
one instant a page at a time and asserts nothing is skipped or repeated.

Visibility is not relaxed for any of it. The feed composes `taskVisibilityFragment` like every other
task read, so an addon connected as a member syncs exactly what that member can see, and the
external-id lookup returns the same null for "no such correspondence" and "you cannot see the task it
names" so it cannot be used to probe.

Five routes, the external links folded into the page read beside the attachments and the time, and
the adapter-author contract written where an adapter author will look: `packages/tasks/CLAUDE.md`.
- The whole-repo security audit is now scheduled: a weekly Claude Code Routine (`MC - Security Audit`, Wednesdays 13:00 UTC, fresh session per firing) runs the vendored security-audit skill in full audit mode over `main`, opens one `remediate-` pull request per confirmed finding with a regression verifier, and reports needs-validation leads by notification. Audit artifacts never enter the repository. The canonical configuration lives beside the audit policy in `docs/conventions/testing.md`, the `maintenance-agents.security` roadmap node moves to partial, and the pull request template gains a row asking whether the security angle was run against the companion files the change reaches.
- Three reads the shipping surfaces need and the subsystem never had: `GET /api/v1/shipments` (the firm's shipments, newest first), `GET /api/v1/shipments/{id}` (one shipment in full), and `GET /api/v1/integrations/shipping/connection` (whether an account is connected, and its health).

The eight routes built in June were all writes or live carrier calls. There was no way to ask what a firm had sent, which is why the register could not be built over them — `selectShipmentStatement` reads one shipment by id and nothing listed them.

The list pages on a keyset over `(created_at, id)` rather than an offset, because a register is read while shipments are being created and an offset skips or repeats rows as the page moves under the reader. It reads one row more than asked for, so whether another page exists comes from the read itself rather than a count that could disagree with it, and a cursor the register did not issue is a 422 rather than a silent first page — which would read as the register having reset.

Two projections are deliberately narrower than the row. A list item carries the recipient's name and not their address, so a list of a firm's mail does not send every recipient's street address to the browser; and the detail says `hasLabel` rather than the storage key the label lives at.
- **`apps/web-worker` — the SvelteKit application on its own Cloudflare Worker, so a change to a
button's label no longer rebuilds and redeploys the API.**

The app Worker binds the SPA's build output under its own `assets` block, which means every UI-only
change rebuilds a Worker that also carries the per-firm data layer, the WebAssembly artefacts and the
Docker steps that produce them. The new Worker carries the same build output and nothing else: no
`main`, no bindings, no secrets. A page request is answered by Cloudflare's asset server and invokes
no script at all.

It is separable because `apps/web` genuinely depends on nothing that reaches a crate — its four
workspace dependencies are `@magna-carta/design-system`, `@magna-carta/design-tokens`,
`@magna-carta/tools` and `@magna-carta/merge-field-catalog-contract`. The WebAssembly imports that
make the app Worker's build slow and Docker-dependent are the API's own: PDF form fill and text
extraction, decryption, and email parsing.

**This stage is additive and changes nothing that is serving.** The app Worker keeps its `assets`
block, so the application answers from one origin exactly as it does today, and the new Worker is a
second door to the same files. Cutting over needs route patterns on one hostname — the SPA
everywhere, the API Worker on its own paths — which needs a zone hostname the account does not have
yet. Removing the app Worker's `assets` block before those routes exist would make the application
unreachable, so the runbook entry says so at the point where somebody would be tempted.

Build settings for the new Worker are the same three uniform fields every sibling uses; the runbook
records them along with its Watch Paths.
- **The time entry is served as a record, not a row.** The listing and detail reads carried eleven fields against a table that stores twice that, so the Time Sheet redesign had nothing to render where the design puts a rate, a code, an enterer or an invoice. `timeEntries.list` and `timeEntries.get` now serve the whole record through one shared read (`readTimeEntryRecord` / the listing queries in `@magna-carta/timekeeping`): the frozen rate snapshot (`rateE4`, `rateSource`, `rateCardId`), the UTBMS task and activity codes with their ids, codes and labels resolved, `source`, `invoiceId`, `createdAt` (the entered date, distinct from the work date), `createdByUserId` + `createdByName` (the enterer, resolved through the member mirror like the timekeeper's name, null where the member row is gone), `timekeeperName` on every read, and `attachmentCount`. Four new surfaces beside it, all per-firm-migrated (`20260901T130000_time-entry-record-surfaces`):

- **Internal memo** — a nullable `memo` column, settable on create and PATCH (null clears), served everywhere the entry is. It is the firm's own note and never client-facing; the audit trail records which fields an edit touched, never the text.
- **Entry number** — an immutable matter-scoped reference minted at capture through `@magna-carta/sequence-numbering` (counter per matter + allocation-key backstop): the matter's number, a dot, a zero-padded sequence (`2026-0147.0042`). Every capture path draws one (create, grid batch, timer stop-commit); existing entries stay honestly null. Served as `entryNumber` and echoed on the capture acks.
- **History** — `GET /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/events` serves the entry's recorded audit events oldest first (actor id + resolved name, redacted detail), the file-history shape; capture now records its source and an update the field names it touched, so the rail can say what happened.
- **Attachments** — a `time_entry_attachment` relation linking an entry to files already in its matter, with list/attach/detach routes. Attach refuses a file on another matter; detach removes the link and never the file; both acts are audited.

`POST /api/v1/time-entries/{id}/convert-to-cost` converts a mis-recorded charge: one idempotent act captures the cost (matter, narrative as description, the entry's amount, work date as incurred date) and voids the time entry so the value is never counted twice, with cross-referencing audit events on both records. It refuses an entry that is billed, void, claimed by a draft invoice, or carrying no amount, and requires `costs:track` on top of `time:track`. Convert-to-fee is deliberately not built: the fee work-in-progress store does not exist yet, and a fee route against invoice lines would bill a charge no one recorded.
- **The Time Sheet is ported from the owner's own surface**, which is an editable grid rather than a
table that opens a window. That distinction is the whole of it: what stood on the matter's Time tab
was a read-only ledger and a record window, and neither is a smaller version of a sheet somebody
captures a day's work in.

Rows edit in place and autosave on leaving a cell, and the leading state mark says which of saving,
saved, saved-but-incomplete, not-yet-written or failed the row is in. Undo and redo carry forty
bounded steps with split menus naming what each step was, and an undo writes the restored values
back rather than only redrawing them. Scope is Today, Yesterday or This week against the firm's own
first weekday, with a custom range that applies as it is picked — and a row just added or re-dated is
never dropped out of view. Search expands from its icon and collapses when left empty; clear-filters
exists only while a filter is in play.

**The timer is the firm's real one, not a local stopwatch.** The single-active-timer routes already
existed, so starting a second row says the first was stopped and kept its time; a row that is already
an entry takes the elapsed time onto its own duration, and a row that is not becomes the entry the
timer commits.

Nothing was simplified because an endpoint is missing. Time Code, Date Entered, Rate, Files and
Entered By render as real columns naming what they wait on, and the capture route requires a positive
duration and a narrative — so a fresh row lives on the sheet holding what is typed into it, marked
not yet written with the reason, and writes itself the moment it is acceptable.

**Two consumer defects were found by measuring rather than reading.** The record pane's field rows
broke on a viewport media query when the pane's width is a property of the window, which is exactly
what collided three labels into one unreadable run. And a Soon badge overflowed the pane by thirty
pixels in a pane that does not scroll sideways, so it was simply cut off. Both are container-width
problems and are now solved with the width the pane actually controls.
- **`lint:doc-links`, `lint:changelog-coverage` and `lint:active-work` — two gaps `documentation.md` named itself, and one rule held up by memory.**

**Dead links.** 1,734 relative links across 1,051 documents; every one now has to resolve, and an anchored link has to name a heading that exists (GitHub's real slug rules — punctuation deleted rather than replaced, emphasis unwrapped, duplicate numbering). External links stay out of scope: a gate must not depend on the network. Building it was mostly learning what a false positive looks like here — a decision fragment's prose is authored at three depths, because the same body lives at `docs/decisions/pending/`, at `docs/decisions/NNNN-`, and rendered into `docs/Decision-Log.md`, so a link is sound if it resolves from any home the prose actually has. That removed 65 of the first pass's 102 findings.

**The 37 that were real say something worth acting on.** Thirty are in numbered decision records and all have one cause: a link that was correct in the pending fragment climbs one directory too many when the assembler numbers the file, so `../conventions/invariants.md` lands at the repository root. The repair belongs in the assembler as a link rewrite on promotion, not in thirty files. Three more are in `CHANGELOG.md` and genuinely dead — `apps/worker` became `apps/api-worker`, `ci.yml` became `gate.yml`, a fixture baseline is gone. One spec points at a design that was deleted rather than moved. One was unambiguous and is fixed in place; the rest are a register that only shrinks.

**Changelog coverage.** A change touching `apps/`, `packages/`, `crates/` or `containers/` source brings a fragment. The carve-outs are a positive list, not a negative one, so a new directory is silent by default and must be added deliberately. Tests are deliberately in scope — they are the largest class of small change, and carving them out would leave the floor holding almost nothing. `tooling/` and `.github/` are out: the custom of changelogging them is worth keeping, but a gate firing on every lint tweak gets routed around in a week. **The gate holds the floor; the custom holds the ceiling.** Manifests and lockfiles are named in the source as the real remaining hole rather than hidden. On `main` and in the merge queue it stands down and prints why, rather than passing silently.

The escape hatch is `changelog.d/exemptions/<slug>.md` with a `reason:` in words — in the diff, where a reviewer reads the claim beside the change it excuses, and counted only as part of that change.

**The stream registry.** Every note under `docs/active-work/` has to sit at a branch-shaped path and carry the four keys the registry reads, with a status from the documented set. `vp run worktrees` only warned, and the root `CLAUDE.md` compensated by telling people to remember to run it. One note declared a status the registry does not document, which is exactly the shape that makes a note invisible.
- **A version chip at the top right of every signed-in screen, and an overlay that says what every
part of the platform is running.** The chip is the web application's own build identifier, baked in
at build time, so it renders even when nothing else answers. Clicking it opens the version overlay:
the web app, the API, and each backend service worker (malware scan, bundle build, conversion,
file repair, password recovery, text recognition, document sealing, discovery, keyword search) with
its commit, commit date, build time, and reachability. Every value is copyable in one click.

The overlay is honest by construction. Each service reports its own identity over a tiny shared
version route (`packages/build-identity`, stamped by each Worker's deploy build; a build without
git identity says `dev`); a service that is absent, unreachable, or too old to answer is named as
exactly that, never given an invented version. The aggregate read
(`GET /api/v1/meta/versions`) probes all bindings in parallel under short timeouts, caches
briefly, and carries `observedAt` so a cached answer states its age. And because the web app and
the API deploy separately, the one skew that matters is called out in words: when their commits
differ, the overlay says "Different Builds".
- **The version chip now sits on the sign-in page too.** It only existed inside the application, which
put it on the wrong side of the door: "which version am I on" is asked most often by someone who
cannot get in, and the one screen they can reach could not answer.

The chip and its overlay ride the shared signed-out frame, so sign in, password reset and the
registration screens all carry it in the same chrome corner, from the same component as the app
shell's. Its identifier is baked into the page at build time, so it needs no connection and no
session to be right.

The signed-out overlay shows the web application alone and says so in a line of its own. The
aggregate that reports the API and the backend services is an authenticated read, and is not
attempted before sign-in: a signed-out panel issues no request at all rather than rendering a
rejection as though something were down. The skew notice, which needs a second version to compare
against, is likewise absent there rather than guessed at.
- **A design for the Worker fleet: what the core Worker stops carrying, where the hosts go, and why the
API and the orchestration stay one program.**

Fifteen entries under `apps/` are three different kinds of thing — entrances, the core, and engines —
and nothing said so. The design names the kinds, records that `apps/api-worker` is the naming convention
applied to the root script rather than an oversight, and refuses the split of the API from the
orchestration on the one fact that settles it: `FirmDatabase` is a Durable Object on that script and
is each firm's database.

The segmentation that is worth doing is different. The core Worker still imports three WebAssembly
packages whose work belongs at Workers that already exist — PDF at the signing Worker, decryption at
the recovery Worker, message parsing at the mail entrance. Moving them makes the slowest build in the
repository need no Docker at all.

It also records that the host cutover was never blocked. `magnacarta.esq` has been a live zone since
June and the status Worker already holds a custom-domain route on it; a stale comment claiming
otherwise is what made it look gated. The design orders the cutover so the `assets` block stays as the
rollback until both hosts are confirmed serving, and names the two same-origin assumptions that stop
being true when the application and the API move to different subdomains.
- **A developer-console gallery of three candidate headers for the document editor, for the owner to choose between.**

The direction is to take the app's rail and top bar off the editor screen and replace both with one band that carries what each of them was carrying. Which band that is, is not obvious: the rail and the bar between them hold a way home, a way back to the matter's files, search, the build chip, notifications, the Time Sheet handle, two transfer registers and the profile menu, and a header thin enough to be worth the change cannot hold all of it.

So the three candidates are rendered rather than described, at `/developer-console/document-editor-headers`, from the shipping components and over a stand-in document canvas at a fixed frame height — the band's cost in canvas is the visible difference between them. **Continuous chrome** seats the document in the app's own ink bar and gives nothing up. **Document masthead** keeps the header the document already has and folds what survives of the app into its action row. **Path bar** makes the path itself the header, every rung from the docket to the document on one row. Each renders four states — editing, saving, read-only, and an editor that has lost its connection — each measured, so a band that grows when the document turns read-only is a number rather than a squint.

Nothing about the editor changed. The real edit route, the app shell and `ScreenHeader` are untouched, and the only file outside the new directory is the fixtures registry that makes the surface findable. Two limits are stated on the page itself rather than left to be discovered: the save readout is driven by a prop, because the editor does not report its save state to the host at all yet, so what is under review is a shape and not behaviour; and the product's one back control has no register for an ink band, which is a design-system gap the first variant would have to close.
- **Three merged designs had no ledger node at all, so the register could not see them and their open
owner flags had nowhere to land. Twenty-five nodes added across three new areas: exhibits, translation
services, and self-serve provisioning with the free evaluation tier.**

**These are not new scope, and the totals moving does not mean new work was promised.** Each of the
three designs is merged, which is to say the commitment was already made; the ledger simply never
learned about it, so the register was under-counting the program rather than over-counting it. This
is the same reasoning under which two shipped trust capabilities were given nodes last week —
recording work already committed is not the same as adding work. The owner reads the headline totals,
so it is worth saying plainly: 708 capabilities became 733, and not one of the 25 is a decision taken
here.

**Statuses are derived, not chosen.** Exhibits carries a merged design _and_ a merged sixteen-task
implementation plan with its slice fragment reporting no build begun, which the vocabulary calls
`planned` — eight nodes plus a root, with trial admission tracking `deferred` because the design
parks it and prints its three columns blank. Translation carries a merged design and no plan, which is
`designed` — six nodes plus a root, with human-attested certification `deferred` to the design's own
fourth slice. Self-serve is the one with code in it: registration is `shipped`, so its root is
`partial`.

**A finding worth stating: half of the self-serve design is already built.** The two-stage
registration split, the three-door role fork, the confirmed-registration outbox row and the
provisioning consumer that runs the existing provisioner off it are all on `main` under ADR-0280,
along with the `firm.display_name` split that took the firm's human name out of the unique resume
identity. What is _not_ built is everything the flags are about: no tier catalog, no tier column, no
quota ceiling, no upgrade-required refusal, and no lifecycle beyond provisioning.

**Eighteen of the twenty-three owner flags placed, on sixteen node lines; five left in their specs.**
The same rule as the last sweep: surface a
flag when the answer changes what gets built, leave out anything that only decides how an agreed
build is written. Placed — exhibits E1 and E4 (letter overflow past Z, which becomes a migration once
a label has been served, plus which numbering presets ship), E2 and E6 (how strict an issued set is),
E5 (package pagination against an already-stamped produced page), E7 (admission tracking at all), E8
(detecting prose references in a firm's existing documents); translation T1 (engine and vendor
posture), T2 (whether the provenance record exists), T3 (human certification), T4 (pasted text
recorded or ephemeral), T5 (derived sibling or new version), T8 (the machine-output statement on
every rendition); self-serve F1 (the free-tier numbers — the flag the founding-a-firm screen's
"starts on the free tier" line is literally waiting on), F2 (the reaping clock), F3 (trust on
verification or on payment), F4 (verification as review or attestation), F6 (metered tool allowances
or a hard lock). Left in their specs: exhibits E3 and translation T6 and T7, which decide wording and
plumbing on agreed builds, and self-serve F5 and F7, a legal-perimeter call and a nod to retire a
reserved route field.

No existing node's `status` was touched. `docs/now.md` is regenerated from the ledger, as always.
- **The period ledger at `/time`, and the cross-matter listing that had to exist first.** The sidebar's Time row was an announced Soon stub for a structural reason rather than a cosmetic one: `GET /api/v1/time-entries` answered one timekeeper on one day, or one matter entire, and returned an empty list for anything else. The top bar's firm-wide Time Sheet was therefore reading nothing at all, and flipping `shipped` would have linked to a screen with no read behind it.

The third listing shape closes that: a `from`/`to` span of work dates across every matter, narrowable to one timekeeper, matter or status, cursor-paged on the same `(work_date, id)` key the per-matter read walks so a cursor means one thing on both. `listTimeEntriesInRange` in `packages/timekeeping/src/queries.ts`; one added index (`time_entry_work_date_index`), because the unnarrowed span had no work-date-leading index to ride.

A period naming no timekeeper asks for the firm's whole record and is gated on `time:viewFirm`; naming somebody else is gated identically. Defaulting an ungated caller to themselves was considered and rejected — a listing that silently answers a narrower question than it was asked is the defect the per-matter status default already was. A span that reads backwards is refused rather than swapped.

The screen reuses what the matter's Time tab already had: the one grid, the entry record window, the status register, and the scope arithmetic the Time Sheet uses (which gains last-week and the two month spans — one function, two menus). It adds a Matter column, resolved client-side against the firm's matters rather than denormalized onto the row, and the period totals. Deliberately no free-text search: the period pages, and a box covering only the loaded rows would report a word missing from a month it never read.
- Time is entered in hours, in units, or as the span between two clock times.

Three ways of saying the same thing, because firms are three. **Hours** — "1:30", "1.5", "90m" — is what everybody understands and is always available. **Units** counts the firm's own billing increment: a practice that bills in tenths thinks in tenths, and asking that person to convert six units into 0.6 hours is asking them to do arithmetic the product already knows how to do. **A span** is the two clock times the work happened between, which is how somebody who was in a meeting from nine to half past ten actually remembers it.

All three are live at once and each is a view of the same minutes: type in any of them and the others follow.

**A unit is whatever the firm bills in, and is asked rather than assumed.** Six minutes is the prevailing default and a firm on quarter hours means two and a half times as much work by "two units" — so the increment is read from the firm's own setting, scoped to the matter and the member, and never guessed.

**How many of the three are on screen is the reader's own setting**, in the record window's menu. All three show by default, because a capability nobody can see is a capability nobody has; a member who only ever thinks in one of them can put the other two away. The last one standing cannot be turned off — a window with no way to state how long the work took cannot record time — so the control refuses rather than obeys, and says so.

A span that ends earlier than it starts is read as crossing midnight, because that is a real evening.
- Trust — bank charges, and the firm's own funds in a trust account. A trust bank account gets charged
by its institution, and until now the ledger had no way to record that: a firm's real bank statement
could not be reconciled, because the one item on it that no member authorized had nowhere to land.
The conduct rules answer that by permitting a firm to keep a small amount of its **own** money in the
account for the sole purpose of bearing those charges, and that is now wired — narrowly.

**A bank charge cannot be turned into a way to move client money, and that is a property of the
structure rather than a rule somebody remembers.** The record beside a firm-funds entry lives in its
own table which has **no column for a client, a matter, a node, or a payee** — so a row of it cannot
describe a movement of anybody else's money whatever a caller intends. The entry goes through a
second composition door that admits exactly two lines, the firm-funds balance and that same account's
bank leaf, and refuses everything else; the door client money goes through still refuses a firm-funds
line outright and was not relaxed to make room. Only two movements exist in the category — the firm
putting its cushion in, and the institution taking a charge out — and there is deliberately no
movement that pays anybody: paying a person out of a trust account is a disbursement and goes through
the disbursement queue with its authorization.

**A bank charge is never borne by client funds, enforced by the database.** The firm-funds balance
carries the same zero floor every matter ledger carries, so a charge larger than the firm's own money
in the account drives it below zero and the whole batch aborts. Recording such a charge is refused
with the remedy named: put the firm's funds in to cover it, then record it. Until then the statement
line sits unmatched and the reconciliation reports the difference, which is the honest state.

**The carve-out is off until a firm turns it on, per account, and it takes a capability of its own.**
`trust:firmFunds` is seeded to Owner/Admin alone — narrower than every other trust key, including the
authority to release a client's money. Opening it is refused on a pooled interest-bearing account:
the researched rules exempt that kind of account from service charges, so there is nothing for the
firm's funds to pay and putting them there would be commingling with no permitted purpose.

**The three-way proof learned about it.** The firm's cushion is a leg of the proof in its own right
and is never folded into the client total — a client leg that quietly included the firm's own money
would tie out while asserting that firm money is client money, and leaving the cushion out of the
comparison entirely would report a `book-to-client` disagreement on every account that enabled the
carve-out, poisoning the one signal that means something reached the ledger without going through the
composition guard. Closing a reconciliation freezes the cushion figure alongside the other three.

---

Trust — unclaimed client funds: the dormancy read and the firm's diligence file. A firm holding money
for somebody it can no longer reach has a continuing duty to make reasonable efforts to locate the
owner and distribute the funds, and to be able to evidence both afterwards. The platform now surfaces
the balances and holds the evidence.

**Nothing here escheats, sweeps, or moves on a timer.** In the jurisdiction researched for this
subsystem, designated client trust accounts are exempt from the state unclaimed-property presumption
outright — nothing escheats, no dormancy period runs against them, and the one onward destination the
rules name is permissive rather than compelled. So there is no countdown, and no screen says a firm
must act by a date.

**Dormancy is a comparison, not a column.** The read lists matter ledgers that still hold money and
have been quiet since a date **the reader states** — there is no default period, because the periods
differ by jurisdiction and several of them gate a permission rather than an obligation. Nothing is
stored, no sweep maintains it, and the same read against a wider window gives a different answer with
no state having changed. It reports two dates rather than one, because the rules' clocks run from
**receipt of the property** and not from the last thing that happened on the matter.

**Every locate attempt is recorded when it is made** — regular mail, certified mail, telephone, email,
a review of the firm's own records — with the address or number actually used, the outcome, and who
recorded it. That is the artifact a certification is built from and the one thing nobody can
reconstruct two years later. The file is append-only and one client ledger carries one open review at
a time.

**Every movement takes a person.** Closing a review as a distribution names a disbursement that
**already posted** through the ordinary authorized path; the closing composer receives no amount, no
payee, no date and no method, so there is nothing it could assemble into a ledger entry. It writes one
row and moves nothing, and the database independently refuses a closure that names a payment out of
another client's ledger.
- **Trust, first production round.** The matter's Trust section stops standing empty: `apps/web/src/lib/trust/matter-trust.svelte.ts` reads the firm's trust accounts, chooses one (the only open account, else the remembered one, else the first open one alphabetically), reads the matter's ledger against it — a 404 is "no ledger yet", a fact the surface states rather than a failure — and the three writes the section was designed around land as dialogs: a deposit, a payment out proposed under the firm's authorization posture (released at once or left pending with the eligible approvers named), and a transfer between two of the client's matters. Pending requests on the matter show in the notices band with approve, reject and withdraw. The sidebar's Trust row lights up over `apps/web/src/routes/(app)/trust`: the accounts register, the act that opens one, and per account the approval queue with its verbs, the statements and reconciliations as recorded, the bank-charge cushion, and the firm's authorization posture with its change. `POST /api/v1/trust/accounts` is the one route the slice lacked — every test had seeded an account through the domain package — and it derives the jurisdiction from the office rather than taking one. The trust-account listing now has one home, `$lib/trust/trust-api.ts`, which the report screen re-exports. The reconciliation workbench, statement entry and import, funding the cushion, and the unclaimed-funds file remain backend-only and say so on the screen.
- Trust — PDF bank-statement import for three-way reconciliation, designed. Owner extension T10. Design only: a spec, a five-slice implementation plan, and one ADR fragment at `status: Proposed`. No application code, no schema, no migration, no route, no parser.

**It adds one producer of rows that already have a home.** The reconciliation built under ADR-0246 is untouched — not the statement table, not the matcher, not the proof, not the close, not what a match means. Everything hard is upstream of the row, which is why the design is small.

**The governing sentence is that a reconciliation records a disagreement between the firm and the bank, and must never record a disagreement between the bank and our reading of the bank.** Both are differences between two numbers and they are opposites: the first is the whole product, which is why an unbalanced proof closes rather than being refused; the second is a defect wearing the first one's face, and once it is in `trust_bank_statement_line` it is indistinguishable from the bank having said it.

**The confidence model is arithmetic, not a score.** A statement states its opening balance, its closing balance, and the items between them, so rows that foot to the parsed closing balance are corroborated by two figures read independently from a different part of the page; a single misread digit breaks the footing by a power of ten, and a misidentified column breaks it comprehensively. Where a running balance is printed the check localizes to the line. A statement that does not foot is **refused**, not stored with the difference recorded. A recognizer's per-line confidence is retained on the row as provenance and used only to order a member's review and to explain a failure — a threshold on a confidence score is the silent-and-usually-right default ADR-0214 exists to refuse, and it cannot see structural uncertainty at all, which is where the damage lives.

**An imported line never causes a movement, and nothing has to be built to enforce that.** Four independent grounds: the line has no client and no matter, and trust attribution is derived from the matter's own client party rather than accepted from a caller; the bank leg is the only independent input in the proof, so a posting import would make the reconciliation compare the bank statement with itself and lose the one signal that means something reached the ledger without going through the composition guard; a movement caused by a parse has no authorizer, and `authorized_by` is a table CHECK; and it is a strictly larger authority than automatic matching, which the shipped matcher already refuses. Structurally, `trust_bank_statement_line` has no relation to the ledger and the only join is a match row a member created.

**Provenance is retained rather than recomputed**, because recognition is server-canonical rather than cross-architecture deterministic and model pins move — so re-running extraction next year is a fresh reading, not a reconstruction. The PDF, its digest, the extraction artifact with geometry and engine provenance, the parser version, the resolved profile, the rows with a locator back into the artifact, and the confirmed preview fingerprint are all kept. This also names an existing defect: the delimited importer takes its file in a request body and drops it after parsing, so a statement already recorded as `imported` cannot be re-derived from anything the platform kept.

**Parsing runs where the platform already parses, and no dependency is introduced.** Native text layer in pure Rust as WASM in the Worker over `crates/pdf-core`; pages that are scans in the OCR Container that is already deployed; table reconstruction in TypeScript beside the money rules it must obey. The one Rust addition is an exposure, not an engine — `textpos.rs` already computes glyph boxes and `textextract.rs` discards them for a single-column reading order that interleaves columns, which is fine for a keyword index and fatal for a table. A PDF table library is refused (the mature ones are Python or sit on a large C++ parser reading untrusted privileged bytes), and reading the statement with a model is refused on three grounds — non-reproducible output, no arithmetic corroboration of a generated number, and a consent question that is not a parsing detail.

**Nine flags (S1-S9) go to the owner**, numbered as their own series so an answer cannot be mistaken for an answer to a trust ledger flag. Four decide what gets built: whether a footing failure may be overridden, whether a scanned statement may be imported at all, how long a client's bank statement is retained and whether subject erasure reaches it, and whether the retention repair is applied backwards to the delimited path. The rest cover a pre-filled bank-charge composer for an unmatched service charge, one line matching several ledger entries, the capability the import runs under, whether a model may ever read a statement, and whether an import needs a second person.
- **Trust, second round.** The reconciliation workbench lands on the firm's Trust screen and its own route (`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/trust/reconciliations/[reconciliationId]`): a statement recorded by hand with its lines, or imported through the preview-then-confirm pair quoting the preview's fingerprint; a reconciliation opened on a statement; the three-way proof as it stands beside what a closed one froze; unmatched lines beside outstanding items with the suggestions' signals marked; matching and withdrawing by hand; closing the proof balanced or not. The cushion's three acts are forms behind `trust:firmFunds`. The unclaimed-funds file is a section of the account's record, reading dormancy against a day the reader states. Three backend additions: `GET /api/v1/trust/accounts/{id}/position` (book, client total, held, cushion, counts, from dated rows through the proof's own leg computation), `GET /api/v1/trust/reconciliations/{id}/matches` (withdrawals included), and the matter's number and title on each queued request.
- **`pnpm run lint:area-notes` and `pnpm run lint:catalog-coverage` — two rules the repository states and nothing held.**

Every code area is supposed to carry its own `CLAUDE.md` for local rules and the invariants that bind there. 55 of 85 workspace packages do. The 30 that do not are now a register that only shrinks, and it includes `packages/data-access` — the home of the firm-scoping golden rule — and `apps/web`. The gate also checks what the existing notes do, and they all pass: each opens with a title naming its own area (so a note copied from next door is caught) and says what the area is before anything else. What it deliberately does not require is the template's full section list: `## Local conventions` appears in 9 notes of 55, so requiring it would mint 46 headings reading "None."

The design system's coverage rule — catalog entry, behaviour test, visual regression — is held at the **component family**, the directory the package's `exports` map names one subpath each, not the file. The per-file version was measured first: 229 of 235 `.svelte` files under `src/lib` are exported, because a compound component exports its parts by design, and only 56 are imported by a story directly. That opens a 173-entry register of parts the family's own story already photographs — a form to fill in rather than a debt to pay. At family level the number is 79 of 83, and the four missing entries are the register: `field-label`, `folder-glyph`, `record-reference`, `service-marks`.

Coverage counts the story an entry is **about**, never a component that merely renders inside someone else's story: rendered-somewhere is enough for a screenshot to move and not enough for a person to find the component, and not finding it is how the second implementation gets built. The behaviour leg is clean from either side (87 of 91 stories carry `storybook/test` assertions). The visual-regression leg is not per-component checkable and is not pretended to be — `catalog.spec.ts` holds no component list at all, deriving its matrix from the built catalog at run time, so the gate asserts that derivation instead and leg three follows from leg one.
- **Account · Security adds, removes and re-issues two-factor. It was the account surface's last Soon
seam.** The sign-in screen had verified a code since the auth backend shipped, and no screen could set
one up. `$lib/account/two-factor.ts` wraps the plugin's `enable` → `verifyTotp`, `disable` and
`generateBackupCodes`, and words each refusal by its code. The add panel is one `ActionDialog` whose
three steps (password, authenticator, recovery codes) turn over in place and end on `"done"`. It is
offered only while the session says two-factor is off: in the pinned plugin, `enable` on an enrolled
account replaces the working secret and marks it verified with no code asked for.
`apps/api-worker/test/account-two-factor.test.ts` pins that behaviour and three other facts the page
relies on (the session reporting the change at once, a refused removal leaving it on, and replaced
recovery codes retiring the old set).

- **`QrCode` in the design system** (`@magna-carta/design-system/qr-code`), over `uqr`: pure
  TypeScript, no dependencies, and it returns the module matrix rather than markup. It is drawn as one
  SVG path in the chrome token pair, the one pair that stays dark-on-light in dark mode. Checked by
  decoding the rendered screenshots in both modes with an independent reader.
- **The authenticator issuer is "Magna Carta".** Unset, the plugin fell back to the library's
  `appName`, so a member's phone would have filed the account under "Better Auth". The fix is
  `TOTP_ISSUER` on the plugin, not the instance-wide `appName`.
- `account-seams` now guards the other direction: no account page claims a Soon badge or a control
  waiting on a backend.
- `ActionDialog` — the one panel an act is asked for in, and `RecordWindow`'s modal peer.

Thirty-four files in `apps/web` composed a modal panel by hand, and each re-derived the same seven mechanics: the open flag, the reset when it opens, the busy flag, the commit, the failure band, the refusal that disables the commit, and the footer. They had already drifted in every way drift was available — thirteen said "Cancel" where five said "Close" for the identical gesture, eighteen suppressed the corner dismiss where twelve kept it. **And not one of the thirty `Dialog` panels asked before it discarded**, so a stray Escape threw away a half-written write-off, credit note or new matter in silence. `RecordWindow` was given a guard for exactly that and could not lend it.

The shell owns what no caller may re-derive, and owns it by having no prop for it: the footer's geometry and the order of its two controls, the dismissal's word, the busy state, whether the corner dismiss shows, which primitive renders the panel, and the one close path every exit runs through. A caller differs on a closed set — a `fields` snippet, a `notice` slot the app puts its failure band in, `kind`, `width`, and a commit that reports `committed` or `refused`. `kind` is the line that carries the most weight: a form is a `Dialog`, a question is an `AlertDialog` with the role and the dismissal behaviour that implies. Four panels reached `AlertDialog` before this and thirty did not, with no rule behind the split.

The unsaved-work guard moved out of `record-window.svelte` into an internal both shells consume, so the product asks that question in one voice rather than in one window.
- **The UI standard has always required looking at the rendered page, and there was no tool that could
look.** `docs/conventions/ui-design.md` instructs the coordinator of a UI stream to verify
empirically before committing — screenshots, computed styles, interaction round-trips — and the
repository configured no browser. Every gate under it reads source text, so "the classes are right"
was machine-checked and "the screen is right" was somebody's word. The Chrome DevTools MCP server is
now declared in `.mcp.json`, and the standard says where to point it and what evidence a review owes.

The same standard delegates UI work to subagents "with the constraints, not just the task", and
there were no agent definitions to carry them — so each delegation restated the rules from memory.
`ui-builder` and `design-reviewer` now hold the binding constraints and the reading order.

**The third gap is the one that cost the most.** The auth flow went through fifteen mockup revisions
before it was built, and most of what those revisions settled was not about auth at all: headers are
title case, user-facing copy takes no em dashes, a duration in a sentence renders from the value
that governs it, every non-initial step of a flow carries the same back control, a resend counts
down visibly from the first send. Those are rules for every screen, and they lived in one task
description. `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md` is now their home — append-only, and read
before composing anything.
- **Undo, redo and reversal are designed as one contract, and the inventory that forced it is the
finding.** The platform ships **seven** distinct ways to take something back — two independent
client-side undo stacks, soft delete and restore, the discovery journal's exact compensation, void
and unvoid, the ledger's compensating entry, and two shapes of hard delete — and nothing joins them.
The emitted contract carries **thirty-three DELETE operations and five reversal operations of any
kind**. The per-firm schema carries **thirteen `deleted_at` columns and exactly one `deleted_by`**, so
twelve of the platform's thirteen soft-deleting tables cannot answer the first question a deleted view
is asked.

**Three things are called undo and only one of them is.** A surface stack reverses gestures inside a
session; a record's reversibility is a property of an operation, independent of who is looking; and
deletion's lifecycle is a third question that ADR-0049 has settled for files and nowhere else. Every
defect found is a boundary crossing between those three. The file manager's stack covers movement and
stops, its module explaining that a delete is already recoverable through Deleted Files — a Layer-A
stack deferring to Layer B correctly, by hand, and only there. The Time Sheet refuses a step for a
void for the same reason and has to say so in a hand-written sentence naming two other surfaces.

**The proposal is that reversibility becomes route metadata.** `RouteMeta` already carries
`operationId`, `permission`, `audited` and `idempotency`, emitted as `x-mc-*` and gated by conformance
fitness functions; a `reversal` field joins them, as a discriminated union over what the platform can
actually do — `inverse`, `compensating`, `none` — required on every
mutating route, with a `none` obliged to carry the sentence that says why. The count of irreversible
operations becomes a number CI knows. The dialog's recoverability line stops being a string in a
Svelte file and becomes the rendering of the declaration, so "It moves out of the list and stays
recoverable" cannot drift from what delete does.

**Three defects verified in the source, each a consequence of the same conflation.** The Time Sheet
announces "Undid {label}" the instant the stack pops while the write-through is unawaited, so a reader
is told the record went back before it has. The same undo writes back **every** row on the sheet
rather than the ones the step changed, because a snapshot cannot know which fields moved — which also
writes over a row somebody changed elsewhere. And `notes.deleteNote` hard-deletes a note whose own
design rules that there is no hard delete in the product and that retraction is a state.

Also proposed: one `HistoryStack` and one `UndoRedoControls` in the design system, taking the inverse-
command model from `MoveHistory` and the bounding, labels and announcement helper from `SheetHistory`,
so the split control exists once instead of twice; a named deletion vocabulary separating soft delete,
detach, deactivate, tombstoned hard delete and unrecorded hard delete, with soft delete as the default
for anything a member authored; the deleted view as a pattern rather than a screen; and the ruling
with the widest reach — that an acknowledgement dialog is offered **only** where the declaration is
`none`, which is the Nielsen Norman Group posture the product already follows by instinct with one
alert dialog in the entire application.

A generic undo journal was considered and rejected on two independent grounds: it would hold prior
values of privileged content, which `audit_log.metadata` is redacted by construction to exclude, and a
generic backward replay cannot know that unvoiding a cost-converted time entry is forbidden or that a
coding act's undo must be exact to the rows it wrote. Those are domain rules and the subsystems
already express them as routes; the declaration points at those routes rather than replacing them.

No code, no schema, no migration, no route. Eight owner decisions, five build slices, and one
deliberate omission — the implementation plan waits, because slice 1's census changes what the later
slices contain.
- Unified identity and authentication methods — the design for passkeys, one-time sign-in links, firm
identity providers and client-portal identity, treated as one surface rather than four bolt-ons.
Design only: a spec, a six-slice implementation plan, and six ADR fragments. No application code, no
schema, no migration.

**The framing sentence comes first and everything inherits it.** A method proves you are the principal;
it never decides who the principal is, and it never decides what the principal may then do. The failure
the design exists to prevent is a method quietly acquiring one of the other two jobs — and one instance
of that is already in the tree, where a credential-issuing event (the invitation's `kind`) is the only
record of whether an account is staff or a client.

**Three nouns carry the whole surface.** A **principal** with an immutable `principal_kind`; an
**authentication-method register** projected over Better Auth's four credential tables, because three of
the questions the platform must answer — may this account use a password, is this the last method, what
was enrolled after that sign-in — are asked across those tables and answerable in none of them; and an
**assurance** level (`mailbox` < `credential` < `multiFactor` < `phishingResistant`) with an
`authenticated_at` stamped on the session. Which methods an account may use resolves most-restrictive-wins
over a platform floor that is code beside the permission registry, firm narrowing through the settings
registry, and actual enrolment.

**Client-portal identity becomes structural, and the load-bearing half is the one usually skipped.**
`principal_kind` is NOT NULL with an immutability trigger, `RouteMeta` gains `principals` enforced by a
new chokepoint admission gate, and a portal principal holds no per-firm `member` row so RBAC grants it
nothing anywhere. But the change that matters is
`CHECK ((principal_kind = 'portalClient') = (firm_id IS NULL))`: `user.firm_id` is what every
firm-scoped surface reads to place a caller, so leaving it populated for a portal client makes a
forgetful surface fail **open** inside that firm, while emptying it makes the same surface resolve no
firm and answer the reserved cross-firm 404. The community board's invitation-counting subquery — whose
own comment asks for exactly this — becomes one session field.

**Recovery is the part the design spends its judgement on**, because recovery is where account takeover
lives and any method can be added. Every recovery path is an authentication method with the ceremony
removed, so it is enrolled, budgeted against the shared ladder, and audited as one — a passkey defeated
by "email us a link" is a mailbox credential wearing a passkey's clothes. The mechanism is a hold:
announced immediately to every channel of record plus the firm's Owners and Admins (never one channel,
because the attacker holds one), delayed, cancellable by any valid session or one click from any
notified channel, and on effect revoking every session and every method enrolled since the request.
Its converse closes the commonest takeover shape — enrolling a method is itself a notified event. The
primary path is firm-administered and reuses the shipped three-fact invitation machinery; platform
recovery is bounded to the sole-Owner case and deliberately not routed through the support-grant
framework, which is consent-anchored and cannot stretch to somebody who by definition cannot consent.
Four paths are refused outright, including knowledge-based answers, since a firm's own data is largely
in public court records.

**Home-realm discovery answers about a domain, never an address.** Silently refusing and silently
allowing are both wrong, and resolving on blur is worse than either. Discovery resolves on submit
against a domain the firm verified by publishing a DNS TXT record — a fact anyone can already resolve —
which is why the map may only ever be populated by verification and never by an administrator pasting a
list of addresses. `exclusive` enforcement removes the password from the register rather than ignoring
it, and cannot be turned on until the firm's Owner holds a passkey, because a provider outage must not
lock a firm out of its own practice-management system.

**The library was verified rather than assumed**, per golden rule 11: Better Auth supplies passkeys,
magic links, email OTP, Turnstile, cross-domain one-time tokens, `session.freshAge`, and — as a separate
MIT package — OIDC and SAML single sign-on with domain matching. It supplies no principal kind, no
method register, no assurance, no domain verification, no interception of a password submit, and no
recovery hold. Two of its defaults are inverted and pinned by test because both are wrong for an
invitation-only platform: magic-link auto-registration, and its documented removal of an unverified
account's password on verify, which lands on exactly the state an invited member occupies between
redemption and setting a password. Account linking is set explicit for the same class of reason. Three
stale facts in the tree are scheduled for repair in slice 1, including the two-factor plugin's own new
lockout, which would otherwise disagree with the platform's published attempt budget.

**Step-up becomes route metadata** over the `stepUpRequired` field the problem contract already carries
for the malware-flagged download, with a counter-rule so the gate does not metastasise: step-up is for
acts that are irreversible or that create a new way in, and everything else is RBAC's job.

Fifteen questions are flagged rather than decided, each shipping as a configurable value with a
recommended default: whether a passkey may stand alone, whether a link may establish a session, whether
a firm may narrow or weaken a control, the second-factor floor and its grace, the three recovery hold
windows, platform-administered recovery, forced re-enrolment after a spent recovery code, the single
sign-on enforcement modes and break-glass, the federated session cap, the step-up list, portal method
strength, whether one mailbox that is staff at one firm and a client of another gets one account or
two, and whether the shared attempt ladder becomes a Durable Object. Every one of them changes the
platform's security posture, which makes it the owner's call and not the design's.
- **`firm-resources.ts` — the one declaration of what a firm owns, because it cannot be discovered.**

A firm's record spans four things created at different moments by different code: control-plane rows,
a SQLite Durable Object, an R2 bucket, and possibly a managed natural-language search instance. None
of them can be enumerated from outside. There is no API that lists Durable Object instances, none
that maps a bucket back to its firm, and `ai_search_instance` is deliberately the sole index of the
instances. So the set can only be DECLARED, and anything missing from the declaration is invisible to
everything that walks it.

That is not hypothetical: writing the platform reset by hand missed the search instances entirely.
They would have been left running and unnameable against an account ceiling of 5,000.

Ordering is part of the declaration rather than a detail of any one caller. `destroyOrder` puts the
control plane last because it is the index of everything above it, and the tests pin the properties
that make a walk safe — control plane last, every orphanable resource strictly before it, positions
unique — so a caller that walks the list in order is correct by construction. Offboarding, a
data-subject export and the reset script read one list instead of three drifting copies.

What is not built yet, and is named in the file: a fitness scan that fails a per-firm resource
provisioning creates and the manifest never hears about, on the model of the PII/erasure registry's
attribution function.
- **In-meeting chat, kept on the record** — the owner's ruling of 2026-09-20, and it makes `meeting_message`
the meeting subsystem's first stored content. Everything the record held until now was identifiers
and instants, because the audio, the video and the screen share are routed between browsers and
reach no storage here at all. A chat message is a thing somebody said, so it carries what a filed
message carries: it is retained under the matter, it is registered as personal data, and it can be
taken back.

**A message hangs from the STAY, not from the member.** Being in the room is what made it sayable,
so the row names the stay it was said from and the member is resolved through it — which means
somebody whose connection dropped and who dialled back in has each message attributed to the stay it
was actually said in, rather than to a person who was present through a gap they were absent for.
The stay is named BY VALUE (`participant_kind` + `participant_id`, no foreign key) because a
member's stay is a `meeting_attendance` row and an external guest's will be a `meeting_guest_stay`
row: `meeting_attendance.user_id` is NOT NULL, so a foreign key onto it here would have barred every
guest from chat, and relaxing that afterwards is exactly the table rebuild this schema refuses on a
table anything references. `@magna-carta/meetings` writes the literal `'member'`; nothing writes
`'guest'` yet, on the call and text log's reasoning for its own producer column.

**Taking a message back is not a delete.** `redacted_at` and `redacted_by_user_id` blank the body and
keep the row, held from both sides by a CHECK — a redacted row's body is empty and a live row's is
not — so the transcript says a message was there and that somebody removed it. A second removal
answers with the row as it stands rather than moving an instant somebody's record already carries.
The author may take back their own words and a member holding `meetings:host` may take back
anybody's, and both stay possible after the meeting has ended: the words outlive the gathering.

**Three routes** — `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` (idempotent, 201),
`GET /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages` (cursor-paged, oldest first, with `since` for a poller)
and `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/messages/{messageId}/redact` — all on `meetings:join`, with
the host question asked inside the redaction handler because the AUTHOR may do it without holding
`meetings:host`. Every one reads the meeting through the same visible-matter gate the rest of the
subsystem composes, so a walled matter's transcript is as absent as its room. The room will later
relay a `message` frame so a message reaches the other browsers as it is said; the route is the
record either way, because a write through the socket would put the firm's record in a Durable
Object's transient storage, which empties when the room does.

**The audit rows carry identifiers, instants and a character COUNT** — never the body, and least of
all on the redaction, where an audit row recording what was removed would be the one place the
removed words survived.
- **Firm Profile is live: the firm's name is set from Settings and reaches the paper.** `PUT /api/v1/firm/profile` sits behind a new `firm:manageProfile`, seeded to Owner/Admin alone.
