list in `tooling/check-scoped/unsafe-autofix-rules.mjs`, alongside the three rewrites already there.
The exclusion is fix-pass only: `pnpm check:scoped`, `pnpm check` and the editor still report the
finding, they simply stop applying it unattended.
- **`check-snapshots` fails on a forked snapshot chain instead of reporting "nothing to do".** Merging
two branches that each added a per-firm migration leaves two snapshots naming one parent, and
drizzle refuses every `generate` against that lineage — but the pinned drizzle-kit reports the
refusal as an `Error:` line and **exits 0**, so `refresh-snapshot.mjs`, which read the status alone,
took a refused generate for "the schema matches the snapshot". It passed through two such merges on
one branch.

Two layers now. `refresh-snapshot.mjs` looks for the fork itself before generating — any two
snapshots sharing a `prevId` — and names the files and the repair: keep the one already on main,
delete the branch's, refresh, then let `generate` report "No schema changes". And any `Error:` line
drizzle-kit prints is a failure whatever its status, which covers the failures that are not forks.
Both are proven against the real pre-repair commit and a stub that errors at exit 0.

The broader gate was not blind: `tooling/migration-integrity`'s lineage check does catch the fork
(checked against the same commit). What it could not do is stop a person who ran the snapshot check
alone — which the repair message itself told them to re-verify with. That message now names the
generate as the proof.
- Two pieces of chrome every surface inherits: a full-screen panel squares its corners, and a table's totals sit on the bottom of its frame.

**A modal filling the screen has square corners.** A radius says the panel is a sheet lying on top of something; at full size there is nothing underneath it, and the curve reads as four notches of desktop showing through the corners of the application. Fixed on the shared modal frame rather than in the record window, so any shell that grows an expand gesture inherits it.

**A totals strip sits on the bottom edge of its frame, not under the last row.** A ledger fills the height it is given, so the ordinary case is a table with room beneath it — and the strip is held down by stickiness, which does nothing while there is nothing below it to scroll past. The totals of a four-row ledger were coming to rest halfway up the screen with a band of empty surface below them. The table now asks for its frame's full height and a scenery row takes the difference, so the records keep the one line each the density gives them.

Table layout does not behave the way it reads, and that row's placement was settled by measuring a real browser rather than by reasoning: in the table's foot, or as a percentage on the cell rather than the row, it is given nothing at all and the surplus is handed to the last record, which stretches to fill; with a zero-height body the records keep their height but are pushed to the bottom, putting the gap above them. As the last row of the body it takes the whole surplus and everything else stays put.

**A date field's label sits its control on the same baseline as the fields beside it.** It was omitting the line-height every other field label sets, so a date field started a few pixels below its neighbours and a row of three read as two fields and a mistake.
- **The pre-push hook took its migration-integrity check through the test runner, so an unrelated suite
running in another worktree could fail the push — under the words "migration integrity", which reads
as lineage corruption.** It failed that way twice in one session while another agent was building
elsewhere; both times the same check passed standalone in about 600 ms, and both times the printed
label sent the reader looking for a broken journal. The second lesson taken from it was `--no-verify`,
which is the expensive part: a hook that cries corruption over contention does not just waste a
diagnosis, it teaches people to switch the hook off.

The checks never needed a runner. They are structural assertions over the committed journal, the
`.sql` files and the `meta/` snapshots, plus one apply of the whole chain into an in-memory
`node:sqlite` — no Miniflare, no browser, no worker pool, no fixtures. They now live at
`tooling/migration-integrity/` as a plain script, and the three callers all drive that one module:
the pre-push hook and the gate's `governance` job run `node tooling/migration-integrity/index.mts`
directly, and a Vitest twin runs the same functions with the normal suite. `packages/database/test/migration-integrity.test.ts`
is gone — its content moved wholesale rather than being copied, so the hook and the suite cannot
drift into disagreeing about what a sound lineage is.

Two things were tightened while the checks moved. A lineage that loads zero migrations now fails
instead of passing: every rule above it is satisfied vacuously by an empty set, and a guard that
clears nothing is indistinguishable from a guard that ran. And any error raised while taking the
checks — an unreadable journal, an absent `drizzle/` directory — is reported as a failure rather than
allowed to look like a clean run.

**The gate's `lint:test-collection` was also reported as counting seven files more than the gate
collects. It does not, and the seven have a name.** Measured on a quiet machine at 949 registered
test files: the lint asserts 656 for `test-node`, an unfiltered run executes `Test Files 656 passed
(656)`, and the two CI shards execute 328 and 328 with no file in both and no file in neither.
`test-worker` reconciles the same way at 238.

The reported 649 came from an invocation carrying **ten** of `test-node`'s **fourteen** positional
paths. The four missing ones — `apps/{recovery,scan,search,sign}-worker` — hold exactly 7 files and
41 tests, which is the whole of the reported gap in both figures (656 − 7 = 649, 7475 − 41 = 7434).
Nothing runs nowhere. The path list wraps over five YAML lines and gets copied short, and a short
list does not fail: it runs a subset and reports green, which is the same property that made the
original mis-scoped filter invisible. `pnpm run lint:test-collection --print-invocations` now emits
each job's command resolved onto one line so a count can be reproduced without retyping anything.

What the episode did expose is that the lint had no way to be checked. It existed to prove something
about the gate, and its own set arithmetic — floor, union, disjointness, drift — had never been run
against a known-bad input, which is the same posture as the workflow comment that confidently claimed
a mis-scoped path "fails loud" and was false for months. So the lint moved to
`tooling/lint-test-collection/`: the arithmetic is now separable and covered by
`collection.test.mjs`, where each assertion is shown to bite on the failure it names and to stay
quiet on the near-miss that is legitimately fine (a file claimed by two projects is two entries, not
a double-payment). One real hole is closed with it — the lint checked that every invocation it holds
still exists in the workflow, but never the reverse, so a fourth test job added to `gate.yml` and
never registered would have taken a share of the suite that the coverage check then credited to
nobody. The invocation list is now closed in both directions.

`docs/conventions/build-performance.md` records what the lint proves and, newly, where that proof
stops: at collection, not execution, with the measurement that currently bridges the two and the
warning not to read a shard's count as a job's.
- **A second person on a guest's link no longer walks into the room under the first guest's name.**
An arrival on a link whose stay is already open still returns that stay, but now puts it back at
the door under the name just typed, so a host sees who is arriving and admits them deliberately.
The room drops the earlier holder's tile and socket at once. The name the stay carried before, and
who admitted it, stay on the arrival's audit row.

**Sending a fresh link closes the stay the old one held**, in the same write, and the fresh link
arrives at the door. Withdrawing a link and replacing one both close the stay `left` rather than
`removed`, so inviting the person again brings them back instead of telling them they were put out.
A fresh link, whether rotated or re-sent, also starts its arrival count again, so a guest whose
connection kept failing is never sent a link that is already used up.

**A link says why it stopped working.** An expired link this deployment signed is answered
`410 guest-link-expired` with no database read, instead of the flat 404 a guessed token gets, and
it is counted under its own reason. An arrival whose link changed under it is told whether it was
withdrawn, replaced, used up or expired. A link whose person has been taken off the event is refused
as withdrawn, and the refused arrival is recorded.

**The meeting socket takes a guest's grant as a WebSocket subprotocol** (`meeting-guest`, then the
grant), and answers with the bare protocol name, so the credential stays out of the socket's
address. The `guest` query parameter is still accepted, on the socket route alone; the messages and
departure routes now refuse it even on an upgrade.

**An invitation whose e-mail could not be sent is no longer remembered as sent.** Nothing is stored
under the request's idempotency key until the mail has gone, so the host's retry sends a fresh link
rather than replaying a success the guest never received.
- **Six corrections to hosting and the door, found in review.**

**A hand-over leaves the outgoing host a co-host.** `grantHosting` now inserts a co-host grant for
the person stepping down, in the same batch as the revocation, so there is no instant in which they
hold nothing. Handing the room over is not leaving it: dropping the outgoing host to an ordinary
member took the mute, the spotlight and the door away from somebody who had been hosting a second
earlier, with nothing on any screen to say so. `revokeHostGrantStatement` takes an optional `role` for
the same reason — a batch that closes one grant and opens another for one member is the only place
"whatever they hold" stops being one row, and the hand-over now names the grant it is closing so a
race is caught by the guard rather than by a raw constraint one statement later.

**A co-host may stand down.** `POST /api/v1/meetings/{meetingId}/hosts/{userId}/revoke` naming
YOURSELF is a resignation and is anybody's to make; the one refusal is the sole grant-holder, because
a host resigning out of a room where nobody else holds anything leaves a running meeting with nobody
running it. Its own audit event, `meetings.meeting.hostingResigned`, because both rows carry the
caller as the actor and one name would make "did somebody stand down or were they stood down" a
question you answer by comparing identifiers.

**Two co-hosts and an absent host no longer leave a room permanently hostless.**
`countOtherHostsPresent` counted every live grant, so each co-host saw the other and neither could
claim a room nobody was holding. It now counts a live HOST grant whose holder is in the room. A
co-host does not prevent the claim; the host does.

**The door is now shut in the same statement as the arrival.** The join path read the lock and the
lobby a round trip before its insert, so a host shutting the door in that instant had the arrival
land in a locked room — and a host turning the LOBBY on in the same instant put somebody straight
into a discussion the door was opened to keep them out of. Both conditions are now predicates on
`insertAttendanceUnderCapStatement` and, inverted, on the waiting insert, so the guarded write rolls
the whole batch back rather than half-landing a stay in a room that is shut.

**Removing somebody who was still at the door leaves no key behind.** The room's release only knew
the `participant:` keyspace, so a removal from the lobby closed the stay in the record and left a
`waiting:` key — the host's own panel went on offering to admit somebody the record says is not in
the meeting, and the key kept arming the door's grace deadline.

**A lock or lobby write that changed nothing no longer disturbs the room.** Both routes now skip the
room call when the service reports nothing moved, rather than spending a room-state broadcast on
every socket to restate what each of them already draws.
- **Four tests that were red on `main` are green again, and two of them found real gaps.** All four had passed through unseen because the gate ran nothing on `main` for a month, and each is a seam between two branches that merged in quick succession.

- When the column controls moved into each header's right-click menu, the trailing-pinned column's held pin did not come with them: the grid model already refused to toggle a `pinnedEnd` column, but the menu offered "Pin Status" as if it could, and the Time Sheet story still clicked a Columns button that no longer existed. The menu now shows a trailing-pinned column as pinned and disabled, titled "always keeps its place at the trailing edge", and the story asserts that through the header menu.
- The masthead's "Compact density" story rendered two page banners for comparison, which axe rejects; the comparison masthead now sits inside a labelled section, where a header is that section's header rather than a second banner.
- The conformance suite's committed operation list still named the four notes operations the edit-and-delete model replaced; it names the four that replaced them.
- The export-snapshot write on a member's shelf (`recordExportSnapshot`) put its object into the firm bucket with no dimensions, which the R2 dimension scan exists to catch: an object nothing can scope. It now carries the new firm-scoped class `export-snapshot` (`@magna-carta/object-dimensions`), on the same footing as `download-bundle`, since its figures may span matters and the shelf is the member's.

One more collision of the same day is recorded rather than fixed here: the matter-status window (#473) composes its own `Dialog.Content`, which the one-shell lint (#466) rejects. It stands as an allowance in `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`, on the reading that it is a record window's shape, and the migration is owed to the stream that owns the screen.
- **A bare `Combobox.GroupHeading` throws when the listbox opens, and four pickers shipped one.**

The heading finds the identity it labels on the `Group` above it, so without one the context lookup throws — on the press rather than on render, which is why it stayed invisible: the "no matches" line is only drawn when the list is empty or fully narrowed. `matter-picker.svelte` was returning a client crash report from the Messaging screen for exactly that reason. `time-zone-picker.svelte`, `participant-picker.svelte` and the time record window's document picker carried the same line and are fixed with it.

The design system had already written this down, in `undo-redo-controls.svelte`: "Both hand-built copies of this control shipped without it."
- **The cost listing narrowed to drafts exactly as the time listing did.** Asking for a matter's costs
with no status returned only the draft ones; everything submitted, approved, invoiced or voided was
excluded, and the contract declared the parameter optional with no default and no note. A matter
that had been billing for a year showed almost nothing.

An absent status now means every status. Narrowing to one remains the work-in-progress question, and
the contract says so.

The listing resolves the vendor's directory name in the same statement rather than answering with an
identifier. A matter with fifty disbursements would otherwise be fifty lookups to print one column.
Two outer joins, because a vendor is optional on a cost and may be a person or an organization; the
screen tells "no vendor recorded" from "the directory entry is gone", which are different facts and
`vendorId` is what distinguishes them.

The Costs section is built over the repaired read, replacing a fixture table. It shows each cost's
status and its hard-or-soft class, and totals what the firm advanced beside what it may recover —
the difference being what the firm decided to absorb, which is a decision worth seeing rather than
one figure hiding it. Voided costs are excluded from both, since a withdrawn cost was never advanced.

**Both silent defaults are now gone, and there were only two.** The other seven query defaults in
the route surface are page sizes and explicit nulls, so this was a repeated mistake rather than a
class needing a gate.
- **Asking for a matter's time answered with its drafts, and nothing said so.** The per-matter listing
defaulted its status filter to `draft` when the caller named none. The contract declares that
parameter optional with no default and no note, so a client reading it would expect the matter's
time record; what came back excluded every entry that had been submitted, approved, invoiced or
voided. A matter with a year of billed work read as nearly empty.

An absent status now means every status, which is what a matter's time record is. Narrowing to one
is still available and is the work-in-progress question, asked by a different caller for a different
reason; the contract now says which is which.

The listing also resolves the timekeeper's name in the same statement rather than answering with the
identifier. A matter with forty entries would otherwise be forty reads to print one column. The join
is outer: a member can be archived while the time they recorded stays on the matter, and that reads
as an honest absence rather than a user handle where a person's name belongs.

The Time section is built over the repaired read, replacing a fixture table. It shows the status of
every entry, because a voided line and a billed line are not the same fact, and it totals only the
billable time that still counts. Starting a timer from the screen waits on the timer surface and
renders as an affordance that says so.
- **Every frame a meeting socket sends now spends from a budget.** The room throttled a `sync`, a
layer change, a hand and a reaction, and nothing else — so `publish`, `subscribe`, `renegotiate`,
`close` and the speaking half of `presence` could each arrive as fast as a browser could write to a
socket. The first four are a billed call to the routing service apiece, presence writes the
participant record, and every refusal emitted an unsampled telemetry event, so the cheapest thing to
send was the most expensive thing to serve. A per-socket token bucket —
`FRAME_BUDGET_PER_SECOND` (20) and `FRAME_BUDGET_BURST` (40) in `@magna-carta/meeting-protocol`,
on the wire because a client has to know the pace it is held to — is now spent in
`dispatchClientFrame` ahead of the parse, so a frame the room will not read costs it no parse
either. Over budget is `refused: rate-limited` with the socket kept open, host frames included.

Underneath it, the four acts that reach the routing service carry per-participant windows on the
existing `syncAt`/`layerAt` pattern (`publishAt`, `subscribeAt`, `renegotiateAt`, `closeAt`),
claimed past every refusal the roster can decide and ahead of the session, so a frame the room was
never going to act on spends nothing. They are refused rather than dropped because the browser is
waiting on an answer to each of them. A request to unmute carries a window kept on the member being
ASKED — two hosts taking turns would otherwise each stay inside a budget of their own — and the
budget's own refusals are sampled into telemetry on the terms the storage budget is, because a flood
recorded frame-by-frame costs more than the flood. The load harness sends six frames per socket
across a whole pass, so its pace is unchanged and its counts are unchanged.

**A room is claimed from inside it.** `claimHosting` asked only whether any OTHER grant-holder had
an open stay, so a member holding `meetings:host` who had never joined could take a live meeting
sixty seconds after the host's tunnel dropped, from outside it — and the record would show a host
nobody in the meeting had met. Nobody hands this grant over, so being in the room, or standing at
its door, is the whole of what makes taking it an act of the meeting rather than of the permission
key. Refused `meeting-not-joined`; the door case is unchanged and the claimer is still admitted by
the same batch, which is how a lobby-on meeting whose host has gone gets a host at all.

**Two smaller ones from the same review.** A reconnect no longer hands back a grant that was
withdrawn while the socket was being opened — an existing participant record keeps its own
`hostRole`, and the routes' `hostingChanged` stays the only writer of truth after the first welcome.
And the platform operator's read into a live room (`routes/meeting-inspect.ts`) is `audited: true`,
writing the operator, the firm and the meeting to the control plane's `auth_audit` before the room
is read.
- **A newly provisioned firm's bucket accepts browser uploads.** The first production upload failed with "Nothing answered while sending the bytes to storage": the browser PUTs bytes straight to a presigned URL on the firm's own bucket, which is a cross-origin request, and the bucket carried no CORS policy — so the preflight was refused before a byte moved, and the app could only report that nothing answered. Provisioning had never configured CORS; the runbook step that applies it was written for the shared platform bucket, and a firm bucket minted by `firm-provisioner.ts` got neither. `firm-resource-provider.ts` now carries `configureBucketCors`, run unconditionally on every provisioning run that reaches the bucket step alongside the notifications and expiry rules, translating the rule set (now a module beside the code that reads it, `apps/api-worker/src/files/browser-upload-cors.ts`, replacing the checked-in JSON artifact, and naming the `workers.dev` serving origins too) into the REST API's shape and folding in the deployment's `APP_BASE_URL`; `pnpm run emit-r2-cors` prints it as the dashboard's JSON for the by-hand path. Buckets that existed before the step — the platform bucket and the one production firm — still take the policy by hand; the runbook's section 15 now says so, and names the read that tells whether a bucket has one.
- **A password is chosen at registration, and the credential is committed with the account.** Every joining path — `registrations.confirm`, the firm-provision consumer's owner adoption, `members.invite`, invitation redemption — created a `user` row with no credential `account` row, on the theory that the mailed password-reset link would bring one into being. It does: Better Auth's reset endpoint inserts a credential account when `findAccounts` turns up none (verified against the installed 1.6.22, `api/routes/password.mjs`). But it only does so if the mail arrives and somebody acts on it, so a deployment with no `EMAIL_FROM` — which resolves the logging adapter and delivers nothing — produced accounts nobody could ever sign in to. The only symptom was the library logging `Credential account not found` from `api/routes/sign-in.mjs`.

`StartRegistrationRequest` now carries `password` (optional at the schema layer, bounded by Better Auth's own configured 8–128; required by the two doors that create something, refused as a field-level 422 naming the rule). It is hashed in that request with the library's own hasher and stored on `registration.credential_hash` — a new nullable column, so a registration in flight across the deploy still completes the account-less way it started. Confirming inserts the `user` row, its credential `account` row and the verified-email flag in ONE batch; the founding door passes the same verifier through `provisionFirm`, which commits it with the owner. `ConfirmRegistrationResponse` gains `next: signIn | checkEmail`. `joining-credentials.ts` is the one home for the hash and the account statement.

Redemption deliberately still mails its link: the code, surname and date of birth prove no mailbox, and that link is the only thing standing between somebody who guessed all three and another person's account.

**And an unguarded send no longer escapes as a 500.** `registrations.start` answers a retryable `503` (`mail-undeliverable`, Error ID, retry window) and keeps the row it committed — both branches identically, so a mail outage cannot become the account-existence oracle the endpoint is built to deny. The reset-based paths could not be guarded at the call site at all: Better Auth's `runInBackgroundOrAwait` awaits the send and swallows what it throws into its own logger, so `api.requestPasswordReset` resolves whether or not a mail left. The guard therefore sits on the PORT `app.ts` hands the library, where the failure is counted (`email.delivery_failed`, dimensions `surface` + `messageClass`) and correlated. No send path anywhere logs a body. `createAuth` also reads `baseURL` from `APP_BASE_URL` when set, silencing the library's cold-start warning.
- **`pnpm test tooling` collected nothing and reported that the directory had no tests. It now collects
all 34 files, and a filter that genuinely selects nothing says which of the two happened.** The
snapshotter also reaps its own working copies again, after ~125 of them filled a disk.

Three unrelated pieces of developer-tooling friction, batched because they live in the same two
directories.

**A directory filter now resolves across projects.** The runner matches a positional filter against
each project's OWN root-relative paths, and every `tooling/*` project roots at its own directory —
so `tooling` matched nothing anywhere: relative to `tooling/clean`, its one test file is
`select.test.mjs`, a string not containing "tooling". `packages` and `apps` had the same shape. That
made the documented idiom — the root `CLAUDE.md` says to filter by PATH, not by test name — fail on
the directories most likely to be filtered that way, and answer with "No test files found", which
reads as _nothing here has tests_ rather than _your filter matched nothing_. An absolute path always
did resolve, which is why the gate's test jobs spell every path `"$PWD/tooling"` — not a style choice
there either, after a relative `packages` filter once collected zero of the packages' tests while the
gate stayed green. `pnpm test` now resolves a directory filter to its absolute path before the runner
sees it (`tooling/test-single-flight/path-filters.mjs`), so the short spelling means the working one
and nobody has to know the gate's idiom. Filters that are not directories — `select.test.mjs`, an
option's value — are passed through untouched.

**And a selection that provably cannot match is refused before the lock is taken**, naming the filter
and saying that it matched nothing rather than that the directory is empty. The one refusal condition
is proof, not heuristic: the project list in `vite.config.ts` is closed, so a directory with no
registered project at, above, or inside it can never yield a file however the filter is spelled. A
directory that does hold a project but whose `include` globs happen not to cover it is left to the
runner — proving that case would mean re-implementing glob resolution, and a wrong refusal blocks a
run that would have worked.

**The load-profile snapshotter reaps its own working copy.** It `mkdtemp`s a directory per load and
copies the whole snapshot database into it; nothing removed them, and ~125 accumulated to ~8 GB until
the box hit 100% disk. Reaping now belongs to the code that created the directory — the only code
that knows its name — on close, in a `finally` so a failed handle-close still reaps, and on process
exit, because the measure CLI is a straight-line script whose mid-run throw never reaches its own
`close()`. That is how they leaked. As a backstop for a run killed outright, `vp run clean` sweeps
abandoned copies older than 24 h. The sweep matches the `mkdtemp` name shape exactly rather than by
prefix, so it cannot take the fixture cache that shares the prefix and belongs to a different
creator, and the age bound is the whole safety argument for deleting by name: without it the sweep
would race a live run and delete the database it was measuring against.

**The inner loop's wasm-artefact precondition is left as it is, deliberately, and now says why.** It
looked like the one unconditional step in a gate that scopes everything else to the diff — svelte-check,
the Rust gate, drizzle snapshots and the fitness sweep all skip with a stated reason. Scoping it to
the diff is nevertheless wrong, and measuring said so: in a fresh worktree `vp run typecheck` fails
with twelve `TS2307`s on the missing generated `.d.ts` files. That step is itself unconditional and
`tsc -b` builds the whole reference graph, so whether the artefacts are needed is a fact about the
build graph, not about the diff — no diff-shaped condition can be both sound and useful. Skipping the
check would only trade one clear message naming its own repair for twelve confusing ones. The
reasoning is recorded at the step and in `docs/conventions/build-performance.md` so the next reader
reaches the same conclusion without re-measuring.
- **A real matter rendered blanks where a sample matter rendered detail.** The client's mapper for a
live matter read hardcoded seven fields to null: the matter type, the Location, the responsible
attorney, the e-billing flag, and all three instants. Only the three in-repo sample matters — the
fixtures the interface is reviewed against — ever showed those, which is the worst way round for a
demonstration to be wrong.

Three of the seven the contract already carried and the client's payload type simply did not accept,
so they were parsed away on arrival. The other four the contract did not carry at all.

The detail read now resolves the type, the Location and the responsible member to **names**, in the
same statement, rather than answering with the identifiers a screen cannot print at a person. That
is a separate statement from the one the lifecycle service uses: deciding whether a matter may open
or close has no business paying for three joins to learn a name it will never render. All three
joins are outer, and an unset type or an archived member reads as an honest null rather than an
identifier standing in for a name.

The three collections stay empty on purpose and now say so in the code. Files, time entries and
costs each have their own list endpoint on their own screen; filling them from the matter read would
be three calls the overview does not need and a record that goes stale the moment one of those
screens writes.
- **The gate of record has executed nothing since 2026-08-05, and the reason is not in this repository.
Ten days of pull requests merged against a status that looked like a failing build and was actually an
account that could not start a job.** The runner labels were never the cause; no workflow change lands
here, and the one action that clears it is now on the deploy queue.

The standing suspicion was that `ubuntu-slim` — introduced by the CI cost-reduction work — is not a
real runner label, and that fixing or reverting it would restore the gate. Checked against GitHub's
current runner reference, `ubuntu-slim` is generally available, needs no plan and no enablement: a
1-CPU / 5 GB container runner, exactly as `gate.yml`'s own `RUNNERS` header describes it. Three
independent observations then rule it out as the cause:

- Run 351 on `main` (2026-08-05, 04:04Z) failed with the identical fingerprint at a commit whose
  `gate.yml` carried **thirteen `ubuntu-latest` jobs and no `ubuntu-slim` at all**.
- `assemble-docs.yml`, which is entirely `ubuntu-latest` and contains no `ubuntu-slim`, has been
  failing the same way on every push to `main` throughout.
- Moving the `changes` job to `ubuntu-latest` on a live branch and pushing it reproduced the failure
  exactly — 2 seconds, `runner_id: 0`, no logs. The proposed fix was measured, and it does not work.

The outage began between 03:16Z and 03:46Z on 2026-08-05, three hours **before** `ubuntu-slim` first
entered the repository, which settles the ordering on its own. What actually happens is that GitHub
refuses to start any billable job for this private repository: the job is created, no runner is ever
attached, and it concludes `failure` in two or three seconds with a log endpoint that 404s. The Free
plan includes 2,000 Actions minutes a month for private repositories and GitHub blocks usage once the
quota is spent with no valid payment method — which is what the austerity note said on the day it was
written, before the diagnosis drifted into "no runner assigned" and then into a label theory.

**What lands:** the recognition rule in `operations.md` — `runner_id: 0` with an empty `runner_name`
is a job that never started, and it must be read as _unverified_, never as _broken_ — plus the owner's
billing step at the top of the deploy queue, a corrected date and cause in `ROADMAP.md` (it read
2026-08-07), and a revert checklist in `build-performance.md` that now keys off an observed non-zero
`runner_id` rather than a calendar month turning over. `gate.yml` itself is untouched, deliberately:
reverting the labels would spend three times the runner rate to fix nothing.
- An export could be downloaded successfully and never appear on the download shelf, with nothing
anywhere saying why. Two defects, and the second is the one that mattered.

**The register's schema requires a finite number on a two-faced cell, and rejects the WHOLE document
otherwise** — so a single unmeasured figure cost the member the entire shelf item. The same class of
defect the spreadsheet renderer already guards against in `cellPlan`, arriving one layer along:
`storedFromExport` now falls back to the printed text face when the number is not real, which loses
nothing a reader can see. `packages/export-document` gains a test pinning what the schema accepts,
and the client pins the fallback.

**The failure was silent by construction, which is why it went unnoticed.** `keepExportOnShelf`
swallowed every outcome so that a shelf failure could never cost a member the download they already
had. That reasoning holds — it still never throws and never blocks — but swallowing made a refused
document indistinguishable from one that simply never arrived, with no Error ID and nothing to act
on. It now returns the outcome, and the export menu reports a refusal with the server's own words
and its Error ID.
- **The file manager's rename field opens with the cursor in it, and does not move the row.** Three
defects with one field between them. The list's in-place field was never focused and never
selected, so making a folder put a name field on screen that nobody was typing in — the reader had
to find it, click it and click away again before it looked right; `beginRename` now focuses it and
selects the stem, the same gesture `file-inspector.svelte` already made for the panel's own field.
The field also pushed its row taller, which is arithmetic rather than styling: `.mc-table-cell` in a
grid is `block-size: var(--mc-control-sm)` with `padding-block: var(--mc-space-4)`, and `.mc-input-sm`
asks for that same full control height, so it could not fit in the box it was in. It gives up the
control's own minimum and takes the cell's content box. A refusal still grows the row, because the
reason has to be readable.

**A table's row mark keeps its space whether or not the row is marked.** `data-table-grid.svelte`
drew the pin in the first cell only while the row was pinned, so pinning shifted that cell's text by
the glyph and its gap — the reader saw the list twitch at the moment they acted on it. Any grid
given a `rowMark` now keeps the slot on every row; a grid that never marks a row reserves nothing.
The condition is the capability, not the current state, because a condition that changes when the
first row is pinned reflows at exactly the moment the reflow would be seen.

**One rename path, two places to say no.** `renameTo` answers with the sentence that refuses rather
than posting it itself, so the list's field sends a refusal to the screen's failure band while the
details panel keeps its own field open with the reason beneath it. The two halves of that seam were
built in parallel and disagreed about the answer's type; the panel's half is the one that was right.
- **A firm database that applied a migration under its pre-rename id now reconciles itself on wake, instead of refusing to start.**

The 2026-09-15 re-stamp of `20260911T000000_office-email-address-lines-and-firm-brand-images` and `20260914T090000_event-conference-link` was taken on the premise that no database could have applied either id — no firm onboarded, both per-firm pools empty and recreatable. A firm database had applied the first of them. From the moment the rename deployed it refused to wake, because the applied-ledger records the TAG and that id named a migration the lineage no longer contained. Every route that needs firm data answered with the build panel's `Firm database: Not answering`, and the runner's sentence for it — `deploy mismatch (code older than schema)` — pointed at the opposite of the truth: the deployment was newer than the rename, not older.

`packages/database/src/re-stamped-migrations.ts` records a rename as data, and `runPendingMigrations` consults it before it refuses. A re-stamp moves the id and not the SQL, so the schema the database has is already the schema the new id names, and the ledger row is rewritten through the `supersedeAppliedMigrations` seam the baseline collapse already uses — one transaction, no schema SQL, resumable if it is interrupted part way.

Three shapes are still refused, each in its own words: a ledger holding both ids of one re-stamp, which the rewrite cannot express and should not guess at; a deployment older than the rename, which is told to roll forward rather than sent hunting for a schema change nobody made; and a genuinely unknown tag, which is the deploy mismatch the original sentence was written for.

The immutability gate reads the registry directly, the way it already reads `LEGACY_BASELINES`, so a rename is recorded once and the gate and the runner cannot drift into disagreeing about which tags a database may still be holding. `tooling/migration-immutability/allowed-changes.mts` is correspondingly narrowed: it is for a tag going away with nothing standing in for it, and the 2026-09-15 rename is now its worked example of an entry that should not be written there — an allowance asserts nothing needs repairing, which is a claim about the fleet that is easy to believe and hard to check.
- **A renderer refusal says which refusal it was.** The safe website viewer signalled every structured
refusal from Cloudflare Browser Rendering by throwing one sentence containing the words "capacity"
and "limit", and both routes then decided the response by matching that sentence with `includes`.
Every distinguishable fault therefore collapsed into the same answer: an account without the
entitlement, a credential lacking the permission and a rejected parameter all reached the member as
a 502 saying the service was at capacity and to try again shortly. The service states its reason in
an `errors` array, and the renderer discarded it — reading only `success`, `result` and `meta` —
before anything could act on it.

The refusal now travels as `RendererFailure` (`packages/safe-browse/src/renderer-failure.ts`),
carrying the service's HTTP status and error code and, deliberately, nothing else: the upstream
message can quote the suspect URL back, so a failure that cannot hold the target cannot leak it
whatever a caller later logs. A status the service documents as momentary (408, 429, 5xx) stays the
transient 502; every other refusal describes how this worker is calling the service, which waiting
cannot fix, so it reaches the standard pipeline as a 500 with an Error ID to quote. Both paths now
log — the transient one answered and wrote nothing before, which is why the first live failure left
no trace at all. A non-2xx and an unparseable body are refusals too, rather than a `SyntaxError`
surfacing as an unexplained server fault.
- Production databases provisioned before the 2026-07-04 baseline collapse were bricked by their own
history: their `_migrations` ledger holds the retired sequential ids (`0000_foundational-tables`, …),
the shipping bundle knows only the timestamp-id baseline, and the runner's unknown-tag guard read
that as "code older than schema" and refused. Every scheduled control-plane pass failed, every
pre-collapse FirmDatabase Durable Object threw on wake, no post-July-4 migration could ever apply,
and `POST /api/v1/registrations` 500ed on its first read.

The runner now recognizes a ledger that is EXACTLY one retired chain — recorded as a committed
constant in `packages/database/src/legacy-baselines.ts`, verified schema- and seed-equivalent to the
baseline that replaced it — and atomically rewrites those rows to the baseline tag before the guard
runs, then applies the pending tail normally. Once, per database; the next run is an ordinary no-op.
Any other unknown tag — including a strict prefix of the retired chain, whose schema the baseline
would misrepresent — still refuses with the same message, because there it really does mean a newer
schema than the deployed code. Both targets (control-plane D1 via the scheduled pass, per-firm
Durable Object SQLite on wake) get the same rewrite through one new atomic `MigrationTarget` method.
No committed migration SQL changed.
- **Participants open their media sessions at the same time rather than one behind another.**
`sessionFor` in `apps/api-worker/src/meetings/room/room-media.ts` held `blockConcurrencyWhile`
across the call that opens a Cloudflare Realtime session, so every arrival waited for the one before
it and one slow upstream answer stalled every frame in the room. The lock now covers storage only:
a per-stay map of openings in flight makes two frames from one participant share one call while
other participants proceed, the session is written onto the record together with the first publish
or subscribe (a first publish still costs five reads), a failed opening is retried on the next frame
with the same refusal and Error ID, and a browser that reconnects or leaves mid-opening is handled
rather than merged into a record it no longer owns. The load harness gains a per-frame-type count of
storage reads beside its count of lists.
- The second wave of Meetings came back from review with seven defects that share one shape: a decision
made from a read that was already stale by the time it was acted on, or a frame nobody was counting.

**A held-back presence transition is now relayed, not dropped.** The room throttles how often one
person's speaking and muted state is relayed, which is what makes a room of three hundred
affordable — but the transition inside the window was discarded outright, and the last transition of
a burst is the one that is still true. A one-word answer left somebody `speaking: true` on every
other screen until they next spoke; a quick mute and unmute left them shown muted for the rest of the
meeting. A suppressed transition now raises `presenceDirty` and arms the room's alarm for the end of
its window, and the alarm relays what is stored. The room's one alarm reconciles three deadlines
where it reconciled two.

**A cancelled event can no longer end a meeting somebody is in.** The cancel read the meeting a round
trip before it committed, and the statement it composed matched `status <> 'ended'` — so a member who
joined in between had the room closed under them by somebody editing a calendar, with the room itself
never told, and a host who ended it in the same window turned the cancel into a server error. The
closing now carries its own precondition (`status = 'scheduled'`, no open stay) and its own guard
label, so the batch rolls back whole and the route answers the 409 it answers from the pre-read —
or, when the host got there first, treats the closing as a no-op and lets the cancellation through.

**Opening a room from the event form asks for `meetings:host`.** The four event mutations ride
`calendar:manage`, which is the key for keeping a diary; a `meeting` field on the form convenes a
gathering, which is a meetings act by another door. Refused with a 403 about that field alone — the
event still records. Cancelling stays on the diary key, because after the fix above a cancellation
can only ever close a room nobody walked into.

**A poller following a chat no longer loses a message to a tie.** `since` was a strict comparison on
an instant, so the second of two messages stamped the same millisecond was gone for that reader
permanently. The continuation is now the `(sent_at, id)` keyset every other list walks: the read
takes `sinceId` beside `since`, and the last page carries a `nextCursor` as a POSITION rather than a
has-more flag, which is what a screen following a live meeting actually needs.

**The words of a chat message are no longer stored in the idempotency record.** That row is replayed
verbatim to whoever retries the key and is not part of the record a redaction reaches, so a retried
send would have served text a member had already taken back. The record's own fields are stored and
the words are not; a first answer is read back off the row.

**Two members taking the same message back together are both answered.** The loser of the race met
the redaction's guard and was handed an Error ID for a message that is, in fact, gone.

**And three costs nobody was counting.** `sync` and `layer` are now throttled per participant, the
way presence is — one whole-roster answer a second and one layer change a quarter second, because a
browser can send either as fast as it can write to a socket and each costs the room a read of every
key it holds or a call to the routing service. A layer change is refused unless it names a media
section the room actually subscribed for that browser, which the roster check it passed never
constrained. A broadcast skips a socket that has been accepted and not yet welcomed, so concurrent
arrivals no longer set every new browser asking for the whole roster at once. And resolving who is
connected walks the sockets once a pass rather than once a participant — ninety thousand attachment
reads per alarm in a full room, before.

The protocol package's frames-have-handlers scan was reading for the frame's name anywhere in a
side's sources, which passes for six frames whose names appear in a type alias or a meeting state; it
now parses the dispatch on each side and compares the set both ways.
- **ADR-0167 has said since June that the Worker-extraction rubric "and the worker template are the
living standard in `docs/conventions/operations.md`," and the rubric was never written there.** A
`grep -i rubric` over that file returned nothing. The cost is not hypothetical: the question of which
subsystems earn their own Worker was re-derived from first principles in a long exchange, by two
people who each looked for the rule where its own decision says it lives and did not find it. The
rubric now lives there, as § 18.

It is written to be decided from — a reader settles "does this subsystem get its own Worker?" without
opening the Decision Log. The five properties are stated as tests rather than labels (property ③ is
"state the contention as a sentence," which is why the discovery and search containers are separate
Workers: extraction saturates CPU for hours during a bulk load while search's premise is staying warm
for sub-second queries). The compute-vs-coordination seam is stated in full, and the fleet is
tabulated as worked examples — the nine container-owning Workers with the properties each cleared, the
four Workers that exist for other reasons and did not come through the rubric at all, and the eleven
coordination Durable Objects that deliberately stayed in the app Worker.

Three things the rubric's own history makes worth writing down. Search reads like a counter-example
and is not one: it failed the statelessness gate as first posed, got a stateful-service design
instead, and reaches its dedicated Worker only because that design moved the index state out of the
container — the rubric was not bent. "One deployable, one origin" (ADR-0069) is reconciled rather
than quietly contradicted: what survives is one public origin, and every extraction since is internal.
And the containment property is what binds, not the literal absence of a route — which is why
`magna-carta-edit` is browser-facing on a cookieless content domain and still satisfies it.

The clause placing coordination Durable Objects in the app Worker carries a short note that it is
under active revision by a decision in flight, since the API surface is being split from background
orchestration. The note names no ADR number and predicts no outcome; it says which sentence moves and
which does not, so the decision that supersedes it replaces one block quote rather than the section.

Nothing in the Decision-Log register was edited — it is assembled on `main`. One inaccuracy in
ADR-0167 is left standing and reported rather than silently corrected in the retelling: it lists "the
pure-Rust PDF engine" among the Container family, and that engine shipped as in-process WASM in the
app and sign Workers, with no container anywhere.
- **Saving in the editor was refused every time, because the host required a lock it never told the editor to take.**

The editor takes a lock on a document only when the host's CheckFileInfo answer says it supports locks. Ours never said so, so the editor never locked; and the host refused any save made without a held lock, answering a conflict, which the editor showed as the document having been changed by another user. The answer now advertises the lock contract it enforces (`SupportsLocks`, `SupportsUpdate`), and states `IsAdminUser` so the editor's server audit stops reporting it missing.

With locks in use, a second defect was waiting behind the first: one container serves a document, and a container that stops without unlocking left its lock in the session record, so the next instance's lock was refused and the document read as held by another editor. A plain lock request carrying a different value is now the successor taking over; releasing or refreshing a lock still requires the held value, so an old instance cannot release a successor's.

Also in the image: the editor's own "what's new" dialog no longer opens on every first open of a document. It remembers having been seen in the browser's storage for the editor's origin, and every document here is its own origin. Help › What's New still opens it; whether the editor was updated is the platform's version report to say.
- **The scoped gate could not pass a change that touched only screens.** `pnpm check:scoped` handed
every changed path to `vp check`, which runs the formatter and the linter together; the formatter has
no Svelte parser and refuses outright when _every_ path in the set is one it cannot format. A change
set of nothing but `.svelte` files therefore failed the gate with "Expected at least one target file"
regardless of what was in it &mdash; and the pre-push hook runs this gate. It stayed hidden because
every screen built so far shipped alongside a route or a transport module, and one formattable path
in the set makes the refusal disappear.

The two passes are now split the way `pnpm fix:scoped` already split them, and for the reason that
script already stated: each pass gets only the paths it can parse. The step construction moved into
its own module so the split is a pure function with a test, rather than something only a real run can
falsify.

**The matter sections kept the previous matter's answer on screen while the next read ran.** Costs,
Time and Parties set their list inside an effect keyed on the matter without clearing it first, so
navigating between two matters left the old table and any old failure standing until the new read
landed. A failure was attributed to the matter now on screen; a list was read as that matter's own.
Each now discards the old answer before asking for the next one.

Parties discards on a change of _matter_ only. Its reload after a sever is the same matter's list
being read again, and blanking it there would flash a skeleton over a table the reader is still
looking at.
- **A session handle means nothing without the room that issued it.** The whole fleet's meetings run
inside one Cloudflare Realtime application, which knows nothing about meetings or firms: it will
forward any session's track to anybody presenting the application credential. The signaling room was
passing a browser's `subscribe` frame straight through, so any participant in any meeting could pull
any other meeting's media — including another firm's — by naming a session id. The room now checks
every (session, track) pair against its OWN roster and refuses the whole frame (`unknown-track`)
without asking the service anything, refuses a subscription to the asker's own session, and refuses a
`publish` whose track name does not carry the publisher's own participant handle
(`foreign-track-name`) — a name is how every other browser resolves a track to a tile, so a foreign
one puts one member's camera under another member's face. Published tracks are recorded from what the
service CONFIRMED rather than from what the browser offered, and a participant is capped at eight.

**The room now closes what it started.** Each published track's media section is kept beside its name,
which is the only handle the routing service accepts for stopping one — so leaving, ending, closing a
track, and the new grace sweep all stop the forwarding they are ending, best-effort and never
blocking the record. A closed track leaves the roster and the room is told, where before a stopped
screen share was offered to every browser that joined afterwards.

**A closed laptop now ends a stay.** Nothing closed attendance when a socket simply went away, so a
stay stayed open for the life of the record. A dropped socket with no other socket for that stay arms
a Durable Object alarm a minute out; the sweep closes the stay through the firm-scoped data-access
layer with its own `meetings.meeting.left` audit row carrying `reason: socket-lost`, drops the roster
entry and stops the media. It never ends the meeting — that is the host's act and it records who took
it. The same alarm retires the ended marker a day after a meeting closes.

**An upgrade joins a participant; it does not reset one.** A reconnect or a second tab overwrote the
participant's routing session and tracks with nulls, leaving live media nothing could name, subscribe
to or close; and closing one of two sockets removed the participant the other was still watching
through. Both are read-modify-write under the object's own gate now, and a stay survives while any
socket for it is open.

**One participant's bad luck no longer ends the meeting.** The routing session was opened inside
`blockConcurrencyWhile`, and Cloudflare terminates and resets an object whose callback throws —
dropping every socket in the room. The failure is carried out as a value and answered on the one
socket that asked, and `end()` now writes its two storage operations under one gate so no frame can
land in the window that answered "the room does not know you" for a meeting that had just ended.

**The database holds the two rules the reads cannot.** A partial unique index on
`meeting_attendance (meeting_id, user_id) WHERE left_at IS NULL` and a capacity-guarded
`INSERT … SELECT` settle the races a read-then-write is a round trip too early for: a double-clicked
Join is handed the stay the first click opened, a thirteenth simultaneous arrival is told the room is
full, and the loser of a simultaneous Start is handed the winner's room — each of which previously
surfaced as a 500 on a raw constraint.

**Signaling is refused cross-origin, failures are recorded, and the attendance record is paged.** A
browser will open a WebSocket cross-origin carrying the member's cookie where it would refuse to let
that page read any other call here, so an upgrade whose `Origin` is not this application's is now a 403. Every routing-service and relay-credential failure goes through the standard error pipeline with
an Error ID — carried on the `refused` frame so the screen can show it — and never the upstream body,
the application id or a session description. `GET /api/v1/meetings/{id}/attendance` is cursor-paged
like every other list, and the relay-credential mint has one home
(`apps/api-worker/src/realtime/turn-credentials.ts`) shared by the meeting join and the connection
tool, each deciding its own fallback.
- **An event held in one of the firm's rooms now appears on that room's calendar.** The owner: "when i set an event to be in a location, it did not populate in to that locations calendar" — and, separately, "location and booking a room seem duplicative of what should be the same functionality". They are the same defect seen from two sides.

The Location field stores TEXT, deliberately: a courthouse, a department number and opposing counsel's office are none of them records this product holds, so the picker offers the firm's offices and rooms and keeps anything else that is typed. A room's own calendar, meanwhile, reads BOOKINGS. Nothing joined the two, so choosing "Boardroom" from the picker wrote the string "Boardroom" and the Boardroom's calendar stayed empty — while Book a Room, on the event's Rooms tab, did the real thing. Two ways to say one thing, and only one of them true.

`room-location.ts` matches the location text back to an active resource of the `room` kind, and the two record forms book it. The column stays free text — nothing dangles when a room is renamed, and a place the firm has no record of is still just typed — so what changed is only that where the text does name a room the firm has, the booking is made.

The match is exact on a trimmed, case-folded name, which is what the picker actually writes. Anything looser books a room off a guess: "Boardroom 2" is not "Boardroom", and a courthouse whose name happens to contain a room's name has not booked that room.

The booking is a second write, because it needs the event's id. So it can fail after the event has landed, and the form says so rather than closing on a room somebody believes is held: the event is never unwound, and the notice names the room and points at the Rooms tab.

Still open from the same round: the wider location model the owner described — offices carrying addresses with rooms inside them, and Zoom or Google Meet as bookable places with their own concurrency ceilings — which is a spec rather than a patch.
- A download or conversion result is checked for in the same bucket the URL handed back addresses.

`files/firm-bucket.ts` resolves a firm's storage as a pair — the name a presigned URL addresses, and the handle the Worker reads through — because presigning against one bucket while reading through another is silent data loss. Five call sites took the name and then reached for the bound binding anyway, which is the exact split the seam exists to prevent.

The bundle and conversion progress resolvers took a bare `bucketName`, signed a URL against it, and asked the bound binding whether the artifact was still there. So did the ZIP download route, for both its cached-artifact fast paths and the inline stream, and the bundle build consumer for the bytes it reads and the artifact it writes. Today the guard's refusal hides this, because a firm whose bucket is not the bound one cannot get that far. Once a firm resolves to its own bucket, the same code would report a live artifact `expired`, or hand back a signed URL for an object it had confirmed in a different bucket.

All five now take the pair, and the two job coordinators resolve it through the same seam rather than reading the binding off their own `env`. The name a URL is signed against and the handle its bytes come from are one decision again.
- **Template registration leaks bytes, and until now nothing could even say how many.**

Registration writes its bytes to R2 inside the idempotent effect and before the scan, so a
registration that throws in between leaves a full copy behind. Each attempt mints a fresh key, so
retries multiply it, and the storage reconciliation never reaches them: that pass lists `files/` and
`bulk/` only, and corrects the meter rather than deleting anything.

A daily pass now **measures** the leak: per firm, it walks `templates/` and counts every object no
`document_template_version` row anywhere in the fleet names, that is not a staged upload, and that is
older than a 24-hour grace period.

**It deletes nothing, and that is the finding rather than a shortcut.** The rule "delete the
complement of the live set" is only as safe as the live set is complete, and completeness cannot
currently be verified. A read that FAILS can be caught, and is — one failure disarms the whole pass.
A read that SUCCEEDS AND RETURNS NOTHING cannot be told from a firm that holds no templates, because
the per-firm database object self-migrates on construction: address it under the wrong name and it
answers zero rows from a brand-new empty database rather than throwing. The residency seam already
documented in the database proxy makes that reachable — the first jurisdiction-bound firm will be
addressed with a jurisdiction its statements carry and this pass does not.

Arming the delete wants the invariant to become checkable, most plausibly by stamping each object
with the firm that wrote it, so an orphan is decided against ONE firm's rows and the fleet-wide union
disappears along with its blast radius. That is a design decision with a real trade, and it is filed
for the owner rather than taken here.

**The retention read is paged.** It crossed the per-firm database boundary in a single response, and
a failed retention read disarms the whole fleet's pass — so a firm large enough to overflow one
response would not have slowed the measurement down, it would have switched it off, every night,
silently. It is a keyset walk over the object key now; the key carries the version identifier, so the
ordering is total and no row can be skipped or repeated across pages.

**Two smaller things the review corrected.** The candidate count is DISTINCT KEYS, not sightings:
template keys carry no firm segment and every firm resolves to the same bound bucket, so each firm's
pass walks the same prefix and a per-sighting count would scale with tenancy rather than with the
leak. And the per-firm cap is a budget per PASS, not per that firm's own objects — the fleet-wide
ceiling is the cap times the number of active firms, which the earlier wording claimed the opposite of.
- **The shipping credential-store defect was a class, and the class has now been swept: seventeen
injection seams in the worker's composition root, each exercised against `createApp()` with no
overrides. Fifteen are honest or legitimate. One more was not — `POST /api/v1/scan/diagnose`
answered `500 Internal server error` with an Error ID where the scan engine is wired but
unreachable — and it now answers `503`.**

**What a member got.** The route's own description promised "an honest `unscanned` verdict until the
scan Container is activated", and that promise only holds while `SCAN_SERVICE` is **absent**.
`wrangler.jsonc` declares the binding, and Cloudflare refuses a deploy whose service binding names a
worker that does not exist — so the state a deployment actually spends time in is bound-and-answering-5xx
(a placeholder worker, a Container that is not up), where `containerScanAdapter` threw a bare `Error`
and the member asking whether a file was safe was told the platform had broken. The
sibling `POST /api/v1/file-type/verify` degrades to a clean `503` on the identical condition. The
tools reality check recorded the inconsistency on 2026-08-15 and left it, because choosing between
"fault" and "verdict" for an unreachable engine is a safety decision; this changes neither — it
changes only how the fault is **reported** on the one surface that answers a person directly.

**The fix, in the vocabulary that already existed.** A 5xx from the scan service now throws
`ScanFaultError` — the error the verdict layer already raises for a deployed engine reporting
unavailable, because it is the same fact: no scan happened and none can right now. A 4xx keeps the
plain throw, since this adapter and the service disagreeing about the request is fixed by neither a
retry nor a deploy. The diagnostic route catches the typed error and returns the registered
`service-unavailable` problem, whose contract — the condition clears when the binding is activated —
is true here. Nothing about the ingest consumer changed: a queued file with an unreachable engine
still throws, still retries, and still never commits as clean.

**Why nothing caught it.** `apps/api-worker/vitest.config.ts` registers a stub worker for every service
binding, and the scan stub answers an honest engine-less result over HTTP 200. A stub that behaves
correctly proves only that the route works against a healthy service.
`scan-unreachable-engine-seam.test.ts` binds a placeholder that answers 503 and pins both states
apart: nothing wired at all is still a verdict a firm can read (`unscanned`, reason `no-engine`), an
unreachable engine is a refusal.

**The count, because it is the result.** Of seventeen seams: eleven are legitimate injections with no
production placeholder to test against (the clock, the logger, the fetch and socket adapters, the
browser renderer, the presigner and firm-resource-provider pairs, the flag evaluator, the assistant's
self-marked deterministic inference port, the recovery backend); four were already honest and now
verified by running them (`esign.seal` → `503`, `ai-detection.detect` → `422`,
`tools/turn-credentials` → `503`, the conversion and search engine ports' `engine-not-implemented`);
one was the shipping defect, fixed already; one is this. So the shipping case was closer to unlucky
than typical — but the reason it survived was systemic, and
[`docs/conventions/testing.md`](docs/conventions/testing.md) now carries the rule: every injection
seam has at least one test that supplies nothing and asserts what a real request gets.

**Not fixed here:** the scan engine's deployment, and the transactional-email adapter, which is the
one remaining seam whose production default is a placeholder — with `EMAIL_FROM` unset the logging
adapter is selected and every verification and reset message is written to a log and dropped while
the API answers success. That is the documented deploy-time activation in the operations runbook, not
a code defect, and it is the seam whose failure no status code can show.
- **`main` was red on a second count nobody had traced: the web app's test project could not resolve
`$lib` at all. Seventeen tests had never run.**

`apps/web/vitest.config.ts` uses a plain node pool and deliberately leaves SvelteKit's plugin out —
it never runs a dev server or a build, and the comment at the top explains why. What the comment did
not account for is that `$lib` is SvelteKit's alias, and its plugin is the thing that resolves it.
`.svelte-kit/tsconfig.json` maps the alias for the type-checker, so the code type-checks; at test
time nothing mapped it at all.

Thirty-six modules under `src/lib` import through the alias. Any test reaching one of them dies at
load with `Cannot find module '$lib/…'` — a whole-file failure that reads like a missing dependency
rather than a missing config line, which is most of why it went untraced. Only one suite reached
one, so the hole waited for `create-document.test.ts` to be written and then looked like that
suite's problem.

The config now declares the alias itself, independent of SvelteKit and matching what the generated
tsconfig maps. `create-document.test.ts` passes, 17 tests; the whole web project passes, 380.

**A guard, not just a fix.** `test/lib-alias.test.ts` imports _through_ the alias, so the hole
cannot reopen quietly — verified to fail with `Cannot find module '$lib/api/request.ts'` when the
alias is removed, and to pass when it is there.
- **A three-day trial is on all three days.** It was on the first one, and every other day it covered read as free (owner, 2026-09-16: "multi-day events are not showcasing through multiple days"). Two independent faults, either of which alone was enough to hide it.

**The READ windowed on the start alone.** `civilDateWindowConditions` compares both bounds against a source's sort column, and for an event that is `starts_on` — so a row running the 12th to the 16th was outside every window that did not contain the 12th. `spanningCivilDateWindowConditions` is the shape a spanning row needs: it starts before the window closes AND ends after it opens. `COALESCE(ends_on, starts_on)` makes a one-day row behave exactly as it always did, because its end IS its start, so the predicate collapses to the plain one for almost every row the calendar holds. Applied to the `matterEvent` and `firmEvent` timeline sources and to `selectFirmEventsStatement`. This does not widen what a source may return beyond its window — it returns rows the window always should have held.

**The TIME GRIDS placed by `entry.date === key`.** The month never had the fault, because `placeEntries` walks every day of a span; the week and the day could not use it, because a span on an HOUR axis is not the same entry repeated — it is a different piece of the day on each of its days. `day-segments.ts` cuts it: the first day runs from the start hour to midnight, a day in the middle is the whole column, and the last day runs from midnight to the end hour. Each piece carries its own id, because two pieces of one record are two things to render and a grid keyed on a repeated id drops all but one, and `continuesBefore` / `continuesAfter` are what let a block reaching the top of a column say it began yesterday rather than at midnight.

All-day entries never reach that module: they have no `startMinute`, they belong in the band above the hours, and both time grids already banded and spanned them correctly.
- **A new firm no longer admits its owner before the member record that makes the workspace usable has landed, and the wait now names the steps it is on.** Activation flips the firm active and attaches the account to it in one control-plane batch; the member row every permission resolves through is written into the firm's OWN database afterwards, by the `member.provision` message that same batch queues. The welcome screen went in on the first fact, so a first sign-in could land in an app where every screen answered as though a role were missing — which is what the diagnostics panel's "Not in the database yet" row was reporting after the fact.

`GET /api/v1/me` gains two optional fields. `joining.build` reports how far provisioning has got, read from the firm row's own marks (`bucket_name`, `wrapped_firm_key`, `status`) and its outbox row rather than tracked anywhere, so a resumed build reports what it has actually done; `membership.state` distinguishes a mirror still landing from a member holding no role, which an empty permission list cannot. Both guards read the second — `(app)/+layout.ts` sends that person to `/welcome`, and `/welcome`'s own load keeps them there, so the two stay mirrors rather than a loop. The words for the five steps live in `apps/web/src/lib/auth/firm-build-progress.ts`, beside the screen, on the same split the database-health panel keeps: the wire carries facts, the browser decides sentences.
- **The instruction that creates an active-work note is shorter than the note format, and the
difference is the part that makes the note findable.** `CLAUDE.md` said to add
`docs/active-work/<branch>.md` with a scope and the files you expect to touch. The registry needs
two more things: the path must mirror the branch exactly, slashes included, and the file needs a
frontmatter block. A note that misses either is not rejected — it is simply never read, so the
stream it describes warns nobody and `vp run retire-note` cannot find it afterwards to clean it up.

The registry already detects both failures and names them, in a section written precisely for this
case. It is only reached by running `vp run worktrees`, which the instruction did not say to do.
Now it does, and the two requirements are stated where the note gets written rather than only in the
format document.
- **Browser-side race safety, plus the Durable Object gate and two property verifiers.** `LatestOnly` (`apps/web/src/lib/api/latest-only.ts`) replaces five hand-rolled stale-answer counters; `pnpm run lint:stale-response` fails a sixth and is what found the fifth. `WriteIntent` holds one idempotency key across every attempt at one intent, so a retry after an ambiguous failure replays rather than duplicating — the double-click that `writeKey`'s comment claimed to cover is already handled by any synchronously-set in-flight flag; the comment is corrected in all four modules. `pnpm run lint:durable-object-gates` scans for a Durable Object deciding across a non-storage await and found `BundleBuildCoordinator.requestBundle` HEADing R2 mid-decision, so two requests for one expired bundle each enqueued a full rebuild; fixed with `blockConcurrencyWhile`. Property verifiers for the number draw (correctness absolute at every N; convergence bounded at five by the retry budget, now pinned) and for concurrent ledger postings against the domain's own fitness queries.
- **`changelog.d/a-firm-puts-its-own-fields-on-an-asset.md` gains the developer entry it was marked
`public` without.** The fragment carried only customer-facing prose under no `## Public` heading, so
`lint:changelog-fragments` had been failing on `main` since it landed — `vp run changelog-build` would
have refused to assemble either changelog. It surfaced the moment that lint moved into the inner loop's
always-on step; a red gate on arrival is exactly what a gate is for, but it belongs fixed in the same
change that starts enforcing it.
- **`pnpm fix:scoped` deleted type assertions the code needed, and the file stopped compiling.** The
rewrite strips the shape assertion off `await response.json()` in the worker's route tests. It is
reproducible: two assertions in, zero out, ten TS2571 errors on a file that type-checked a moment
earlier, and it reaches every such assertion in the file rather than only the ones just written.

The two tools disagree about the same call. `typescript/no-unnecessary-type-assertion` reads
`.json()` as returning `any`, against which any assertion is a no-op worth deleting; the type-check
of record resolves it to `unknown`, against which the assertion is the only thing making the
property access legal. The fixer trusts its own answer and rewrites.

It joins the two rewrites already held back from the unattended fix pass. The finding still shows in
every check path, as those do — seeing it and deciding is the point; having it applied while you
look away is not.
- **A resource's availability could report a room as free when it was double-booked.** The read caps at
two thousand bookings in the window, then pairs overlapping bookings over the rows it was handed. A
booking past the cut that overlapped one inside it was a conflict the grid never painted — a _wrong_
answer rather than a short one, and wrong in the direction that says a room is available.

The cap was reachable with ordinary data, not only pathological data: the window is capped at 366
days, and a well-used meeting room booked six times a working day crosses two thousand inside one
year. The read now **refuses** past the ceiling and names the remedy — ask for a shorter window —
taking the posture the continuance walk and the stocktake reconciliation already take when an answer
cannot be given accurately in one pass. The ceiling is injectable so the refusal is provable at a size
a test can seed rather than by writing two thousand rows.

**The resource picker's silent backstop now reports itself.** Five hundred was a magic number in the
route handler; it is `MAX_FIRM_RESOURCES` beside the statement, and the response carries `capped`. The
picker still returns the whole catalog rather than a page, because a picker missing a room says the
room does not exist — but a firm that somehow holds more bookable things than one answer carries is
now told to filter by kind or office instead of being shown a short list that looks complete.

**The event-type catalog and the continuance chain are recorded as bounded by construction**, each
with what bounds it: a firm's own event vocabulary, and `MAX_CONTINUANCE_CHAIN_DEPTH`, which
`readContinuanceChain` already asserts on every step because a chain longer than that is corrupt
rather than continued. The chain must also stay whole — it is the procedural history of one hearing,
and half of it is a different account of what happened.
- **A guarded write refuses its batch instead of being reported on after it commits.** A statement whose WHERE repeats the precondition its caller read is marked `guarded(statement, label)` in its effect; affecting no rows now raises from inside the transaction, so the audit row and outbox message riding the same batch roll back with it. Previously the WHERE clause protected the row and nothing else — `batch()` surfaces no per-statement row count, `commitEffectBatch` returned void, the route answered 200, and the unguarded audit statement recorded the refused edit. Both SQLite adapters enforce it, the Durable Object returns it as a typed `unaffectedGuard` outcome beside `uniqueConstraint`, and `commitEffectBatch` refuses a guarded effect handed to an adapter that has not declared `enforcesGuardedWrites`. The fee and cost ledgers adopt it and map the refusal onto the 409 they already return, so no contract moves. `pnpm run lint:guarded-writes` holds the line.
- **An empty table no longer lights up under the pointer, and a table says when there is more to the side.** Two findings from one owner walk over the tables.

The first was reported as "the hover does not extend down the entire table, it stops about halfway", and the table it was reported on was an EMPTY one. The empty, filtered-empty and loading placeholders sit inside the table so the frame holds its height, which makes each of them a `<tr class="mc-table-row">` in the same body as the records — and the row hover found them there. Hovering an empty register painted a grey band exactly as tall as its message (measured at 70% and 78% of two frames on the table-states page, and about half of a taller one) with the rest of the frame left white: a hover that appears to give out partway down the table. The ruling against this was issued on 2026-08-30 and only half carried out — marking the placeholder's CELL does nothing, because the treatment being withheld belongs to the ROW. The row now carries `data-placeholder="true"`, and the shared recipe passes it over for the hover fill and for the `cursor: pointer` that promised a click there was nothing to click. Records are untouched. The story tests hold the cursor half of the treatment on both sides — a record offers itself, a placeholder does not — because the fill answers only to a real pointer, which the browser-mode driver does not supply.

The second is the gilt scroll-edge hint, which existed only inside the sidebar: a thin gold rule that DRAWS in at the edge of a scroll area while more content lies that way, the affordance the rail's hidden scrollbar gave up.
