tallying them in application code, which broke in two ways past that cap — and broke in the direction
that makes a rule look _less_ consequential than it is, on precisely the screen where a firm decides
to let rules file without confirmation.

Every count understated. And a matter whose links all fell past the cut was **absent from the answer
entirely**, not undercounted: the matter set handed to the access filter came from that same truncated
page, so a rule on such a matter contributed no entry at all.

The matter set now comes from the **rules**, not from the links. A rule is bound to one matter, so the
rule catalog names every matter a rule could have filed to — and it puts the ceiling on a quantity a
person controls (how many matters the firm has set rules on) rather than one that activity drives.
Revoked rules are included, because a rule that filed for three weeks and was then stopped is exactly
what a reviewer is looking for. The counting then happens in the database, grouped per rule over the
matters that survived the wall, so there is no ceiling on links at all and the numbers are exact.

`matterScopeCapped` on the response says when the firm holds rules on more matters than one answer
carries — a rule may then be missing from the list, which is a different and far rarer failure than a
count being wrong.

**Neither read is paged, and that is unchanged.** The existing argument stands: a cursor over a set the
access filter can shrink hands out short pages and calls it the end of the list. What was wrong was
never the absence of a cursor — it was the silence about the cut.
- **The back button on the editor's bar shows the matter's number beside the arrow.** The editor's shortcuts bar draws no words for any button (its builder switches labels off and keeps a button's text as its `data-cooltip` tooltip), so the number the host sent as the label was a tooltip and nothing more. The stylesheet the edit worker serves now draws the words from that attribute in a `::after` rule on the host button, cut to `BACK_LABEL_CHARACTERS` (12) with an ellipsis; the editor's own tooltip shows the whole number on hover.
- **The build panel's copy control is the copy symbol, and its repository link is GitHub's mark.**

Copy carried Lucide `clipboard-copy` — a clipboard with an arrow into it, which is the picture of PASTE — so the one control a person reaches for during an incident was drawn as its opposite. It is Lucide `copy`, the two-sheets glyph, everywhere else in the industry.

The repository link carried `git-branch`, which names a git concept rather than the service on the other side of the link. Lucide has no GitHub mark and could not: brand marks are not iconography. So the mark follows the brand-asset track instead of the icon rule — `@magna-carta/design-system/service-marks` is a new, deliberately quarantined home for a third party's own published mark, self-hosted and unaltered, taken in `currentColor` as the monochrome use GitHub's guidance provides for, with a row in `docs/conventions/third-party-trademarks.md` recording whose it is and on what terms. `lint:one-ui`'s hand-drawn-glyph rule learns the second exemption beside the brand mark's, with the reasoning on it.

**Counsel sign-off is outstanding** on that register row (policy 5, the ADR-0090 legal track) — the mark ships behind that flag rather than ahead of it.
- **The calendar no longer waits for every matter the firm has ever opened before it paints.**

`calendar-context.svelte.ts`'s `ready` included `firmMatters`, and `calendar-controller.svelte.ts` refuses to issue the calendar's own reads until `contextReady()`. `FirmMatters` walks the whole matter listing — up to ten pages, and `listEveryMatter` issues two requests per page because the numbered and consultation streams are separate — one page after another, because each needs the previous cursor. So up to twenty requests across ten serial round trips completed before the grid's rows were even requested. Time to first paint scaled with how many matters the firm had ever opened, which is the wrong thing for it to scale with and gets worse every year a firm uses the product.

**What that walk contributes to the grid is a matter NUMBER on a chip** — the one thing on a chip that does not come back with its own row. Everything else a chip says (its kind, its type's name, its hour, its tone) is in the entry's own read.

So `ready` now waits for exactly what a chip cannot be painted without: the event-type catalog and the firm's week start, two parallel reads of fixed size. The matters are still read, in parallel, off the critical path — and `numbered` in `calendar-entries.ts` fills the number in from the controller's existing `visibleEntries` derived when they arrive. **Nothing is read a second time**: the chips re-label from state that is already in the browser.

`detailIsMatterNumber` on `CalendarEntry` is what makes that safe. Without it a later pass cannot tell a detail that WANTED a number from one that was complete as it stood, and would overwrite "Hearing · Department 12" on a matter's own calendar — where every row shares the matter, so the number is the one fact worth saying nowhere. `numbered` returns the same object where nothing changed, so a grid never re-renders a row nothing happened to.

**One consequence had to be handled rather than accepted.** A record form can now open before the matters land, and `MatterPicker`'s empty state said "No matters were read, so there is nothing to file this on." — which would have been false for a second on a large firm. An empty list means two different things and they look identical from inside the picker, so the caller, which holds the read, now says which: `reading` renders "Reading the firm's matters" instead. It defaults false, because a caller handing over a list it already has is never in that state.

Unchanged: the walk itself, its bound, and the Time Sheet's use of it. A firm past the bound still gets a capped list — and a chip whose matter is beyond the cap simply keeps no number, which is what it did before.
- **The work canvas lays its children out as a column, so a full-height screen shrinks under the platform notice.** `<main>` in `app-shell.svelte` is `flex flex-col`; `NavigationLayout`'s root is `min-h-0 shrink`. A two-sided screen sized itself to the whole canvas as a block child and kept that height whatever stood above it, so the platform notice pushed it past the bottom edge and the canvas grew a third scrollbar. The page-inset lint reads the canvas's class list, so its inert-grow rule retires itself on the same change. `personInitials` moves from the time sheet's column helpers to the design system's name formatters beside `personName`, which is the one home the account corner and the time ledger now share.
- **The capture waits for something every page reaches.** The first refusal the safe website viewer
could actually read said `http=422, code=6004` — which the rendering service documents as being
unable to complete the action because of an issue with the site, most often a timeout. The cause was
ours: the snapshot asked the browser to wait for `networkidle2` before shooting, and a page holding
a socket, a poll or an analytics beacon never reaches two-connections-idle, so the wait ran to its
own 45-second limit and the service gave up. Every capture against a live commercial page failed
that way, and the answer on screen blamed capacity. The capture now waits for `load`, a condition
every page reaches, and the bounded settle afterwards is what covers the painting that idle was
there to wait for.

A page that still will not finish gets a second attempt with everything expensive turned off — no
lazy-load sweep, the earliest ready signal, the first viewport only. A worse screenshot is worth
more than none on a surface whose whole purpose is looking at pages chosen for being suspect. Only
a page failure earns that retry: a capacity shortage and a configuration refusal fail identically
on a second ask, so retrying either would spend a second render to learn nothing.

A failed render is now its own answer (`page-render-failed`, HTTP 422) rather than borrowing one
that fits it badly. It is not the capacity 502, which invites a retry the server has already made,
and it is not the 500, which hands the member an Error ID for a page that is merely slow.
- **The capture waits for the page, shoots all of it, and narrates while it works — and a WHOIS
query for a hostname finds the domain's record.** The renderer was shooting a client-rendered page
mid-load (skeleton placeholders where content goes) and only the first viewport: the snapshot call
now passes `gotoOptions.waitUntil: networkidle2` with a timeout, a settle beat for lazy content,
and `screenshotOptions.fullPage`. A new streaming route (`POST /api/v1/safe-browse/stream`,
newline-delimited JSON stage lines) reports the redirect probe's settled facts while the renderer
still works, via a `CaptureStage` callback on `captureSafeView`; the page's loading viewport
narrates them ("Landed on youtube.com after 2 redirects. Rendering the page…") instead of a
generic line. And `lookupRegistration` walks a hostname up to the registrable domain that actually
answers — `www.youtube.com` is a registry 404 while `youtube.com` is the record the member meant —
stopping at the two-label floor and never walking an IP. Screen side: the tab strip aligns to the
address bar's height, the Different Site indicator (landed URL, badge, copy) lives only in the
Overview tab, the Soon marker survives only on the Live control's hover, and the WHOIS page
renders its result frame at rest.
- **The conflicts screens were built, and the sidebar said Soon.** The surface under `/conflicts` —
the check runner, the firm's own check history, one check read back with its candidates and their
adjudications, and where a matter stands — has been real Svelte for some time, over an API that
serves every read the read-surface design named. The sidebar destination never noticed: the entry in
`apps/web/src/lib/navigation/destinations.ts` still carried `shipped: false` with `announced: true`,
which is the one combination that renders a row **disabled and without an href**, and the Ctrl+K
palette listed it as `Conflicts Check — soon`. Every one of those screens was reachable only by
typing its address.

Nothing failed on it, and nothing could have: a registry flag disagreeing with the routes beside it
is not a type error, and the flag is the whole mechanism by which the sidebar decides what exists.
`apps/web/test/conflicts-surface.test.ts` now asserts the destination is shipped, has its href, and
carries no Soon treatment, so the surface and the promise cannot come apart again silently.

**A matter's conflicts record moved inside the matter.** Where a matter stood was served at
`/conflicts/matters/{matterId}`, outside the matter shell, and reachable in practice only from the
intake checklist. It is now the matter's own **Conflicts** section, on the strip directly after
Intake — separate from Intake rather than folded into it, because running a check is not one of the
intake procedure's steps, it is the act a step asks about, and the record it writes outlives the
intake that prompted it. The old address survives as a 308 rather than a 404.

The section claims the `conflictsCheck` timeline source, which `sections.ts` had declared as one no
section owned. `packages/calendar/src/sources/all.ts` was already building
`/matters/{id}/conflicts?entry={checkId}` for those rows — the seam was placed and pointed at a
route that did not exist — so a conflicts check on a matter's Activity chronology opened nowhere and
explained itself instead. It now opens the check it names, honouring the deep-link obligation in
`entry-from-url.ts` by going to the check's own record rather than landing the reader on the
standing.

**And the link to the conflicts record stopped vanishing the moment it mattered.** The intake
checklist offered its way through to a step's fact only while `step.record === null`, so ticking
"run the conflicts check" removed the only route from the matter to the check that was run. That is
precisely backwards: "we checked" is a question asked months later, by somebody who was not there
when the box was ticked. The link is now offered whether or not the step is recorded, and says
which of the two it is.
- The discovery processing slice landed a load-profile measurement harness that prints its latencies,
and the console-ban fitness function failed on `main` the moment it merged. The harness is the same
class as the measurement CLI already on the allowlist — a developer tool whose stdout is its product,
printing machine-relative numbers precisely because asserting them against a threshold would turn a
busy laptop into a red build — so it joins the allowlist rather than losing the print.

Two things this exposed rather than caused. The ban scans `src/`, which includes a `.test.ts` living
there, so a measurement test is held to a rule written for application code; the existing measurement
files avoid it only by keeping the logic in a plain module and letting the allowlisted CLI do the
printing. And the ban's own comment said "the ONLY two source files" above a list of five.

It merged green because the check that catches it lives in `packages/telemetry` and the verification
run covered the packages the change touched. A repository-wide fitness function is not in the package
whose code it governs, so scoping a test run by the diff can skip it entirely.
- **Moving between a matter's sections threw, because the create control treated an ordinary navigation as a defect.** The header's control checks that the claim behind it answers for the section the reader is standing on — a real guarantee, since the label comes from the address and the behaviour from the page, and a mismatch would mean the label says one thing and the press does another. It enforced that by throwing.

Leaving a section updates the address _before_ the outgoing page's effect cleanup releases its claim, so for one flush every ordinary navigation holds a claim for the section just left. The check fired on that window, inside a `$derived`, which crashed the screen: `The create control is claimed for "files" but the reader is on "parties"`, on every pair of tabs.

The decision moved into `honouredClaim` in `create-action.svelte.ts`, which ignores a claim belonging to another section rather than throwing. The guarantee is unchanged — an unhonoured claim is not pressable — and the control falls back to disabled carrying the line it already shows in the moment before a section claims. A genuine mismatch, a page answering for a section it does not render, now surfaces as a control that never becomes pressable instead of a white screen. Four tests pin the predicate, including the navigation window itself.

The slot's other rule is untouched: a second claimant while a first still holds the control is still refused loudly, because that one really is two parts of a screen believing they own the same action.
- **The custody register's nine list endpoints each carried a different defect, and one fix would have
been wrong for most of them.** Traced individually rather than paged for symmetry.

The overdue check-out sweep and the holds report now page over the platform's keyset cursor. Both are
ascending, and the direction is the point: a page of the most overdue check-outs, or the oldest holds
still in force, is the answer a firm wants, and paging forward walks toward the merely late.

The holdings-per-owner report and the stocktake list are **capped with a signal** instead. Their
answers now carry a `capped` flag, true when the firm holds or has counted more than the response
names. Neither can take a cursor honestly: holdings-per-owner is ordered by `packets_held DESC`, a
count the query computes rather than a column any row carries, and a keyset over it would page by a
value that does not exist in the table. The stocktake list answers which count is running now and what
the last one found — a short answer was the right shape all along, and only the silence about it was
the defect.

The item-type vocabulary, the location tree, and the per-location occupancy report are recorded as
bounded by construction with what bounds each. The location tree is left whole for the same reason a
matter's folder tree is: its callers resolve a packet's shelf to a path through its ancestors, and
half a tree resolves to a wrong path rather than a short one.

Two are left as they were, with the reason written down: the sighting list orders on three columns and
the reminder collector merges two streams, and each needs a design decision rather than a fix applied
for consistency.
- **Four surfaces named the wrong day, and the gate that would have caught them now exists.** "Date Entered" on the time details panel and the time print sheet, the attachment date on the time record window, and "Created" on the invoice print sheet each rendered `createdAt.slice(0, 10)` — the **UTC** day of a stored instant — through a formatter that pins to UTC.

A record entered at 18:30 in Los Angeles has a `createdAt` of 01:30Z the next morning, so all four named the following day for every entry made after late afternoon in an American office. Two of them are print sheets that reach clients.

They now use `formatInstantDate`, which reads the day in the viewer's own zone. The two print-sheet contexts gained an `instantDate` member beside their existing `date`, because the two are not the same question: `date` is contracted as "a work date as a reader sees it" and pins to UTC so a recorded day never moves, and passing an instant's first ten characters through it was a misuse of that contract rather than only a formatting slip.

The date gate missed this: its rule matched `.toISOString().slice(0, 10)` and not a slice of a value already holding an instant, which is the form all four took. It now reads the receiver — a name that can only mean a moment — and found twenty-three more sites in the same shape. Those genuinely wanted the UTC day, so `civilDateOf` gained the string form and they say so by name; a slice is invisible to every scan, which is the whole reason the four bugs were written that way. `validFrom`/`validTo` are deliberately not read, because those columns hold a civil date at one end and an instant at the other by design.

Worth recording: this is the case a compile-time brand could not have caught. `createdAt.slice(0, 10)` produces a perfectly well-formed `YYYY-MM-DD`, so a branded type obtained by parsing accepts it. The value is not malformed — it is the wrong day, and only knowing where the string came from tells the two apart.
- **The file manager's details panel renames what it is showing, in the panel.** Pressing the name called `onRename` back into `file-manager.svelte`, which set `manager.renamingKey` — so the field opened on the ROW, which may be scrolled out of view or in another folder. The reader pressed a name and watched a selection happen somewhere else. The panel now hosts the field itself: `file-inspector.svelte` keeps its own editing state, seeds the draft through `renameFieldValue`/`renameSelectionEnd` so only the stem is selected, commits through `committedRename` so a hidden extension reattaches, and takes one seam from the host — `onRenameCommit(name)`, answering null or the sentence that refuses. The behaviour is Magnus's `conversation-name.svelte`, which had already settled it: Enter commits, Escape abandons, blur commits, and a refusal keeps the field open holding what was typed with the reason beneath it, because a name that collides is fixed where it was written. The field takes the resting control's own height (`mc-input-sm` and `mc-button-sm` are the same `--mc-density-control-sm`), so opening it moves nothing else in the header. Six mounted tests in `apps/web/test/file-inspector-rename.test.ts` — the claim is about a rendered panel, so a source scan could not make it.

**A safety check says what it ran under, and a request that never ran says so.** Three facts the platform already recorded and did not show. The re-scan route audits `enqueued` on every request, and nothing read it back: a request that reached no queue — no engine recorded, or none bound — showed as "Check requested" and the reader waited for a verdict that was never coming. It now reads **Not queued** in the warning register with the reason beside it, derived from the second unread fact, the engine recorded at the moment of asking (`currentEngineVersion` in the same metadata, which `scanFactsFromMetadata` dropped). Third, the firm's own scan settings: the history response carries the four the File Safety page writes, so the Safety tab states the engine decomposed into its three parts beside the depth, the threshold, the treatment and the re-authentication choice — and says, in its own last row, that only the ENGINE is recorded per check. What a check ran under, when somebody has since changed the depth or the threshold, is recorded nowhere; stating that is more useful than a number that might describe a different configuration.

`FileScanEvent` gains `queued`, `FileScanHistory` gains `scanSettings`, and the reading of the policy on this route is deliberately open to any member who can read the file — reading a verdict means reading what it was looked for with, where CHANGING the policy stays behind `firm:manageScanPolicy`. The four settings' words moved into `scan-policy-words.ts` so the settings page that writes them and the Safety tab that reads them cannot name one setting two ways.
- **The `.dev.vars` placeholder guard was red on `main`, and with it the standing merge bar.**

`apps/api-worker/test/dev-vars.test.ts` pins the tracked `.dev.vars` byte-for-byte against a literal in the test. The two had disagreed since the header comment in `.dev.vars` was rewritten without the literal being updated in the same commit — which that test's own docstring asks for. Every key and value matched; the difference was one sentence of prose about which firm-provisioning adapter runs locally. So `pnpm test` failed for every branch, on a file most branches never touch, and the failure said nothing about the branch that ran it.

The literal now carries the file's current header word for word, and the test says out loud why the prose is pinned at all: a byte-for-byte guard cannot tell a rewritten explanation from an inserted credential, so it refuses both and a person decides which it was. That is the guard working, not a flaw in it — the cost is exactly this, and it is the right trade for a file whose whole job is to never hold a real secret.
- The version and database-health reads no longer go dark when the firm database is the thing that is broken.

Both are firm-scoped, and the chokepoint resolves a firm by checking that the session's member row is active — a read against the firm's own database. When that database cannot be reached at all, the check does not answer, it throws, and every firm-scoped route answers 500. That includes the two routes whose entire subject is whether the firm database can be reached. An unreachable database took out the panel built to say the database is unreachable, and the reported symptom became an unrelated version read failing.

`RouteMeta` gains `firmDatabaseOutage`, defaulting to `"reject"` so every route that has not thought about it still fails closed: membership could not be verified, so no firm data is served. A route declaring `"tolerate"` is admitted with the context the control plane alone could build, and no permissions. Registration refuses that declaration alongside a named capability — permissions are read from the same unreachable database, so a route claiming one could not be honoured — which makes the misconfiguration a startup failure rather than a discovery during the outage it was written for.

Nothing is relaxed while the database is up: the member-active check runs exactly as before and a deactivated member is still absent. Nothing leaks while it is down: the reads that would carry firm data are the reads that cannot complete. The health handler already caught every probe and reported `unreachable` per check — it simply never got to run.
- **The Directory has a listing.** It never had one: the screen was designed to be searched and not browsed, so `MINIMUM_QUERY_LENGTH` characters had to be typed before anything appeared, and a firm that had entered twenty clients opened it to an instruction. The reasoning was half right — a ranked, capped answer must never be dressed as an index — and drew the wrong conclusion; the answer is to build the index.

`GET /api/v1/directory/entities` is the new read: both node tables unioned into one sequence, ordered by a name key computed per table so a row never sorts under one name and prints another, cursor-paged over `(sort name, id)` through the existing opaque token, and carrying `total` for the whole record rather than the page. `kind` narrows it. Deleted and merged-away records are excluded. It lives in `packages/directory/src/entity-listing.ts` and reaches the firm database through the chokepoint like every other directory read. The ordering key is computed rather than stored, so the read scans the node tables; a stored normalized sort column is the change if that ever stops being cheap enough.

The screen now shows the index at rest and the search answer only when a query is asked, as two visibly different objects: the index is the platform's one table (sortable, filterable, paged, counted), and the search answer keeps the firm's relevance order, is never re-sorted client-side, and keeps its capped line.
- **Five discovery reads that grow with the corpus answered with a page and no way to reach the rest.**
Each carried a LIMIT and no cursor, so a review set larger than a page returned a prefix that read
exactly like a complete answer.

The coding history is the one that mattered most. It is the record a challenge to a production is
answered from — who coded what, when, under what criteria, and who reversed it — and its whole value
is that it is complete. Truncated to the most recent fifty acts, it omitted precisely the history a
meet-and-confer is about. It now pages, newest first.

The matter's review sets, a review set's loads, its Custodians of Record, and a document's other
copies page too. Two of them needed their sort key made total first: `display_name` alone does not
order two custodians who share a name, and the occurrence list ordered on the duplicate's identifier
with nothing behind it. Both now carry the row's own identifier as the tiebreak, so the keyset cannot
skip or repeat at a page boundary. The custodian list stays alphabetical and ascending, because that
is how a person looks a name up; the copies list is the read behind "which custodians held this
document", and a boilerplate announcement held by every custodian in the matter is exactly the
document that question gets asked about.

Every one of these composes the review-set access predicate into its SQL. The keyset clause is placed
between that predicate and the ORDER BY, so the predicate still precedes the LIMIT and the visibility
fitness pass holds unchanged.

**Two are recorded as bounded by construction, each with the index that bounds it.** A review set's
access list holds one row per member (`review_set_access_member_unique_index`), and a document's live
coding holds one row per tag (`review_document_tag_live_unique_index`), so the bounds are the firm's
headcount and its own tag catalog rather than the corpus.

**`keysetClause` joins the cursor helpers.** The existing helpers push onto a conditions array, which
does not fit a statement assembled by string concatenation around an access predicate whose position
in the WHERE clause is load-bearing. Five reads needed the same clause; it now has one home.
- **The documentation says what the repository does.** A review pass over the root and conventions
docs, changing only what could be verified against the code, the account or the git history: the
README's quickstart now gives the install order the root `CLAUDE.md` insists on (`pnpm install`
first, because `vp` is a devDependency) and the single-flight `pnpm test`; `CLAUDE.md` says that
`pnpm install` activates the tracked hooks through `postinstall` and that four packages, not three,
carry git-ignored WASM output; the maintenance runbook stops claiming the per-merge docs assembly
keeps the changelog current minutes after a merge (GitHub Actions has been blocked account-side since
2026-08-05, and 401 changelog fragments and 171 pending decisions are waiting) and stops saying the
docs-sync Routine has not been created (it was, twice); the documentation standard names the lint
rules that exist instead of a link checker and a changelog gate that do not; the conventions index
lists the four rulings ledgers and the engine-host seam it omitted and no longer calls `code-style.md`
and `typescript.md` stubs; the gate workflow's and the pre-push hook's comments stop describing
`git push main:release` as the only deploy; the roadmap stops placing the file-manager primitives on
a branch that no longer exists and stops saying Directory pronouns await a pull request; and the
relative links that broke when `apps/worker` became `apps/api-worker`, when decision fragments were
numbered, and when the calendar's time-zone module moved to `@magna-carta/civil-time` point at the
files again. Fifty-two `docs/active-work/` notes whose branches had landed are retired, with their
`status.d/` pointers cleared — twenty-seven of them the registry itself could not call landed from
the shallow clone a cloud session starts with, and could once the history was fetched in full —
along with the two July notes (`file-surface-web`, `slice-0-7b-app-shell`) whose streams the
notes themselves or the later auth-interface pull requests had superseded. The firm-usage stream's
one document that never reached `main`, the per-firm R2 bucket-isolation options brief that
`docs/specs/2026-09-01-per-firm-r2-bucket-isolation-review.md` reviews by path, is landed at the
revision that review read, and the download register's ledger evidence names the save-target seam
that is already on `main`.
- **The template library rendered as the crash screen on every visit.** `CreateControl` refuses a noun longer than its fixed width holds, `/documents` shipped `noun="Template"` against a budget of seven, and the refusal is a `throw` raised while the screen renders — so the render boundary replaced the whole page and the defect read as a 500 rather than a label that did not fit.

The owner's ruling was to re-measure the one width: `size.create-control` is 140px (was 136px) and `CREATE_NOUN_MAX_LENGTH` is eight (was seven), so every create control in the product moves together rather than one screen stretching the control for its own label. The budget is written down as the measurement it is — "New Template" sets 81.6px in the reading face at the small size, and a 140px control leaves 80px of label after the padding, the glyph and its gap.

Two gates now read a noun before it renders. `pnpm run lint:matter-create-control` read create nouns only out of the matter section registry, where they are declared as data, and never out of a screen's own markup, where this one was written; it reads both now and names the file and line. `apps/web/test/documents-library-screen.test.ts` mounts the screen under the real root layout, so a render-time throw of any kind there fails in the battery instead of on the deployed site.
- **An office document could not open in the browser editor, and the screen never said it was trying.**

Two defects, found on one real open, that compounded into a blank frame.

coolwsd composes its `frame-ancestors` from the two origins it knows — its own, and the WOPI host it was configured with — which is correct for the ordinary integration, where the WOPI host is also the page doing the framing. It is wrong for this topology by construction: the WOPI host here is `wopi.magna-carta.internal`, a non-routable name the container reaches only through outbound interception, and the page doing the framing is the firm's own app origin, which coolwsd is never told and cannot derive. The policy it sent named the editor origin and an internal host, the browser found the app origin missing, and refused. No document could have opened through this path.

The app origins are now added to that policy by the worker in front of the container (`apps/edit-worker/src/embedding-policy.ts`), not by coolwsd's own configuration. `net.frame_ancestors` is obsolete and ignored from CODE 24.12.4.1 onward, and its replacement `net.content_security_policy` is truncated at the first space when passed through the image's `extra_params` — which a list of origins always contains. Beyond that, who may embed the editor is a fact about this deployment's app domain rather than about the editor image, and nothing in this repository can exercise the container's configuration, where the rewrite is a pure function with tests beside it. The sources coolwsd put there are kept, because the editor frames pages of its own. Widening costs no tenancy: the access token names one version of one file in one firm and is re-verified on every callback, so the framing origin was never the gate.

The waiting state ended at the wrong moment. Opening is two waits — the launch call, which answers at once, and the editor container, which starts on first address — and the screen fell quiet between them, exactly when the long wait began. It now runs until the editor itself reports the document on screen, through the frame message protocol, and states it with Retry when the editor stays silent past a budget that allows for a cold start. For the editor to speak at all the host must tell it where: the launch now carries the origin that asked for it in the signed token, and `CheckFileInfo` returns it as `PostMessageOrigin` — carried rather than configured, because per-firm subdomains mean there is no one app origin a deployment could name.
- **The editor refused its own WOPI host, because the allow-list was being set through a channel the image does not reliably read.**

Once the frame loaded and the WebSocket connected, coolwsd answered "Unauthorized WOPI host": the WOPISrc host `wopi.magna-carta.internal` was not in its allow-list, even though the container's `aliasgroup1` environment variable named exactly that host. That variable is read by coolwsd itself, and only when the image's entrypoint passes `--use-env-vars`; and the mode switch it writes lands on the key `alias_groups[@mode]`, without the `storage.wopi.` prefix that `parseAliases` reads, so a group defined that way sits under the template's default mode `first`, which is the one state parseAliases refuses. The variable was set, the socket was up, and the host was still rejected.

The allow-list is now three `--o:` overrides in `extra_params` — the group's host, its allow flag, and the mode spelled `storage.wopi.alias_groups[@mode]=groups` — which the entrypoint expands onto coolwsd's command line and coolwsd folds into its highest-priority configuration layer. It is the channel every other setting in that file already uses, and the one this deployment proves works: `ssl.enable=false` from the same string is why the editor serves over HTTP behind the edge at all. It reaches coolwsd whether or not a given image version's entrypoint reads environment variables.

Recorded beside it: the editor worker gains its area note (`apps/edit-worker/CLAUDE.md`), the home for the container's operational knowledge — how the allow-list is set, what "Unauthorized WOPI host" means, and the three coolwsd log lines that decide it.
- **Production deploys stopped failing Worker validation: the app worker's entrypoint no longer
spends the startup budget.** Every deploy after the route count grew past a threshold failed with
error 10021 ("Script startup exceeded CPU time limit"), leaving `main` merged but undeployed. The
cost was the aggregate of the entrypoint's static import graph — every route module builds its zod
schemas and OpenAPI metadata at module scope. `src/index.ts` now keeps only the Durable Object
class re-exports (the one thing that must be synchronous at startup) and reaches the Hono app, the
Cron pass router, and the queue router through one dynamic import of the new
`src/event-dispatch.ts`, which the runtime evaluates on the first event instead of at validation:
roughly 1.5 s of local startup work became 0.24 s under `wrangler check startup`. The rule is
recorded in `docs/conventions/build-performance.md` (a Worker entrypoint keeps no static imports
beyond its Durable Object exports; measure entrypoint changes with `wrangler check startup`).
- **The matter's file list is the only part of that screen that scrolls, and undo reaches the acts a reader performs on it.** Five corrections to the file manager, from the owner's walk of the deployed screen.

Scrolling a long folder used to scroll the whole page: the matter's title, its row of sections and the folder path all left the top of the screen while the counts strip walked off the bottom. The cause was one utility and it reached every working surface in the product. A screen of this shape renders inside a column whose height is a minimum over an auto height — deliberately, so an ordinary document section can still grow past the fold — and the section inside it asked for its share with `flex-1`, whose zero basis is a PERCENTAGE. Against a column sized by its content that resolves to the item's own content, so the section reported the whole table as its base size, the column grew to meet it, the minimum never applied, and nothing was ever capped. A definite basis gives the column its minimum back. The four money ledgers take the same fix.

Undo and redo were wired to one act out of five. A move between folders was recorded; renaming, deleting and pinning were not, so the controls sat disabled through most of a session and read as broken — the stack and the pair of controls were never the defect. Each of those acts now records a step with a real inverse, and each says what it will take back ("Undo renaming Motion.pdf to Answer.pdf"). A move records only what actually moved, which it did not before: an origin written before the write meant a refused move still landed on the stack, and undo would have offered to put back something that never left. Deleting a folder has no restore behind it, so it records nothing and the screen says so instead, naming Deleted Files, where the documents it held can still be recovered one by one.

In the left rail, a chosen folder and a chosen view now look like one state rather than two. The view rows wore the ordinary selected surface, which on that sunken rail is very nearly the rail's own colour, so the open view read as barely marked beside a folder that was plainly lit.

In the icon layout, a long file name used to run over the tiles beside it and both became unreadable. A name now wraps onto a second and a third line and then ends in an ellipsis, with the whole name on the tile's hover; the pin's space is held open on every tile, so pinning lights a glyph and moves nothing.

The details panel's rename commits through the panel now and runs the list's own path — the same collision check, the same write, the same undo step.
- **Five corrections against the deployed file manager, one of which was never the file manager's.**

The toolbar's own search field is gone. The matter is searched from the matter header and nowhere else; this surface had a second field, and the ruling that put the search in the header predates the header having one. What reaches the file manager's Search Results view now is the query in the address (`?q=`), read the same way `?entry=` already hands a section a record, so a search still opens the view, losing it still leaves, and a search survives a reload.

The rail's "No folders yet" sentence is gone — the root row and the control that makes a folder had already said it. The table header menu's display settings moved out of the Columns submenu into the menu's own root: Columns holds columns, and a setting filed under a noun that does not name it is a setting nobody finds. The icon view's settings control moved to the LEFT of the list-or-icons swapper, so the swapper stops sliding sideways every time a reader changes view.

**The breadcrumb reading black in dark mode was a document-wide defect wearing a file manager costume.** The app declared no `color-scheme` and gave the root no text colour, so the browser painted its own light-mode system colours underneath every dark theme, and any element written without a colour took `canvastext` — black — however dark the band behind it was. The tokens were correct the whole time, which is why it looked like one screen's bug. `packages/design-system/src/lib/styles/base.css` declares both, in the `base` layer, imported by the app entry and the catalog preview alike; it also hands the browser the dark canvas behind an overscroll, dark scrollbars and dark form controls, none of which a token reaches. Measured before and after on the running app: an uncoloured element computed `rgb(0, 0, 0)` without it and the theme's ink with it.
- **The file manager's folder path no longer moves the toolbar, and Home is always in reach.** Opening
a folder deep enough for the path to outrun its strip used to put a horizontal scrollbar under it,
and the scrollbar took its own height out of the toolbar: every control on the row shifted the moment
a reader went deep, and shifted back when they came up. The path also carried Home at its head, which
made it the first thing to scroll off the left — the one crumb always worth reaching.

Home is pinned beside back, forward and up now, outside the part that scrolls. A path deeper than its
room folds its middle behind an ellipsis, keeping the folder under Home and the last two, and
pressing the ellipsis opens the folded folders as a menu: one press to any of them. What still does
not fit scrolls, with the scrollbar hidden and the gilt edge rule drawn in its place, so the toolbar
is the same height at every depth; the strip holds itself at its far end, so the folder the reader is
standing in is never the crumb that scrolled out of sight.

The fold itself is the design system's one collapse rule (`collapseBreadcrumb`), shared with the
`Breadcrumb` component, so the two surfaces that draw a path cannot fold it differently. Hiding a
scrollbar is now the shared `mc-scrollbar-hidden` recipe, which the sidebar's nav list had written
out for itself.
- Eight failures the scoped gate never sees, found by the full test battery on the shipping branch.

Four were pinned state that the shipping work deliberately changed, each mechanism working as designed: the Owner/Admin permission list in `me.test.ts` and `auth-provisioning-e2e.test.ts` (which gained `integrations:useConnection`), the back-navigation exemption register — pinned by name precisely so a new exemption cannot be added without a second person reading its reason — and `tool-destinations`, which used shipping as its example of a `soon` tool. Shipping is `alpha` now; the case is about the STAGE, so it follows one of the three tools that still has it.

Two were real mistakes. A bare `window.open(url, "_blank")` in the shipment window bypassed `$lib/navigation/open-beside`, the one helper every new-tab opening goes through so the isolation a second tab gets is decided in one place rather than per caller. And the object-dimension scan read `credentials.put(...)` as a bucket write; it is the integration credential store and reaches no object storage at all, so it carries the sanctioned marker with that as its reason.

Two were one obsolete file: `shipping-unbuilt-credential-seam.test.ts` asserted that connect, rate, purchase, track and refund all refuse with 501 "because the per-firm credential read is still a seam". That read is built, so the file's premise is gone and the file with it.

Not fixed here, and not from this branch: `discovery-routes.test.ts` > "converges rather than duplicating when the same selection runs twice" fails with 409 where it expects 202. Verified against a clean worktree at `origin/main` — identical failure, same assertion — so it is pre-existing and belongs to whoever owns that lane.
- **Two corrections from the owner's pass over the deployed rail.**

The Customize row's **grip was inert**. `onpointerdown` sat on the row's label button and the grip
was its sibling, so the one thing on the row that says "move me" was the one thing that would not.
The press is caught on the row now — grip, glyph, name and badge all start the drag — with the
trailing eye/star/lock let out by `event.target.closest(".mc-sidebar-row-control")` rather than by a
handler on each, so a control added to that row later is covered without anybody remembering to. The
row takes `role="presentation"`: it is a layout box, and the accessible path is the button inside,
which keeps its role, its `aria-roledescription` and the Alt+Arrow it announces.

The **sub-menu step was too shallow to read**. The rail's rows carry an 8px inset of their own, so a
24px indent put a child's glyph barely a glyph's width right of its parent's and a cluster read as a
flat list with a hairline through it. It is 32px now — 20 of margin, which the hairline sits on, and
12 of padding, which keeps the rule off the rows.
- **The registration and sign-in path now works end to end, and its failures identify themselves.**
The confirmation mail carries a link to `/register/confirm?token=` (origin from the request) plus
the typed code as fallback, instead of the bare token as its whole body; the password-reset mail
links straight at the new `/login/reset-password` screen (origin from the request, or
`APP_BASE_URL` on the request-less firm-provision consumer path — `password-reset-link.ts`), never
at the library's own redirect hop, which spent the token on a bare GET and stranded the visitor on
an error page. The reset screen itself replaces its holding card: request a link, set the new
password, both enumeration-safe. A server fault on any joining screen now surfaces its correlated
Error ID under the message (`joiningSupportErrorId` + `CredentialNotice`), per
`docs/conventions/error-logging.md`. Local development no longer 500s on a fresh database: a
dev-only middleware (`dev-control-plane-bootstrap.ts`, gated on the same fail-closed signal as the
dev seed route) brings the control-plane schema to head before the first API request, closing the
"no such table" failure `wrangler dev` hit because it never fires the migration cron. The
terms-of-service and privacy-policy confirmation rows on the registration form flow as sentences
again instead of scattering across the label's flex row.
- The lint cost proxy stops counting work nobody does.

CI does not lint the whole repository on a pull request. It lints a computed scope, and it defers the one package whose lint is effectively a whole-repo lint — `apps/api-worker` — to the post-merge pass. Which package that is gets decided by a cost proxy: the number of lintable files the type-aware linter has to pull into a type program.

The proxy counted every file in a package's dependency closure, tests included. A dependency's tests are never pulled into a dependent's type program, because nothing imports a test — so across api-worker's 61-package closure that was 609 phantom files, 30% of the one number the rule is decided by. Its weight falls from 2022 to 1413 once they are dropped. A package's own tests still count, because linting a package does lint them.

The share that selects a sink moves from 0.50 to 0.35 in the same change and not independently of it: on the honest numerator, api-worker is 46% of the workspace rather than 65%, so at 0.50 it would have stopped being selected and the deferral would have become a silent no-op. The new share is set from measured lint time rather than from the proxy that was in question — api-worker takes 11.7s against 2.6s for `apps/web` and 1.4–2.1s for a typical domain package, and its per-file cost is superlinear, so a file-count proxy understates the outlier it is picking.

Two guards that compared a sink against its neighbour, or against how far past the bar it sat, are gone. Both fired on ordinary growth in `apps/web` rather than on anything about the deferral, and one could have deselected the expensive package while keeping a cheaper one. Selection is already the outlier test; what is left asserts the two failure modes worth failing on — no sink selected, so the deferral does nothing, and more than two, so it has stopped being about outliers. Simulated against this dependency graph, the rule now stays green from today through +1200 files in `apps/web`, while `apps/web` joins as a genuine second sink and api-worker eventually ages out of one.

Separately: a package with no lintable files of its own can never be a sink. `apps/web-worker` has zero and depends only on `apps/web`, so it carried `apps/web`'s weight exactly and forever — deferring it would defer no work while spending one of the two sink slots.
- **The file list's geometry, the scale control, and two panels that grew when they were pressed.** Six defects from the owner's round of 2026-09-16, five of them in one screen and one of them in two.

The grid reserved its row-mark slot as an inline box in every first cell. Every surface that composes a first cell out of an icon and a name composes it with flex — which is block-level — so the mark took a line of its own above the content: a band of empty space over every file name, a name reading low in a row whose other cells were still centred in a row a line taller than it should have been, and a list a third taller than the density asked for. The slot is now the cell's own leading padding with the pin painted into it (`data-table.css`), so the cell holds exactly one in-flow child whatever the surface renders there. The reservation is unchanged: a table that can mark a row still reserves the width on every row, so pinning moves nothing.

`DataTable.Grid` takes a `frame` of `card` or `flush`. A card's last row drops its hairline because the card's own bottom rule runs a hairline below it; a flush grid has no card — the file manager's toolbar and counts strip are its frame — so the rule left the last file as the one row in the list with nothing under it. Flush keeps the hairline and fills the frame. It replaces the `rounded-none border-0` incantation four file-manager grids and five money ledgers were each spelling out, which is the right trade: giving up the card changes three things that have to move together.

The scale control now scales the list. It moved one thing in list view — a single flip between two densities, at one threshold in the middle of a ten-step range — so nine of the ten steps changed nothing a reader could see. The grid reads `--mc-table-grid-scale`, a multiplier defaulting to 1, for its text, its row height and the glyphs inside its rows; the file manager publishes it once on the file area, so every view including the inside of an archive takes it. The header band and the counts strip do not scale: they are the frame around the list, and growing them pushes the rows a reader asked to see more of off the screen.

Location leaves the file list's browse columns, where a folder listing already answers "where is this" in the path above it and the tree beside it — it had to ship hidden for exactly that reason. It stands in Search Results and File Analysis, where rows come from different folders. File Type gives up the monospace face and reads in the table's own.

The Change Status panel is two sides: the steps down the left, and the step under discussion — what it does to the record, what it requires, and the field it asks for — down the right. It opens on the step the lifecycle runs toward, so `Choose a step first.` is struck along with the state that produced it.
- The platform's one table now obeys the rulings it was built to carry, and it can group and mark its rows.

Four settled rulings were already contradicted by the table that shipped days ago, all of them in the per-column filter. The set filter's narrow field said "Type to narrow the choices" and the text filter said "Contains…" — both struck, because every ghost text is the FIELD'S NAME and never a description of what to do; each now carries the column's own label. The set filter's select-all was a static checkbox that stated what IS; it is now one control that states what pressing it will DO, reading "Select none" while everything is on and "Select all" the moment anything is off. And the set filter carried a "Clear This Filter" button, which said the same thing that control already says: a set filter with everything selected IS no filter, so it now carries no clear control at all. The other filter kinds keep theirs, and still only while a filter is in play.

A fifth was in the columns menu: an unpinned column's control drew the crossed-out pin, a different glyph for what is meant to be one glyph in two states. There is one pin everywhere the pin state shows — pinned rows and pinned columns alike — and fill is the only difference.

Alongside the conformance work the table gained the two things every list says about a row before it says anything about the row's data. **Row groups:** pinned items sit above everything, separated by a rule, in the order the member arranged them rather than the table's sort — a pinned file leads a list whose folders would otherwise sort ahead of it. A pinned key whose row a filter excluded contributes nothing, so the footer's "n of m" stays true. **Row marks:** one vocabulary — the filled pin on the row's first cell, a dashed edge while a row waits on a cut or a copy (a cut row speaks quieter, because it is leaving), and that same quieter voice for a row present but not of the list's own kind, which is what a deleted match among live search results and an event inherited from a folder act both need.

Every fixed ruling is pinned by a test that asserts the property the ruling names, so the next round finds them asserted rather than remembered. The developer console's table-states gallery gains the groups-and-marks specimen.
- **The repo-wide fitness sweep reaches CI.** `tooling/check-scoped/repo-wide.mjs` has always defined the repo-wide set as two halves — the `lint:*` scripts, and the Vitest checks that self-register with an `@repo-wide-fitness` directive — and the gate's `governance` job called only the first. The second half is where the encryption chokepoint scan (`no-plaintext-escape`), the telemetry console ban, the design system's off-token and `bits-ui` boundary scans, the PII registry coverage check and the schema conformance checks live; twenty-six members in all.

They were not unenforced, exactly: each runs under its own package's Vitest project. But the test battery is asked for on a pull request rather than automatic — the `run-tests` label, always on a queued merge — so on an unlabelled pull request nothing looked at them and the first report came from the merge queue, which is the most expensive place to learn that a protected-field read escaped its chokepoint.

The sweep is now a step of its own in `governance`, both scopes, unconditional: about four seconds for twenty-six read-only scans in one un-isolated process. Deciding whether to run it would cost more than running it. `lint:lints` holds the workflow's `MAGNA_CARTA_FITNESS_SCOPES` value identical to `FITNESS_SCOPES_ENV` in the module, so a rename cannot quietly halve what the sweep covers.

The derivation was never the problem and is worth restating: neither half has a roster, and adding a check to either is a line in `package.json` or a comment in the check's own header. A derived set still has to be called, and this one was half-called for as long as it existed.
- The database panel names the fault instead of only the symptom, and the docket stops rendering `[object Object]`.

A firm database bricked by a failing migration read as "Firm database: Not answering" and nothing more. The cause was in hand the whole time — the durable object throws a specific error, and the health read was catching it in a bare `catch` and discarding it — so a reader went to the logs for a fact the panel already held. The firm-database check now carries that message, scrubbed and bounded to the same length the error pipeline gives any `messageHead`, because a constraint failure names the constraint but a UNIQUE violation can carry the offending value out with it. Where the database gave no reason at all, the row says that plainly rather than implying none exists.

Separately, the docket's failure branch interpolated the failure RECORD into its Alert, so a reader got `[object Object]` where the sentence belonged — and no Error ID, which is the one thing that makes a report actionable. It goes through the standard failure surface now, which reads the problem's own detail, keeps this screen's words for when the server sent none, and carries both the correlation handle and the retry.
- **The sweep that activates a new firm now carries the chain to its end, instead of leaving the owner's member record for the next cron fire.** Activation and the member mirror are two outbox rows, and the second is written by the consumer that applies the first — from inside the pass, after `sweepOutbox` had already read its pending set. So the firm went active within seconds and the row that every permission resolves through sat pending for up to five minutes: a founder attached to a firm whose own database had never heard of them, which is what the joining screen's last step and the database-health panel's "Not in the database yet" have been reporting. Redeeming an invitation never had the problem, because its `member.provision` row is committed by the request itself and is already pending when the sweep reads.

`sweepOutbox` gains `maxRounds`: a pass may re-read the pending set, taking only rows it has not already tried — a row whose publish failed keeps its remaining attempts for the next fire rather than spending them seconds apart — and stops as soon as a round finds nothing new. It defaults to 1, so every per-firm sweep is unchanged; those publish to a Queue and cannot feed the table they are reading. The control-plane sweep asks for four, which is headroom over the deepest chain its consumer map can make.
- **The sign-in password field carries a "Password" placeholder, matching the email field above it.**

The email input has read "Email Address" inside the box since the screen shipped; the password input
had nothing. The two sit one above the other, so the empty one read as the odd element rather than as
a deliberate difference.
- **The honorific field takes a second pick.** It holds several on one comma-separated line and the
list narrows against the part after the last comma — which while somebody types is the word they are
typing and at rest was the honorific they had just chosen, so the list offered exactly the one entry
already held. The reading moved out of `honorific-field.svelte` into `$lib/names/honorific-line.ts`,
where `typedPart(query, typing)` makes a settled line narrow nothing and the pick sequence is pinned
step by step. Two smaller faults went with it: the rows now carry a per-pick sequence number in their
value, so the primitive's "clicking the row it already holds is a deselect" can never leave an act
unreported, and the empty string that deselect reports is no longer appended as a token — which used
to leave a dangling comma in somebody's stored name.
- `vp run worktrees` printed two views of the active-work registry and they disagreed completely. The
streams list was empty — it required a non-agent worktree, and every stream here runs in an agent
worktree it explicitly omitted. The touch-overlap list, three lines below, named twenty branches
colliding across twenty-five paths. Every one of those branches had already landed: measured, twenty
of twenty. The section a new stream is told to consult before editing a shared file was wrong in
every entry it had.

Overlaps were computed from every note file on disk with no liveness test of any kind. A note is a
file, and a file outlives the work it describes — nothing deletes one but the hand that wrote it, and
the cue to do so, the branch disappearing, never fires here, because this repository cannot delete
its remote branches. Two hundred and thirty of them are still on the remote; exactly one note named a
branch that was actually gone.

The registry now decides for itself. "Has this branch landed" moves to `tooling/branch-landing`,
shared with the build-artifact cleaner, which already had to answer it for the opposite purpose — one
implementation, because a wrong answer either deletes a live workspace's build output or hides a real
collision. A stream is in flight while it has a workspace or an unlanded branch, so a forgotten note
can no longer manufacture a warning, and work on another machine is visible even though this checkout
sees none of its worktrees.

Three failures it used to swallow are now named rather than dropped: notes for branches that have
landed (thirty-six of them, swept here), notes whose branch resolves to no ref, and notes with no
frontmatter block — nineteen of those, half the directory, all silently collapsing onto one empty key
so that eighteen were discarded and their declared touch lists warned nobody. A note's branch is now
read from its path, which is why a malformed one still has an identity to report. Drift for a branch
that is not checked out locally reads as unknown instead of `+0/-0`; the live UI stream, which the old
output called perfectly in sync, is four hundred and eleven commits behind.
- **Dragging a sidebar row to reorder it stuttered, and it was three faults stacked.**

The slot size came from the pressed element's own height, but rows are separated by a gap, so every
slot was measured short and travel of two rows read as travel of two-and-a-bit. `Math.round` flipped
the landing index at exactly half a row, which is precisely where a hand rests while it is deciding,
so the whole list reflowed on every tremor. And each `pointermove` wrote state — several times per
frame on a high-rate mouse — reflowing the list between two paintings of it.

`DragReorderController` measures the real PITCH from two rows marked `data-reorder-row`, moves the
landing index only once the pointer is six tenths of a row past the boundary (and four tenths back,
so a boundary is crossed once), and coalesces the offset into one write per animation frame. The rows
also carry a grip now: the grab cursor only answers once the pointer is already on the row, which is
an answer to a question nobody asked.
- **Report an Issue from the Build Information panel now stays open, and the panel links the
repository its commits belong to.**

**A dialog cannot be a child of the surface that dismisses it.** The panel mounted the issue
reporter inside itself, and the panel is the body of the chip's popover: pressing Report an Issue
closed the popover (correctly — a popover cannot be read from under a modal) and the popover's exit
then unmounted the dialog it had just rendered, about a second after it appeared. Both surfaces went
at once, which read as the report refusing to open. The flag and the diagnosis it carries now live
in `$lib/components/issue-report.svelte.ts` and the shell mounts the one dialog — the same move
`build-panel.svelte.ts` makes for the panel's own open flag, and for the same reason.

**One dialog, one draft.** The profile menu and the command palette each mounted a copy of the
reporter too. Those two worked, because a menu that closes does not own the dialog's DOM, but three
mounts meant three drafts: a half-written report begun from the palette was invisible from the
profile menu, and the other door opened on an empty field. All three doors now open the shell's one
dialog and contribute nothing but the gesture.

**The panel links its own source.** `repositoryUrl()` joins the commit and dashboard links in
`$lib/versions/deployment-links.ts`, and the panel's header carries it at the end of the control
cluster so the three controls beside it keep their seats. It is `BUILD_IDENTITY.sourceRepository` —
resolved at build time from the git remote, the same value every commit link is already built on —
so a build that resolved none renders no link rather than a dead one, and it is signed-in only by
the same rule the commit and Worker links keep.
- **Two defects found by reviewing the provisioning work against a fresh firm that still could not upload.**

**The runbook told the operator to create the R2 S3 token scoped to the platform bucket.** That
instruction is from 2026-06-22; per-firm buckets began being signed with "the same account-scoped
credential" on 2026-09-03, and nobody reconciled the two. A key scoped to one bucket cannot sign a
valid request for any other, so a token made to the runbook's instruction refuses every per-firm
presigned PUT with 403 — after the reserve has succeeded, which is exactly the shape the owner has
been seeing. The row now says "Apply to all buckets in this account", and says why.

**The reset script treated a bucket that was never created as a failure to delete**, which would have
blocked the whole reset behind every firm provisioned under the dev adapter (which records a bucket
name and creates nothing). A 404 on the listing now counts as already gone.
- **The Database section reported `Schema: Up to date` for a firm database that was refusing every request because of its ledger.**

The schema check compared two head tags and nothing else. The runner rejects a ledger holding a tag it cannot place _before_ it applies anything, so the tags already there are untouched and the ledger can sit exactly at the expected head — which read as health. The panel then showed `Firm database: Not answering` and `Schema: Up to date` together, two rows describing one subsystem contradicting each other, with the reassuring one wrong. That is the reading the section exists to prevent, and it shipped in the section's own worst case.

`migrationState()` was already returning the fault; `readSchemaState` read the object and used two fields of it. The schema state gains `refused`, read from the fault first, and the row says `Not applied` with the count and head the database does have — the refusal's own sentence stays on the firm database row rather than being copied into a second place free to drift from it.

**Two signals the firm database computes and sends were being dropped in the same function.** `outOfOrderArrivals` names migrations that reached this database behind its own ledger head, which has no other symptom — everything is applied, but this database ran the pair in an order a newly provisioned firm will not, and for dependent migrations those orders do not reach the same schema. `restorePoint` names the instant the object can be restored to and the migrations it sits in front of, which is the question a database broken by a migration raises next. Both now appear as lineage notes beside the row, on the same "said only when there is something to say" rule as the provisioning backlog, and both travel in the copyable report — a pasted report is how a diagnosis reaches anyone who can act on it.

The restore point's Cloudflare bookmark is deliberately not on the wire: restoring is an operator's act with dashboard access, and the opaque handle does nothing for the member reading the panel.
- **The screen search clears, closes, and goes somewhere.** Four corrections from the owner's first
walk of the matter search, all made in the one shared control so every list screen inherits them.

A live query now carries an **X** at the field's trailing edge. Escape always cleared the field, but
Escape is a key and nothing on screen said so — a person reaching for a pointer had to select the
text and delete it. Both paths now run the same code.

**Clicking away closes an empty search.** It did not before: focus landing on the page's background
was read as focus going nowhere, so the field stayed open behind whatever you did next. A search
with something in it still stays open, because a narrowed list has to carry its reason on screen.

**Enter opens the full results**, flushing whatever you typed last so it never opens a search one
keystroke behind the field.

**The panel opens with the field** rather than with your first keystroke, so the scope and the way
through to the full search are reachable before you have typed anything — including going straight
to the full search page with nothing typed at all.

**A matter search finds folders.** Searching a matter for a folder by name answered nothing while
the folder sat in the tree: the Files source only ever matched file names, and consulted folders
only to say which one a file was in. Folder names are now matched alongside file names, in the same
Files group, each labelled so a folder and a file of the same name are told apart.

**The control opens in two directions, and the downward one is now a seam on the component.** The
icon opens to the inline start into the field (writing the query) and downward into a `panel` snippet
(aiming it, and reading what came back). That panel renders INSIDE ScreenSearch's own root, which is
load-bearing rather than tidy: the collapse watches measure against that root, so a panel rendered
beside the control is read as "outside" and shuts the field on the first click into it. The matter
search's scope moved out of the `scope` seam and into that panel — the seam seats a control inside
the field's leading edge, and "Everything on this matter" spelled out there took most of the field's
width on a header line.

The results page follows the same arrangement, through the same component. `MatterSearchSettings`
is the scope, the deleted toggle and a trailing slot, rendered by the header control inside its
panel and by the results page as the row under its field — two seats, one object. It holds no state:
both surfaces already keep the scope somewhere authoritative and disagree about where (the control
on its `MatterSearch`, the page in the address), so a third copy could only be right when neither of
theirs was.

One fitness rule was widened to allow it, deliberately and narrowly: a percentage on a logical
`inset-*` property means "this element's own extent", which `styles/animations.css` already
establishes cannot be a token. Only bare percentages, only on the four inset properties.
- **The load-profile snapshot tests stop failing on a busy runner.** Every test in `packages/fixtures/test/load-profile-snapshot.test.ts` seeds a real SQLite snapshot — the version-bump case seeds two — and all six ran under Vitest's five-second default, which is sized for tests that compute rather than tests that do a second or more of genuine work. On a loaded node shard that is not enough: the version-bump case timed out twice on one pull request, and it passes in 1.36 s on an idle machine, so what failed was a measurement of the runner rather than anything about the code.

The five seeding tests now carry an explicit `60_000`, matching `load-profile-smoke.test.ts` beside them, which was given the same treatment for the same reason and is why the pattern was already in the file next door. The sixth test seeds nothing and stays on the default, which is honest — it really is a unit test. Sixty seconds is deliberately generous: nothing here measures how fast the seeding is, so a timeout that trips on a slow machine only ever reports the machine.

Nothing about what the tests assert changed. The timeout is the clock, not the claim.
- **Three corrections on the signed-out surface.** The sign-in card's footer line is gone. The quiet
inline links beside a field — Register, Forgot Password, and every other side door sharing the
`QUIET_LINK` register — now carry `cursor-pointer`: they render as bare `<button>` elements to stay
out of the control chrome, and Tailwind v4's preflight sets `cursor: default` on a button, which the
design system's own Button recipe answers for itself but a raw-class link does not. And the chrome
band's four destinations now resolve through `ECOSYSTEM_SITES` instead of a local list of hardcoded
`#` hrefs, so Status links to the live status page and the three sites that are not stood up yet stay
inert until their registry entry carries a URL.

The band having its own copy of each address is what let the status page be live and unreachable from
here at the same time.
- **The `Tooltip.Provider` moved from the app shell to the root layout**, so every route group sits beneath it. The version chip reached the signed-out surfaces on 2026-09-02 and brought a tooltip with it; a `Tooltip.Root` with no Provider above it throws (`Context "Tooltip.Provider" not found`) rather than rendering bare, and the only Provider lived inside the app shell, which the sign-in, password-reset and joining screens never mount. Clearing cookies and reloading therefore crashed the sign-in screen before it drew. The shell's own Provider is gone (one, at the root, is the design system's stated placement), and `apps/web/test/root-layout-tooltip-provider.test.ts` pins that a bare tooltip throws and the same tooltip renders beneath the root layout.
- **The matter status window's "read again on every opening" only ever read once.** The engagement read
was an `$effect` guarded by a plain `arrangementAsked` flag that `reset` — the shell's `onOpen` —
cleared. `ActionDialog` calls `onOpen` from an effect of its own, and a child component's effects run
after the parent's, so the guard was read before it was cleared: the window read the fee arrangement
on its first opening and never again for the life of the component.

Both facts the window re-reads (the engagement, and now the office the paper file is kept at) are
read from the opening transition itself rather than from an effect. The readiness reads stay effects
deliberately — they ask about the matter's own status, which only this window changes, so once per
visit is the whole of it.
- **Full-page captures load what scrolling would, and the viewer fits the monitor.** Below-the-fold
images lazy-load on scroll, so a full-page screenshot without a scroll captured gray placeholders
under the first viewport: the snapshot call now injects a bounded scroll sweep (`addScriptTag`,
viewport steps to the bottom or thirty steps, whichever first, then back to the top) with the
settle timeout raised to cover the loads it triggers — bounded so an infinite-scroll feed cannot
hold a capture hostage. And the viewer's full-height column double-claimed the canvas: the page's
`h-full` took 100% of the canvas height on top of the Back-to-Tools row above it, so the frame's
bottom edge always sat below the fold and the screenshot's inner scrollbar with it. The tools
layout now owns the height column (nav row fixed, slot takes the remainder), so the viewer sizes
to the monitor exactly and normal-flow tool pages keep scrolling the canvas as before.
- The time surfaces stop saying "not recorded yet" about eight things the server had been serving all along.

The Time Sheet, the matter Time tab and the shared record window were built whole against a record fuller than the listing answered, and every field the contract could not fill was rendered honestly as a gap — the right call, and each one was written down in a register. What nobody re-asked is whether the contract had caught up. It had, in the same commit that built the Time Sheet. So the entry number, the entered date and who entered it, the resolved rate, both UTBMS codes, the internal memo, the attachment relation and the per-entry event history were all being served while three screens went on refusing them. The web type declared 12 of the 28 fields the server sends, which is what let it last: a type naming a subset is not a smaller truth, it is a screen that cannot see what arrived.

**What is now real.** The **entry number** on the ledger column, the sheet's Time Code cell, the record window's subtitle, the details panel and the printed sheet — and an entry captured before the sequence existed says it has none rather than being given an invented one. **Both dates and both people**, on every row rather than only the delegated ones. The **resolved rate**, read and not typed, naming where in the chain it came from: an entry keeps the rate in force on its work date for ever, so this states a fact rather than offering a change. **Category and Activity** as typable comboboxes over the firm's own UTBMS catalogue, one component rendered twice; a catalogue this account may not read costs the picker and not the field, because the entry's own code and label ride the listing. The **internal memo**, written and saved on the sheet's third row line and in the record window, and shown on a read-only record too — internal is not the same as hidden. Its exclusion from the printed sheet is now proved against a real rendering holding a real memo, not asserted in a comment. **Attachments**: what an entry points at, attaching one of the matter's own documents, detaching without deleting. And the **History tab** reads the served events, translating the audit's own names into a reader's words, reading an unknown event back rather than dropping it, and quoting only a reason somebody actually wrote — the audit's metadata is a field list by construction, and a field list is not prose.

**What is still a gap, and still rendered as one:** moving a written entry to another matter, recording one member's work under another's hand, the review gate as a served setting, unsubmit, delete-draft, billing disposition beyond the boolean, the rounding increment, capture before an entry has a description and a duration, the non-billable category, and the invoice's own number beside its identifier.

The register that got this wrong now says what it is for: a list of gaps is only honest while somebody re-asks it against the contract, and unasked it states the opposite. A test holds the retired eight out of it.
- **Every write on the Time surface except creating an entry was answered `400` before the handler
ran.** The contract declares `Idempotency-Key` required on update, submit, approve, kick-back and
void; the client sent one only on create, and the transport adds the header solely when a caller
supplies it.

So a row typed into the Time Sheet saved once, and every keystroke after that settled into "Not
saved. The server answered 400." Striking a row failed the same way. Saving from the record window
failed the same way. The autosave was architecturally present and could not succeed.

**No test could have caught it.** Nothing anywhere in the web application asserted what a surface put
on the wire — method, path, headers or body — so the whole suite passed with this live. The key is
now a required parameter of every write, making an omission a type error at the call site rather than
a failed save, and the new test asserts the header on all six writes from a table that a new write
cannot be added to without carrying it. The defect was reintroduced deliberately to confirm the test
fails: seven failures across two files.

Seven further defects went with it. "New Entry" created two rows and left one permanently phantom.
Undo announced "Undid striking this entry" when nothing un-strikes one, because no unvoid route
exists — it now refuses the step and says so at the moment it happens. Submit and approve discarded
their outcomes, so a refusal was silent. Two capabilities the code claimed were "rendered disabled
