It records `unavailable`, as it does on a deployment without the binding, and `unavailabilityReason` for `files` names both causes. The search worker's warm cron stays off. Not yet shown: a real file indexed and found by the deployed engine (`docs/deploy-queue.md`, _Search engine activation_).
- **The hosted gate divides the test battery across four machines and writes its caches even when a
run is red.** `ci.yml` was one job that ran `pnpm gate` end to end: 60 to 86 minutes on 2026-11-09,
of which the battery was 52 to 74. It is now `prepare` (the plan, and one build of the WASM
artefacts when no cached copy matches), `checks` (`pnpm gate --skip tests`), four `tests` jobs
(`pnpm gate --only wasm,tests`, each with one slice of the suite) and `gate`, the required check,
which is green only when the others are. The gate reads the slice from `MAGNA_CARTA_TEST_SHARD`
(`tooling/gate/plan.mjs`, `parseShard`) and hands it to the test runner as `--shard`; unset, as on a
laptop, it runs the whole suite as before.

**The WASM cache was never being written.** The combined cache step saves only when its job
succeeds, and no hosted run had succeeded, so every run compiled the artefacts from cold (251 to 320
seconds). Each cache is now saved by its own step right after the build, the cached paths are
every `packages/*/src/pkg` instead of a list that had fallen two artefacts behind, and the cargo cache is kept on failure.
Home: `docs/conventions/build-performance.md`, _The hosted run_.
- **The repository is ready to be made public.** A full-history scan of every branch and pull-request ref (gitleaks and trufflehog) found no live credential, so nothing was rotated. What would have been published is removed from the current tree: the real network address in the speed-test tests and plan is now a documentation address (`203.0.113.10`), and the owner's personal mail addresses are gone from the operations runbook and the company-email decision. Every action the workflows use is pinned to a commit rather than a movable tag, because a public repository runs pull requests from forks. A `LICENSE` file states all rights reserved, and `package.json` says `UNLICENSED`.
- **A typeable dropdown opens its list when you click or tap the box itself.** Before, the list opened only from the small arrows at the end of the field or once you started typing, so seeing the choices meant aiming at a narrow target. Now a click anywhere in the box shows the list, and you can still type straight away to narrow it. Moving into the field with Tab does not open it, so tabbing through a form stays quiet; Down Arrow or any letter opens it from the keyboard as before. Fields that only offer suggestions once you type, such as the street line of an address, are unchanged.
- **The address index leaves out two more share-alike sources.** A re-read of OpenAddresses' source records found the Austin-area regional layer (`us/tx/capcog`, CC BY-SA) and the Portland Metro layer (`us/or/portland_metro`, a share-alike database licence) recorded as share-alike but missing from the licence register, so the next build excludes them; the Texas and Oregon statewide layers still cover both areas. The runbook now says how to re-read the register, and the cost note prices a build at the three hours its instance stays awake.
- **The public changelog has one address: `community.magnacarta.esq/changelog`.** The second custom
domain, `changelog.magnacarta.esq`, is gone from the board's worker, and the Changelog page on the
board's own host is now the one board page search engines may list.
- **The community board's sign-in secret now comes from the account's Secrets Store.** `magna-carta` and `magna-carta-community` both bind `COMMUNITY_HANDOFF_SECRET` from the store, so the one value is kept in one place instead of being set on each Worker.
- **No signer's record on the Certificate of Completion runs across two pages.** The signer details are laid out two signers to a page and the audit log is filled a page at a time by the height its rows are expected to take (`SIGNERS_PER_PAGE` and `auditPages` in `packages/signing/src/certificate-sheet.ts`), and every page of a section that runs past one carries its heading and its place, as `Signer Details (1 of 3)`. The two Contact lines are labelled `Document` and `Certificate of Completion`. The document hash prints as two lines of 32 characters, each in eight groups of four set on a grid, so the groups of one line stand under those of the other. Every page is headed with a letterhead (a bar in the accent colour, the lockup, the certificate's name over its reference) in place of the lockup and title that opened only the first page, and the footer is the page number alone, centred under a rule. The PDF composer (`crates/pdf-compose-core`) gains the two things this needs, each off unless a document asks: a `letterhead` drawn in the top margin of every page, and `grid` on a field, which sets the value's words in columns of one width. The audit log gives the name and the address columns more of the width, so an IPv4 address no longer wraps.

**The certificate is set in Atkinson Hyperlegible and says where each signer signed from.** The sheet names its typeface (`typeface` on the composed document), and the composer bundles Atkinson Hyperlegible Next (SIL Open Font License 1.1) beside Liberation Sans. Atkinson draws Latin only, so the sign Worker reads the composer's `missingCharacters` and sets the sheet again in Liberation Sans when a name is in Greek or Cyrillic. The seal route records the city, region and country the network gives for the connecting address as `SignerAttribution.location` (server-observed, like the address itself, and absent where the runtime gives none); the certificate prints it under the address as `Location (by IP Address)`. Page one gains a `Documents` section (name, pages, hash) between the summary and the signers; the summary drops its `Time Zone` line, since every time names its zone, and its `Reference` line, since the letterhead of every page carries the reference, now with a small label beside it. The signers table and the audit log are banded (`banded` on a composed table: a shaded heading row and every second row, no rule under each row), a rule parts two signers who share a page, and the audit log's consent step reads `Agreed to E-Sign` so the event column does not wrap.

**The certificate's sections are cards, its margins are one measure, and it can be laid out for A4.** Summary, Documents, Signers, Contact, each signer's record and each page of the audit log are drawn as cards: a rounded frame with the section's name inside it over a rule. The summary is set in two columns. Every edge of the sheet is half an inch from the paper's edge on all four sides (the sides were an inch, the bar 32 points and the page number 27). `certificateSheet` takes `paper: "letter" | "a4"` and fills the audit log's pages for the paper's height and width; the seal path issues Letter until a firm can choose. The lockup in the letterhead is the mark and wordmark on the paper itself, with no dark tile behind the mark. The composer gains `cardStart` and `cardEnd` blocks, `twoUp` on a fields block, and, under a letterhead, a footer measured from the content (`Letterhead::FOOTER_HEIGHT`) so a caller can place it from the paper's edge.

**Each signer's record carries their signature, and the cards are quieter.** A caller of the seal route may send a signer's signature as a picture, and the certificate prints it at the foot of that signer's record at one height. A picture that cannot be read is left off and the certificate is still issued. Where a one-time code was sent is printed as `Code Sent To` when the caller gives `attribution.codeDestination`; the code itself is never printed. The first card is named `Request Details`, its counts read `Total Signatures` and `Total Initials`, and a signer's `Signature` line reads `Signature Type`. A card's name now sits in a bar in the accent colour with gently rounded top corners, its frame is a pale hairline, column headings are gray text with no shade, and every row is ruled off from the next with a pale rule that is never doubled against the frame.

**Initials print beside the signature, and the certificate names a support address.** The seal route accepts `signatureImages` and `initialsImages` on a signer, each a list of pictures with the pages it was placed on (`SealRequest.signatureImages` and `initialsImages` to the sign Worker), and the signer's record closes with them two to a line, each under a small label. A signer who used more than one signature has every one printed, numbered and with its pages, as `Signature 1 of 2 (Pages 1-3)`; a signer with more pictures than fit beside a second record has a page to themselves. The composer's image block gains `label`, a small bold line above the picture, and `beside`, which sets a picture on the line of the image block before it. The sign Worker's `CERTIFICATE_SUPPORT_EMAIL` is set in its `wrangler.jsonc`, so the Contact card gives an address for questions about the certificate itself.
- **A conflicts check's account of its search is in sections, in plain words.** `describeCheck` (`packages/conflicts/src/report-text.ts`) returns keyed sections instead of a numbered sentence list. Each section has a heading, plain sentences and an `attention` flag. The sections are Searched, Names and identifiers, Relationships, Firm Employees, one per place beyond the Directory, Not searched, and Results. The check read's `statement` (string array) becomes `report` (`CheckReport` in `packages/conflicts/src/contract.ts`). The web files each place's section under its own place by key, where it used to match a sentence prefix. No reader-facing line carries a dash, and the unavailable-source reasons in `packages/conflicts/src/sources.ts` are now plain sentences. Results still ends "0 results." on an empty search that recorded everything it found. The printed and downloaded report has one section per part. No migration.
- **A crash in the browser now states what was thrown and where.** `crashSignature` in `apps/web/src/lib/diagnostics/crash.ts` gives the kind, the engine's own message for a TypeError, ReferenceError or RangeError (never a message our code or a library wrote, and never a SyntaxError, whose JSON.parse message quotes its input), and the first stack frame. It goes into the breadcrumb ring, onto the failure record as `cause` (a Cause row on the crash screen and a `cause` line in the copied trace), and into the uncaught-error and unhandled-rejection breadcrumbs. A client Error ID had nothing behind it before, because a client crash never reaches a server log.
- **Dropdown lists put the tick at the end of the row, and both kinds of choice field share one chevron.** `Select.Item` (also the Combobox and EntityPicker row) renders its text first and a trailing indicator box, so options line up with the field's own text instead of sitting behind an empty tick gutter; the chosen row is set in the medium weight with an accent tick. Group headings are semibold with more room above. `Combobox.Input` swaps its up-and-down chevrons for the Select trigger's single ChevronDown.
- **Fields, choices and buttons get a visible edge, a hover, one focus ring and a distinct disabled look.** New semantic tokens `border.field`, `border.field-hover`, `border.control` and `surface.field-disabled` (light and dark, held by the contrast gate at 3 to 1 for the edges) feed the Input, Textarea, Select, Combobox, date, date-time, Checkbox and Radio recipes: the edge darkens on hover, focus is the ink edge with the accent ring, a disabled field is dashed on a pale fill, and Textarea, Select and the date field gain the danger edge for an invalid value. The secondary button is now outlined instead of a borderless grey fill, and every button's focus ring uses the accent.
- **The files host is live.** `FILES_ORIGIN` is now `files.magnacartausercontent.com`, which the zone
routes to the `magna-carta` Worker, so a preview grant's stream address answers from the cookieless
host instead of the `files.example.com` placeholder.
- **The Google Places key is read from the Secrets Store.** The app worker binds `GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY` from the Cloudflare Secrets Store, with a per-Worker secret as the fallback, and the System Status page now counts the Google key as setting address suggestions up.
- **A DropdownMenu behind an icon-only trigger no longer opens on hover.** `DropdownMenu.Trigger` checks its own text when the pointer arrives: a trigger with no words (every "..." menu, a cog, any button named only by its `aria-label`) skips the hover controller and opens by press, key or tap. Menus behind a word keep hover opening. Pinned by the DropdownMenu story "An icon-only trigger opens only when pressed".
- **Meetings have a nine-digit address, and personal rooms an address by name.** `meeting.join_code` (nine digits, partial unique index, backfilled) and `meeting_personal_room.address_name` (the owner's first name, then first-last, then a number; backfilled) are added columns with their own CHECKs. `GET /api/v1/meetings/by-code/{joinCode}` resolves a code to its meeting through the visibility gate, the meeting summary carries `joinCode`, and the room link routes read a room by its address name only. The web room is one screen (`meeting-room-screen.svelte`) at `/meeting/{code}` and `/meetings/{id}`, which shows the code address in place; `/room/{name}` replaces `/meetings/rooms/{linkCode}`, which is gone (no redirect, at the owner's word). My Room no longer offers Get a New Link.
- **Meeting Connection Details is wide and short instead of narrow and tall.** The popover takes the record-pane width (capped to the window) and at most 70% of the window's height, in two columns that scroll on their own: this browser's numbers and Copy Diagnostics on the left, the people and the wire events on the right.
- **Connection Details in a meeting say what the numbers mean, and which server the meeting runs through.** The panel shows the Cloudflare site (read from `/cdn-cgi/trace` when the panel first opens) and the media server end of the candidate pair in use (direct or relayed, UDP or TCP, its address), the picture in pixels, the camera size in words ("Full size" rather than `f`), what each quality reading means, and Upload and Download over every stream (`ConnectionSample.uploadBitsPerSecond` / `downloadBitsPerSecond`). The empty-room line and the event rail are gone; the wire events stay in Copy Diagnostics, which gains upload, download and the transport. The camera's three sizes are capped at 1.2 Mbit/s, 350 kbit/s and 120 kbit/s.
- **Leave is pinned to the meeting band's bottom-right corner, and the side panel has a stronger edge.** Leave is the band's last element, pushed to the end of its line (`ms-auto`), so it stays in the corner however the groups before it wrap; End Meeting moves before it. The side panel takes `border-border-strong` and `shadow-elevation`. The reserved meeting tab now opens through `reserveBeside` in `$lib/navigation/open-beside.ts`, so the open-beside source scan passes again.
- **A meeting opens in a tab of its own, with the whole window.** Start, Join and Open My Room open the room in a new browser tab named for the meeting, so pressing Join again brings the same tab forward. The room has no application rail or top bar, and Leave closes the tab. Where the browser blocks the new tab, the room opens in the current tab as before.
- **Meeting questions are part of chat, and a meeting's picture no longer flashes when a tile is re-rendered.** The chat panel takes the question queue and draws questions in its timeline (`chatTimeline`), with an All / Questions filter and an "Ask as a question" box; the side panel's Q&A tab and the control bar's Q&A button are gone from the member's room. A tile now sets `srcObject` only when the stream is a different one and clears it only on teardown, and the video keeps one compositing layer whether or not it is mirrored. Copy Diagnostics gains `picture`, `camera-track` and `view` events.
- **The meeting room's chat, Q&A, polls and roster are one side panel with four tabs, and the control bar is three groups.** `meeting-side-panel.svelte` holds the screen's snippets as tabs; the chat, polls and questions panels take `inline` to draw without their popover or dialog, and the room page derives each one's "open" (which drives the unseen counts) from the panel's tab. The band reads left to right as what this member sends, what they do in the room, and where they look and leave; the host's room acts sit behind a "..." (Host controls) menu. The guest page keeps its popover chat for now.
- **The meeting room opens in speaker view and draws every picture at the camera's shape.** `MeetingClient.speakerView` now starts true and survives a rejoin; the room and guest pages seed it from `meeting-view-preference.svelte.ts` (layout and mirror, per browser). `meeting-layout.ts` picks the gallery's column count that draws the largest 16:9 tile for the measured space, and speaker view puts the others in a strip along the top. A speaking tile carries an accent outline and an audio-lines mark; a shared screen is shown whole (`object-contain`). The room header's Share menu copies the firm link and, for a host, opens Guests; Effects gains a Mirror My Video switch that flips only the local preview.
- **The Meetings page lists every member's room, and its History says where each meeting was filed and what became of its recording.** A new Firm Rooms card shows each colleague's standing room with Copy Link at any time and Join while it is open (`GET /api/v1/meetings/rooms`). My Room's settings (lobby, audio call, Get a New Link) move into a "..." menu beside the card's title. Recently Ended is renamed History and gains Filed To (the matter's title, now carried on every meeting summary as `matterTitle`) and Recording columns.
- **A record's sections are folding cards, and New Person reads the person back as a contact card.** `record-sections.svelte` draws each section as a bordered card whose header (a button with `aria-expanded`) carries the section's icon, name and count and folds the card; a jump from the rail unfolds it. The sections no longer repeat their name as a second heading inside the card ("Ways To Reach Them", "Addresses", "Sealed Identifiers", "Belongs To", "Other Name"). New Person's right column is `new-person-context.svelte`: the duplicate check states where it stands in one sentence, and the read-back shows the photo, name, pronouns and dates, then each fact marked by kind (`PersonSummaryLine.mark`).
- **Soon hovers name what is missing, in plain words.** Every disabled "Soon" control and not-yet-built column now reads "Not built yet: <what is missing>." (for example "Not built yet: recording payments.") instead of naming the internal dependency ("Waiting on the payments slice, whose first step is ..."). About 70 dependency phrases across billing, costs, fees, time, trust, discovery, custodian, matters, reports and the file tools are rewritten; the small "Soon" badge is unchanged, at the owner's request. The rule in `docs/conventions/ui-design.md` records the wording.
- **UI copy rewrite, third batch.** About 200 strings on the matter, file manager, document, calendar, communications, custodian, discovery, report, tool, notification and account screens rewritten in place, with no behaviour or layout change. Explanations of internal mechanics are cut to what the reader needs to act, "corpus" becomes "review set" in the UI, "the platform" becomes "Magna Carta", and "every X" summaries read "all X". Conflicts, meetings, the directory and person screens, signing, Magnus and the PDF editor are left for later because other work is open there. Tests that quoted the old copy move with it.
- **UI copy rewrite, second batch.** About 250 strings on the settings pages and the money screens (bills, trust, time, costs and fees) rewritten in place, with no behaviour or layout change. "Invoice" becomes "bill" everywhere a person reads it (identifiers and wire names keep `invoice`), "colleagues" becomes "staff", and explanations of how the system works are cut to what the reader needs to act. The "Not built yet. Waiting on ..." hovers are untouched until the owner settles their wording. Tests and the `lint:one-ui` placeholder allowances that quoted the old copy move with it.
- **A record's picture opens to look at, its Contact card edits all at once, and relationships are grouped.** In the Directory record window, pressing the picture now opens it large over the record (a `Dialog` in `entity-photo.svelte`) with Edit Photo and Download, instead of a Change, View or Remove menu, and View Full Size no longer opens a new tab. Edit Photo opens the cropping window on the current picture, where it can be re-centred, replaced or removed. The cropper takes JPEG, PNG, WebP, GIF, AVIF, BMP and SVG up to 20 MB (`PHOTO_FORMATS` in `photo-crop.ts`), names them on a `Dropzone` and in the picker's `accept`, and marks a refused file with the Dropzone's new `invalid` state. Also: the Preferred star on a contact line is a toggle, and jumping to a record's last section scrolls only the content pane, where `scrollIntoView` used to lift the whole window out of its frame. The record's Contact card (`contact-card-editor.svelte`) is a plain list behind one Edit that opens every line at once, with Preferred and Do Not Use as two-way switches and one Save turned into single writes by `contact-edit-plan.ts`. The relationship list is grouped under headings (`EDGE_TYPE_GROUPS`), A to Z within each, and seven family edge types are added (`spouse_of`, `parent_of`, `child_of`, `sibling_of`, `grandparent_of`, `grandchild_of`, `family_member_of`), classed `family` for conflicts traversal; no migration, as `edge_type` is an open catalog.
- **UI copy rewrite, first batch.** About 260 user-facing strings across `apps/web` rewritten in place, with no behaviour or layout change: the "Nothing answered" transport-failure lines (about forty wordings) become "Couldn't connect." plus what did not happen, em dashes leave UI strings, and the matter section descriptions in `apps/web/src/lib/matters/sections.ts` are cut to one line each. Conflicts, meetings, directory, signing, Magnus and the PDF editor are untouched until their open work lands. Tests that quoted the old copy move with it.
- **Settings › Versions becomes System Status, organised by feature.** `GET /api/v1/meta/versions` now
carries `features` (each Working, Not set up or Not working, from
`apps/api-worker/src/system-status/feature-roster.ts`) and, for a platform operator only,
`featureRequirements` (the presence of each setting a feature needs, never a value). The new
operator-only `GET /api/v1/platform/recent-errors` reads the last day of `error.captured` and
`operation.failed` events back from Workers Logs and folds them by Worker, place and error name. It
needs the `OBSERVABILITY_API_TOKEN` secret (`docs/deploy-queue.md`). The page has counts and tabs for
Features, Deployment, Workers, This Firm, Recent Errors and Feature Flags. The header chip is trimmed
to the deployment, the features that are not working, and the firm's records. The old
`/settings/versions` address redirects.
- **System Status has a button in the sidebar's foot.** The pulse icon beside Customize in
`apps/web/src/lib/components/app-shell.svelte` links to `/settings/system-status` and marks itself
active there.

### Security

- **Every npm dependency is on its newest compatible release, Wrangler is on 4.158.0, and every Cargo lockfile is refreshed.** The catalog in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` moves each pin to the newest release on its own major line that is past the three-day cooldown, including `wrangler` 4.110.0 to 4.158.0 (Worker Previews need 4.135.0 or later), `@cloudflare/workers-types` to `5.20261106.1`, `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` to 0.23.0, `better-auth` to 1.7.18, `zod` to 4.6.7, `svelte` to 5.57.3, `bits-ui` to 2.20.6 and Storybook to 10.6.6. `happy-dom` crosses to 21.0.4, the first release clear of two HIGH advisories (an import-alias escape to host code and an SSRF through parsed iframes and stylesheets). Two overrides are new: `tinypool@2` at 2.1.2 clears two CRITICAL prototype-pollution-to-code-execution records reached through `vite-plus`'s formatter, and `zod` at 4.6.7 reaches the copy the Workers test pool hard-pins at 4.4.3. Upstream bits-ui now restores the body's style through CSSOM, so `patches/bits-ui@2.20.6.patch` keeps only the preventable-`onFocusOutside` half. better-auth 1.7 types the two-factor enrolment answer as a union with an emailed-code shape, which `apps/web/src/lib/account/two-factor.ts` now refuses by name. Svelte 5.57 flags the safe-browse canvas's deliberate `role="application"`, now ignored with its reason beside it. Terrazzo 2.10 writes zero-length shadow lengths more compactly, so `packages/design-tokens/generated/` is regenerated with no change in meaning. `yara-x` moves to 1.23, which requires wasmtime 48, so the accepted `RUSTSEC-2026-0269` entry leaves `osv-scanner.toml`.

**The Rust supply chain crosses the majors that carried advisories.** Every `zip` consumer in `crates/` and `containers/*` moves to 9.4.1, which clears nine zip advisories (several of them CRITICAL: a dual-header parser differential, an AES-entry HMAC bypass, extraction outside the target directory). zip 9 returns entry names as a `Result`, and each call site falls back to a lossy decode of the raw name, so no entry is skipped. `tantivy` 0.27 lifts `lru` to 0.18.5 (RUSTSEC-2026-0253). Also moved: the RustCrypto family (aes 0.9, cbc 0.2, md-5/sha1/sha2 0.11 and the rest, with cipher 0.5's trait renames), `cfb` 0.16, `chardetng` 1.0, `zune-png` 0.5, `tower-http` 0.7, `base64` 0.23, `lopdf` 0.46 and `oar-ocr` 0.9.2. Held, each for a stated reason: `lopdf` 0.47 rebuilds a missing cross-reference table on load and so reports a broken file as intact; `hayro` 0.9 replaces the device trait the bad-redaction detector implements; `quick-xml` 0.42 rewrites the event model under the untrusted OOXML walk; `sevenz-rust2` 0.25 makes private the internals the 7z parser reads; `reqwest` 0.13's rustls feature pulls in `aws-lc-sys`, a C library; `mail-parser` 1.0 needs rustc 1.98; and `rand` 0.10 is held because `ms-offcrypto-writer` takes a rand 0.9 generator.
- **Only an administrator can connect, replace or disconnect the firm's postage account, and the
platform's fee on a label is the server's number, not the caller's.** Two findings from a security
review of shipping, both closed before any firm could reach them.

**The account.** The connect and disconnect routes were gated on `shipping:manage` — the same
permission as drafting a shipment — and the credential store does no check of its own on a write, by
design, because it defers to the route. So any member who could draft a shipment could replace the
firm's EasyPost key with one on an account they control, and every shipment an administrator bought
afterwards, with its clients' names and addresses, would go to that account; or disconnect the firm's
postage outright. Both routes now require `firm:manageSecrets`, the right the Settings navigation
already tagged the page "View" without — but whose controls the page itself never checked, so it also
now shows that member the account's health and a sentence saying only an administrator can change it,
instead of a key field the server would refuse. Reading whether an account is connected stays on
`shipping:manage`, since the register uses it to tell exactly that member when no account is
connected. Not reachable under the
default roles, where only Owner/Admin holds `shipping:manage`.

**The fee.** `POST /api/v1/shipments/{id}/purchase` took `serviceFeeMinor` from the request, with no
upper bound, and a positive fee becomes a billable charge on the shipment's matter when the firm
recovers the shipping service fee. A member who could buy a label could put any amount on a client's
bill without `costs:track`. The field is gone from the request, and the fee is set on the server:
zero, since the platform charges nothing per label today. A client that still sends it has it
ignored rather than refused, so a browser tab left open on the old page can still buy its label.

Both are pinned by tests that fail when the hole is put back.
- **The toolchain moves to Vite+ 1.5.0, and the Workers test pool to its renamed successor.** `vite-plus` 0.1.24 and the Vite 8.0.16 it brought carried GHSA-587h-7wmj-h5pm (HIGH, CVSS 7.5) and four lower advisories (GHSA-698v-4r3x-3vcv, GHSA-r825-w8mm-5pxw, GHSA-rq7h-c2jc-7f22, GHSA-9jrq-w75r-8gcw), fixed only from vite-plus 1.1. Vite+ 1.x runs upstream Vitest instead of the rebundled `@voidzero-dev/vite-plus-test`, so the catalog's `vitest` is now 5.1.0, the version vite-plus 1.5.0 depends on, and the `vitest` alias leaves the `overrides`. `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` 0.23.0 peered only Vitest 4; its successor `@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` 1.6.0 keeps the same `cloudflareTest()` plugin and `cloudflare:test` module, so every worker's `package.json`, `vitest.config.ts` and `worker-env.d.ts` change only the package name. The design-system story tests import the Playwright provider from `@vitest/browser-playwright`, now a catalog pin kept equal to `vitest`, because upstream Vitest has no `vitest/browser-playwright` entry.

**One Vite in the tree, at last.** The `vite` override alone never reached a `vite` peer: the alias reports its own version (1.5.0), which no `^8` peer range accepts, so pnpm auto-installed upstream Vite for SvelteKit, the Svelte and Tailwind plugins, Storybook and Vitest — the Vite 8.0.16 the advisories named. The root `package.json` now declares `vite` as the same alias, so every peer resolves to it, and `peerDependencyRules.allowedVersions` silences the version warnings that leaves (`vite`, and Storybook's optional `vite-plus` peer, which still names only 0.1/0.2). The lockfile was resolved fresh to drop the stale peer resolutions; outside the toolchain the only version that moved is `@types/react` 19.2.17 to 19.3.0.

**Two overrides leave.** `zod` was there only to reach the 4.4.3 the old pool hard-pinned; the new plugin pins 4.6.6, past the 4.6.6 floor. `tinypool@2` pinned 2.1.2 under the formatter; oxfmt 0.76 and Vitest 5.1 both pin 2.2.0, and the override would now drag them back. Oxfmt 0.76 and oxlint 1.91 come with the move: the formatter now hugs a single arrow-function argument that carries a return-type annotation and indents a list item's continuation line that opens inside an inline code span, which reformats 58 files (8 source, 50 Markdown), and oxlint-tsgolint 7 reports more `no-unnecessary-type-assertion` and `consistent-function-scoping` warnings (none are errors).

**`@cloudflare/vitest-plugin` is patched so the API worker's suite can run under Vitest 5.** When each test file after the first starts, Vitest 5 asks the pool for a snapshot of the modules the server has already transformed. workerd cannot read the host disk, so the plugin inlines every one of them into a single WebSocket reply. For the API worker that reply is about 65 MB across 4,254 modules, and workerd closes the socket with 1009 "Message is too large". The runtime then restarts in a loop that leaks a Vite server each time, until the run reaches about 14 GB. `patches/@cloudflare__vitest-plugin@1.6.0.patch` answers that one request with an empty map, so modules are fetched one at a time, as under Vitest 4. With the patch, all 319 API-worker test files pass (2,959 tests). Plugin 1.6.1 carries the same code, so the patch stays until a release bounds or chunks the reply.

## The blind spot, measured

The previous pass reported that rule 1 skips any path a has-code node already claims, so a `partial`
area root naming `packages/custodian` immunises every `deferred` child beneath it. Three candidate
rules were measured against three states of the ledger and **none of them can close it.**

- **Tighten rule 1's accounting to be at-least-as-specific** (a strict ancestor no longer accounts
  for a path). Against the ledger as it stood when all twelve wrong statuses were live: **6 hits, all
  six false positives, and none of the twelve.** Against the post-evidence-sweep ledger: 10 hits, 2
  true. The reason is structural — the rule's only input is the node's own prose, and a mis-statused
  node's prose is the sentence that is wrong. It says "no such thing exists" and therefore names no
  path, so no path-keyed rule can see it at any precision.
- **The absence-about-a-resolving-path shape** ("no X in `packages/Y`"): **22 hits, 3 true.**
- **Widening rule 7 (`sliceAlreadyDelivered`) past `not-started`**: `deferred` alone gives 1 hit and
  1 false positive; the full widening to `deferred`, `designed` and `planned` gives **10 hits and 10
  false positives** — the reports sub-slices, the matter-assets tail, and the discovery clustering
  node, every one of them correctly pre-code. That is worse than the +2 the rule's own header already
  measured and rejected, and it is rejected here on the same terms.

What is worth doing instead is smaller and honest about which job it does. **A regression guard, not
a detector:** a node whose `evidence` or `notes` says something landed while its status says nothing
is built. Measured across three ledger states: **0 hits before the drift was found, 6 hits and no
false positives in the window where the evidence had been corrected and the status had not, 0 after
this change.** It cannot find drift nobody has noticed — its recall on that is zero by construction —
but it makes the specific mistake the previous pass made twelve times impossible to commit again.

And one number that bounds every slice-keyed rule: **220 of 265 pre-code and parked nodes carry no
`slices:` tag at all**, so rule 7 is blind to eighty-three per cent of them whatever its status
filter. Tagging is a cheaper lever than a rule, and it is the one that would move that number.

**The rest needs a human pass on a cadence.** Both the areas swept so far were read by a person
against the code, and both found drift running one way: nodes describing work that has since landed.
That is a reading job, and the docs-sync routine is where it belongs.
- **`vp run retire-note <branch> --with-merge` retires a stream note in the pull request that lands the work, instead of a second merge afterwards.**

`main` is production, so a follow-up pull request whose only content is deleting one file is a production deploy to delete one file. Four of the last ten merges were exactly that.

The landing check that made the second merge necessary is the right guard for the workflow it was written for — retiring on `main` after the fact, where the deletion takes effect the moment it merges, so removing a note early really does erase the one collision warning other worktrees get. It is the wrong question for a deletion committed on the branch: that reaches `main` when the branch does and not a moment sooner, so `main` keeps the note for as long as the pull request is open. And it cannot be satisfied anyway, because a branch has not landed while the pull request landing it is still open. What `--with-merge` checks instead is that HEAD is on the branch whose note it is, which is what makes "the deletion travels with the merge" true rather than asserted.

It does the paperwork only — clearing every `status.d/` pointer at the note, re-rendering `STATUS.md`/`STATUS.json`, deleting the note. Removing a worktree and deleting a branch cannot happen from inside that branch, so that half stays a later local `vp run retire-note <branch>` and keeps its landing check. The command no longer refuses that pass: a workspace with no note left is exactly what a landed `--with-merge` leaves behind, and it used to be told there was nothing to retire by the retirement that had worked.

The guard moved out of the runner into `retirementRefusal` in `tooling/retire-note/dependents.mjs`, on the same pure-rules / impure-runner split the migration gates keep, so the decisions now have tests — they had none before.
- A firm database whose lineage is stuck now says so, instead of refusing every question including that one.

Migrations run in the `FirmDatabase` durable object's constructor, and a constructor that rejects takes the entire object with it — every read, every write, and, because the diagnostic reads are firm-scoped like everything else, the surfaces whose only job is to explain what happened. One statement in one migration put a firm completely dark, with the fault legible nowhere. That happened twice in a day.

The object comes up either way now. The fault is recorded rather than rethrown, and what it costs is business data, which stays refused: the schema is at a consistent state but an older one than this build's code was written against, and serving reads across that gap would trade an outage for wrong answers. The refusal carries the fault, so it explains itself instead of surfacing as a bare platform error.

What it no longer costs is the ability to ask what is wrong. The durable object answers a migration read outside that gate — a question about the fault cannot be refused because of the fault — and the health panel's schema row asks through it. That row used to be an ordinary statement, which meant the one check that could name a stuck lineage was the check a stuck lineage silenced: it reported "Not read" about its own subject. It now reports which migration the database reached.

The database section's own copy control is gone with it: the panel's copy control takes the whole diagnosis from the top, and two copy gestures differing only in scope is a choice a reader has to make without being told which is which.
- **A task is read and changed in the product's one record window, and a new one is that same window
with nothing in it yet.** `task-record-window.svelte` carries the fields, the attachments tab, the
print sheet and the acts; `task-list.svelte` keeps the rows, the search, and the one act a list is
for. Everything that used to unfold inside the list is gone with it — the composer above the rows,
the row that turned into fields, the attach picker, the cancel-reason form and the per-row assignee
select — because each was a second place to learn where a task's fields live.

Two things fell out of it. `note-attachable-documents.ts` becomes
`record-attachable-documents.ts`, typed on the shape a document association has rather than on a
note's name for it: a note and a task attach a matter's files identically, and a second copy would
have been six lines free to drift. And the reason the firm is not doing a task is asked for in its
own action panel (`task-not-doing-dialog.svelte`) whose commit says "Record the Decision" — every
panel in the product leaves through a control that says Cancel, so a commit that also said it would
be two controls with one word and opposite meanings.

The owner's ruling was on the books for records that already had a window. A task had none, and the
tempting half-step — an action dialog for making one, the row still editing it — produces exactly
the defect the ruling names, with the panel and the row free to disagree about the record's own
fields. That half-step and its correction both happened here; only the second was the fix.
- **A task's state becomes four rungs — To Do, In Progress, On Hold, Done — and cancelling is replaced
by archiving.** The rungs are one control group in the record window's action bar; beside them sit
the only two other things that happen to a task, and they differ in one thing: archiving keeps the
data, deleting takes it. Archiving is orthogonal to the rungs — a task is archived FROM where it
stood and comes back there — so the list's foot now offers **Show Done** and **Show Archived** as two
questions rather than one. The archive reason is optional, which is the whole lesson of the state it
replaces: cancelling required one, and nobody used it.

**The schema route is the finding, not the change.** `matter_task.state` is a CHECK-constrained enum
on a table `time_entry`, `matter_task_document` and `matter_task_external_link` all reference — plus
its own `blocked_by_task_id`. SQLite cannot alter a CHECK, and the rebuild that would has to drop the
table, which a durable object refuses at the commit for every child row: the migration applies to an
empty database and takes every real firm's offline on wake, which has happened here before. Six
mechanisms were probed against real durable-object storage and all six fail — including
`PRAGMA writable_schema`, SQLite's own documented way to change a constraint with nothing dropped,
which workerd's authorizer answers with `SQLITE_AUTH`.

So `state` narrows to the one thing the database pairs it with by CHECK — is the work finished — and
the three open rungs arrive as an added `progress` column, with `archived_at`/`archived_by`/
`archive_reason` beside it. `ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN` drops nothing, so it lands on a parent, and the
same probe file proves the three properties the route rests on: an added column may carry its own
CHECK, that CHECK may name a second column, and existing rows take the default. The reader's four
rungs are reassembled from the two columns in exactly one function. Recorded as
ADR-a-vocabulary-on-a-parent-table-grows-by-adding-a-column, which is the general answer for this
fleet rather than a note about tasks.

`20260914T120000_task-rungs-and-archive` carries every cancelled task onto the archive columns with
its reason intact, and `packages/database/test/task-rungs-migration.test.ts` runs it over rows rather
than over an empty database — the gap both of this repository's migration outages came through.
- **The conflicts graph walk is now budgeted per kind of relationship rather than by one integer, it
stops at a recorded closure cap instead of running unbounded, and it costs a number of queries that
follows the channel count rather than the entity count. The rule that carries the change is that a
truncated expansion is never reported as a completed one.**

**One integer could not express the question.** "Follow a company's rename and merger chain as far as
it goes" and "do not walk from a spouse to her employer's other directors" are different instructions,
and the shipped `depth` answered both with the same number because it could not tell them apart. The
traversal now spends a budget per **edge class** — corporate family (transitive, no hop cost),
control, family, representation — each a firm setting with the design's recommended default of one
hop, each resolved per run and recorded verbatim on the check row. The shipped `depth` request field
and column both keep working: supplying `depth` sets every budgeted class to that number, which is
exactly what it always meant, and the column now carries the widest resolved budget so a reader of it
alone is never told the traversal was shallower than it was. A stored firm policy that predates the
typed budgets keeps its own `defaultDepth` for every class rather than falling back to the shipped
default — falling back would silently narrow the search for precisely the firms that widened it.

**The cap, and the sentence that makes it acceptable.** Corporate-family edges cost no hops, so a real
holding structure can put thousands of entities in one closure; a bound has to exist. The per-run
closure cap (firm-set, recommended default 500) is that bound, and it is never applied silently. On
reaching it the walk stops and the check records **that it was truncated**, the caps in force, the
entities it reached, how many further entities it had discovered and refused to admit, and how many
entities it did match but never expanded from. The posture read carries the record; the report
statement says in words that the search of the graph is incomplete. A check row written before the
record existed reads `traversal: null` — "the row does not say" — which is a third state and is never
flattened into either of the other two. This is the depth analogue of the shipped rule that a source
recording `unavailable` never reads as searched and clean, and it fails the same way if broken: the
platform telling a firm it looked somewhere it did not look.

**Degree-based hub suppression is refused, and the refusal is in the code.** Skipping any node with
more than N edges is the obvious way to keep a closure small and it silently narrows the search — a
clearing bank on five hundred matters is exactly where a positional conflict lives. The bound is on
the SIZE of the closure, where reaching it is a recordable fact, never on the SHAPE of the graph,
where stepping around a hub leaves nothing on the record at all. A test holds it.

**Ended relationships are traversed.** A divorced spouse or a subsidiary sold last year is walked, not
skipped, and the path step carries `expiredAtCheck` so the reviewer weighs it — the rules that most
often decide a conflict are about _former_ clients and _former_ relationships, so a walk that stopped
at currency would drop the dimension they turn on. Expiry is judged against the check's own clock
rather than an ambient wall-clock read, so a long walk cannot hold two opinions about when a
relationship ended.

**The N+1 goes in the same change as the widening, not after a measurement.** Widening a traversal
without batching would have regressed the shipped load profile on the first deep corporate group: the
per-entity path is one or two subject reads plus four matching queries **per reached entity**, which
at a 500-entity closure is roughly 2,500 queries in one invocation. Now there is one subject-facts
read per node table over the whole closure, one batched edge read per traversal round rather than one
per node, and each blocking channel run once over the whole closure — phonetic, trigram, blind-index,
and the exact-name probe — with per-subject attribution kept exact rather than approximated. Every
set-valued read chunks at D1's hundred-parameter cap, so the count is proportional to channels times
ceil(entities / 100) and not to entities times channels.

**Proved, not asserted.** The batched matcher is held to returning _exactly_ the per-entity matcher's
hit set — same entities, same evidence, same tiers, at both strictness levels — over a real migrated
corpus carrying sound-alike surnames, typo variants, an exact-name twin, a name-mismatched identifier
twin, former and alias name rows, a merged-away subordinate resolving to its master, a mononym too
short for trigrams, and organizations alongside persons. A performance change to a conflicts engine
that alters which hits come back is not a refactor; it is a missed conflict. The per-entity path is
kept as the thing the batch is measured against, and a second test counts prepared statements on both
paths so an accidental read inside a loop fails the build rather than waiting for a corpus large
enough to show up in a timing.

**Batching the trigram channel naively is slower than not batching it, and the harness caught that
too.** The union query returns each candidate once, but re-deriving "does this candidate share a
trigram with this subject" inside the per-subject loop is quadratic in subjects times candidates. The
union's rows become an inverted trigram-to-entities index once instead — the shape the phonetic
channel already had — and attribution is a union over each subject's own trigrams. On the same corpus
that took a 613-entity closure from 5,684ms to 394ms for the same 211,199 candidates. Query count is
the right target because a D1 query is a network round trip, but a batch that trades round trips for
quadratic arithmetic has moved the cost rather than removed it.

**Measured.** The load profile gains a deep corporate group — a twelve-deep successor lineage with a
six-hundred-wide subsidiary fan, sized past the default cap on purpose — plus a complete deep-graph
run, a deliberately truncating run, and a statement-count bound on the batched matcher printed beside
the timings.

**Two findings the harness produced, recorded rather than fixed under this change's cover.**

The design says "the candidate set the channels return is still bounded by blocking", and over
multi-word ORGANIZATION names it is not. The trigram channel matches on any shared three-character
window, and company names share " an", "and", "nd ", "inc", "llc" with nearly every other company
name, so each reached organization returns most of the organization corpus as candidates. Nothing is
suppressed — that is the no-threshold rule, and it is right — so **hit rows scale as closure size
times corpus size**, not as closure size. The closure cap therefore bounds the wrong quantity. The
recommended default of 500 ships as designed, because the number is the owner's, but it ships beside
this finding rather than in place of it.

And the second, which is how the first was noticed: at that scale `composeEffectBatch` in
`packages/data-access/src/effect-batch.ts` fails on `statements.push(...effect.statements)` with
`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. A spread argument list has a hard engine ceiling, so
the shared batch composer has an undocumented upper bound on statement count that applies to every
domain composing a large batch. Not this change's seam to fix.

The load-profile measurements consequently run at closure caps of 40 and 15, with the reasoning
stated at the constant, so the harness measures the traversal rather than the engine's argument
limit. The gap between those numbers and the shipped default is the size of the finding.

**Not in this change, and deliberately.** The three flags that decide what the platform asserts about
a firm's ethical position are the owner's and are untouched: whether the balanced band searches
former, maiden and alias names; whether an imputed conflict follows a lateral hire and whether a
screen cures it; and whether a matter may refuse to open over undisposed hits. The firm-marked
non-expandable-entity mark needs a Directory write path and belongs with the slice that owns it.
- Three corrections to the Excel export on the owner's review: the menu now offers both layouts
(`Excel, Sheet per Table` behind a cover sheet, and `Excel, Single Sheet` with every section
stacked), both workbooks open with the report's title and the instant it was generated, and export
filenames are human (`Firm Usage 2026-08-31 19-48-43.xlsx` — the report's own name, the date, and
a readable time to the second, filesystem-unsafe characters dropped). Worksheet names are deduped
defensively so a title colliding with a section can never produce a workbook Excel refuses.
- Records one shared decision for widening the `firm_account_role` vocabulary, which the payments and general-ledger slices were each about to carry separately, and corrects the payments plan's step that added a role to a TypeScript constant without mentioning the DDL constraint that would refuse it.
- **The account surface states facts and builds the controls its small text was standing in for.**
`SettingDefinition.description` is optional rather than required (owner correction, 2026-09-18) and
`SettingsRow` renders the muted line only where there is one; `AccountMasthead` lost its `meta` prop
outright, since all three of its pages were restating their own headings. Three of the four rows the
`account-seams` guard was written for are built, so that guard now tests the named seam rows
(Two-Factor) rather than disabling every control on a page that carries one.

- **Profile · Photo.** `member_photo` in the per-firm database keyed by the member's user id, bytes
  in the firm's bucket under their own SHA-256, `me.photo` / `me.setPhoto` / `me.removePhoto` and a
  content route beside them. Content-addressed and written object-first, the firm brand-image
  reasoning. Registered in the PII registry as a hard-delete at the subject, with the note that the
  row is the only thing naming the object.
- **Security · Password.** Better Auth's `/change-password` behind the product's action panel, with
  `revokeOtherSessions` offered and defaulted on. `password.changed` joins the auth audit through an
  endpoint after-hook — `internalAdapter.updateAccount` passes no context to the account hooks, so
  the endpoint is the only place the door has a name, and the hook guards on the returned value
  because an after-hook runs over failed requests too.
- **Profile · Identity.** The address is engraved from the session bootstrap. No change control: the
  decision and what a change would actually cost are in `docs/decisions/pending/`.

`advanced.ipAddress.ipAddressHeaders` now reads `cf-connecting-ip` ahead of `x-forwarded-for`. The
library's default reads the latter alone and, with no trusted-proxy list, refuses any multi-hop
value — which is the only shape Cloudflare sends — so every session recorded an empty address. The
signed-in-devices row omits the clause where one is genuinely absent, and `REVOCATION_LAG_NOTE` and
`UNRECORDED_ADDRESS` are gone with the banner and the caption that carried them.

`member-name-api.ts` moved onto the generated client and `member-photo-api.ts` was written on it, so
the `lint:screen-data` hand-written-transport budget stayed flat at 56; the adapter both use
(`outcomeOf`) lives at the seam.
- **A node's evidence can say "no conflicts check exists to trigger" and be wrong for weeks, because
nothing in the repository can check an English sentence. The obvious fix — make the sentence name a
path — was measured at 96 hits over 708 nodes and rejected. Eight capabilities that existed were
being counted as work not begun, with seven further claims saying so in prose, and every one of them
was found by running the matcher by hand instead.**

**The idea, and why it does not survive measurement.** You cannot check a sentence against a
filesystem, but you can refuse it: require evidence asserting something does not exist to also carry
a repository path, so `no conflicts check exists` becomes `no caller of packages/conflicts exists`
and the three path rules in `tooling/lint-ledger-staleness/` can finally see it. An unfalsifiable
claim becomes a falsifiable one and the existing machinery does the work. The measurement says
otherwise. **96 raw hits, 14% of every node** — not a lint finding but a migration — and the hits are
not a fixable tail. They are the ledger's most correct idiom: _"no code"_, _"none exists"_,
_"Backend only — no UI"_, each naming a capability with **no location on the tree at all**, because
it was never built anywhere. Forcing a path onto those means inventing one, and rule 4 correctly
suppresses an unresolved path inside an absence claim, so the invented path is never checked until
somebody happens to create a file at exactly that name. The convention also cannot make anybody look:
writing `no packages/conflicts caller exists` requires having checked, and checking is what corrects
the belief.

**A better formulation appeared while measuring, and it fails too — by one.** Drop the filesystem and
compare the ledger against itself: a node's prose asserts a named capability does not exist, where
that capability is another area root the ledger holds at a has-code status. No English resolved
against a tree, just two committed statements disagreeing, the same shape as the roll-up and
slice-delivery rules. **8 hits, 5 true, 3 false**; narrowed to a standalone word followed by a
subsystem noun, **6 hits, 5 true, 1 false**. The survivor is `ai.magnus.record` — _"belongs to the
discovery surface and is not built **here**"_ — a node scoping an absence to itself while naming a
subsystem that exists. That is ordinary English, and the narrowing that would suppress it is fitted
to the one sample rather than derived. One false positive is one too many for a scan whose entire
argument is that it fires rarely and is right when it does.

**So the matcher ships as a search tool and not as a gate**, which is the division the design already
draws: judgement reads prose, the gate does not. Run over `roadmap.d/` by hand it found five stale
claims, and following one of them found a sixth seam nobody was looking for.

**Conflicts, corrected in one direction throughout.** Slices 1 and 2 shipped and six nodes still read
as though nothing had. The matching engine is `shipped`, not `researching`: four blocking channels
over the Directory corpus, related-party edge expansion as a 0-1 BFS that costs corporate hops
nothing, and a deliberately scorer-free evidence tier that orders and never filters. The immutable
log is `shipped`: three append-only tables with nine `RAISE(ABORT)` triggers, a runtime fitness probe
that refuses a plaintext-identifier-shaped digit run in recorded evidence, and the plain-language
statement of what a check searched. Human clearance is `shipped` — four disposition kinds, a required
rationale, a reversal that is a second row rather than an edit — and firm-wide imputation is
`shipped`, matching the firm's own people by identity and never by name, with the party class unioned
back into the floor on every read so no stored policy can drop the firm-wide corpus. Strictness and
search depth are `partial` rather than shipped, and for stated reasons: the strictness floor has no
write path behind it, and the content source is registered with no corpus and records `unavailable`
on every check so the log can never read as searched-and-clean for document text.

**Billing was carrying the same shape.** `financial.billing.invoice-composition` read `not-started`
with "no invoice model in tree" over eight invoice tables and a composer that builds fee and cost
lines from claimed work-in-progress; `financial.billing.wip-to-ar` read `not-started` with "no
posting service exists" over a `finalizeInvoice` that locks every claimed entry into billed and
writes the receivable in the same batch. Four further notes lines across time, costs and the billing
parent still called that slice unbuilt. Composition is `partial` (tax is a declared line kind and a
posting role with nothing computing it) and the posting is `shipped`.

Shipped moves 249 → 254 and partial 192 → 195, so shipped-plus-partial goes 441 → 449 of 708, 62% to
63%. The Conflicts area moves from 11% done to 56%.
- **An Error ID says when and where it came from.** Its body carries 9 base36 milliseconds since the
epoch, a 3-character service code and 9 base62 random characters; `describeErrorId` in
`@magna-carta/telemetry/ids` reads it back. Both facts are on the log record already, and being on
the record is no help while the record is the thing being searched for: a member quotes an id days
later, and whoever reads it has to choose a Worker and judge whether retention still holds the
window before the search can start.

**The fields are packed INTO the existing 21-character body, never appended.** That body's shape is
pinned in three places that know nothing about the telemetry package — the per-entity identifier
validators, the `pattern` emitted for every identifier field in the OpenAPI document, and the
scrubber's whole-handle exemption. The last is the sharp one: a handle the scrubber stops
recognising is rewritten to `[scrubbed]` on the way out, destroying the very Error ID a failure is
keyed by. Keeping the budget means every previously minted id stays well-formed and no contract
moves. The random part drops from ~126 bits to ~53, which is ample for a correlation handle that
grants nothing and addresses no record, and would not be acceptable for a handle that names one.

A 9-character timestamp rather than 8 because 8 runs out in 2059 and would have truncated silently
into a confidently wrong date; the test that pins both ends of the range is what found it. A Worker
announces itself once through `setServiceIdentity`, from the module its events pass through rather
than its entrypoint, which is held to a startup CPU budget the telemetry import would spend. A
Worker that never announces mints `unk`.

**And one failure now mints one Error ID.** `logOperationFailed` returns the id it minted. A caller
that had to show the member an id used to mint its own and call this too, which minted a second —
so the record's `errorId` field named a failure nobody held, and the member's id survived only if
the caller had buried it in the message. A support search against the field found nothing, which is
the one thing that field exists to make possible.
- An error in the matter file manager used to say only that something went wrong, and its two buttons did nothing. It now leads with the fact that the record itself is unaffected — the first thing anyone needs to know — then names the request that failed, the status that came back, the time it happened, and the Error ID worth quoting.

Three first steps follow, each with the reason it is worth trying, so a person can tell a connection problem from a platform one before anyone else is involved. Retry re-runs the request. Report a Problem opens a real reporter rather than an inert button: it lists exactly what is sent, keeps the screenshot opt-in and unticked, and states plainly that no document, file name or matter content is included. The report goes to the firm's own pipeline, not an outside service.

The error view also scrolls inside its own pane. That ruling had been marked settled off a dialog fix, and the error view is a pane, not a dialog — the cap had never applied to it.
- **An identifier is a shape, checked before it is sealed.** `packages/directory/src/identifier-shape.ts` declares what each kind is made of — SSN nine digits, EIN nine in two groups, licence region + number, bar number jurisdiction + number, account held-with + number + username + secret — and `checkIdentifier` refuses a value that does not fit with the sentence the screen shows beside the field; the API runs the same check on `AddIdentifierRequest` (now `type`, `label`, `number`, `username`, `secret`) and on every identifier in a create. `directory_identifier` gains a nullable plaintext `label` (migration `20260903T090000_directory-identifier-label`) so the enumeration can say what a sealed value is of. An account's sealed value is the JSON of its three parts; its blind index normalizes the number alone, so the username and secret never reach an index; the reveal route hands the parts back apart.

**The `dob` kind is gone.** A date of birth is a date on the person, in the clear, beside the date of death; a sealed birthday could be neither shown nor used to tell two people apart. The sealed `client.dateOfBirth` merge field went with it — a plain field from the person's date column is a document-assembly follow-up.

**Email and phone rules are shared.** `packages/directory/src/email-address.ts` is the one email check, used by the API's `prepareAddress` and the screen's live refusal. The web app takes `libphonenumber-js` (already in the lockfile through `class-validator`) for dial codes, as-you-type national formatting and E.164 submission; the server's own parser is unchanged and receives the international form with the region beside it.
- **Both surfaces that had their own undo now render the design system's, and both old stacks are
gone.** `apps/web/src/lib/file-manager/move-history.ts` and
`apps/web/src/lib/time/time-sheet-history.svelte.ts` are deleted; the file manager's footer and the
Time Sheet's toolbar each render `UndoRedoControls` over a `HistoryStack`, and the four hand-built
split controls become one. What a surface still varies is the register — quiet ghost buttons in a
counts footer, bordered secondary ones in a toolbar of secondary buttons — because that is a fact
about the chrome the pair sits in rather than about undo.

**The file manager's recorded move became the first inverse command.** Each key goes back to where
IT came from, which is exactly what the old `RecordedMove` already held and what a snapshot of the
surface could never have said. A write that refuses now throws, so the stack keeps the step and the
reader gets another attempt at the same move rather than the one beneath it; the refusal goes to the
same band every other refused act on that surface uses. The revision counter the controls needed in
order to re-derive is gone with it: the shared stack's steps are reactive, so there is nothing to
bump and nothing to forget to bump.

**The Time Sheet's snapshot became a pair of field writes, and that is where its two defects were.**
An undo now writes **the row the step changed** — the snapshot could not say which field moved, so
putting one back meant writing every row on the sheet, over rows the step never touched and over
whatever somebody had changed in another window meanwhile. And the announcement now waits for the
write: `runUndo` used to say "Undid {label}" the instant the stack popped while
`#writeBackEverySavedRow` was unawaited, so a reader was told the entry went back before the record
agreed, and heard nothing when it then refused.

**An inverse whose entry has left draft refuses rather than writing.** The void, the submission or
the approval is the newer fact, and putting a value back on an entry somebody voided in between
would be a second act wearing the first one's name. The step stays on the stack and the walk says
which act it stopped at. Two existing tests already pinned the behaviour through the snapshot model;
they now pin the refusal, and assert that the walk reports it.

Two new tests cover what the port is for: that an undo writes the row the step changed and no other
row on the sheet, and that a walk answers only once the write has answered. The design system gains
leaf export paths — `@magna-carta/design-system/history-stack` and `/history-shortcuts` — because a
module with no Svelte in it must not pull the control's component tree in; doing so fails as
`Unknown file extension ".svelte"` deep inside bits-ui, which reads like anything but the import
that caused it.

And the defect the shared control was built with: all four undo and redo dropdowns rendered
`DropdownMenu.GroupHeading` with no `DropdownMenu.Group`, which throws when the caret is pressed. It
went with the markup that carried it.
- **The register counted 133 roll-up parents as if they were work, and it could not tell a screen
somebody uses from a backend nobody can open. Both are fixed, and there is now one page for
answering the questions the build is waiting on.**

Three corrections to how the feature ledger is read, all raised by the owner reading the register.

**A roll-up is not a unit of work.** Hierarchy is encoded in the dotted id, so a node with children
is a summary of them — and its status goes `partial` the moment its children stop agreeing. Counting
those parents beside the leaves did not add work to the totals, it added the same work a second time
under a status nobody chose. The distortion was not evenly spread either: of 133 parents, 107 were
`partial`, so it landed almost entirely on the one status a reader is most likely to mistake for
progress. Every share in the register now runs over the 621 units of work, with the parent count and
its `partial` share stated in its own section rather than quietly dropped. The numbers move
accordingly: shipped reads 41% where it read 35%, and `partial` 16% where it read 27%.

**`surface:` — a new ledger key, because `status` never held reach.** A backend nobody can open and a
screen somebody uses every day are both `shipped`, and reading those as one number overstates the
product by the entire amount of interface that has not been built. The key takes `screen`,
`awaiting-screen` or `internal`, is required on every leaf whose status is `shipped`, `partial` or
`in-build`, and is refused on roll-up parents and on nodes with nothing built — a parent's reach is
its children's, and a capability nothing has been written for has no reach to record. It is recorded
rather than derived because deriving it was measured and rejected: prose in `notes` carried a usable
signal on 63 nodes of 754, and an `evidence:` path naming a screen on 14 of the 359 leaves with code
behind them. The register gains a section reading the answer back, and the interface debt is now a
stated figure rather than something inferred from `partial`.

**`docs/decisions-open.html` — the decision desk.** The `awaiting-owner` questions were recorded
where each piece of work stopped, one line inside one area file, and reachable only as a list part
way down the register. That is somewhere to read them, not somewhere to answer them. The desk is a
third rendering of the same ledger, built by the same `vp run register-build`: every open question as
a card, sorted by whether anything is built behind it, with the reach chip from `surface:`, an answer
box that persists in the browser, filters by area and by unanswered, and a copy-out block that names
each decision by node id. It has no network of any kind — that is what lets it be read from the
repository, from a published copy or from a laptop with no connection and be the same page — so the
answers come back by paste, in a format written to be applied without anybody matching them up by
hand. `pnpm run lint:roadmap` holds it to a fresh render like the other two, so a question leaves the
desk exactly when its node's key does.
- Custodian's number draw now runs on `@magna-carta/sequence-numbering` instead of its own copy of the
idiom, leaving one home for how a sequence number is allocated.

Custodian grew its counter and allocation statements before the shared package was extracted out of
matters, so the same read-render-commit — ensure the counter row, increment it guarded on the
observed value, and claim the drawn value in an allocation row whose composite primary key is the
actual backstop — existed twice. `packages/custodian/src/numbering/counter-statements.ts` is now the
same thin shim `@magna-carta/matters` uses: it binds `custody_number_counter`,
`custody_number_allocation`, and the `packet_id` owner column to the shared builders and keeps the
`CustodyPacketId` typing on the allocation. Every export it had, it still has.

**Behavioural identity was the bar, and the SQL is unchanged.** The shared builders emit the same
statements for these table names, character for character, so a custody number renders exactly as it
did — the shape is printed on physical labels and read out over the phone, and a format change would
not be a refactor. The one difference in reachable behaviour is a widening that cannot fire:
`isNumberAllocationConflict` also recognises the append-only refusal that an allocation table with a
no-overwrite trigger raises ahead of its primary key, and `custody_number_allocation` has no such
trigger. Custodian's existing suite is the proof — the concurrent-draw test still walks three
simultaneous draws out to `CUS-00001`/`00002`/`00003`, the allocation ledger still records one row per
drawn value and none for a manual number, and the retry still steps past a manual number the counter
would have rendered. A new case pins what the shared, table-parameterised predicate must not lose: a
collision on `matter_number_allocation` is not a custody draw race and is never retried as one.

**The retry loop deliberately stays in `packet-service.ts`.** `drawWithBoundedRetry` cannot express
two things custodian's loop does: it gives up as a named `CustodyValidationError`
(`custody-number-exhausted`) that the route maps to a problem type rather than as a bare `Error`, and
it retries a manual-number collision that consumed no counter value and therefore has no observed
draw to advance past. Matters keeps its own loop for the same kind of reason. The statement builders
are what was duplicated and what is now shared; a loop growing an option per consumer's error
vocabulary would be shared in name only.
- **Discovery's attribution reads "Custodian of Record" wherever a person meets it.** The owner named
the label; the code word does not move. Every user-facing string now carries it — the OpenAPI
`description`s on the record-custodian routes, the refusal sentences the discovery services raise
that a route surfaces verbatim as a problem `detail`, and
[`docs/user/features/review-sets-and-loading.md`](docs/user/features/review-sets-and-loading.md).
Identifiers, tables, columns, route paths (`/api/v1/review-sets/{reviewSetId}/record-custodians`),
schema names, and refusal codes stay `record_custodian` / `recordCustodian`, so nothing on the wire
changes shape. `tooling/lint-custodian-vocabulary.mjs` now recognises both permitted forms and
nothing else: the leading-`record` family for code, the full phrase "Custodian of Record" for
readers, and a bare `custodian` still fails in every casing and position — with self-test rows for
the near-misses ("the custodian of the estate" is still a violation). No screen was touched; the UI
surfaces are the owner's to schedule.
- **Discovery's three screens take the product's search and create controls, and the search is a real
one.** The register, a review set's document list and its Loads screen each shipped without
`ScreenSearch`; Loads carried a button per act — "New Custodian of Record" beside "New Load" — which
is the shape the standing list-screen ruling names outright, and the register listed corpora with no
way to start one.

**Every one of the three searches on the server, over the whole record.** A field that narrowed the
rows already fetched would have answered about the first page of a cursor-paged listing and read as
the whole of it, which on a corpus a firm certifies the contents of is the most expensive kind of
wrong. So the reads gained the parameter instead: `ReviewDocumentListFilters.search` over
`source_name` and `source_path`, the two review-set listings over `name`, and the loads listing over
`source_description`. Each is a LIKE scan placed AFTER every clause that can use an index — the
review-set predicate, the access predicate and the equality filters — so what it walks is one corpus
the member may see, stopped by the page limit; `likePattern` escapes the reader's own `%` and `_`
once, in one place, so a production whose files are named `100%_final` does not silently match
everything.

**The cost is measured rather than argued.** The load-profile harness runs both cases
(`discovery-review.list-page-by-name-search` and `-no-match`), and at the 250,000-document ceiling a
search that matches costs 0.4 ms — flat against the unsearched page, because the LIMIT ends the walk
— while one that matches nothing costs 62 ms, the pass over the review set. The plan is an index
search with no temporary sort at both volumes, which the existing fitness assertion there now holds
for the search too. Both numbers sit in the read that pays them, so the day one of them stops being
acceptable the answer is visible: the review set's own search index, not an index on a column a
leading wildcard cannot use.

**On the document list the search is a CRITERION, not a control beside them.** It is a built provider
in `criteria.ts` like every other narrowing, so it rides the address — a searched queue is a link a
supervising attorney can send — it composes with the Custodian, load, family, state and exception
filters as an intersection, and a bulk coding act over the result works unchanged, because what it
holds is a criteria set rather than a page of identifiers. Providers gained `setFrom` for the two
whose control is not the popover (the family, named by opening a document; the search, set in the
action row): they still render there, saying where they are set and offering the way to clear them,
because that popover is the one control answering "why is this list short".

**Keyword stays a separate criterion, and the difference is now legible on screen.** Searching what a
document is CALLED composes into this listing; searching what is INSIDE it composes into the review
set's own index, is still `soon`, and sits next to the name search in the Narrow control so a reader
choosing between them can see which is which.

**Loads' two buttons are one `CreateControl`** reading the bare "New", each choice carrying its own
refusal, and its "Each Load" panels follow the table rather than the read. **The register creates
too**: it shipped read-only on the reasoning that a create control would have to ask which matter
and would therefore be the matter's screen in disguise, which the Conflicts Check ruling settled the
other way a day later — `NewReviewSetDialog` now takes `chooseMatter` and asks, over the caseload,
exactly as the conflicts composer does from its own two doors.
- **Downloads is a register on the platform's one table.**

A fixed list of seven columns served a shelf that held one kind of thing. It holds five now — an export, a bundle, a converted file, a discovery production, a file taken off a matter — and they answer different questions, so the columns are declared (`apps/web/src/lib/export/download-columns.ts`) and the reader chooses: sort, per-column filters, show and hide, reorder, pin, and a layout that survives the visit. Type and Standing declare their whole vocabularies rather than reading them off the rows in hand, so a member with no conversions loaded this week is not told the register cannot hold one.

**Standing is the column the screen could not do without.** Now that the row outlives the bytes, "is this still here" stopped being answerable from the other columns: Available, Preparing, On the matter, and Record only are four different answers to "can I have it again", and the Download control is offered from the same reading.

**The read is paged and the search is the server's.** `GET /api/v1/downloads` answers the house `{ data, nextCursor }` envelope and takes a `search` that narrows the whole register — the register has no bound now, so filtering the rows a client happens to hold would answer confidently about a fraction of it. Taking several at once routes by kind rather than by "artifact or not": snapshots render into one archive, a matter file and a stored artifact each open on their own, and a record that never held bytes is reported as short rather than silently missing from the zip.
- **Attorney License Lookup lists all fifty-one registers instead of asking which one you want.** The
state `ChoicePicker` and the single revealed register card are gone; the screen is now
`DataTable.Grid` over `attorneyLicenseRows()`, one row per state, sorted by state name. Every answer
the tool could ever give is a hyperlink and there are only fifty-one of them, so the picker was
hiding fifty links and, with them, the two questions a list answers for nothing: is a state covered,
and which registers are not encrypted.

`attorney-license.ts` keeps its DOM-free split and swaps its API — `licensingStateChoices()` and
`registerForState()` out, `attorneyLicenseRows()` and `attorneyLicenseColumns()` in. The columns are
State (anchored, carrying the link), Code, Register, Connection, and Address hidden by default. The
plain-HTTP caution stops being an `Alert` that appears only for a state already chosen and becomes
the Connection column: a `set` filter over the declared `CONNECTION_STANDINGS`, so narrowing to the
unencrypted two is one gesture and the filter offers both values whatever the rows on screen hold.
Encrypted reads as quiet text; the two that are not carry the warning badge with what it means.

A register opens two ways, per the table's own convention: the row's gesture (`onActivate` →
`openBeside`) and the state's name as a link, which is what buys the browser's new tab and copied
address.
