- **Every date on the platform is now entered through one control.** Sixteen surfaces held a native `<Input type="date">`; all sixteen are the design system's `DatePicker`, and `pnpm run lint:date-handling` fails a native date field wherever it is written — the design system included. There is no allowance list any more: it is empty and a test asserts it stays empty.

It had been recorded rather than failed, because whether the native control was good enough for some fields looked like a design question with real trade-offs. It was not one. The design system's own notes had already called the native date types "a thin interim", and only the component can carry a firm-configured week start or a locale-aware week — the native `type="week"` is hard-locked to ISO 8601, Monday-start, not configurable. Two controls also meant two behaviours on the same screen, and the split was quietly growing: it reached sixteen entries on a merge while the gate stayed green.

Three things had to exist first. The picker gained the Input's own `size` scale, imported rather than redeclared, so a date field and the text field beside it can be set to one row height — that is what let a column's date-range filter, two boxes inside a menu, keep its compact geometry. It gained an `aria-label` that reaches the segment group: the property spread goes to a root element that renders no DOM, so an `aria-label` written the obvious way disappeared without a warning and left the field unnamed. And the conversion between the picker's value and the `YYYY-MM-DD` text a record holds moved to sit beside the picker, because a design-system component cannot import an app; screens still reach it at the same import path.

One thing was given up, recorded here so it is not rediscovered as a defect: the invitation screen's birthdate field carried `autocomplete="bday"`, and a browser fills a birthday only into a native date input it recognises as one. The picker has no `name` or `autocomplete` to pass through, so that date is typed now, like every other one.

Two smaller repairs came with it. `startOfCivilMonth` joins `endOfCivilMonth` in `@magna-carta/civil-time`, so the draft-bill dialog's billing period starts from the month's parts instead of `` `${today.slice(0, 8)}01` `` — correct, unreadable, and one edit from being a day out. And the `FieldRow` catalog specimen now holds a real date field, which makes it the specimen for the one thing the two label recipes have to agree on: they must measure the same, or a date field starts a few pixels below the fields beside it.
- **The download register admits every download, and the row outlives the bytes.**

`download_item` was built as a shelf of what the platform MADE you, and only exports were ever written to it — `bundle` and `conversion` were named in its vocabulary from the start with no client able to create one, and a file downloaded from a matter had nowhere to go at all. So "I downloaded something and it did not appear in Downloads" was the correct behaviour, which is the definition of a design that needs changing.

One reviewed rebuild widens it. `producer` gains `file`; `kind` gains `reference` and `record`; `object_key` and `expires_at` become nullable, tied to the kind by CHECKs. `download_item` is a LEAF — nothing in the schema references it — so this is the `invoice_wip_claim` shape rather than the parent rebuild the repository forbids, and the audit is written out in the migration's own `-- contract:` header.

**`reference` is a safety boundary, not a vocabulary.** An artifact fetch presigns the stored object key with no further check, which is right for a frozen bundle the member already had and wrong for a live matter file: a member screened off a matter afterwards would keep a working handle to its files. A reference carries no key — the CHECK makes that unrepresentable rather than remembered — and the fetch hands back this platform's own `/api/v1/files/{id}/download` address, so the matter capability check runs again at the moment they ask. **`record`** is the register being complete without lying: a bundle streamed inline assembled its bytes for one response and never retained them, and filing those as an artifact would report "expired" for something that was never stored.

**Retention splits.** The bytes are privileged content in a second place and keep the seven-day rule; the row is a title, a producer and two instants, and is kept. The sweep marks `expired` and takes the object where it used to delete both, and the read it drives excludes what it has already marked so that marking terminates. The shelf read is paged for the first time, on the `(created_at, id)` pair the index already leads on — its old comment reasoned that a whole read was safe because the shelf was short-lived by construction, and keeping rows takes that premise away.
- Every read and write of a firm's objects resolves the firm's bucket through one seam.

`src/files/firm-bucket.ts` is the one home for "which bucket holds this firm's bytes", and it answers as a pair: the name a presigned URL addresses, and the handle the Worker reads through. Twenty-one modules reached the bound binding directly instead, past that resolver. Eight of them were genuinely a firm's bytes — the email capture consumer, preview delivery, the search index consumer and its compaction sweep, the natural-language feed, the storage tiering sweep, the WOPI host, and the document editing session — and now resolve through the seam.

Several already had the answer and did not use it. The capture consumer carried the bucket name on its own message and passed it to attachment extraction while reading through the binding. The preview delivery token has carried a `bucket` field all along, with a comment calling it a forward seam. The tiering sweep's comment described this exact change as future work.

The seam grew a second entry point for callers holding only a firm id — a queue consumer whose message predates any bucket field — so nothing needed a new message field to be correct.

Four modules keep the binding because their bytes belong to the platform or to local development: the status reachability probe, the development presigner's staging objects, the development upload leg, and the development seeder. `pnpm run lint:firm-bucket-seam` fails any new direct use, and fails a stale allow-list entry too, so an exemption cannot outlive its reason.
- **Every main screen states its name the same way, and the sidebar agrees with it.** The screens had
drifted into four ways of introducing themselves: Home greeted the reader with the time of day,
Notifications titled itself "Notification Center" while the sidebar row opening it said
Notifications, Downloads and Notifications each carried an eyebrow repeating their own title back,
and Conflicts Check, Tools, WHOIS Lookup and Assemble a document each carried a sentence under the
title restating what the title said. Matters, Directory and Custodian carried a title and nothing
else, because the ruling that got them there reached the list screens in 2026-08 and stopped.

Every main screen now takes the Matters shape — `ScreenHeader` with the destination's own name from
`navigation/destinations.ts`, no `eyebrow`, no descriptive `meta`. The rule is not new ("a heading
carries no explanatory sub-text"); it had only ever bound lists, and now binds every archetype,
recorded under a new "Screen headers" heading in
[`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`](docs/conventions/design-corrections.md) and restated
on `screen-header.svelte` itself so the next author meets it at the call site. A meta line still
carries facts — Home's date, a room's kind and seat count, the speed test's run time, Assemble a
document's alpha badge — because the test is unchanged: removing the line must lose a fact.

**The `my-work` destination becomes `tasks`.** A matter's own section was already Tasks, so the
registry and the matter used two names for one noun. That screen also had no page heading at all —
its name was a `FieldLabel as="h2"` inside `TaskList`, so the route rendered no `h1` — and it now
carries a real `ScreenHeader`. `TaskList`'s `heading` turns optional for exactly that reason: a
matter's Tasks section still names itself, because the matter's masthead carries the matter's name,
while the firm-wide list lets the page's own header speak. `mergeGroupOrder` skips stored ids it no
longer knows, so a member who had dragged the old row to a custom sidebar position finds Tasks at
its canonical position and keeps the rest of their arrangement.

**What a header gives up, the page takes back.** Neither line that carried a real fact was deleted;
each moved to where the fact is used. The safe website viewer's isolation notice now renders in
`WebsiteShell`'s new `note` band, at the address bar beside the control it qualifies, yielding to
`invalidHint` because a fault with the address in hand outranks a standing fact. The seventeen
settings pages give up their masthead descriptor the same way: `SettingsMasthead` no longer takes a
`meta`, and the sentence renders through `settings-description.svelte` as the first line of the
page's own scroll area, so it travels with the plates it describes. `SettingsPage` still takes
`meta` and passes it there, so a standard settings page is unchanged at its call site.

**And the rule becomes a gate.** `pnpm run lint:screen-headers` (`tooling/lint-screen-headers/`,
nineteen unit tests) refuses an eyebrow on any screen, a destination screen titled something
`destinations.ts` does not call it, and a meta line that is fixed prose rather than a read value.
It earned itself immediately: the uploads screen landed on `main` mid-consolidation carrying
`eyebrow="Uploads"` over `title="Uploads"`, and the file workbench was found stating three fixed
sentences under its title — including the same "Runs outside any matter" removed from Tools — from a
header in `lib/` that the route-level pass never saw. Its privacy consequence now reads full width
under the header, where the narrow file rail could not have held it. Membership derives from the
`lint:*` scripts, so the scan joins both the inner loop and CI's governance job with no further
wiring.

The `tasks.my-work-*` load-profile measurement names are left alone — recorded measurements, not
user-facing text.
- **Every number the firm issues is drawn from one register.** The segment-template scheme engine
moves out of `@magna-carta/matters` into `@magna-carta/sequence-numbering` beside the counter
mechanism it already held, under a static register of purposes (`purposes.ts`) naming what each
sequence is, when it is drawn, whether the firm shapes it and with which parts, and what renders
until it does. Conflicts checks and custody packets join as scheme-shaped purposes: a check draws
through the shared planner and its own counter tables instead of `MAX + 1` under a hard-coded
`CC-` prefix, defaulting to `CC2026-00001` restarting each year; a packet draws from the
`custody_packet` purpose with its old `CUS-00001` shape as the default, and custodian's dead
fixed-shape model is deleted. Invoice, time-entry and call numbers are registered with their fixed
shapes. `GET /api/v1/numbering-schemes` lists the register; `Settings › Practice › Numbering`
(formerly Matter Numbering, which redirects) shows one plate per sequence. Decision:
`docs/decisions/pending/every-number-the-firm-issues-is-drawn-from-one-register.md`.
- **An intake is numbered the moment the enquiry is written down.** The lifecycle ruling of 2026-09-06 said no number of any kind existed before a matter became active. The consultation sequence reversed half of that on 2026-08-31; the owner reversed the rest on 2026-09-14: "everything should have a number, intake would have a number as well."

An intake was already work — somebody took the call, a person is named responsible for it, a conflicts check may have run, procedure steps are being cleared against it — and the only name the platform had for it was its handle, which is what the platform joins on and what nobody can read back down a telephone.

**A third run, not a number moved earlier.** `matter.intake_number` is drawn at creation from a scheme whose `purpose` is `intake`, rendering `I2026-0001` until a firm configures its own. Drawing the consultation number at intake instead would have been cheaper and is the wrong shape: most enquiries are declined, so the consultation run would fill with numbers issued to nothing and stop being readable as a run of consultations — the same defect the consultation sequence was created to avoid on the matter run.

**Nothing is replaced.** Graduation adds the consultation number beside the intake number and opening adds the matter number beside both, so a file that came the whole way answers to three names and a note filed under any of them still resolves. Every surface that quotes a matter falls through to the newest number it has drawn; the matter list, the communications log and the intake desk search all of them.

The draw rides the existing `matter_number_counter` / `matter_number_allocation` mechanism under an `intake/` scope prefix rather than a third pair of tables. What each sequence IS — its prefix, its label, its retryable collision, whether a built-in default exists — moved out of the service's conditionals into `numbering/sequences.ts`: two sequences were two branches and read fine, three made the shape visible, and a fourth run is now one row rather than four edits. The migration backfills every row currently at status `intake` and seeds the counters to match.
- **Every screen's title now comes from one component, and a screen entered from another names where it came from.** The two are the same change: the reason three detail screens shipped with no way back is that there was no one place a header rule could live. Twenty screens assembled the design-system Masthead by hand in eight different combinations of its parts; four more hand-rolled an `h1` over a letterspaced `p` outside the design system entirely; and three area wrappers (settings, account, matter) had each partially centralized it for themselves, duplicating the same framing verbatim. Nothing was wrong with any one of them — the problem was that "what does a screen header look like here" had twenty-four answers.

`apps/web/src/lib/screen/screen-header.svelte` is now the one answer: the way back, the eyebrow, the title, the citation line, the actions, and a `trailing` column for a band that shares its height with something else. The Masthead recipe stays the primitive underneath — the register, the display serif, the density step — and this is the one assembly of it. Twenty-four call sites became one; `Masthead.Root` now appears exactly once in the application.

**The way back is named, not drawn** (owner's direction, 2026-09-03). A screen passes a destination **id** — `back="directory"` — and the href, the user-facing label and the glyph all come from the sidebar's own registry, so a back link cannot point at a screen that does not exist, cannot call it something the sidebar calls something else, and cannot go stale when a path moves. `DestinationId` is a literal union derived from the registry, so a typo is a type error rather than a link that renders and goes nowhere. The arrow shows the destination **in miniature** — its own sidebar mark beside its own name — because the point is to learn where the link lands, not merely that there is a way out. A screen outside the sidebar (the developer console) passes a spelled-out target instead, deliberately more work to write than an id.

The matter band takes the one shape too, which costs it a row it had spent two rounds saving: its way back was an unlabelled arrow inside the citation line, which cost no height but said only "back". It now leads the band, named and marked, in the same place as on every other screen.

`pnpm run lint:back-navigation` answers three questions from the route tree and the registry rather than from a list: every route whose nearest ancestor route renders a page passes a `back`; the destination it names resolves to that ancestor's own path; and nothing in the application assembles `Masthead.Root` itself or builds its own back link out of `EyebrowLink` and an arrow icon. The third is what keeps the first true — a screen with a hand-made header is free to grow its own idea of the way back, or none. It runs in the inner loop and in CI by derivation (every `lint:*` script in the root manifest is repo-wide), and its nineteen tests feed it deliberately broken route trees, including the one that would make the whole gate pass vacuously: a component walk that followed the import into the shared header and found the back link every screen's answer flows through.
- **Every shipped Workspace screen searches itself through `ScreenSearch`, in the screen header's `actions` snippet, or records why it does not.** The Matters docket, the Directory and a matter's Notes each carried their own search — a `type="search"` field beside a Lucide search glyph, its own debounce, its own toggle behaviour on a live query — so both 2026-09-02 corrections against the shared control (the clear glyph, collapse-on-click-away) had reached the component and none of the three. All three now use the control. Downloads and Uploads gained one; both hold their whole list in the browser, so they narrow on `searchOn="keystroke"` with nothing leaving the machine.

**Four screens gained a search by gaining a query on their read**, which is where the work was. Notifications, the Conflicts Check log, Magnus and the Calendar were first recorded as declining on the grounds that their reads took no search parameter; that is a reason to add one.

- **Magnus** matches the conversation title and what was SAID in it — nothing generates a title, so a transcript search is the only way a conversation is found again. Content is in scope only for a member's OWN conversations; the firm-wide administrative read matches titles alone, because `packages/magnus/CLAUDE.md` holds that transcripts may not be swept across the firm's records until the discovery surface owns an include-or-exclude control for it. `searchesContent` is the one place that boundary is decided.
- **Conflicts Check** matches the matter a run was made against and the NAMES it surfaced, through `directory_name.normalized_display` so a term normalizes the way the corpus did. The closed labels stay with the column filters, which match them exactly. "Has this firm ever checked this person" is now one question rather than a walk through the log.
- **Notifications** carries no sentence in the record by design, so the client resolves the term into the kinds and categories whose WORDS match (`kindsMatching` / `categoriesMatching`) and sends those with it; the server OR-s them against the matter number. An empty `kinds` means the term matched no kind, never "match no row". The unread badge is deliberately not narrowed.
- **The Calendar** narrows the window on screen, because its three reads cap their horizon server-side and refuse a wider one rather than clamping it. The view states how many entries in the named window match and that other dates were not searched, so the control never implies a reach it does not have.

`@magna-carta/data-access/like-search` is the new one home for escaping a reader's text into a `LIKE` pattern. Two copies of that rule already existed (the discovery review reads and the communications log), agreeing by luck; a third was about to be written here. A test caught the bug that makes it worth having: `normalizeName("%")` strips to the empty string, and a contains-pattern built from an empty term is `%%`, which every stored name matches — a reader typing one stray character would have been handed the whole conflicts log.

`pnpm run lint:workspace-search` is the new fitness function. It reads the Workspace group out of `navigation/destinations.ts` and the pages out of the route tree — no roster kept by hand — and refuses four things: a Workspace screen that neither searches nor declines, a control seated outside the header's action row, a decline left standing after its screen got a search, and a second implementation of a search box anywhere beneath a Workspace destination. Coverage follows the render rather than the file, walking each page's `$lib` component imports, so Tasks passes on the search `TaskList` owns. Thirteen of the fourteen shipped Workspace screens now search; Home declines, being a summary of other screens rather than a list.
- Exporting no longer saves a file. It GENERATES the item onto the member's download shelf, so several
can be gathered over a morning and taken together — the owner's direction, and the reason the shelf
existed in the first place. The format menu stays on the export control, because the format is what
the item is made for and what its download defaults to; that choice is kept on the new
`download_item.requested_format` column, distinct from `downloaded_formats_json`, since "what this
was made for" and "what has actually left the platform" answer different questions and are both true
at once.

The register learns the difference: `POST /api/v1/downloads/snapshots` takes `taken`, defaulting to
false, so a format asked for is not recorded as a format downloaded. Claiming otherwise would tell a
member they already hold a file that was never made.

**Multi-select and one archive.** `/downloads` gains row selection and a bulk action that appears
only while a selection is in play. Snapshots render and travel in a single `client-zip` archive
rather than firing a download each — several simultaneous downloads make the browser prompt and then
scatter the files, which is the mess the gathering exists to avoid. An artifact cannot join the
archive and that is structural, not an omission: its bytes reach the member over a presigned URL the
browser downloads directly, and pulling them through the tab to repack them is what
`network-resilience.md` rule 2 forbids. Those open on their own, and a partial result is always
reported as partial.

**`Settings · Downloads`** carries the one preference: save a file as soon as I export. A user-tier
scoped setting, so it follows the member between machines, audited on the
`notificationPreferences.update` precedent, and written to the member's own tier and nothing else.

Where a file LANDS is deliberately absent, and stays absent: a page cannot choose the folder, the
local-disk pickers are Chromium-only, and they could never apply to a bundle whose bytes never pass
through the page. The browser's own "ask where to save each file" already covers every download; the
platform-side answer belongs to the desktop app.

Also repaired, and not from this stream: the matter-notes routes landed without their conformance
entries, so `main` was failing two fitness assertions — the six `notes.*` operations are added to the
committed operation list and the `notes:` namespace bound to the matter resource.
- Several fields on the time and cost windows stop explaining themselves and start working.

- **Every code field carries a `(None)` row, for every firm.** A firm that does not code its time is the commonest configuration in the product, and it was getting two paragraphs apologising that it had no codes turned on, under two fields it could not use. `(None)` is also what the field READS at rest rather than a blank: an empty box says nobody has filled this in, and `(None)` says the entry carries no code. The explanatory line survives for the two states that really are inabilities — this account may not read the catalogue, or the read failed.
- **The internal memo moved under the description and lost its badge.** They are one act of writing that differs only in who reads it; down beside the arithmetic the memo was a stranded field a reader met after they had finished with the entry. The "Internal" chip beside the label said in a second voice what the word Internal in the label had already said.
- **The Billing dropdown lost "No charge, on the bill at nothing".** It is non-billable under a longer name — both mean the client is charged nothing and the entry carries no value, and the only difference anybody could name is whether the line prints, which is a question about a bill rather than about this entry. Two rows for one disposition make a member choose between them, and there is no right answer to that choice.
- **A document can be attached before the entry is saved.** "Save the entry first" is a true statement about the route and a wrong one about the work: the person writing up an afternoon has the document open in front of them. The picks are held and applied the moment the entry is written.
- **The cost window writes the same pair in the same shape** — Description then Internal Memo, stacked and full width — and commits with the same words, "Save & Close". A cost and a time entry are recorded minutes apart by the same person, and the fields they share should not move between them.
- **Voided, never struck.** One word for the act, across the history rail, the sheet, the ledger and the record window.
- **File Analysis is a plain file table, and the file manager's header holds still.** The strip above
the File Analysis table is gone entirely — the Safety column already filters, so a second row of
controls above the table said the same thing twice. The view's own acts moved to the footer beside
undo/redo: the door into the set-aside issues and the report download (the copy button is gone; the
download produces the same text). Browsing inside a zip likewise adds nothing above the table: the
archive's crumb, its badges, the extract seam, and the way out sit on the archive's own line just
above the footer, so entering and leaving an archive never moves the header and never costs the
footer a tool.
- **The file manager now matches the owner's settled Docket design, and Fees stands beside Time and
Costs.** The work-in-progress fee ledger left the Billing tabs for its own matter section, and
Billing (the bill register) wears the Alpha mark instead of Soon. On the Files surface: the
breadcrumb and navigation controls sit directly above the file list rather than spanning the whole
surface, the counts footer is pinned to the bottom of the screen and tallies folders and files with
a select all/none toggle, the New control anchors the toolbar's far end, and the matter's status
seal moved beside the matter number in the masthead's top-left corner. Toolbar and footer controls
are quiet glyphs — no resting box, no grey plate behind a disabled undo/redo, an active toggle
reading through its glyph and a hairline — the columns control included; the file area's edges are
square; the pane dividers lost their grip handles; and both side panels sit on the sunken surface
so they read as panels. Collapsing or reopening a side panel now hands the space to the file list
alone instead of resizing the opposite panel. The folder tree's right-click grew the full file
menu — open, download, pin, rename, cut, paste, delete, colour and mark. Uploading no longer waits
on the destination question: files start uploading the moment they are picked (drag-and-drop onto
the list included), the Upload dialog shows each file's own progress while the destination —
Current Folder, Home, or Select Folder over the real folder tree — is chosen, and a failed upload
now names the stage it failed at and quotes the Error ID.
- **The floating surfaces share one alignment, one width rule and one stacking layer — settled in
the design system, not at each call site.**

A listbox, a menu or a popover now opens aligned to the right-hand edge of the control that opens
it and grows leftward, never extending past that edge and never wider than the room the screen has
for it: a long option wraps inside the panel instead of running the panel off the screen. Before
this, the components set no default of their own and the alignment was written by hand at
ninety-five call sites, with a settings row's listbox — its control pinned to the right of the
row — running off the right-hand edge of the screen. The Combobox now anchors its list to the
whole field a person sees rather than to the text box inside it, so the list's edge sits on the
field's. A caller whose control is left-anchored still says `align="start"` and wins.

The two context-menu parts move to the layer every other floating surface already sat on, above
the modal layer, so a right-click menu raised inside a dialog — the Upload dialog's queued files —
renders above the dialog and can be used, instead of painting underneath it.
- The four financial ledgers' details panels become one shell, and a refused control says what it would have done.

Time, Costs, Fees and Billing each carried their own details panel, and the four were the same panel: the same three faces, the same header, the same ruled runs of facts, down to identical class strings. `$lib/details-panel` is the shell they now compose — Root, Header, Title, Subtitle, Close, Body, Section, Facts, Fact — and what stays in each surface is what only that surface knows. `DetailsPanel.Toggle` takes the pane control with it: four ledgers had written that out identically, copied comment included.

The shell keeps two deliberate seams rather than pretending they do not exist. `Fact` takes a snippet where a value is a mark rather than a figure, because the fee panel's standing badge is neither tabular nor right-aligned; and it takes a class where one figure has to carry a warning the column does not, because a bill past its due date is that case.

A refused control was explained in two competing sentences: seventeen call sites naming the act and the permission, and seven more naming only the permission. `permissionRefusal(act, permission)` is the one home. The seven that said only "This account does not hold the billing:credit capability" now also name the act, which is the half a reader can take to whoever administers their account — so those seven tooltips read differently than they did. One more said "capability" where the other twenty-four said "permission", and now says "permission" too.
- **The quality gate now stops at the first failure.** Matrix fail-fast is on and the heavy jobs (WASM,
Rust, containers) wait on the cheap format tripwire, so one red job stops the rest from spending
runner minutes. The dependency audit is deliberately not gated on it. Part of the temporary CI
austerity, marked for the September 1 revert.
- Live mode in the Safe Website Viewer streams the remote browser instead of returning a screenshot per step, on the owner's ruling that live websites should be streaming. `GET /api/v1/safe-browse/live/stream` upgrades to a WebSocket (same-origin only, through the chokepoint on `tools:safeBrowse`) and hands it to the member's `SafeBrowseSession` object, which holds the socket and a CDP connection to their browser: `Page.startScreencast` JPEG frames go out one in flight at a time, paced by the page's acknowledgements, and pointer, wheel, key and pasted-text input comes back through one shared, bounded protocol (`@magna-carta/safe-browse/live-stream-protocol`). The SSRF guard now covers every document the browser requests for the whole session through CDP's Fetch domain, not one navigation at a time. Popups fold into the visible tab, downloads are denied, the file chooser is intercepted, dialogs are dismissed and reported. A second tab opening Live takes the browser over; idle is now three minutes without input. `POST /api/v1/safe-browse/live/navigate` is retired. The cross-origin upgrade check the meetings socket carried moved to `chokepoint/same-origin-upgrade.ts` so both sockets share it.
- **Dropdown menus open on hover.** `DropdownMenu.Root` now owns a hover controller (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/dropdown-menu/hover-open.ts`), shared with Trigger, Content, and SubContent through context: a mouse pointer resting on the Trigger for 120 ms opens the menu, the menu follows the pointer between the three, and it closes 250 ms after the pointer has left them all. A press, a key, or a tap opens the menu exactly as before and a menu opened that way is not hover's to close; a press on a hover-opened trigger keeps the menu rather than toggling it shut; a hover-opened menu leaves focus where it was unless focus has entered the panel; and hover-opening one menu closes another hover had opened, so Money and Record on the matter strip never overlap. On for every menu, `openOnHover={false}` keeps one click-only. Select and Combobox are unchanged: a form control that opened as the pointer crossed a form would fight the reader.
- **The sidebar's Messaging row is calls and texts, and the four things wearing that name are down to
one.** The row had an id meaning the whole three-channel Communications layer (`communications`), a
label meaning one channel (Messaging), and a description meaning two ("Client and portal messages") —
while the matter section wearing the same label described a fourth thing again, the client portal's
`comment`/`message` grant capability. Nothing in the tree agreed, and every future reader of either
registry would have had to guess. The owner settled it on 2026-09-07: **Messaging is voice and
SMS/MMS** — the two channels ADR-0047 already decided and neither of which has a line of code — for
logging what occurs, routed through the carrier so the logging happens by itself, with recording and
transcription over the voice half.

**Email is refused from the row on purpose, and the refusal is argued rather than assumed.** The case
for folding it in is real: captured mail that routes to no matter lands unrouted today —
`apps/api-worker/src/emails/capture-consumer.ts` says so outright — and **no screen anywhere in the
product shows those**, so mail is being captured into a place nobody can look at. It loses anyway,
twice. Email already has a home the platform deliberately does not replace: the whole posture is
_file from the mailbox into the matter_ — the add-in's pane, the forward/CC capture address, the
auto-file rules — so a row that opens a mail list competes with the client the member already has
open. And calls and texts have no other home at all; there is no mailbox for the firm's SMS number,
and a phone call leaves no artifact unless the platform makes one. The verbs are different —
_route what exists_ against _cause a record to exist_ — and one row cannot carry both. The unrouted
mail gap survives as an open question rather than being quietly absorbed.

**The design names the log as the durable thing and the carrier as a producer into it**, which is
what takes the surface off the vendor's critical path. One `communication` record — channel,
direction, counterparty, member, nullable matter, instant, duration, body, attachments in per-firm
R2 — written by three producers in the order they can be built: a member logging a call by hand, the
Telnyx adapter writing the same row from a signed webhook, and transcription enriching a row that has
a recording. A2P 10DLC registration is weeks of procurement lead time by ADR-0047's own account and
gates only the second of those, so the record model and both screens are blocked on nothing.

**The global row and the matter section are split by one sentence: the global row holds the
unassigned and the cross-matter, the section holds the assigned and the case-bound.** An inbound text
from an unrecognised number belongs to no matter, which makes filing a conversation onto a matter an
act that exists only globally; inside a matter the reverse act exists (unlink, as filed mail already
has) but routing from scratch does not. The gate is where they actually diverge: a section inherits
the matter's own access, while the global screen must narrow routed rows to matters the member may
see before anything hydrates — the email add-in's suggestion ranking is the precedent to reuse — and
unrouted rows, having no matter, fall through every matter-based gate and need a permission of their
own rather than "any member may read the firm's inbound traffic."

**Recording is sequenced last for a legal reason, not a technical one.** ADR-0047 gates call-recording
consent on the jurisdiction-profile machinery — roughly a dozen states require all-party consent where
Nevada requires one — and that machinery is still in design. Text logging, manual call logging and
carrier call _metadata_ carry no such gate; the audio does.

**And it is built, not only designed.** One per-firm `communication` row behind
`@magna-carta/communications` and seven operations; the firm-wide `/communications` screen and the
matter's Messaging section over ONE listing component, so the section cannot drift from the log it is
a view of; the section off `soon` with a search source, a timeline source and a create noun, which
answers all three coverage lints rather than deferring them; the destination flipped to `shipped` at
`alpha` in the same commit as the screen, per the registry's own rule. The audit log carries
identifiers, enums and instants and never the words or the number, asserted by a test rather than
trusted. 45 tests.

**Building the gate found a real hole in it.** `readRoutableMatter` selected from an unaliased
`matter`, and the visible-matter predicate composes as `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM matter WHERE matter.id
= <expression> …)` — so the subquery's table shadowed the outer one, the correlation degenerated to
`matter.id = matter.id`, which is true of every row, and the anchor check silently passed **every
matter in the firm**, the platform-owned custody holding matter included. The outer table is now
aliased `anchor`, and the test that caught it is kept beside the one that proves an unrouted row is
unreachable by id without the capability. Anything else composing this predicate over `matter` itself
is exposed the same way.

Five open questions for the owner remain, including where portal secure messaging now lives and where
the unrouted **email** queue does — the one part of the cross-channel argument that survives the
refusal above, and still the one screen the product does not have.
- **The conflicts check, the waiver disposition and the cost record pick people through the one
picker.** `subject-party-picker.svelte` and `cost-payee-picker.svelte` are deleted; the check runner
uses `EntityPicker` in multiple mode, the disposition dialog and the cost record window in single
mode, all over `directoryPickerSearch`. A source scan (`apps/web/test/entity-picker-gate.test.ts`)
refuses any other caller of `searchDirectory` outside `$lib/directory`, naming the one standing copy
— the custodian's `owner-picker.svelte` — with the reason it stands: the custodian-refinements
stream rewrites that file and its dialog, and folds it when it lands. The allowance fails the scan
the day the copy is gone.
- **The file manager's Upload dialog comes first, and nothing is sent until Upload is pressed.** `apps/web/src/lib/file-manager/upload-dialog.svelte` replaces the destination dialog: it opens on Upload, on a drop onto the list and on the empty folder's button, holds the file, files or whole folder chosen in it (the design-system Dropzone gained `onEntries`, which walks a dropped folder through the entry API instead of handing the consumer a zero-byte stub named after it), asks the Upload Location beside them, and starts the transfer only on its commit — "Upload", not "Save". A folder is recreated under the location, level by level, before its files go in. The running commentary is gone with the early transfer: no "each is uploading now" subtitle and no "closing keeps what has already landed" line, which read as something saved behind the reader's back. A file that did not go reads "Upload failed", with the stage and Error ID as before. A download that fails on the Downloads page or in the top-bar tray now states so on its own row with a Retry beside it, instead of a toast that vanished.
- The display vocabulary and the caps label each become one thing, and the registry starts naming the surfaces it had been leaving out.

Money, counts and civil dates were presented from inside the table's typed columns, which is where a column author found them and nowhere a details panel would think to look. They move to `packages/design-system/src/lib/formatters/`, beside the answers for how long, when, who and which version, and the table re-exports them so every existing import still resolves. The move is not a bug fix and the note in `money.ts` says so: the float path only starts disagreeing with an exact minor-unit sum once a single row passes roughly a trillion of the major unit, which was measured rather than assumed. Two of the four answers to "how long" — `hoursFromMinutes` and `decimalHoursText` — turned out to have no callers at all outside one test, and are gone.

The caps field label existed 101 times, hand-written, in two tones that disagreed: the invoice window alone used both. Worse, 77 of those sites reached for an inline `letter-spacing` style to put back the tracking every design-system recipe already carries, which is raw CSS in a codebase that forbids it. `FieldLabel` takes the register the masthead eyebrow and the eyebrow link already agreed on and stops it being retyped; it renders whichever element the caller's document structure needs, because the alternative is the callers that need a `dt` or a heading carrying on by hand.

`Badge` gains `caps` for the same reason. Six badges that label a standing rather than count something — a matter's status seal, the "View" marker on a settings section — were each written as `class="uppercase"` plus an inline letter-spacing style; uppercase without the tracking is wrong, and the tracking is not expressible as a utility, so every one of them reached for raw CSS. One more inline style, on a table header, was restating tracking `.mc-table-head` already sets. The app carried 77 of these; it now carries 2, both in surfaces whose colour varies with state and which are somebody else's stream to touch.

Eight shared surfaces the one-implementation registry had never named — `DataTable`, `Masthead`, `TopBar`, `EmptyState`, `LabelledField`, `FieldRow`, `StatusMark` and the new `FieldLabel` — now have entries. The registry's promise is that no second file claims the name; it had not been making that promise about the components most likely to be forked.
- **One create control, at one width, on every screen — and on a matter it sits beside the search.** Every matter section carried its own create button in its own action row, a different distance down the screen on every tab and a different width on every one of them: "New Fee", "Record a Cost", "Log Time", "Write Note", a bare "New". The owner's ruling on 2026-09-03 moves the affordance up into the matter header beside the search, as ONE control that reflects the section it is on without ever changing size.

`CreateControl` is a design-system component: a primary Button held at a token width (`size.create-control`), reading "New" and one noun, pressing straight through or opening a menu in the same footprint, and rendering disabled with its reason rather than leaving the row. The noun grammar (`create-label.ts`) refuses a phrase or a noun the width cannot hold, so the truncation the recipe carries is theoretical.

On a matter the control is answered from two places. `sections.ts` gains a required `createNoun` — a noun, or `null` with a `createWaitingOn` line — so the label is settled by the address before the section has mounted and never flickers between tabs. The section's page claims the behaviour through `claimMatterCreate` (`create-action.svelte.ts`) while it is mounted: a ledger exports `openNew()` and the page hands it over; Files hands over a three-item menu; Calendar states the refusal it used to draw as two disabled buttons. The slot refuses a second claimant, and a mount test pins the assumption that refusal rests on — a page swap releases the leaving claim before the arriving one lands.

The docket, the directory and the firm's custody register render the same component in their mastheads, and the custody register gains the register search beside it, so the pair reads the same way everywhere. Empty states no longer carry a second create button; each names the control at the top instead.

`pnpm run lint:matter-create-control` is the gate: every section answers, every noun fits, and no `<Button>` or menu trigger wearing the plus glyph — or reading as a create verb — survives on a screen that carries the control.
- **There is one record form for an event, and its first question is who the event belongs to.** `record-firm-event-dialog.svelte` is deleted; `record-event-dialog.svelte` is the only one.

Two forms meant a reader had to know, before opening anything, whether the thing they were about to record was firm business — and had to close one panel and open the other on finding out they had guessed wrong. They asked nearly the same questions in nearly the same order and drifted anyway (owner, 2026-09-16: "firm events and events should be the exact same").

**Two choices and no third** (owner ruling). Matter writes a `matter_event`; Firm writes a `firm_event`. There is no None, because there is no third table for one to land in, and inventing a third word for the same row would put two records on the calendar that nothing could tell apart afterwards. A personal appointment is a firm event with only the one person on it, which is what the `participants` audience already means.

**What the choice reveals is only what genuinely differs.** Matter reveals the matter picker beside it, on the same line — "a matter" and _which_ matter are one answer given in two presses. Firm reveals the audience (everyone at the firm, or the people listed) and the office, which is a real foreign key on a firm event because it is what says which rooms are nearby; and it hides the court reference, which a firm meeting has no court for. An all-members firm event hides the participant list too, because that list is one the record ignores.

The `Record` menu offers two kinds rather than three. A third item would be a second way to open one panel, and the reader would still have to decide before opening anything — which is the thing that was wrong.

This supersedes the 2026-09-14 arrangement, where leaving the matter picker empty was what made the record a firm event. That was the right shape for the data and the wrong shape for the reader: an absence answered a question nobody had been asked.
- The pane system moves out of the record window into a frame both modal shells sit on.

The record window's frame — the header band and its quiet controls, the body, the primary pane that stops at its measure beside a context pane that takes the rest, the action bar of fixed geometry, and the fit-first/cap-second rule they all obey — is now `styles/recipes/modal-frame.css`, an internal recipe rather than a component. The record window keeps every class name as a hook and every pixel as it was: its four frame-bearing stories were screenshotted from the static catalog before and after, and all four are byte-identical.

Extracted because the alternative was measured. The largest panel in the app had rebuilt every one of these rules from utilities in 647 lines, quoting the record window's own doctrine in its comments, because there was nothing to reach for. A pane system that lives in one shell is a pane system every other panel rebuilds.

`ActionDialog` moves onto the same frame and gains a `context` pane — the record window's right pane, lent to a form. A context pane implies the record width whatever `width` asked for; a primary pane with no context beside it fills the frame. The notice band now sits outside the scroll, directly above the action bar, where the reader is looking when a commit comes back refused. Focus lands on the first field rather than the header's own dismiss.
- The four financial ledgers — Time, Fees, Costs and Billing — now hold their chrome in common, and an empty table centres in what the reader can see.

**They take the screen and keep it.** Each ledger capped its table at the viewport height and then grew past it, so the counts footer walked off the bottom as entries arrived. They now sit in one `FullHeightSection`, the frame the file manager already used: the table scrolls inside itself, the footer stays on the bottom edge, and a page never reflows because a row landed. The panes below it are one `LedgerPanes` component rather than four copies of the same geometry — a difference between two of these tables was already a defect by the one-table ruling, and the frame around the table is the same argument one level out.

**The empty state stops running off the right.** A placeholder row spans every column, so its cell is as wide as the TABLE — wider than the frame whenever the columns are, and far wider once anybody has widened one. Centred in that cell, the empty state's watermark and heading landed off past the inline end with the sentence trailing after them: measured in a 660-pixel frame, the heading sat entirely past its right edge, centred at 691 where the frame ended at 680. The grid now measures its own visible width and the placeholder's content sits in a block stuck to the frame's leading edge and sized to it, so the state centres in the visible width and holds its place when the table is scrolled sideways. Two rules had to be beaten for that to land, and both were found by measurement rather than by eye: the cell's own inline padding, and the transparent border every row's first cell reserves for the selection rail — two pixels of silent offset on a row that is not a row and is never selected.

**One pane toggle, the file manager's.** All four wore a bordered secondary button; they now wear the same quiet chrome affordance the file manager does, last in the row on every ledger. The divider between the panes loses its centred grip handle — resizing is unchanged, and the whole edge always dragged.

**The Time tab drops its Time Sheet button.** The sheet opens from the top bar on every screen including this one, so a second door here took a reader somewhere they were already standing. Its handle in the top bar also loses the border that made it read as a different kind of control from the download tray and the bell beside it.

**The Fees toolbar is one row.** View, Amend, New Fee and the pane toggle sat across two lines with the arrangement's facts; they are now one row, and the second line is back.
- The version panel's three carets are one component, and a shut heading says what it hides.

The three sections each computed their own collapsed badge, and the differences had stopped being decisions. Deployment carried a count of Workers without a version and dropped the sync read entirely — so folding it hid whether the two Workers serving the app agree, which is the one fact a reader opens that section for. Workers carried the same warning with no sense of how many Workers were behind the fold. Database carried a mood, "Needs attention" or "Not working", with no count at all, so one bad row out of four and four bad rows read identically. And all three said nothing whatever when healthy, which looks exactly like a section that never loaded.

The heading is now one component every fold renders through, and all three hand it the same shape from the model: a **count** of what the fold hides, always, then a **status** pill only where there is something to say beyond the count. A count present when things are fine is what makes a quiet heading meaningful — "13 Workers" with nothing beside it is a section reporting health, where an empty heading was a section reporting nothing.

The wording changed with it. "Without a version" named the missing field rather than the condition, and reads now as "2 not reporting" — a reader wants to know the Worker did not answer, not which column is blank. The database mood becomes "1 not working" or "2 needs attention" against a "4 checks" count. Deployment's shut heading carries the sync read it used to lose: "3 parts · In sync".

`collapsedHealthBadge` and `summarizeSilentWorkers` are gone, superseded by the pill builders, along with the dead worst-reading derived they fed.
- **Every failure in `apps/web` renders from one record through one component family.** The client
kept four of the twelve fields an RFC 9457 problem carries; it now reads all of them, and
`requestAccess` / `stepUpRequired` — emitted at six places in the API worker and previously read at
none — become the control the member presses instead of another apology. Four private copies of the
problem parser collapse into `lib/api/problem.ts`; `PagedList` holds the failure rather than a
string, which is what made nine surfaces structurally unable to show an Error ID; and
`failure-state` / `failure-band` / `failure-details` in the design system are extracted from the
costs and billing pair rather than invented. The copy path assembles the whole trace once
(`lib/diagnostics/failure-trace.ts`), states absent facts rather than dropping them, and falls back
to a selection copy where the async clipboard is refused. `lint:failure-surface` is the fitness
function that keeps it.
- **The navigation column's row is one design-system part, and the catalogue column has its own home.** `NavigationLayout` gained a `Row` export (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/navigation-layout/navigation-layout-row.svelte`, recipe `mc-navigation-layout-row`): the control-height rounded row, the quiet hover tint, and the lit row's selected fill with the gilt start-edge bar drawn as an inset box-shadow. Three places had written that treatment out by hand — the settings layout, the catalogue column Tools and Reports share, and the inline `style` strings in both — with the file manager's folder tree already foreseen as the fourth. All three now compose the part, and `apps/web/test/{settings,tools,reports}-navigation.test.ts` each fail if a row grows a class list or an inline style of its own again.

Two judgments moved into the part. The element follows from `href` and nothing else: a string is an anchor, omitting it is a button, and `null` is an entry designed with nowhere to go yet, which stands unlinked and quiet with its Soon mark rather than dressed as a disabled control — the same spelling `CatalogueEntry.href` already used. And a name wraps rather than truncating: the control height is a `min-block-size` and the recipe carries no `white-space` or `text-overflow`, because a row reading "Property Listin… Soon" has stopped naming the thing, which is a navigation row's one job. The layout still imposes no structure on what the navigation holds; taking the row is a choice.

`catalogue-navigation.{svelte,ts}` moved from `apps/web/src/lib/tools/` to `apps/web/src/lib/catalogue/`. It serves Tools and Reports equally, so Reports had been importing a column out of the Tools directory; the catalogue framework's third view now sits beside its list and tiles views, and `apps/web/src/lib/catalogue/CLAUDE.md` says so.
- **Recording a call and reading one are the same window, because there is no reason for two.** A call
was recorded in an action dialog and read in a record window. Both rendered the same fields through
the same component, and both disagreed about everything around those fields: one had tabs and the
other did not, one printed and the other did not, one called its commit Save under a heading and the
other under an action bar. Two surfaces for one record is two things for a reader to learn and two
places for the next field to be added to only one of. There is one now, and the only difference
between its states is whether it opened with a record in it — a new one opens straight into the
fields, asks where it belongs, and carries the number it is about to be given.

**A call's length is typed, and it is allowed to disagree with the clock.** The round before this one
worked the duration out from a start and an end, which is right until somebody is put on hold: an
hour on the line and twenty minutes of call are two true facts about one call, and computing either
from the other asserts they are the same number. `communication.ended_at` is now stored beside
`duration_seconds`; the length is typed and reads `20`, `45m`, `1h 5m` or `1:20`; and an end fills an
EMPTY length and never overwrites one somebody wrote. Where the two differ, the form and the record
say both, so the gap reads as the hold it is.

**Every call and text carries a number a person can say out loud, and it exists before the record
does.** `2026-09-08-0042` — the day it happened, and that day's own sequence. A handle is what the
platform joins on; it is not something a receptionist can write on a message slip or read back down a
telephone, and a call is quoted out loud more often than any other record a firm keeps, because the
person on the other end of it is still on the line. So the window shows the number the next record
for that day WOULD draw, before anything is saved, and says that it is a preview rather than a
reservation; the record's own number replaces it the moment there is a record. The migration that
adds the column numbers every row already on the table, so the log has no rows without one.

The sequence is the shared counter idiom (`@magna-carta/sequence-numbering`) with one departure worth
naming: it has **no allocation table**. The general warning that a unique index on a rendered number
cannot stand in for one is about schemes carrying a segment that varies within a counter scope, and
this scheme carries none — the day IS the scope key — so two draws that observed the same value in
one day render byte-identical strings and the partial unique index aborts the loser exactly as an
allocation primary key would.

**The description is the row's second line rather than a column.** It is prose, and usually longer
than every other fact on the row put together, so as a column it was either truncated to a few words
— which is not a description — or wide enough to push the facts off the screen. It has the row's full
width underneath the facts now, through the one table's own row-detail, which is the same mechanism
the time sheet's description already sat in.

**Digits past the end of a phone number are an extension, not a formatting failure.** `AsYouType`
stops formatting silently once the digits exceed what a country's numbers hold, so typing a direct
dial onto the end of a number turned `(312) 555-0148` into a run of fourteen digits under the cursor.
The overflow now rolls into an extension the shared phone field owns, and the split is the longest
prefix libphonenumber calls possible rather than the country's digit count — so a North American
number typed with its trunk 1 is not cut a digit short. The two halves store as one string,
`+13125550148x4102`, which the formatter reads back into both. The Directory's contact rows had built
their own extension input beside the shared field; they use the field's own now, which is the last
half of that pair that was still built twice.

**And an intake starts from the form, not only from a record.** Save And Start An Intake records the
call first and hands the saved row up — an intake with no account of the call that caused it is what
the control exists to prevent. The provenance tab is a History rail, in the shape every other record
window uses.
- **Enter commits in every `ActionDialog`.** The primary pane is a `<form>` and the commit in the bar is its submit button by `form` attribute, so the platform's implicit submission does the work and a disabled commit stops it; Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter commits from a textarea via the form's keydown listener. No caller changed.
- **Production stack frames name the source file, line and function.** The web build now emits source maps without the source text (`sourcemapExcludeSources`) and stops renaming identifiers (`mangle: false`, compression and whitespace removal kept), on both the page build and the Web Worker build in `apps/web/vite.config.ts`. The sign-in crash was diagnosed from `De.get (naXSyiPE.js:5:816)`, which says nothing; the minifier's map does not record the original of a renamed identifier, so a map alone left the `De`. `magna-carta-web` is an assets-only Worker, so the `.map` files are public assets: carrying mappings and paths but no text, a fetched map gives away no code and no comment. Measured cost on the day's build: 897 KB to 1.12 MB gzipped over the whole app, a fraction of that per chunk.
- **The messaging form's second review round: two columns, every closed choice a combobox, one phone field shared with the Directory, and a start and end time the duration is worked out from.**

`communication-fields.svelte` is laid out as the measurable beside the written — type, direction, contact, number, the three time fields and where it belongs on the left; the description on the right, where the transcript and the recording tabs will go once the carrier is connected. The split is a container query on the fields themselves, so the record window's narrower pane stacks them without a second layout. Switching between Call and Text moves nothing: a text's end and duration stand refused rather than disappearing.

`$lib/components/choice-picker.svelte` is the one field for a closed set — a Combobox over `ChoiceOption`s with per-option search words, so a country answers to "44", "+44", "GB" and "United Kingdom" alike. Type, direction and the country are on it. `$lib/directory/phone-number-field.svelte` is the country and the digits as ONE field, used by the call log and by the Directory's contact rows, which had each built the pair by hand.

`formatPhoneAfterEdit` fixes the defect that made a number unshortenable: backspace over a grouping character deleted a character `AsYouType` put straight back, so the key did nothing. A deletion that removes no digit now removes the last digit instead. `phoneNumberPlaceholder` derives a country's grouping from libphonenumber's own example number (4 KB of `examples.mobile.json`), which is the one placeholder in the product that is not its field's name.

Country flags are vendored SVGs under `apps/web/static/flags` (country-flag-icons, MIT) served as static assets, never the flag characters: those are emoji (golden rule 2) and Windows has no font for them. A test asserts a file exists for every country the picker offers.

The duration is derived rather than typed. `LogDraft` still stores `durationMinutes` — the record stores a length, and keeping it as the draft's own field is what makes a correction round-trip without recomputing through a clock — and `draftEndTime` / `durationFromEnd` are the bridge to the two clock fields. An end before the start is a call that ran past midnight.

`MatterPicker` gains `extraChoices` / `extraHeading` / `extraValue`, so "Belongs to" is one searchable field carrying every answer the question has: a matter, a reason there is no matter, or the queue. `EntityPicker` gains `createBeside={false}` and `Textarea` gains `resizable={false}`; both default to what every other surface already does.
- **Registration asked a stranger to classify themselves before anything about them existed.** The
front door opened on a three-way fork — a client of a law firm, somebody who works at one, somebody
founding one — and two of those three led to the same place, because membership of an existing firm
is that firm's decision and never a visitor's. Only the third created anything. So the first question
the platform ever asked was a question about a **relationship**, put to somebody who was not yet a
party to one, on the one screen whose whole job is to establish who they are.

**Joining is now two acts in the order they actually happen.** `/register` makes a person — a name,
an address, the two acknowledgements, one confirmation email, and no fork. Confirming that email
creates the account and sends the link that sets its password. Signing in lands on `/welcome`, a
dedicated in-app screen that settles what the account IS: start a law firm, or redeem an invitation
into one that already exists.

**The account that belongs to no firm is now a real state rather than an unrepresentable one.**
`user.firm_id` was `NOT NULL`, so a signed-in person with no firm could not exist; it is now nullable,
by a reviewed control-plane table rebuild (the tag is in `REVIEWED_REBUILDS`, and the migration's own
`-- contract:` header audits the copy). That nullability is what makes the state fail **closed**:
`RouteMeta` gains `firmlessSession`, defaulting to `reject`, so a session carrying no firm gets the
same reserved 404 a cross-firm request gets on every one of the platform's routes except three. The
bootstrap (`GET /api/v1/me`) declares `allow` and answers a null firm plus what to do next; the two
onboarding mutations declare `only`, which makes them unreachable for anybody who already has a firm
— and that is what lets them carry `permission: null` honestly, since a principal with no firm holds
no capability in any firm to name.

**`disableSignUp` does not change, and this is the part worth being precise about.** Better Auth's
signup route stays refused; the account is created by our own confirmation handler, exactly as
invitation redemption already creates one. The reflow is a **restructuring of the existing
registration and confirmation machinery**, not a new public signup endpoint: same route, same
chokepoint, same tightest rate-limit bucket, same dormant Turnstile gate, same identical answer for a
taken address and a free one. What moves is only what a confirmed token buys — and it moves in the
safe direction. It used to buy a firm, an R2 bucket, a minted key and a second email; it now buys one
`user` row and one email. Firm provisioning moved **behind** an authenticated act by a proven mailbox.

**Invitations keep working in both orders, and the possession proof survives both.** Somebody who
arrives with a code and no account still redeems it anonymously at `/register/invitation`, unchanged.
Somebody who makes an account first redeems into it — and the invitation must name that account's own
address. That rule is not tidiness: in the anonymous flow the proof that the redeemer holds the
invited mailbox is that the password link is sent to it, and no mail is sent on the signed-in path, so
without the check anybody holding a code, a surname and a date of birth could attach **their own**
account to somebody else's firm. A code in a link is carried across the flow per-tab so nobody has to
hold it in their head; only the code, never the two facts that make it worth anything.

**The one refusal is now literally one.** Both redemption routes resolve the three facts through
`invitation-redemption.ts`: one lookup, one unmatchable-digest comparison, one balancing write, one
sentence, both budgets. A mismatched address answers byte-for-byte what an unknown code answers, which
`apps/api-worker/test/account-first-joining.test.ts` asserts by comparing the whole observable body
including the attempt budget.

**A firm's own name was being shown as its internal handle.** A self-serve firm's `firm.name` is the
registration's handle — deliberately, because firm names are not unique in the world and a unique
column over them would let a stranger probe for any firm by trying to register its name — while the
readable name lives in `display_name`. The chokepoint resolved `name`, so the bootstrap reported
`registration_an4N2sZ…` as the firm. Found by the founding test landing in the app one step earlier
than the old flow ever did.
- **`ROADMAP.md` stops restating per-capability status and goes back to being the answer to "what is being worked on".** It had accreted into running build commentary — a single Next bullet could carry the design date, the plan link, the ADR numbers, what was built, what was deferred, the seams, and a mid-sentence status correction — and it had duplicated: the integration port system appeared twice, once ending "the framework is built and on `main`" and once ending "Build pending", with nothing flagging the contradiction. The tree settles it: `packages/integrations` exists, the ledger holds `integrations.port-framework` at `shipped`, and the false bullet is deleted. The property external-links resolver was duplicated verbatim, and both the OneDrive move and the continuous-deploy cutover sat in a "deferred, do when convenient" list marked DONE while also appearing under _Recently shipped_ — all now single entries in one place.

**The register is what made this possible.** [`docs/now.md`](docs/now.md) is generated from the feature ledger and gated against it, so it carries every capability at its real status and cannot drift. The roadmap no longer competes with it: what is per-capability status is linked, and the file keeps only what the ledger structurally cannot hold — which stream is live, what it does next, what order the rest comes in, and the cross-slice gates. Roughly 57% of the file's words are gone (17,400 to 7,600) with no stream dropped; what left was build history that already has a home in `docs/specs/`, the Decision Log, `CHANGELOG.md` and `STATUS.md`.

**Gates were kept as gates.** A real cross-slice prerequisite — deploy `magna-carta-sign` before the app worker because the `SIGN_SERVICE` binding blocks it, the attorney review that blocks any compliance surface over the Nevada profile, the CASA/Microsoft verification that blocks the first credentialed adapter, Costs before Billing — stays in the italic idiom the file already used, because those are ordering facts rather than commentary.

**Corrections made against the sources rather than from memory.** Phase 5 and Phase 6 slice numbering was contradicting `STATUS.md` (the roadmap still listed 5·2 as search and 6·2 as tasks; the status fragments have 5·2 as Discovery review and 6·2 as calendar firm events). Slice 2·7 (exhibits) and slice 4·3 (matter assets) were tracked in `status.d/` and absent from the roadmap entirely. Financial reporting's first sub-slice and the register's own history reconstruction had shipped without appearing. Two hardening items — malware scanning and async bulk-download jobs — were still written as deferred after shipping with slice 2·1, and now record only the options genuinely left behind the port.
- **Price the discovery semantic half against the keyword half's measured read profile, and name the
experiment that decides flag D4.** Cloudflare's queried-vector-dimension metric counts a Vectorize
index's resident corpus once per month at twenty times the storage rate, so a queried index costs about
twenty-one times what pricing its storage alone suggests — the earlier sizing recorded only the storage
line. For a 250,000-document review set that is roughly $53.81 per month against the keyword half's
derived eleven cents, plus a one-time embedding charge of roughly $261 to $522 at the platform-pinned
model's published rate. Convergence stays unmeasured, and the blocker is not the deployed-only Vectorize
binding — the binding is substitutable, while no corpus in the repository carries the relevance
judgements a recall claim has to be scored against. Analysis in
`docs/research/2026-08-14-semantic-half-convergence-and-cost.md`, with every figure labelled measured,
vendor-quoted, or derived; the recommendation to defer on a named trigger is a Proposed decision
fragment awaiting the owner. The operating-cost register gains the Vectorize and embedding lines.
- **One bounded-retry loop draws every sequential number.** `drawWithBoundedRetry` could only give up
as a bare `Error`, and it rethrew immediately whenever an attempt failed without having observed a
draw — so `@magna-carta/matters` and `@magna-carta/custodian` both kept private copies of it and only
the statement builders were actually shared. Two widenings close that. `nonConvergenceError` is now a
required option: the loop composes the "did not converge after N attempts" wording once and hands it
to the caller, which returns the error to throw — custodian a named `CustodyValidationError` its
route maps to a problem type, matters a plain `Error`. A mapper rather than a result type, because
every caller's translation is the same throw and a result type would have pushed that wording back
out into each consumer, and required rather than defaulted so a new sequence has to decide what its
route surfaces. And retryable-ness is now independent of observed-ness: a declared collision that
consumed no counter value is retried without advancing anything, which is the case custodian needs
when a concurrent first use of the shared custody holding matter loses on `matter.system_key` before
the counter is ever read.

Both consumers now run on the shared loop and their copies are gone. Behaviour is unchanged for both:
the give-up messages are composed from the same parts and stay byte-identical, the retryable sets are
the same predicates, and the out-of-band advance uses the same observed value and start value. The
one difference is unreachable and in the safer direction — custodian's private loop inferred "a draw
happened" from `scopeKey !== "" || observed !== 0`, which silently stopped advancing the counter on a
firm-wide scheme whose start value was zero; the explicit signal has no such blind spot.
- **The settings surface consolidates: one page shape, one choice field, one table, one version report.** The owner's first Settings round (`docs/conventions/settings-rulings.md`, R1). The hand-rolled scroll region twenty pages carried by copy is one component (`settings-scroll-region.svelte`); the standard page (`settings-page.svelte`) is rewritten around the server-backed draft every firm page actually holds, and Billing, Calendar, Reports and File Safety render it; a plate's closing line is a component of its own. `SettingsRow`'s `select` kind renders the product's combobox, and every hand-placed `Select` under Settings (the notification matrices, the catalog dialogs, Matter Plans, Intake Procedures, the numbering editor, the Text page's Soon seams) is that same field, with sentinel values where "none" was an empty string. The five settings tables are `DataTable.Grid` over column models in `catalog-columns.ts`, so they sort, filter from their headers, offer their column roster and count themselves. The version chip's popover body is `version-report.svelte`, rendered by the chip and by the Versions page alike; the page's histogram workaround is gone. The Beta Access switch is bound to the session's channel through a getter/setter so a cancelled consent leaves it off, and its plate reads "Beta Branch". The scan depth options read "Core", "Extended", "Full", with the engine's reading and the chosen depth's meaning beneath them on File Safety. The matter numbering editor is a table of parts inside the settings anatomy, arrows leading the row.
- Seven more panels open in `ActionDialog`, and the shell gained the outcome one of them needed.

The file manager's three (delete a folder, restore a file, the upload destination), the note and party removals, the settings recap before a save, and the attachment detach inside `RecordAttachments` — the last a design-system component that composed its own `AlertDialog` while registered. The file-manager panels stop taking a `running` flag from their host: the host returns the outcome and the shell owns the busy state; their host-worded failures render in the notice slot. The upload panel's report column becomes the context pane beside its decision, and its bar hint moves into the body.

`ActionOutcome` gained `"done"`: the panel stays open with nothing left to ask — the commit leaves the bar, the dismissal reads Close, the guard stands down — and `fields`/`context` are handed `done`. The upload panel saves its destination and stays to show the batch landing; the two send panels still to migrate will use it the same way. Seven allowances leave `tooling/lint-one-ui/registry.json`; nineteen remain, eleven of them named exclusions.
- Ten more panels — eight in billing, two in costs — open in `ActionDialog`.

Write off a balance, issue a credit note, draft a bill, finalize one, edit a line, record a delivery, void a draft, amend an agreement, kick back a cost, void a cost. Each lost its own open flag, its own busy flag, its own hand-built footer and its own `$effect` that reset the fields; each gained the guard that asks before Escape throws away a half-written correction.

Two of the twelve turned out not to belong here, and naming them is the point. `arrangement-dialog` reads a record — the fee arrangement in force, its terms and its version history — and its one act opens a different panel; that is `RecordWindow`'s shape, not this one's. `apply-trust-funds-dialog` is an act whose commit is not served yet: its control is wrapped in `SoonAffordance`, the product's own primitive for a designed-but-unbuilt capability, and it becomes a plain `ActionDialog` the day a route hands out a trust account. Both keep an allowance, but the allowance now names which shell they belong to and when rather than recording them as debt.

The commit's icon is gone from the eight that carried one. `RecordWindow`'s commit has always been text, and a glyph beside "Write Off" under a heading that already reads "Write Off a Balance" was decoration the two shells disagreed about. Where a footer carried an explanatory line — what opening a draft actually does, which permission finalizing needs — it moved into the body: the action bar is the shell's, and a sentence is content rather than a control.
- **The header's Build Information panel now says what it knows in one grammar, files what it is
showing, links what it names, and reports what a probe cost.** Its paste, the issue reporter's trace
and the panel's four sections were each built by hand; they are now one report model, one section
component and one registry apiece.

**One grammar for every diagnosis in the app.** `$lib/diagnostics/diagnostic-report.ts` owns the
shape — a row is `key: value`, a group indents under its heading — and both the issue reporter's
trace and the panel's paste render through it. They had invented their own formats independently
(`key: value` against `Label: commit · committed …`), so a reader who received both parsed two
documents; and each carried what the other lacked, the trace all the browser facts and none of the
fleet, the paste the reverse. The trace's output is byte-for-byte what it was — its own test pins
every line — and it now shares its environment block with the panel.

**A failed read is in the paste, which is the case the copy control exists for.** The panel's copy
was a single function inside the deployment model, which could not import the database or the
readiness models without a cycle, so both reached it as one pre-joined opaque string — and a section
whose value was `null` vanished silently. Somebody looking at "The version read failed · Error ID
error\_…" copied a report that never mentioned it. The assembly is now a list of contributors over one
state object (`$lib/versions/panel-report.ts`): each owns a section, states its own failure with its
Error ID, and returns null when it has nothing. A fifth section appends one function instead of
gaining a sixth parameter.

**A refused clipboard says so.** The three copy paths each called `navigator.clipboard.writeText`
inside a `catch { return }`, so on an insecure origin or under a managed-browser policy the control
did nothing at all and said nothing at all — and the fallback that works in exactly those cases
already existed in the design system. All three now go through `copyText`, which falls back to the
selection route and reports which happened; a copy that did not happen puts a line on the panel.
