The applied-ledger in every database records the tag, not the SQL behind it, so an edit to a deployed migration is never seen by the databases that already ran it, and a rename leaves them holding a tag the runner cannot recognise — which blocks every later migration for the life of that database. Neither is fixed by deploying again. The check measures from where the branch left `main`, not from `main`'s tip, so a migration that landed while the branch was open is not mistaken for one the branch deleted. Deliberate exceptions are recorded with the reason no database could have applied them; a baseline collapse is not one, because `LEGACY_BASELINES` reconciles those at runtime and the gate reads that list rather than asking for the same fact twice.
- **The firm's Time, Fees, Costs and Billing screens lose their header controls, and their column filters reach the server.** Each carried a period dropdown (worded three different ways), a billing or status dropdown, and a meta line beneath the title that no other main screen has (`docs/conventions/time-tab-rulings.md`, round twelve). The screens now open on their whole record and the table is the only thing that narrows them; the Date, Status, Billable and Timekeeper filters are sent to the listings as `from`/`to`, `status`, `billable` and `timekeeperUserId` (`apps/web/src/lib/money/listing-scope.ts`), so a filter holds across every page rather than over the page in hand, and the same choices ride the address. The three listings take either date bound alone or neither — nothing named is the whole record over the date index, where they used to answer empty — every one of the four takes a status LIST given repeatedly (`status=draft&status=submitted`), and every one gains a `search` (`packages/timekeeping` and `packages/billing` took the predicate for time and invoices), so all four screens carry the live `ScreenSearch` and a multi-state Status filter reaches the server whole. Billing gains "+ Bill": the draft dialog the matter register already uses grew a matter-first shape, resolves the client from the party record (`client-party.ts`), and goes to the matter's Billing section with the draft open. The messaging screen's four scope tabs are gone for the same reason; the Matter column's filter reaches the server as the listing's scope, and the count waiting to be filed stands in the counts strip.
- **The five money sections render inside one surface, `MoneySurface` (`apps/web/src/lib/money/`), wearing the file manager's frame.** Time, Fees, Costs, Billing and Trust each hand the surface their grid, cells, figures, acts and details panel; the surface draws the toolbar flush under the section strip (a coins glyph, the five sub-parts as quiet links with the current one marked, Clear Filters while a filter is on, a ledger's own acts, the density and layout switches), the notices band, the list, an optional line above the footer (where Time and Costs now keep Load more), and the counts strip with the pane toggle last. Two reader preferences are shared by every money section under one key each: the layout (`flush`, the default, or `framed`, the previous rounded-card look) and the row density. Four copies of the frame, the Clear Filters control and the pane toggle became one.

**Trust takes its first surface.** `apps/web/src/lib/trust/` holds the client (`readMatterTrustLedger` over the matter ledger read), the column set, the figures (Balance, Held, Available), the gap register and the ledger, built whole against the trust movement record. The one dependency is named where the fee ledger names its own: the matter ledger is read against a trust account, and no route lists the firm's trust accounts yet, so the list stands empty with the Soon line and the header's New Deposit is disabled with that reason. The trust activity contribution moved out of `awaiting/` and beside the surface it belongs to.

**An empty table no longer lights up under the pointer.** The shared grid's row hover and pointer cursor (`packages/design-system/src/lib/components/data-table/data-table.css`) now exclude the placeholder row, which the standing ruling on placeholder rows already required and which the flush layout made visible: with the grid's own frame gone, a tinted placeholder read as a band of a different surface.
- **Opening a document in the editor names each stage as it happens, and a stall names the stage it stopped at.**

Opening a document is a chain: the editing session is opened, the editor's container starts, the editor page loads, the editor asks the host about the document, fetches its contents, and shows it. The screen showed one sentence for up to ninety seconds and then a failure that could not say which link had broken — and every failure this path has had was in a different link. The wait is now a staged list that advances as each stage completes, with the time elapsed beside it.

The two stages the screen cannot see from the browser — the editor asking the host about the document, and fetching its contents — are the ones that failed most, because they happen inside the container. The host now records each of the editor's calls against the member's open (which call, what it was answered, and the Error ID where it was refused), and the screen reads that record while it waits. So a stall says "the editor came up but never asked the host about the document", or "the host refused the editor's request for the document's contents (answered 404)" with the Error ID, and the failure details list every stage with when it was reached, as one block a member can copy into a report.
- **The opening panel's stages are renamed, stamped with their own durations, and its details are the open's log rather than a second copy of the stages.** `DocumentEditorContainer` now records its phases (`requested`, `started`, `listening`, `served`, `stopped`, `error`) in its object's storage through a `fetch` override and the library's lifecycle hooks (`apps/edit-worker/src/container-phases.ts`), served at `/magna-carta/status` on the document's origin; the session object keeps every callback of an open, not only the last; and `GET …/edit-session/progress` carries both (`callbacks`, `container`), the container's record read over `EDIT_SERVICE` under a 1.5 s budget and null when the worker is unbound. `openFeed` stamps each line with its stage's own duration; `openLog` merges the three sides by instant into the rows the details show. The platform gives no sight of coolwsd's own output, so the boot shows as the gap between `started` and `listening`.
- **The document-opening panel streams the open instead of ticking boxes.** `openFeed` in `apps/web/src/lib/documents/editor-open-progress.ts` turns the stage marks into lines as they happen (a finished stage is one past-tense line with its second; the stage under way says what it is doing and why it takes the time); `openPace` fills a `Progress` bar over `TYPICAL_OPEN_MILLISECONDS` (30 s, the owner's own opens) with the usual time said beside it, never a fraction of the stages; Retry now waits for `RETRY_AFTER_MILLISECONDS` (45 s) rather than the loading region's 15 s; the full ProgressSteps sequence and the failure rows sit behind a Show details control, shown unasked once the open has stopped. The "N seconds so far" line is gone. The editor container moves from `standard-1` to `standard-2` (one vCPU, 6 GiB) on the owner's ruling after the editor's hardware warning; `docs/operating-costs.md` carries the new figure.
- **The owner's round of 2026-09-17, in five parts.** The favourite star in every screen header no longer announces itself pressed (`favorite-control.svelte`): the ghost button recipe rings a pressed control with an accent hairline, which drew a box around a glyph that already carries the state by filling. The settings column folds by band and by group through a new `NavigationLayout.Group` part (`packages/design-system/.../navigation-layout/`), remembered per browser as departures from everything-open (`settings-navigation-folds.svelte.ts`), never folding away the page the reader is on; `NavigationLayout` caps its height against the canvas it sits in instead of guessing from the viewport, and the conflicts settings page is on `SettingsScrollRegion` like the other twenty-three. The Directory searches its own table: `GET /api/v1/directory/entities` takes `search`, answers with listing rows in the firm's relevance order and says when the answer is capped, and matching matters ride the same grid as rows of kind Matter while a query is live; the separate hit table is gone. A fourth rule in `lint:workspace-search`, `second-results-surface`, refuses a Workspace screen that draws one table under the query and another under the else. The calendar fits a laptop: one scroll region under the action row (the agenda is its own), the month sized by a cell minimum that fills its column, and a toolbar that fits one line by measure rather than wrapping — the controls stay over the grid, as the owner ruled in the same breath as naming the escape.
The next morning's corrections ride the same branch: `ScreenSearch` no longer takes a placeholder, so every screen's search field reads the one word "Search" (twenty-three per-screen hints struck). The office editor launch form now carries `ui_defaults=UIMode=tabbed`, so Collabora opens in its tabbed interface with the font and paragraph controls on the Home tab instead of behind the Format menu. The top bar holds one open panel at a time: `TopBar.Root` declares an overlay band (`packages/design-system/src/lib/internal/overlay-band.svelte.ts`) that every popover, menu and dialog seated in it joins, because a hover label counts as a dismissible layer in Bits UI and could keep a neighbour's panel from closing; the account menu is click-only and shows the member's name and firm from the cached session bootstrap. In the file manager, folders form their own run above the files in every view under every column sort (`orderFolderRowsFirst` on the grid's `orderRows` seam; ledger row L59).
- **The build register's web page is rendered from the feature ledger instead of hand-authored.** The
register has always had two readers: `docs/now.md` for anyone in the repository, and a self-contained
page for the owner, who reads it as a page rather than as a file. Only the first was generated. The
page was 350 KB of hand-written HTML carrying the same facts, so every merge that flipped a ledger
node left it wrong, refreshing it meant a person re-authoring it, and in practice it ran several
merges behind — one source of truth with one generated rendering and one copy of it.

`tooling/doc-fragments/register-artifact.mjs` now emits that page from the same `areas` structure the
Markdown renderer takes — a pure function, no filesystem, no clock — and `vp run register-build`
writes `docs/now.html` beside `docs/now.md` in the same run, the way `status-build` writes
`STATUS.md` and `STATUS.json`. One command refreshes both, deliberately: two renderings refreshed by
two commands are two renderings that disagree the first time somebody runs one of them.

`pnpm run lint:roadmap` now re-derives and diff-gates the page exactly as it does the document, so
the published page cannot silently fall behind the ledger either. The counts are not recomputed for
it: `roadmap.mjs` exports `countByStatus`, `share`, `STATUSES_WITH_NOTHING_BUILT` and
`AWAITING_BOUNDARY`, and both renderings use those. A percentage that differs between two views of
one ledger is a defect neither view can be blamed for, and the page had already drifted to its own
wording of the owner-list boundary — including an assertion that the Actions budget is exhausted,
which is a live operational state `docs/deploy-queue.md` owns and no ledger change could ever make
false again.

Three things the hand-authored page got away with do not survive being generated, because a wart in
one file is a wart and the same wart in a generator is a policy. Where `partial` ranks by size is
derived rather than typed, so the sentence cannot go on asserting "the second largest" after
something overtakes it — and it says "joint" instead of picking a winner when two statuses are level.
Inline code spans in `scope` and `notes` render as `<code>` instead of printing their own backticks.
And the boundary paragraph comes from the shared constant. The renderer handles exactly the two
Markdown constructs the ledger and that constant actually use, code spans and one link, and
deliberately no more: an unused branch is an untested branch, and anything else renders as its own
source characters, which reads as a bug rather than swallowing content silently.

The design of the page is otherwise unchanged from the hand-authored one it replaces, down to the
token names and the two dark-theme definitions.
- The control that shows and hides a side pane now ends the counts strip, on every surface that has one.

It used to sit above the table. On Time, Fees, Costs and Billing that meant a row whose only occupant, most of the time, was one glyph — 41 points taken off a table already fighting for them, spent on something that is not an act on the records at all. Those rows now render only when something has to be in them: the way out of a filter, and Costs' Review where the firm runs review. An unfiltered ledger draws no row and its table starts at the top of the screen.

The strip is not free either, and does not need to be: it grows from 32 points to 41 to seat the control. Against the row's 41, that is a net 32 points back to the table and one less band between the reader and the records.

The file manager's two toggles came down as well, though it never had the complaint — theirs ended a toolbar the screen draws anyway. They moved because the answer has to be in one place: a reader should not have to remember that it is at the top of one screen and the bottom of four others. The folder tree keeps its toggle for now.

The five details-panel toggles render through `DetailsPanel.Toggle`, which is what stops four ledgers drawing it four different ways. The folder tree's stays written out in the file manager's footer: one surface has a folder tree, and a component shared by a single caller is indirection rather than reuse. Every glyph control in that footer stepped down to the small square with them, so one band wears one chrome and the strip is four points shorter than it was.
- `docs/specs/2026-08-25-pdf-active-content-analysis.md` — the PDF scrub removes metadata, attachments, XFA and prior field values, and removes none of `/Names/JavaScript`, `/OpenAction` or `/AA`. Verified against `main`; `generate.rs::split` drops them only as page-subsetting fallout, not as protection.

It matters most on the fillable-PDF template path, where a firm registers a form obtained elsewhere and the platform fills and sends the result under that firm's name. The scan heuristics do detect active content — and the standing never-block ruling means a flag admits it anyway. That ruling is right for a file in someone's own matter and cannot serve as the control for an input the platform executes over on a recipient's behalf, which is the real tension here rather than an oversight in either position.

Three postures set out with costs; the recommendation is strip unconditionally on every path where the PDF is a record, and the existing macro-strip consent gate's shape at template registration, where a script can be legitimate and a person is present to say why. Nothing built — the posture is an owner call.
- The per-firm lineage collapses from 105 migrations into one baseline.

Every firm provisioned after a collapse replays the whole history on its first wake, and the history is where the accidents live: a table rebuild that cannot run against a populated database stays a permanent hazard for as long as it is in the chain, because every new firm meets it again. Five such rebuilds were in this one, including the pair that put a firm's database out of reach for a day. They are gone, not grandfathered.

The baseline is not written by hand and not edited from the old one. `scripts/collapse-baseline.mjs` DUMPS it from a database built by applying the existing chain, so the only thing it can express is what the chain actually produced, and `--verify` applies both and compares every object and every seeded row. It was checked against the real pre-collapse chain reconstructed from git: **767 objects and 408 seeded rows, identical.**

The verify pass earned its place immediately. The first dump silently dropped the three triggers that keep the directory's full-text index in step with the table it indexes — their names share the virtual table's prefix, and the shadow-table exclusion was written as a prefix test. A baseline missing them would have built a directory whose search quietly returned only what existed at the collapse. The exclusion now names the shadow set exactly.

A collapse retires migration SQL, and the honest consequence is that a database left behind cannot be carried forward by it. Reconciliation rewrites the ledger of a database sitting at the chain's head, which every live database is; a database that stopped part way through the retired history has a schema no baseline describes, and there is no hop that reaches it — reconciling always lands a ledger on exactly one tag, and no collapse retires a single migration. So the runner refuses that database, and now refuses it in its own words: told "code older than schema", whoever is holding the outage goes looking for a rollback that cannot help.
- **The serial front of every API request loses its two control-plane reads.** The session now rides
Better Auth's HMAC-signed cookie cache for five minutes at a time (`resolveSession` forwards the
refresh `Set-Cookie` so the cache renews past its first window, and a FIRMLESS answer is always
re-read against the store — founding a firm attaches `user.firm_id` by a direct write the library
never sees), and the firm row is cached per isolate for one minute, provisioned rows only — its
three carried values never change after provisioning. The member-active gate and RBAC still read
the firm's own database on every request. The trade and its bounds are the pending decision
`a-session-is-believed-for-five-minutes-and-a-firm-row-for-one`.
- **The gate is ready for a merge queue, and the conventions say what is true again.** Every red check the first full battery found on 2026-09-02 was two branches merged minutes apart and never tested together, which the pull-request tier cannot see by construction. The `merge_group` tier now resolves its diff base from the queue's own payload, and while the austerity holds it defers the fan-out sinks exactly as the pull request does (the sink lint alone is a 2-core runner for twenty-six minutes per merge). The setting that turns the queue on is a repository ruleset, so `docs/deploy-queue.md` carries it as its first entry, with the values to pick and why; it replaces the billing-block entry, which cleared on 2026-09-01.

The conventions stop describing a blocked gate: `build-performance.md`'s austerity section records what happened in August and what the revert is now a decision against, `operations.md`'s quality-gates section names the jobs the gate actually has and the tiers that actually run, and `CLAUDE.md` no longer says the gate of record is blocked.

Two things found on the way. The generated OpenAPI client was behind the committed snapshot for the third time (#445, #459, and now #486 each regenerated the snapshot and left the client), and is regenerated; a queued merge runs the drift check on the tree that lands, which is what stops a fourth. And `check:scoped`'s format step refused a change whose every script file the formatter ignores, which is exactly what a client regeneration looks like; it now carries `--no-error-on-unmatched-pattern` as its lint-only sibling already did, with a test pinning that shape.

And one real regression, found because this change runs the full battery: #477's grid publishes the frame's visible width to CSS from a resize observer, and it wrote the property inside the observer's own callback on every notification. Under the story suite's load that churn made the column-filter field lose focus to its menu while a word was being typed. The write now lands on the next frame and only when the width changed; the full story suite passes.
- **The merge queue is not on offer here, and the conventions stop promising it.** GitHub offers merge queues only in organization-owned repositories (public, or private on Enterprise Cloud); this repository is private and user-owned, so the setting that #488 documented does not exist for it. The owner declined the transfer that would make it available (2026-09-03), so the deploy-queue entry now records why it cannot be clicked, the decision, and the habit that stands in — one merge at a time, the next branch synced onto the `main` the last merge produced — with the up-to-date-before-merge ruleset option deliberately left off because it spends a full battery per open stream per merge. `build-performance.md`, `operations.md` and `CLAUDE.md` describe the pull-request tier as the only run between a merge and production, which is what is true; the `merge_group` tier stays wired for the day the ownership changes. Recorded as a decision.

**And the node test job stops running into the runner's cap.** On #488's battery the second of two node shards was cancelled at fifteen minutes with every test it had reached passing: the slim runner caps a job at fifteen minutes regardless of the job's own timeout, and the suite has grown to where two shards sit on that line. The job now runs four shards, each well under the cap for the same test minutes.

**And the column-filter story stops racing the menu it opens.** The grid's ColumnFilters story failed about one run in six under the suite's load, with focus on the header menu's panel instead of the filter field being typed into: the menu takes focus on open on the next animation frame, not with its mount, and a step that reached the field first had that frame land afterwards. The story now waits for focus to be inside the menu before opening the submenu, and sends the filter keys to the field directly since the rule it asserts is the keyboard one. Six consecutive full-suite runs pass.
- **The entry window's Relate button says Link, and names what it links.** The owner: "Not sure what the relate button means."

One act had two names. The tab is called Links, the model calls them links (`entry-links.ts`, `createEventLink`, `RelatedLink`), and the button alone said Relate — so the word a reader met first was the one the rest of the product never used, and a bare verb with no object told them nothing about what it would act on.

It reads **Link Settings** on a matter's setting and **Link Events** on a firm event, matching the action bar's own verb-and-noun grammar (Continue Setting, Book a Room, Cancel Event). The dialog is "Link Two Settings" / "Link Two Events", its commit reads Link, its refusal says which choice is missing, and the tab's own heading and empty line read Linked rather than Related.

Nothing about the records or the contract changed: a link is the same link, written the same way.
- Ten merges landed in one stretch and the roadmap's _Now_ section still described the state before
them. Discovery's next step was the processing lane that had just shipped. Notifications' next step
was the comparison sweep that shipped two slices ago. Human verification on the anonymous endpoints
did not appear at all.

The per-capability ledger was correct the whole time — every slice flipped its own `roadmap.d/` node
in its own commit, and the build register renders from those. What goes stale is the narrative, which
is hand-written on purpose: it is the one place that says which stream to pick up next and why, and
that judgement cannot be generated from a node's status.

Three streams now read true, and each names its gate where it has one. Discovery says privilege review
is waiting on two owner flags and which two, and separates them from the pair that gate the production
slice after it. Notifications says what its three production paths are and which two answers stand in
front of the remainder. Auth records that human verification is shipped and dormant, with the
inversion that matters — the widget is a prerequisite for its own activation, because the registration
screens are live and mint no token, so provisioning the secret first would refuse every real signup.
- The operations runbook and the owner action queue no longer record any current value of Cloudflare account state — connected Workers, production branches, root directories, build commands, Build Watch Paths, build caching, hostnames and routes, deploy dates, build outcomes. Each is replaced by the runnable command that returns it.

The reason is a count. `operations.md` wrote those values down and disagreed with the live configuration four separate times: a connected-Worker roster short by five; the edit Worker's root directory, deploy command and branch, all three true when written and all three false when next read; two Build Watch Paths matching no file, which suppresses rebuilds silently rather than failing; and a conclusion drawn from `apps/api-worker/wrangler.jsonc` that no custom domain was attached to the app Worker, when the account has an active zone bound to it as one. Each was corrected. Each correction decayed the moment somebody used the dashboard, which leaves no commit behind.

A drift-detecting check was considered and rejected: it needs a committed copy of the truth to diff against, which is the same snapshot in a format that compares, and it cannot run in the gate of record because that gate has no Cloudflare credentials and must not require network.

What stays is what no API returns — the decisions and why, the operator procedures, the failure modes that have each cost a deploy, and the invariants. `operations.md` now opens with the rule and the four drifts as its evidence, so the next person tempted to paste today's values back in reads the reason first.

Falsified along the way, and corrected: the fleet-wide production-branch reconciliation and the missing `packages/build-identity/*` watch paths were both carried as open owner items and are not; `magna-carta` is reachable at a custom domain, not only at `workers.dev`; and it does have Build Watch Paths rather than rebuilding on every push.
- **The step whose whole purpose is removing what a PDF hides leaves its executable content
untouched, and the question of what to do about that now reaches the decision desk.**

`crates/pdf-core/src/scrub.rs` removes thirteen document-level surfaces — `Info`, `Metadata`,
`StructTreeRoot`, `MarkInfo`, `Outlines`, named destinations, optional-content properties, field
values and appearances, `XFA`, embedded files, `Collection`, file associations and file-attachment
annotations — (one of them, the destinations name tree, only in its modern form — the legacy catalog `/Dests`
dictionary is neither cleared nor checked) — and then checks its own work: `verify_scrub_absence` walks the document model before it
is serialized, gating all seven option groups across thirteen checks, and refuses to emit anything at
all if a surface is still reachable. (A model check, not an output-byte one — the weaker of the two
forms the crate uses; `redact.rs` re-reads what it actually wrote.)

What it never looks for is executable content. No document-level JavaScript name tree, no open
action, no catalog actions on save, print or close, no page or field additional-actions, no
annotation action. A document scrubbed before production to an opposing party can still carry code, and this is a live
path rather than a hypothetical one: `prepareFormTemplateVersion` runs the scrub on every PDF form
template a firm registers.

The finding sharpens against the tree rather than against the design: the page-split path in
`crates/pdf-core/src/generate.rs` removes some of the same entries, and does so for safety — but a
different safety, that no byte of an excluded page survives into the output. It drops the catalog
`OpenAction`, `AA` and `Names` because they reference pages across the whole document, and strips an
action from an annotation on a kept page only when that action points at an excluded one, with a
fail-closed gate behind both. An action pointing inside the kept range survives. A split is not a
scrub, and neither path settles what the other should do.

**Surfaced, not built.** Detection is not the missing half. `inspect_pdf` in `containers/scan`
already recognises JavaScript, auto-actions, launch actions and embedded files, with a byte-scan
fallback for a compressed catalog, and records the finding as `active-content` on the verdict.
Nothing is done with it: it blocks no upload unless firm policy flags the file for some other reason,
and `scanAndGateStatements` activates a template version even on an `unscanned` verdict, discarding
`verdict.activeContent`. Stripping is not free either, and the cost falls on fillable forms a _firm_ uploaded: a
court form uses field actions for validation and formatting, so a scrub that removes them hands back
a form that looks right and computes nothing. The node's `awaiting-owner` line states the three
answers — strip always, strip with an exception a firm marks at upload, or surface without removing — the last of which is
closer to wiring up an answer the platform already computes than to building one —
and says why a fourth that sounds obvious is empty: an exception keyed on templates the platform
authored would exempt nothing, because every fillable template in the tree is a firm upload and
whether the platform ever authors its own is itself an open question on
`document-automation.filing-grade-generation`. `documents.pdf.scrub` is `shipped`, so
the question sits under the questions that change something already running rather than under the
ones holding a build.

Also moves this stream's active-work note to `docs/active-work/claude/passive-dev-orchestrator-m7f9jw.md`.
It was written at a flattened path, so the registry reported the branch as resolving to no ref while
two design specs linked the correct path and found nothing there. The path mirrors the branch name,
slashes included, which is what makes the registry collision-free.
- The vendored `security-audit` skill (`.claude/skills/security-audit/`, Cloudflare, MIT) is refreshed to upstream commit `c1c8a8c` of 2026-09-14. The copy landed on 2026-09-11 was already three months behind: it carried the seven original files and none of the domain companions upstream had added since July.

What arrives: a coverage ledger (`coverage-ledger.json`, with its own validator and test suite) so a run records what it checked, not only what it found; a third verdict, `needs_validation`, for a lead with an exact unresolved fact and no severity, so a blocked lead is no longer either inflated to confirmed or dropped; a guidance mode, so loading the skill for a security question no longer starts the six-phase audit or writes files; an execution-safety rule that runs target code only inside an OS-enforced sandbox and otherwise keeps the lead as needs-validation; and ten domain hunting files, of which the tenant-isolation, cloud-and-deployment, supply-chain, resource-exhaustion, and AI-and-LLM ones map onto this platform directly. `VENDORED.md` in the skill directory records the pinned commit and the refresh procedure; the directory joins the formatter's ignore list in `vite.config.ts`, because upstream owns the bytes and because the formatter corrupts one of its files on a second pass; and the security angle of the 7-angle review in `docs/conventions/testing.md` now names the companion files a slice picks from.
- The three send panels open in `ActionDialog`, and each stays on `done` to show what it came to.

Report an Issue and Report a Problem file through the firm's pipeline and then stay open with the reference the report was recorded under, the bar ending at Close; their Copy control moves out of the bar and sits beside the diagnostics it copies, since the bar holds one commit. Request a Change hands the shell `commitSoon` for the filing that is not wired yet, seats Copy beside the request it copies, and asks the shell not to restore focus to its row trigger on close — `restoreFocus={false}`, a new closed seam for the one trigger shape (revealed on focus) that a restored focus keeps latched open. The issue report and the change request keep their drafts across an ordinary close by design, so both tell the shell there is nothing to lose. All three lay their fields out with `LabelledField`.

Three allowances leave the registry; twelve remain, eleven of them named exclusions. Two wording changes: "Request a change" is "Request a Change", and the copy controls lost their bar seat, not their icons.
- `ActionDialog` gained the seams its first fifteen callers were writing by hand, and the design system gained the maturity family and two field primitives.

The primary pane is a real `<form>` and the commit is its submit button by id, so Enter commits in every panel and a disabled commit stops it; Ctrl+Enter or Cmd+Enter commits from a textarea. `subtitle` takes a string (twelve of fourteen were plain text; the eight that could be are now one attribute). `commitSoon: { reason }` renders the commit inside the Soon affordance for an act not served yet — the shell wraps its own control, so the bar still holds one commit in its source and `footer-set` is unchanged.

`apps/web/src/lib/maturity/` moved whole into `@magna-carta/design-system/maturity` — the stage model, `MaturityBadge`, `MaturityDot`, `SoonAffordance` and its wording — because the shell cannot import the app; thirty-five files changed an import path, the two tests moved with the module, and `SoonAffordance` is registered in `lint:one-ui`'s one-implementation registry with three stories in the catalog.

`LabelledField` (label, control, hint, error; the id minted, the description joined, an error marked invalid, the control's attributes handed over as `props` to spread) and `FieldRow` (two or three across) replace the column written fifty-six times and the row written sixteen. The field's gap is the panels' space-8 where the superforms-bound `Form.Field` uses space-4; the recipe says so rather than picking for the owner.
- The export generation stamp splits into two lines — the date, then the time on its own line — and
the time now names its zone (`12:57:56 PM PDT`), rendered from the reader's own clock via the two
shared helpers in `$lib/export/tabular-export.ts` that all four renderers now draw from. The stamp
was always browser-local; naming the zone is what makes that self-evident to whoever a file is
forwarded to. Verified by generating in a headless browser pinned to Pacific time on a UTC machine.
- **The matter status seal is a pillbox again, and one control changes the status.** The dropdown of lifecycle steps that shipped three days earlier is gone: `matter-status-dialog.svelte` renders the Badge inside a plain button that opens the status window, and the window's status row carries one `Change Status` beside the seal. That opens `matter-status-change-dialog.svelte`, an `ActionDialog` of `ChoiceRow`s — one per step the lifecycle allows from where the matter stands, each carrying the block sentence or the standing line, with the chosen step's consequence and requirement rows beneath and the footer commit reading that step's own verb.

The checks moved with it. The close, open and graduate readiness reads, their requirement lists and the hold's reason field are in the change panel; the number, the engagement and the paper file stay in the window, because they are standing facts about the record rather than anything a step does. `matterStepStanding` in `matter-lifecycle.ts` answers where any step stands from one readiness record, so the panel renders one structure where the window rendered three shapes, and every step gained a `consequence` sentence while `takenFrom`/`confirmation` went with the separate confirm panel. The lifecycle contract is untouched.
- **Where a data table will hold the rows, the table renders first.** The owner's ruling of
2026-09-18, on the Downloads and Uploads registers: "downloads and upload pages should show the
table data would populate in, even if there is no data. i want this as a lint and standard rule,
that data tables will still appear before data is in the area. this prepares users for the proper
shape." The header row now stands from the first paint and the words about the emptiness live in
the table's own empty body, under it.

`DataTable.EmptyRow` is the new part that carries them for a hand-composed table: one row, one cell
spanning every column, one line in the table's muted register, styled by the same recipe as the
grid's own empty state and marked `data-placeholder` so it takes none of a row's treatment. Surfaces
built on `DataTable.Grid` needed no part — the grid already draws its header over its own empty body
and says "No Results" there — only the gate in front of it removed.

The fitness function gained a third rule, `table-behind-absence`
(`tooling/lint-structured-empty/`), which reads a Svelte file's markup tree for a data table gated
behind the absence of its own rows: a conditional whose absence branch renders the product's one
`EmptyState` where its other branch renders the table, and the same arrangement one layer in, where
a region is handed an `emptyState` snippet that replaces the table it would otherwise render. It
follows the table through any depth of snippet, and it deliberately leaves a refusal and a failure
alone — a member who may not see the table, and a read that broke, are not tables waiting to fill.
The inline `<!-- structured-empty-allow: <why> -->` works for it as for the other two.

What it found, and what changed: Downloads, Uploads, the directory record's names, categories,
matters, relationships and near-matches panes, the matter calendar's deadlines and events, an
event's bookings, the matter activity register, and the file inspector's versions and checks.
- **The controls a table's control row and counts strip are made of are now table components, and the
count of hand-built copies they replace is the argument.** The clear-filters control was built
**seven times in three shapes**; the labelled figures strip **five times**, one of them already
reading in the opposite order; the load-more control **three times in two places**, one of them
below the strip entirely where it read as an act on the page rather than on the list. All twelve
grid consumers assembled the footer's trailing area through the one escape hatch it had.

**`DataTable.GridFigures`** owns the arrangement and never the formatting: label first, figure
second, tabular, `·` between, and "In view:" before the first one under a filter — because a total
that silently changed meaning when a column was filtered is the most quietly wrong thing a footer
can do. The value arrives as text, since money, durations and counts each format through their own
home and a strip that took minor units and a currency would have to learn all three. The Bills
register's reversed label/figure order is corrected in the move.

**`DataTable.ClearFilters` is two acts and says which.** Column filters alone read "Clear Filters";
a surface whose own search or scope is also holding rows back reads "Show Everything", because
clearing a search under a button labelled Clear Filters is a lie about what the press will do.
Neither is configured — both are derived from what is actually narrowing the view. Its `grid` is
optional, since a surface can be narrowed before its grid exists.

**`DataTable.LoadMore` says the noun** — "Load more matters", not "Load more" — and leaves when
there is nothing more, on the same rule every control that undoes a state follows: absence is the
answer, never a disabled control.

**Two owner placements, recorded as rulings.** The clear control lives in the control row above the
table, where the filters were set (`L42b`, revising L42's footer placement; `TB2c` for the time
surfaces, where TT2 had already put it there). The undo and redo pair lives in the footer on every
surface that has a stack (`A15c`, `TS9`) — the Time Sheet's toolbar pair moved down to join the
worked / billed / value figures. The footer's inline "Show all" stays: it is part of the tally
sentence, not a control in a control row, and the two are different things.

What is left in a surface's own hands is what genuinely belongs to it: the file manager's scale
control and File Analysis's own acts still ride the footer's `extras` slot, which is the slot
working as designed — one escape hatch at the end of a declared order, rather than a declared order
that exists nowhere.
- **The gate's test battery runs only when asked for.** The node shards, the Miniflare shards and the story suite are the bulk of the Actions bill and the whole of a pull request's wall-clock, and the node shards outgrew the 1-vCPU runner's fifteen-minute cap twice in one day. By the owner's ruling a pull request now runs them only under the `run-tests` label (attaching it re-runs the gate with the battery); a manual dispatch asks with its `test_battery` input; a queued merge always asks. The checks stay on every pull request. The branch's own full `pnpm test` is the standing merge bar, stated in the pull request. The node battery is also six shards rather than four. `docs/conventions/build-performance.md` carries the ruling and the trade.
- The three surfaces excluded as "full-screen" open in `ActionDialog`, now that the frame owns expand.

The time sheet is a reading panel that opens filling the screen, its toolbar the first row of the pane and its identity the frame's header; the flag, the two icons and the three utilities it had rebuilt by hand are gone, and the frame's corner control shrinks it back to the record width. The safe-browse screenshot viewer is a reading panel opened expanded. The cost review was never full-screen: it is a reading panel whose three answers — Skip, Kick Back, Approve — sit under the facts they decide, and it walks on rather than closing.

Three allowances leave the registry; three remain, every one a named exclusion: the command palette (a launcher), the settings ledger (a Sheet), and the fee-arrangement window (a record's shape, and a layout the owner is rethinking).
- **The Time Sheet opens from the top bar and belongs to the firm.** The owner's design puts it there —
it lives in the top bar and opens over whatever the person is doing, so capture never forces
navigation — and the port made it a per-matter modal reachable only from a matter's Time tab, removing
the Matter column and recording that removal as a design decision. It was not one.

One component now serves two doors: the Time Keeper chip opens it with no matter assumed, and a
matter's Time tab opens the same sheet pre-filtered to that matter. The chip was the last disabled
control in the shell saying it waited on a surface that had already arrived.

**A row without a matter is legal, because that is how time is actually captured** — somebody records
what they did before deciding where it belongs. Such a row holds typing, runs the timer, carries a
client-minted provisional code, counts in the incomplete tally, and never falls out of view when the
date scope moves. It is simply never sent: the capture route requires a matter, so the row states what
it still needs and writes itself the moment a matter is picked. No failed request, no error a person
has to interpret.

Two adjacent honesty calls came with it. A run started before a matter is chosen cannot become an
entry, so its seconds land on the row and the row writes itself through capture rather than through
the timer. And the permanent matter-scoped entry number the design mints cannot be minted here — no
route serves one — so a written row names that gap and says which provisional code it was held under.

Setting a matter on a row that is already an entry is refused out loud, because nothing moves an entry
between matters yet.
- **The rail regroups on the owner's direction of 2026-09-16.** Six groups, each answering one
question: `favorites` (member data, not registry), `desk`, `work`, `money`, `firm`, `tools`. Home,
Notifications, Tasks, Calendar and Magnus left the old fourteen-row `top` group for My Desk — that
group had "your morning" in the same list as "the firm's evidence", and the split is what says so.

The tool rows are the catalog projected into the Tools group and folded into subject clusters; Firm
Usage left the catalog for a hand-written Firm destination at `/firm-usage`, keeping the
`tools:firmUsage` key through the new `Destination.permission`; the File Workbench went the other way
and is a catalog tool again, in the Files cluster.
- **Every tool is a row in the left sidebar, and a tool opens onto the whole canvas.**

The Tools area was a two-sided screen: a navigation column of every tool on the left, the chosen tool beside it. The owner's direction of 2026-09-16 ends it for two reasons, and the second decided it. The tools are not a family — a postage rate, a WHOIS record, a county recorder's site and a bandwidth measurement share a sentence in the catalog and nothing else, so a column listing the other eight beside the one you opened is a column of things you are not doing. And it cost every tool the width of that column permanently, which the surfaces that will carry the most use — mailing and postage first, where a label, a rate table and an address want to sit side by side — can least afford.

`navigation/tool-sidebar.ts` projects the tool catalog into sidebar rows, so nothing about a tool is restated: the catalog still owns identity, subject group and the permission that gates it, the presentation layer the descriptor, stage and glyph, and `toolRoute()` the address. The registry gains a `tools` group headed by the index row (now "All Tools", and `exact` so it no longer lights up under every tool beneath it); `/tools/<id>` is unchanged, because that address is the catalog's and breaking saved links to shorten a URL is not a trade. `/tools/+layout.svelte` is a passthrough. A tool's rail row is `pinned`: what a member sees there is what they are permitted to run, and a star beside it would be a second, inert answer to a question access control has settled — which is also why Customize mode leaves the group out.

Sidebar groups fold, in the same pass: Workspace, Money, Firm and Tools each carry `Sidebar.GroupTrigger` — the heading itself, with a chevron and the full width as its target — and the fold is remembered per browser. The collapsed icon rail never folds, because a rail with no visible heading has nothing to fold by and nothing to press to bring the rows back. Folding is the sidebar's alone: every destination in a folded group is still one Ctrl+K away.
- **Downloads and Uploads left the Workspace group for the sidebar's footer utility tray.** The
owner's ruling of 2026-09-07: the two transfer registers describe what the application is doing —
often both at once, since a download and an upload can run together — rather than naming a place in
the firm's work, so they belong beside Settings and Customize at the rail's foot and not among the
destination rows.

The mechanism is the registry's existing `footerPinned` tier, which until now held Settings alone:
`sidebarGroups()` and `sidebarEditingGroups()` already skip it, so marking the two entries takes
them out of the scrolling groups AND out of Customize mode in one move, with each row keeping
exactly one home. Both are `pinned` as well, so they are fixtures rather than stars — there is
nowhere else for them to be, and nothing to hide them from. A member who had arranged or unstarred
either one keeps a stale id in stored preferences, which `mergeGroupOrder` has always filtered
against the visible set, so no migration was needed.

The tray has TWO ENDS, which is how it tells its two kinds of thing apart without a divider: the
rail's own controls lead — Settings, then Customize — and the registers lean to the inline end on an
auto margin. Settings leads the row outright because the collapsed rail shows the tray's first icon
and hides the rest; the trailing pair is one element, so that rule takes it away and brings it back
whole. Which end each fixture belongs to is stated in the shell rather than derived, because it is a
fact about the tray and not about the registry, which orders by where a destination sits in the app.

`.mc-sidebar-controls-trailing` carries the auto margin rather than the tray carrying
`justify-content: space-between`, which would also have spread Settings and Customize apart from
each other — the same reason the choice row's trailing part uses one.

The top-bar trays are unchanged, and the two levels are deliberately distinct: the tray beside the
timer is a summary with quick actions, the footer icon opens the full surface.
- **Uploads and Downloads are one frame rendered twice**, and the upload half now has a memory.

`$lib/transfers/` is the shared half: `transfer-tray.svelte` is the top-bar frame both registers render through — the tooltip and the popover sharing one button, the attention dot that takes the maturity dot's corner while it is raised, the titled panel, the way to the full surface — and `transfers.ts` holds the words neither is allowed its own copy of. The Upload control had never named itself on hover, which made the one control in that band that starts a transfer the one a reader could not identify; it does now, because the frame does it for both. The tables stay apart on purpose, and the module's header says why: a download is a stored document any format can be taken from, an upload is a file on a matter.

`upload-history.svelte.ts` is the new half. A transfer still dies with its tab — the files are the browser's own handles — but what a finished batch DID is a list of names, a matter, a folder and the file each one became, none of which needs a handle. That record is kept per browser (the shared persisted-preference primitive, bounded at 50 batches and 250 files each), so the Uploads screen answers "where is the thing I sent yesterday" instead of "nothing uploading", and every file that landed carries a Download straight to its own route on the matter. Nothing privileged is kept: no bytes, no digests.

Both empty states are two words now — "No Uploads", "No Downloads" — which is the standing empty-state ruling (`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`) reaching two screens that predated it with a paragraph each about the mechanism.
- **The Upload dialog holds one height, tabs its intake, states every file's readiness, names what
failed, and no longer asks whether to send files the firm already holds.** The source pane pins the
frame's height (`upload-dialog.svelte`, the record windows' own measure), so tabs, folders and rows
scroll inside it; the intake is `Tabs` — Location, Advanced Settings — in place of the accordion; Add
is one secondary button wearing the dropdown menu, with File and Folder as its items. The digest
register (`upload-digests.svelte.ts`) now asks the firm the moment a hash is in and reports each file
as reading, ready, held or not read, the batch starts every item from that readiness
(`UploadBatchPlan.readiness`), and `checkDuplicates` is gone from the plan: the hash is always read.
A failed item carries a one-line `failure` (the server's problem detail, or the transport class)
beside its full `reason`; the row and the top-bar tray both show it. On the server,
`purgeableVersionObjects` in `@magna-carta/file-manager` is the one door to destroying a version's
bytes, and it refuses while any other version row, live or soft-deleted, holds the same content or
key; the DELETE route's contract says so.
- The Firm Usage masthead byline and page footer are removed on the owner's direction (the tables are
the page), and a Download Report action renders the same response the tables drew as a dated
plain-text file (`$lib/tools/firm-usage/firm-usage-report.ts`, unit-tested). Also fixed at the
shell: the work canvas is now `position: relative`, so an absolutely positioned descendant (a
screen-reader-only table caption on any tall page) resolves against the canvas and clips with it,
instead of stretching the document into a second window scrollbar with bare background beneath the
shell.
- **The Build Versions panel reads the pair that serves you at a glance, and stops resizing itself
while you watch.** The fixed sentence explaining that `magna-carta-web` and `magna-carta` deploy
separately and may report different builds is gone. In its place, the leading pair carries a
colour-coded badge: green **In sync** once they match, amber **Web behind** when the web build is
the one that has fallen behind (the one case actually worth reloading for), or a calm **Different
builds** for any other gap — shown only once both sides have a real version to compare. Separately,
the "Checking services" / "Services checked … ago" line under the header no longer appears and
disappears as a read moves from in flight to freshly answered to aged; it now holds its place at a
constant height, so the panel's size never depends on which sentence happens to be showing.
- **The version chip reports the whole fleet, names every row by its deployed Worker, and tells you
when a newer deployment is live.**

The Build Versions panel's roster was eight workers short of the fleet and its rows carried invented
product names ("Malware Scan") beside, or instead of, the thing an operator would actually open.
Four changes, one panel:

- **Every magna-carta worker is listed.** The aggregate's roster is now the whole fleet — the edit,
  email, status and web workers join it — and a fitness test pins the roster to the wrangler configs
  on disk, so a worker added under `apps/` cannot silently stay off the overlay. The edit and status
  workers now mount the shared version route (and stamp their builds), the email worker gains a
  version-only `fetch` surface for the day it deploys, and the assets-only web worker answers
  through a static `/__version` file its build emits.
- **One name per line, and it is the real one.** Each deployment row is headed by the Cloudflare
  Worker it reports on, carried on the wire itself (`service` replaces `label` in
  `GET /api/v1/meta/versions`), with its state sentence beneath. The web app's own line stops
  borrowing the `magna-carta` name: the build the browser is running is its own line ("This page"),
  separate from the deployment list.
- **A newer deployment announces itself.** The app polls its own version (each build is named by
  its commit) and when a newer bundle is live the chip carries a warning dot and the panel leads
  with the notice and a Reload control. The page-versus-API skew check remains as the second
  detector.
- **Refresh means now.** The panel's Refresh and Retry pass `fresh=true`, which skips the server's
  brief cache and re-probes every worker — so the "checked N seconds ago" line starts over instead
  of climbing through a cache window.
- The version panel copies the whole diagnosis, from a control at the top, and Workers is a section rather than a drawer.

Copy sat at the FOOT of the Database section and put four health rows on the clipboard. A member reporting a fault therefore pasted the database's state and nothing about which build was serving it — the one fact that says whether a fix has even shipped yet — and copying part of the diagnosis reads exactly like copying all of it. The control is now at the top, where a reader reaches for it before scrolling past everything they wanted copied, and it takes the whole panel: this page's build, the API, every Worker the read named, and the database line. Multi-line, because a dozen facts on one line is a paste people summarize from memory instead. A Worker that reported nothing says so rather than going missing, since "absent from the paste" and "reported nothing" are different faults.

Workers has left Deployment and become a caret of its own, beside Deployment and Database. Nesting it made the fleet something a reader reached THROUGH the deployment, when in practice the two are asked about separately: "what build is live" and "is anything not answering" are different questions, and one of them was two folds deep. Each shut heading now counts only the Workers its own fold hides — one count across the whole read would have both headings claiming the same silent Worker.

Three source assertions that pinned the old shape were rewritten to the rules they were actually guarding, rather than to the layout that happened to satisfy them: section order is asserted over the markup instead of the whole file, and the refresh rule is that every gesture a person makes probes fresh rather than that there are exactly two such gestures. One of them required a hand-written `aria-busy` on the refresh control, which the later ruling that every loading state runs through one region forbids outright — the two rules contradicted each other, and the test was the older one.
- **The Build Versions panel stopped saying the same thing twice, and its two gestures moved into one cluster.** Five owner rulings from a deployed-site walk, recorded in [`docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`](docs/conventions/design-corrections.md):

- The standing **"This page / committed … · built …"** row duplicated `magna-carta-web`. That Worker serves the interface, so its commit and timestamps already are this page's, said once under a name someone can open in a dashboard. `showsPageBuildRow` in `apps/web/src/lib/versions/version-overlay-model.ts` keeps the line as a fallback rather than deleting it outright: signed out, a read that failed, or a web row that came back silent all leave nothing else able to state this build, and a panel reporting no version at all is the opposite of the point. While a first read is still in flight it stays away, so it cannot appear for a moment and then vanish when the answer lands.
- **"Services checked … ago"** sits under the header instead of beside the controls. Its length changes on a clock, and on the header row that motion pushed the Refresh button around while a reader was aiming at it.
- **Reload** is now a warning-tinted `rotate-cw` symbol beside Refresh, appearing only while the version poll has a newer bundle in hand. It reads as the answer to the chip's dot rather than as a second refresh, and the Update Available block keeps the badge and the sentence without a second copy of the gesture.
- The **Workers** beneath the leading pair fold behind a caret, remembered per browser on the shared persisted-preference primitive (`version-panel-preferences.svelte.ts`). It defaults to open, and a shut heading counts the Workers that came back without a version, so folding hides rows and never hides a fault: the fleet list is exhaustive precisely because an omission reads as health.
- **Copying a version** darkens the control for a second instead of growing a check beside the commit. The glyph widened the button on every press, and the width change read as the identifier itself changing.
- **The safe website viewer is `shipped`, because a capture came back.** The feature-ledger node
stayed `partial` through the merge that repaired the render, on the rule that a capability's status
follows evidence rather than a deploy; the first successful capture against the deployed service
arrived on 2026-09-18 and the node follows it. Its `notes` no longer claim the page answers every
capture with a renderer-unavailable state, which stopped being true with that merge.

**The Browser Rendering entry in the deploy queue closes, and not the way it was written.** It had
stood open for weeks as the suspected cause of every failed capture — the one dependency no session
could verify from the repository. The entitlement had been serving the whole time. The captures were
failing on a wait for `networkidle2` that a page holding a socket never reaches, which the service
answered 422 and the route reported as a capacity outage.

The entry is closed with that correction rather than a tick, because the shape of the mistake is
what the file invites: an item naming something no session can check attracts any failure that might
plausibly be it, and the attribution is never re-tested. The renderer's own refusals were being
collapsed into a single sentence and never logged, so for weeks there was nothing to read. Make a
failure readable before blaming an open entry for it.
- **The Safe Website Viewer composes as one window and leads with an Overview.** The shell and the
information tabs unify into one framed composition; clickable addresses (outbound links, redirect
hops — still buttons that capture in the viewer, never anchors to the suspect site) wear the
standard hyperlink register, now a standing rule in `docs/conventions/design-corrections.md`
alongside the unmistakable-toggle rule the Static/Live control is restyled to. The landed-URL row
gains its own copy control; the screenshot gains Download Image and a full-screen overlay; the
loading viewport shows the URL being captured, elapsed seconds, and one honest status line. A new
Overview tab leads the right side with facts derived from the capture already in hand (final
status, content type, server, redirect and link counts, captured-at, duration, the different-site
flag), and a Registration tab runs the WHOIS lookup in place for the captured host through the
shared lookup seam (lazy on first open, cached per host, with the same visible retry ladder) — no
redirect to the WHOIS page. Facts needing new backend probes (resolved IP, TLS certificate,
hosting provider) are recorded as seams, not faked.
- **The document's opening wait is one centered panel over the frame, and the way back to the matter is a button on the editor's own bar.**

The staged wait sat above the frame, the "taking longer" sentence and its Retry arrived above that at fifteen seconds, and when the editor came up the panel went away and the frame moved up into its place: three reflows on a screen a member was staring at. The panel now sits over the frame, centered, with the frame beneath it at its final size from the start; the sentence, the Retry and a failure all appear inside the same panel, which grows downward only. Time is written out ("12 seconds so far"), never abbreviated.

With the editor the whole screen, the way back is a button the editor draws for us: **Matter**, on the editor's shortcuts bar, inserted through its message protocol and labelled with the matter it returns to. The editor's own Close is routed to the same exit. Both ask the editor to save first and leave when it says the save is done, or after three seconds if it does not; the editor saves on its own when the last view drops, so the wait protects the member's time, not their work.

Three corrections from the editor's own integration guide, now that it could be read: a save's answer carries `LastModifiedTime` as the JSON body the editor reads (an empty body was logged as invalid and left its change detection off); `CheckFileInfo` names the member (`UserFriendlyName`), so co-authors see a name rather than an unknown user with an identifier; and the frame allows full screen, which a slideshow needs. In the image, the kit's jail is set up by copying rather than by a bind-mount the container cannot make.
- **The back-to-matter button sits first on the editor's bar, carries the matter's number, and takes the editor's icon colour.** The editor appends a host's buttons after its own and shows the icon as given (`insertBefore` is honoured only by its classic toolbar), so the edit worker now serves the platform's stylesheet on the editor's origin (`apps/edit-worker/src/editor-stylesheet.ts`, at `/magna-carta/editor.css`, linked into the page's head as it streams through, under the page's own `style-src 'self'`): the shortcuts row is laid out as a flex line with the host's cell ordered first, and the icon is inverted under the editor's dark theme. `backToMatterButton` takes the matter's number as the button's word, threaded from the edit page's matter record; a matter without one reads "Matter".
- **The week and the day are time grids, and a setting is a block from its start to its end.** The owner's 2026-09-14 round on the calendar, in four parts.

**An entry stretches.** "Start and end time need to properly show themselves on the calendar, not just on the start, should stretch accordingly." The day grid used to park a chip in the row of the hour a thing began in and say how long it ran in words, on the argument that a two-pixel sliver for a fifteen-minute call is unreadable. The sliver is now answered by a MINIMUM block rather than by refusing to stretch: a block is never shorter than one that can hold a line of text, and an entry that outgrows its true duration says so by overlapping what follows it, which is the truth about a day with a fifteen-minute call in it. An entry with no end — half of what a firm calendar paints, since the federated read declares a time of day and no duration — gets that minimum rather than a guessed hour.

**The week is one.** "Week view should be taller since we can include time." It was seven civil-day cells in the month's grammar, each holding a list of chips, which answers none of what a week is read for: who is where on Wednesday afternoon, what Thursday morning still has room for. It is now the day's shape with seven columns — hours down the leading edge, a day across the top — with a band above the hours where what is true of a whole day sits, and where a multi-day run is still drawn across its days and marked at each end.

**What runs at the same time is the reader's call.** "There should be a setting to allow for overlapping events on one calendar, or showing them next to each other." Side by side divides the column between the things in a cluster, so nothing hides; overlapping steps them over one another, so each block keeps more of its width. The choice is held per browser beside the calendar colours, and offered on the toolbar only where there is an hour axis to be concurrent on — the month and the agenda are lists of days, and a list has no concurrency to present.

**The view switch and the window sit beside New.** "Move month view controls to next to the new event button." `CalendarView` hands its action row UP to the host's `header` snippet, so the screen seats the controls on the masthead's own line; a host that ignores the snippet still gets the row above the grid.

Two pure modules carry the arithmetic, asserted without a browser: `time-placement.ts` (the span an entry occupies, the clusters it falls in, the share of the column it takes) and `time-blocks.ts` (which cell it renders in, and the style that draws it there). The block lives in the DOM cell of the hour it begins in — where a screen reader reading the table row by row should meet it — and is positioned out of that cell over one hour step, so the grids stay real tables.
- The frames a meeting's two ends exchange are now one package — `@magna-carta/meeting-protocol` — imported by the `MeetingRoom` Durable Object and by the browser client alike, with the signaling room and the client each split into the concerns they had grown.

They were declared twice, and had to be: a browser bundle cannot import from a Worker, so the room stated the wire with zod and the client re-stated it by hand. Three slices added frames to both ends by prose agreement, and the drift that produces does not fail a build — it shows up as somebody's tile staying black.

The package holds the schemas, the builders, the refusal vocabulary, the version and the caps, and a fitness function asks four questions of every frame in it: the room has somewhere to put each one a browser may send, a browser sends each of them, the browser has somewhere to put each one the room may send, and the package builds each of them. Its first run found `renegotiated` — the room's acknowledgement of a browser's answer — had no handler in the browser at all, falling through the receive switch's `default` since the day it was added.

Beside it, the room is now an orchestrating Durable Object over six modules (state, roster, presence, media, lifecycle, frames), each taking the object's context explicitly so it can be driven without the runtime; the SFU client and the relay credentials moved under `meetings/sfu/`; and the browser client is the same split (signaling, negotiation, subscriptions, capture, presence) with the media-effects stage seamed in at capture as the identity. Mechanical throughout — every test passed with its assertions unchanged.
- **The File Workbench becomes a sidebar destination in the Firm group, at `/file-workbench`, starred by default.** The tool catalogue had it inverted: of its twenty manifests, eleven are the `files` subject group, and ten of those eleven map one-to-one onto the workbench's own capability tabs, so the listing offered eleven doors into one room with the room filed alphabetically between two of its own doors. Firm rather than Workspace on a scope test rather than an importance one, since nothing brought here is filed, versioned, or remembered.

The route moves off `/tools/` because destination currency is a path-prefix match, so a workbench still under `/tools/` would light up the Tools row alongside its own. The manifest row stays, since contextual surfaces query the catalogue by context tag, so `ToolManifest` gains an optional `route` and `toolRoute()` becomes the one derivation every link-builder goes through. The palette's tool provider skips a promoted tool, which the destination registry already lists. `FILE_WORKBENCH_BACK` is deleted and the screen header drops its `back="tools"`: a top-level destination has no way back.
- **The hard and soft cost distinction is gone from the cost surface.** The owner struck it in plain
words — it is not a real thing — and the ruling was recorded as settled: not renamed, not moved to
settings, not kept as a hidden field. It does not exist in the model, the capture form, the columns,
the filters, the review pane, or any copy.

It shipped anyway, because the surface was ported from a superseded draft rather than from the round
that struck it. Gone now: the class column and its filter, the class labels and their meanings, the
class field in the capture form, the class row in the details panel and the review window and the
print sheet, the class clause in the draft refusal, and the hard and soft figures in the panel
summary. Payee drops to three states, because the fourth existed only to carry the distinction, and
the largest-payee ranking now considers every cost that names somebody rather than only the hard
ones.

**The review gate reads off, matching the Time tab.** The two tabs of one matter disagreed about a
firm setting nothing serves: costs assumed review was on and showed Submit, Approve and Kick Back,
while time assumed off and showed none of it. A reader moving between them saw two different firms.
Off is the settled default, and off means the review vocabulary is absent rather than disabled. The
review window and its dialogs stay wired behind one flag, so serving the setting later is a single
change.

Column order, labels and figures come to the settled round: Description leads and is called
Description rather than Info, Recoverable is Billable, Receipt (one) is Attachments (many), and the
footer carries three figures — unbilled, billed, absorbed — rather than four.

Two stale affordances go with it. "Open in Billing" waited on a section that has shipped, and now
waits on the invoice reference it actually lacks. Unsubmit is rendered against a submitted cost,
marked, as the Time tab already does.

**One write still carries the struck field**, because the create contract makes it required: it is
supplied internally as a constant and no caller sees it. The field remains in the schema and, more
consequentially, in the finalize path, where it selects the ledger account — so removing it there is a
decision about accounting rather than a deletion.
- **Three indexes added, three retired, and the eight that were not added written down with the numbers
that declined them.** The second half of the follow-up to the custodian and calendar volume sweep;
the first half rewrote the due-back reads and needed no schema change at all.

**The member filter's participant lookup.** "What is on this member's calendar" resolves as an
`EXISTS` supplying both the event and the member, but only `member_user_id` was indexed, so each
candidate event paid a walk proportional to how many events that member is on.
`matter_event_participant_member_event_index (member_user_id, event_id)` makes it a covering seek,
and the single-column index it strictly subsumes is dropped in the same migration — the table carries
the same number of indexes it did before. Keyed on the member first rather than widening the existing
`(event_id)` index, which measured identically but would have given up seeking by member alone.

**The register list's sort.** `custody_packet` is ordered by `(created_at, id)` on every page, keyset
pages included, and nothing covered that ordering — so every page was a full table scan into a
temporary B-tree, which is the cost keyset pagination exists to remove.
`custody_packet_created_index` costs one B-tree insert when a packet is created and nothing
thereafter: both columns are immutable, so the status and location updates every movement makes do
not touch it.

**The firm calendar's custody movements.** The 31-day firm-wide window reads movements by date with
no packet to key on, so it walked the whole ledger — and that ledger is the one table here that grows
without bound, because a firm holds originals for decades and appends to their history the whole
time. `custody_movement_occurred_index (occurred_at, id)` is insert-only on an append-only table: one
entry per movement a person physically records.

**Two indexes retired for having no reader.** Nothing queries `custody_movement` by `item_id` — every
read goes by `id`, by `packet_id`, or now by `occurred_at` — so `custody_movement_item_index` was
pure write cost on the subsystem's largest table, and it was the cheap-looking entry that made the
due-back reads walk the whole ledger. The partial `custody_movement_due_back_index` was built for the
overdue sweep, and neither that sweep nor the timeline's due-back source seeks by `due_back_on` any
more. `custody_movement` ends with one fewer index than it started.

Measured on the profile corpus against the committed baseline. The first two are harness
measurements; the register pages are direct statement probes, because the harness measures the
register under its filters rather than unfiltered.

| Read                                   | Before   | After    |
| -------------------------------------- | -------- | -------- |
| `timeline.firm-window-member-filtered` | 8.64 ms  | 0.65 ms  |
| `timeline.firm-window-31-day`          | 18.58 ms | 10.80 ms |
| register list, page 1 unfiltered       | 0.32 ms  | 0.09 ms  |
| register list, page 2 keyset           | 0.42 ms  | 0.07 ms  |

The register's two filtered reads plan exactly as they did before — the planner keeps the temporary
B-tree where the filter has already narrowed to a handful of rows, which is the right call and the
reason the new index buys nothing there.

**What was declined.** The firm-wide window scans seven more sources, and none of them gets an index
here. Each costs at most 1.7 ms of that one read at this corpus, and between them `file`,
`time_entry`, `cost_entry`, `email_matter_link`, `document_assembly`, `conflicts_check`, and
`trust_movement` are the platform's hottest write paths — seven indexes on seven constantly-written
tables to save a few milliseconds on federation's weakest read is the wrong trade, and taking it
would spend the evidence that is meant to decide whether a projected read model is ever built. The
scan allowlist still names every one of them by hand, now with the reasoning and the numbers beside
it.
- `GET /api/v1/firm-usage` now composes the three AI meters that were written but read by no route
(`token_usage_meter`, `ai_search_usage_meter`, `ai_detection_usage`), plus new per-domain reads:
matters by type and by location (`@magna-carta/matters/queries`), the file versioning breakdown with
sizes (`@magna-carta/file-manager/usage`), location rows with staffing counts
(`@magna-carta/locations/statements`), Directory people/organization counts
(`@magna-carta/directory/usage`), and the active member count. Everything is computed on the
request — no cache, no snapshot — so a page nobody opens costs nothing. The roadmap's claim that the
token meter feeds the firm-usage surface, which had drifted ahead of the code, is now true.
- **The version overlay now explains each non-answer instead of leaving a two-word badge to be read
as an outage.** "Not deployed", "Unreachable" and "Not reporting" are three different facts about a
deployment, and a bare badge separated none of them: a service this deployment was never wired to
looked identical to a service that failed the read, which looked identical to a healthy service
whose build simply predates the version route. Each row now carries the sentence that says which
one it is, on the line the reported rows use for their timestamps.

Two smaller repairs ride along. The build-identity stamp reads the build runner's own commit
variable (`WORKERS_CI_COMMIT_SHA`, `GITHUB_SHA`) when git cannot answer for the checkout, so a
Worker built on a runner without a usable `.git` reports the commit it was built from rather than
`dev`; a commit that no source can name still reports `dev`, unchanged. And the web-versus-API skew
call compares commits by prefix rather than by equality, because the two sides abbreviate the hash
independently and an equality test would raise "Different Builds" over a deployment that is in step.
- **Tools and Reports render through one catalogue framework, and both search.**

They had always been the same screen — sections with an engraved heading, and under each a run of entries carrying a glyph, a name, one line saying what the thing does, and a maturity mark deciding whether the entry is a link — written twice. Twice had already drifted: Tools registered a tiles view and a list view with the multi-view shell, Reports hand-rolled one list and no switch, and neither could be searched.

`apps/web/src/lib/catalogue/` is now the shape, and only the shape: the entry vocabulary, the pure narrowing, the row, the tile, the two grouped renderers, and `catalogue-screen.svelte`, which assembles the screen header with ScreenSearch and the view switch in its action row over the multi-view shell. Each registry projects into it beside itself — `tools/tool-catalogue.ts`, `reports/report-catalogue.ts` — so nothing about a tool or a report moved into the shared layer, and the shared layer cannot name either. `href` decides launchability from each registry's own rule (`hasSurface`, `isBuiltReport`); the row and the tile read only whether it is null.

The narrowing runs over the sections rather than inside a view, so both views narrow identically and switching mid-search keeps the answer. It matches a word anywhere in an entry's name, descriptive line, `waitsOn` dependency, section heading, or unshown keywords, and every word of a query must match — `catalogue-search.test.ts` pins those rules.
