The lay search synonyms moved from `tool-destinations.ts` into the presentation layer, its own comment's stated durable home, so the palette and the catalogue cast one net.

Removed: `tool-row.svelte`, `tool-tile.svelte`, `tools-list-view.svelte`, `tools-tiles-view.svelte`, `report-row.svelte`, and the tools view-preference pair — the view choice is now one factory over the string-union codec, keyed per catalogue.
- **Tools and Reports are two-sided screens on the design system's `NavigationLayout`.** Each area's routes now render inside a layout (`apps/web/src/routes/(app)/tools/+layout.svelte`, `apps/web/src/routes/(app)/reports/+layout.svelte`) that draws the catalogue as a navigation column on the left and the chosen tool or report on the right, on the same component Settings adopted first — the owner's 2026-09-11 ruling that a screen with a navigational menu and a content area is one component, and that it reaches Tools and Reports.

The column is `$lib/tools/catalogue-navigation.svelte`, one component for both areas, and it reads the same projection each landing index renders (`tool-catalogue.ts`, `report-catalogue.ts`), so a registry entry reaches the column, the index and the command palette with no edit. The current entry is decided by `catalogue-navigation.ts` on the path boundary, so the workbench's password-recovery screen still lights the File Workbench. A soon entry stands in its group unlinked with its mark and its dependency on the hover title, never omitted. The landing route keeps its catalogue index in the content column, so the column is never beside nothing.

The content column is the page's scroll region unless the page claims it: the File Workbench and the Safe Website Viewer stage their own full-height frames and say so through their route data (`content-column.ts`), and the Tools layout hands them a bare column. Every tool and report keeps `back` on its own header; the column is a finding aid beside it, not a replacement for it.
- Every list endpoint is now either cursor-paged or recorded with what bounds it — the pagination gate's carried-over list of unpaged endpoints is empty, down from forty-seven. A matter's staffing assignments and a matter asset's value history now page; the other sixteen were traced to their statements and are bounded by a firm's own configured vocabulary, a fixed platform catalog, or a schema-declared ceiling.
- **The Upload panel, after the owner's 2026-09-08 round, plus the diagnosis behind it.**

The Add menu becomes one press (files; the folder ask rides a chevron on the same control, because
no engine offers a picker taking both). Where the File System Access pickers exist they replace the
hidden `<input>`s, so choosing a folder no longer makes Chrome raise its own "Upload N files to this
site?" over the panel. The batch-wide document type is gone: it is a column on the source table set
on the selected rows, so `UploadBatchPlan` carries `documentTypeIds` keyed by intake key rather than
one id. "On Arrival" is a folded **Advanced Settings** accordion holding the dating basis and a new
`checkDuplicates` setting. `DataTable.ClearFilters` joins the panel's control row, which is the one
table companion the source table lacked.

Hashing moves out of the upload lane into a new register, `upload-digests.svelte.ts`: reads start
when a file is CHOSEN, run one behind another (there is one worker), are memoized per intake key,
and report to a caller that arrives mid-read from wherever the read has got to.
`UploadQueueDependencies.hash(file, …)` is therefore replaced by `digest(entry, …)` — the seam any
stand-in for the queue's network implements. The pace line beside the progress bar takes a fixed
measure from the new `size.transfer-pace` token, so a changing byte count no longer resizes the bar.

The failed upload in the owner's log was the CORS signature from §15 of the operations runbook — a
201 reservation, no part calls, an abort seven to nine seconds later (the retry ladder), and no
Worker-side error at all, because the refusal happens between the browser and the bucket. That
signature is now written into the runbook, and a transport failure on the byte write says the
storage did not answer rather than the flat "nothing answered" that sent readers to check their own
connection.
- **WHOIS retries registry faults itself, visibly, and the Safe Website Viewer becomes a real
browser shell.** The lookup seam gains `lookupWhoisWithRetries`: a transient upstream fault (the
502 the worker maps `RdapUpstreamFailure` to, or nothing answering) is retried up to three
attempts with short backoff, each attempt reported to the page, which shows "Trying again, attempt
2 of 3" in the loading card instead of stalling silently; the platform's own 429 is deliberately
never retried. Recorded as the standing rule "Retry a transient upstream fault yourself, visibly".
The viewer's result structure now renders at rest (the "result region is furniture" ruling): the
URL entry moves into the shell's own address bar as the one entry ("Load Website"), the landed URL
appears as a secondary row when a capture ends on a different site, back/forward/refresh navigate
a client-side capture history (`capture-history.ts`, unit-tested), outbound links load in the
viewer as new captures (buttons, never anchors), the URL is click-to-copy, tab panels are boxed
structures, and a Static/Live toggle renders with Live seamed behind the Soon affordance until the
interactive remote-browsing seam is built.
- The register's "Waiting on you" section is a flat list, and at thirty entries a flat list stops working. "Whether a separate gender field is ever added to a Directory person" was sitting between two decisions that each hold an entire unbuilt subsystem still, and nothing on the page distinguished them.

It now splits by what the answer costs. A question on a capability with **nothing built behind it yet** is holding work still: nobody can start until it lands, and answering it late means somebody waited. A question on a capability that **already runs** is refining something that works — it deserves an answer and it is blocking nobody. Each group leads with its own count, and a group with no entries prints no heading rather than a zero.

The split reads the node's own `status` rather than a second key declaring it. A `blocking: true` field would be the same fact recorded twice, and the two copies would eventually disagree — which is the failure this document has spent the week correcting everywhere else.
- **Where data will arrive, the structure that will hold it renders first, empty.** The owner's
ruling of 2026-09-14: a screen that puts a sentence where its table, list or rail will stand
prepares nobody for what is coming and hides the shape a reader would use to spot a gap. The words
about the emptiness now live inside the structure's own empty state, and the structure stands from
the first paint.

Three design-system changes carry it. `EventRail` draws its frame with zero events — one hollow,
dashed marker where the first event will land and `emptyMessage` in the body beside it — and takes
a `note`, the one line a caller may hang beneath the events inside the frame for what the history
does not yet carry, instead of a paragraph loose on the canvas. `DefinitionList` is new: named
values, framed, with `DefinitionList.Row` drawing the table's empty-cell mark for a value not known
yet and `DefinitionList.Empty` as the row beneath the terms that the words about why go in.
`DataTable.GridFigures` takes a per-figure `scope`: a `whole-record` figure (a server-side count of
what is waiting, a total the loaded rows do not add up to) stands before the "In view:" sentence in
its own group, so a filter on the loaded rows never presents it as narrowed.

The gate is `pnpm run lint:structured-empty` (`tooling/lint-structured-empty/`), which reads a
Svelte file's markup tree for the two shapes the ruling named: a prose branch opposite a structure
in one conditional (and its `{#each}` and `{#await}` cousins), and a muted paragraph immediately
beneath a structure in the same block. It fires only where the prose branch's condition speaks of
absence, treats a non-breaking-space spacer as no prose, and takes an inline
`<!-- structured-empty-allow: <why> -->` whose reason sits beside the code it excuses; an allowance
that excuses nothing is itself a finding. The rule is recorded in `docs/conventions/ui-design.md`.

What it found, and what changed: the file inspector's Hashes tab, the speed test's server facts and
sample table, the matter status window's engagement list, the bill window's history and delivery
tabs, the trust-transfer dialog's ceiling, and the developer console's resource meters.

### Security

- **Post-quantum cryptographic posture** (white paper _Encryption and key management_ → _Post-quantum posture_, `security.md`, ADR-0046): an agility-first readiness stance — the symmetric corpus (AES-256) is already quantum-resistant and needs no migration; harvest-now-decrypt-later on data in transit is met by Cloudflare's hybrid X25519MLKEM768 TLS; public-key signatures (passkeys, the PAdES e-signature seal) are seamed but deferred to upstream standards (ML-DSA/SLH-DSA). Mandates AES-256 everywhere, SHA-384 where free, algorithm-versioned ciphertext/signatures, and symmetric-preferred primitives.
- **Upgraded `hono` 4.12.23 → 4.12.27 (catalog).** Closes five upstream advisories in the API framework, including a high-severity one where the CORS middleware reflects any `Origin` with credentials when `origin` defaults to the wildcard, plus a `serve-static` path-traversal on Windows via encoded backslash. The Worker does not use the CORS or `serve-static` middleware, so this is a proactive bump with no behavior change. (`pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `apps/worker`, `packages/data-access`)
- **Cleared twelve HIGH osv-scanner advisories by upgrading their dependency carriers to patched versions.** The CI dependency-audit gate began failing after advisory-database drift surfaced twelve HIGH (CVSS ≥ 7) npm advisories across eight transitive/direct carriers — `better-auth`, `fast-xml-parser`, `postcss`, `undici`, `sharp`, `js-yaml`, `fast-uri`, and `brace-expansion`. Rather than accept them, each carrier was pinned forward to the version that fixes its advisory: `better-auth` 1.6.16 → 1.6.22 (catalog) and `fast-xml-parser` → ^5.10.1 (direct), with the rest pinned through the pnpm-workspace `overrides` block alongside the existing Vite+ aliases (`postcss` 8.5.18, `undici` 7.29.0, `sharp` 0.35.0, `js-yaml` 3.15.0/4.3.0, `fast-uri` 3.1.5, `brace-expansion` 1.1.18). The `better-auth` upgrade also required adopting its new `twoFactor` brute-force lockout fields (`failed_verification_count`, `locked_until`) into the control-plane schema via an additive migration, so the two-factor enable/verify flow stays green. The osv-scanner gate now reports zero HIGH/CRITICAL npm advisories.
- Hardened and consolidated the dependency-audit setup around the osv-scanner CI gate. The gate now pins the osv-scanner binary by SHA256 (verified against the release's published checksum before it runs, failing closed on any mismatch) so a swapped or compromised release asset can't execute. The pre-push git hook's local `pnpm audit` step is removed — it covered only npm, depended on npm's retiring audit endpoint, and duplicated the authoritative CI gate that now audits both the npm and Rust supply chains — and the `package.json` `pnpm.auditConfig` it read is dropped. `osv-scanner.toml` is now the single home for accepted advisories.
- CI dependency-audit gate migrated to osv-scanner, now covering the Rust supply chain alongside npm. The gate previously ran npm-only `pnpm audit`; it now runs osv-scanner (v2.4.0) over the npm lockfile and every first-party `Cargo.lock` (`crates/` + `containers/`) against the OSV database (GHSA + RUSTSEC), failing on any HIGH/CRITICAL (CVSS >= 7.0) and failing closed on a scan error. This immediately surfaced four real high-severity advisories the npm-only audit could never see — including a stack-overflow DoS (`RUSTSEC-2026-0187`, lopdf) on the untrusted-PDF-parsing path — now accepted with cause and a time-boxed `ignoreUntil` in `osv-scanner.toml` and tracked for remediation by carrier upgrades. The pre-push hook still runs `pnpm audit` for fast local feedback (migrating it is a follow-up).
- **Refreshed the npm dependency catalog and recorded verified remediation verdicts for the advisories the
audit gate still accepts.** `hono` moved 4.12.27 → 4.13.0, which crosses 4.12.34 — the release that fixed
four security defects reachable from a Worker: cross-request data disclosure in JSX, a whitespace-tolerant
CORS origin regex (ReDoS), an algorithmic-complexity denial of service in the Language middleware, and
response-header leakage in the proxy helper. Alongside it, `@hono/zod-openapi` 1.4.0 → 1.5.1,
`@tanstack/svelte-query` 6.1.34 → 6.1.38, `@internationalized/date` 3.12.2 → 3.12.3, `@lucide/svelte`
1.17.0 → 1.28.0, `@cloudflare/speedtest` 1.11.0 → 1.13.0, the three self-hosted font packages → 5.3.0, and
the dev tooling `@faker-js/faker` 10.5.0, `@types/node` 26.1.2, `@stoplight/spectral-cli` 6.16.3,
`@stoplight/prism-cli` 5.16.0, and `happy-dom` 20.11.1.

The accepted-advisory list in `osv-scanner.toml` also lost a dead entry and gained real verdicts.
`GHSA-gv7w-rqvm-qjhr` was removed: GitHub withdrew it on 2026-06-17 because the affected package was
misidentified — the flaw was in the esbuild Deno module, not the npm package — so the gate had been
carrying an ignore that matched nothing. The remaining tracked entries now record what was actually
checked rather than a bare "upgrade the carrier": the `quick-xml` advisories (RUSTSEC-2026-0194/0195) are
fixed in quick-xml 0.41.0 but reached only through `office-crypto`, which still requires `^0.38.4` as of
its newest release (0.3.0, published 2026-07-22), so no carrier upgrade can clear them; and the npm `uuid`
advisory (GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq) is fixed in uuid 11.1.1 but arrives through `postman-collection`, which
hard-pins uuid 8.3.2 through its newest release (5.3.1) — so an override, not an upgrade, is the only
remediation. Both entries keep their 2026-10-14 `ignoreUntil` forcing function.
- Upgraded lopdf to 0.42.0 across every first-party Rust workspace (`crates/` and the `scan`/`ocr`/`recovery`/`file-repair` containers), remediating RUSTSEC-2026-0187 — the stack-overflow denial-of-service in lopdf's PDF parser, on the untrusted-file path. The osv-scanner CI gate's accepted-advisory list drops that entry. The scan container's structural-PDF SIGABRT guards are retained as defense-in-depth. The three remaining tracked advisories (quick-xml x2, npm uuid) stay accepted with corrected, documented reasons: quick-xml is reachable only through office-crypto 0.2.0 (its latest release, which pins quick-xml 0.38, so it cannot be cleared without a newer office-crypto), and the npm uuid advisory is a transitive dev-tooling dependency of postman-collection with no production-runtime exploit path.
- **Telemetry's redact-by-default posture now holds on the counter path and against non-string values.**
The event allowlist was structural for field NAMES but not for field VALUES: a declared field typed
`FieldValue` could still be handed an object by any call site that reached the builder through `any`,
and `JSON.stringify` then wrote that object into the log line with every nested key intact — past the
allowlist, and past the scrubber, which only ever walked strings. Values are now forced back to a flat
primitive at the same boundary as the keys; anything else is replaced outright rather than serialised,
and the Workers logger raises a `telemetry.unloggable` counter naming the event and field so the call
site is visible instead of silent. As a side effect, a `bigint` or a symbol in a field can no longer
throw inside `JSON.stringify` and take the emit down with it.

`Logger.count()` was the other door, and it was unguarded end to end: free-form metric names and
free-form dimension values reached Analytics Engine with no allowlist, no scrub, and no tripwire — the
cheapest way to get privileged content into the dataset, and the one nothing would have caught. The
queue consumer's `costs.recovery.unhandled_topic` counter was already passing a value straight off a
queue message. Counters now go through a **metric catalog** (`@magna-carta/telemetry/metrics`), the
counter-side twin of the event catalog: each metric declares its ordered dimension keys, blobs are laid
out from that declaration, dimension values are scrubbed, and anything undeclared — a metric or a
dimension key — is dropped rather than guessed at, against a tripwire counter. A fitness scan over
every `apps/*/src` and `packages/*/src` fails a `count()` call site naming a metric the catalog does
not declare, or building a metric name by interpolation.

Declaring the dimension keys fixes a second, quieter problem: the Analytics Engine column contract used
to be whichever order each call site happened to write its object literal in. Reordering two keys in a
literal — an edit no reviewer would question — silently re-labelled every column of that metric in the
dataset. The layout is now one declared fact.

The scrub backstop also stopped missing the shapes people actually write. Its denylist caught an
unbroken run of nine or more digits, so a card number typed the way a payment form asks for it —
`4111 1111 1111 1111` — and any phone number at all passed through verbatim with the tripwire silent,
in `messageHead`, the one free-text field in the catalog and the one carrying a user's own words.
Separated 12-to-19-digit groups and phone numbers (dashes, dots, spaces, parenthesised area codes,
country codes) are now scrubbed and tripped.

Finally, the scrubber's minted-handle exemption no longer restates the token length and alphabet that
`@magna-carta/identifiers` owns; it and the package's own per-entity validators both build their
patterns from one exported fragment, so changing the token shape cannot leave a stale copy behind that
starts mangling Error IDs.
- **The uuid advisory is fixed rather than accepted.** `GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq` (missing buffer bounds
checks in uuid's `v3`/`v5`/`v6` when the caller supplies an output buffer) reached the tree only
through the API-contract tooling — `@stoplight/prism-cli` and `@stoplight/spectral-cli` pull
`postman-collection`, which hard-pins uuid 8.3.2 through its newest release, so no carrier bump
cleared it. A `pnpm-workspace.yaml` override now forces uuid 11.1.1, the newest release that still
ships a CommonJS entry point (uuid 12+ is ESM-only, and `postman-collection` does
`require('uuid').v4()`). Its accepted-advisory entry is gone from `osv-scanner.toml` rather than
carried to a later date.

**Password-protected Office uploads no longer scale an attacker's cost.** `office-crypto` parses the
agile `EncryptionInfo` descriptor with quick-xml, and every quick-xml before 0.41 scans a start tag's
attributes for duplicate names in quadratic time (`RUSTSEC-2026-0194`) — so a crafted upload with one
enormous start tag could pin a CPU core for minutes. `office-crypto` 0.3, its newest release, still
requires `quick-xml ^0.38`, so the fixed parser cannot be resolved. `crates/decryption-core` now caps
the descriptor at 64 KiB before `office-crypto` sees the bytes, which bounds the scan to well under a
second and stops the cost scaling with the uploaded file — the same defensive-perimeter pattern as the
existing `EncryptedPackage` size-prefix guard.

**The remaining quick-xml acceptances say what was checked.** Both quick-xml entries in
`osv-scanner.toml` were re-checked before their 2026-10-14 lapse and extended to 2027-02-14 with the
reachability analysis written into the file: `RUSTSEC-2026-0194` is reachable but now bounded, and
`RUSTSEC-2026-0195` is not reachable at all — it affects only quick-xml's `NsReader`, and
`office-crypto` builds a plain `Reader` that never resolves namespaces.

**The operations runbook stopped duplicating the advisory list.** Its dependency-audit section still
described the retired `pnpm audit` gate and restated two accepted advisories, one of which GitHub had
withdrawn. It now points at `osv-scanner.toml` as the single home and records the working rules for
adding, extending, and pruning entries.

**PDF handling picks up upstream decompression-bomb guards.** lopdf moved 0.42 to 0.44 across all six
lockfiles, adding bounded stream decompression, a `LoadOptions.max_decompressed_size` limit for
load-time object and cross-reference streams, and a fix that rejects incremental saves of encrypted
documents. `Document::get_page_content` is infallible in 0.44, so its five call sites in
`crates/pdf-core` dropped their `Result` handling.
- **The `office-crypto` dependency is gone; `decryption-core` decrypts Office documents itself.**
`crates/decryption-core` already owned the ECMA-376 agile verifier, the iterative password hash,
block-key derivation, its own descriptor parser, and the compound-file validation. The only thing
`office-crypto` still did was the package decryption loop, which is now implemented in-house:
MS-OFFCRYPTO agile encryption's 4096-byte segments, each an independent AES-CBC chain under an
initialization vector derived from the `keyData` salt and the segment index, plus the session-key
unwrap that precedes them. ECMA-376 **standard** encryption (Office 2007 — AES-ECB under a
SHA-1-derived key) is ported alongside it, so no document that opened before stops opening; its
legacy RC4 CryptoAPI variant is refused by name, exactly as it was before.

**This removes both quick-xml advisories from the tree rather than accepting them for another
review cycle.** `office-crypto` was quick-xml's only consumer in every audited lockfile, and no
`office-crypto` release resolves the fixed quick-xml 0.41, so replacing it was the only remediation
that existed — the exit the accepted-advisory entries themselves named. `RUSTSEC-2026-0194` and
`RUSTSEC-2026-0195` leave `osv-scanner.toml`, which now holds no accepted Rust advisory at all.
Sixteen crates leave the dependency graph (`office-crypto`, `quick-xml`, `base64`, `bytemuck`,
`derivative`, `ecb`, `packed_struct` and its codegen, `bitvec` and friends, `serde`, `syn` 1.x);
none are added — the in-house loop is built on the RustCrypto primitives already in the workspace.

**Three panic paths on untrusted input close with it.** `office-crypto` computed
`total_size - 4096` as unsigned arithmetic with no bounds check, unwrapped its XML reader outright
on a malformed descriptor, and read `spinCount` from an uploaded document with no cap — so a
crafted file could crash the process or pin a core for hours. The in-house path is checked
throughout: the size prefix is read as the 64-bit quantity it is and converted rather than cast (a
32-bit concern on the wasm32 target), a prefix promising more plaintext than there is ciphertext is
refused before a segment is decrypted, and the spin-count cap that guarded hash extraction now
guards decryption too. Every guard that already existed is kept.

**A wrong password is now refused by the ECMA-376 verifier rather than inferred.** Both schemes
carry a password verifier and both are checked before any package byte is decrypted, so a wrong
password costs one key derivation instead of a full decryption, and a genuinely corrupt document is
reported as malformed rather than as a bad password.
- Dependency audit — three new HIGH advisories are remediated by version, not accepted. `quick-xml`
moves 0.38 to 0.41 in `crates/discovery-core`, the discovery engine's OOXML and OpenDocument text
walk. 0.41.0 is the release that fixes both RUSTSEC-2026-0194, where the start-tag
duplicate-attribute check cost `O(N²)` byte comparisons so a single crafted tag could pin a core for
minutes, and RUSTSEC-2026-0195, where namespace resolution allocated one binding per `xmlns`
declaration with no upper bound, inside the reader and before the consumer ever saw the event. The
first is directly reachable here: the spreadsheet walk iterates a cell's attributes, and this
engine's whole input is files an opposing party chose. `js-yaml` moves to the 3.15.1 and 4.3.1
backports for GHSA-5p4m-2wfm-xmqj, whose `!!omap` key-uniqueness check is quadratic on the default
schema, so a plain `load` of untrusted YAML blocks the event loop for the whole document. The
earlier quick-xml acceptance is not re-opened — it left this repository when its carrier was
replaced, and the carrier today is a different one that arrived with the discovery core. There is
still no accepted Rust advisory.
- **New dependency versions wait three days before they can be resolved.** `minimumReleaseAge` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. A version published minutes ago is the shape a compromised release arrives in: the attacker publishes, the weekly automated upgrade opens its pull request, and the package is in the tree before the registry has heard the report. Every recent npm compromise of this kind was caught in public within days, by other people, at no cost to us — the cooldown is how that work gets used.

It applies at resolution, so nothing already in the lockfile moves, and it is a floor rather than a wall: a security fix that has to land the day it ships is `pnpm add <package>@<version> --config.minimumReleaseAge=0`, a deliberate act with a reason.
- **Eleven of the twenty open advisories across the two supply chains are remediated, and the acceptance
file is empty for the first time.** Nothing had audited them since 2026-08-04: the CI dependency gate is
the only thing that looks, and no runner had been assigned since 2026-08-07. The enumeration was rebuilt
by querying the OSV API directly with the coordinates parsed out of `pnpm-lock.yaml` and all nine
`Cargo.lock` files — the same database and the same lockfile scope the gate's own scanner uses. Its npm
half reproduces GitHub's reported count exactly (four high, five moderate, two low), which is what makes
the rest of the list trustworthy; the nine RustSec findings are additional, and invisible to that count.

What moved, all within an existing major:

- `nanoid` 5.1.11 to 5.1.16 in the catalog — the one **direct production** dependency in the set
  (`packages/identifiers`). Two infinite-loop advisories, and at CVSS 4.0 8.2 the only findings in the
  sweep that were over the audit's fail threshold. Not reachable: the seam imports the secure entry
  point rather than `nanoid/non-secure`, and every size it passes is a compile-time constant.
- `@sveltejs/kit` 2.69.3 to 2.70.2 — quadratic `Accept`-header negotiation. The shipped SPA is
  prerendered by adapter-static and runs no SvelteKit request handler, so the exposed surface was the
  dev server.
- `postcss` 8.5.18 to 8.5.26 in the overrides — an arbitrary `.map` read through a crafted
  `sourceMappingURL`. Taken above its 8.5.23 floor because 8.5.26 is the first release requiring
  `nanoid ^3.3.17`, and that dependency was the only thing holding a vulnerable `nanoid` 3 in the tree.
- `lodash` pinned to 4.18.1 — this retires the long-standing accepted advisory. `postman-collection`
  hard-pins 4.17.21 and never moved, so the acceptance had been sitting on "drops when the carrier
  upgrades" indefinitely; the override is the same move already used for `uuid` on the same carrier, and
  4.18.1 is what every other consumer in the tree already resolved.
- `esbuild` scoped to 0.28.2, and patch bumps of `crossbeam-epoch`, `anyhow` and `memmap2` in the Cargo
  lockfiles.

Nine advisories remain and none is accepted, because an entry in `osv-scanner.toml` is for something
that would otherwise fail the gate and every one of these passes it. Each has either no published fix
(four unmaintained-crate notices, plus `rsa`'s Marvin sidechannel) or no fix reachable without a carrier
moving first (`cookie` behind SvelteKit, `esbuild` 0.18 behind a deprecated `@esbuild-kit`, `lru` behind
tantivy, `wasmtime` behind `yara-x`). The reasoning for each is in the `osv-scanner.toml` header, which
now documents what is deliberately left visible rather than only what is forgiven.
- **Every npm advisory with a fixed release is cleared. The only npm findings left are the two the
`osv-scanner.toml` header already names as out of reach.** Ten advisories had opened since the last
sweep, all below the gate's fail threshold, so nothing had failed. All moved within their existing
major:

- `hono` 4.13.0 to 4.13.5 in the catalog, the only one with production reach: unbounded dot-notation
  nesting in `parseBody()` (a memory DoS through any form body), the query parser reading past a `#`
  fragment, and `toSSG()` writing outside its output directory.
- `devalue` pinned to 5.9.2 (a parser DoS on malformed input), through svelte, SvelteKit and
  sveltekit-superforms.
- `joi` 17 pinned to 17.13.8 (two prototype-pollution paths), reached only as superforms' optional
  validator adapter.
- `js-yaml` 4 to 4.3.2 and 3 to 3.15.2 (merge-key exhaustion), behind the OpenAPI client generator.
- `sharp` to 0.35.4 (an out-of-bounds read in its bundled libheif), behind miniflare.
- `extract-zip`'s two symlink-traversal advisories have **no fixed release**, so their carrier is
  removed instead. `@cloudflare/puppeteer` hard-pins `@puppeteer/browsers` 2.2.4 for its Node launcher,
  which downloads a local Chrome. A Worker never runs that launcher: the entry point drives the
  Browser Rendering binding, and a dry-run bundle of the API worker contains none of
  `@puppeteer/browsers`, `extract-zip` or `yauzl`. Removing it with a pnpm override drops about 600
  lockfile lines and adds no baseline entry.
- **Five HIGH advisories that turned the governance job red on every branch are cleared, one by a bump and four by removing a carrier.** On 2026-09-02 osv-scanner began reporting four advisories on fast-uri 3.1.5 (host confusion and server-side request forgery through URI normalization, CVSS 7.5 each) and one on @faker-js/faker 5.5.3 (`helpers.fake` code execution, CVSS 7.8) against a lockfile identical to `main`'s, so no pull request could merge past a failure none of them caused.

fast-uri is fixed in 3.1.6; the override in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` moves to 3.1.7. It reaches the tree only through ajv, whose declared range already admits that line, so nothing else resolves differently.

faker had a wall. Its sole carrier, postman-collection, hard-pins 5.5.3 through its newest release and reads the v5 API at module load, so forcing the fixed line (10.5.0, a different major) makes the package throw on require. postman-collection reached the lockfile only through the Prism mock server's HTTP layer, and nothing in the repository ran Prism: no script, tool, test, plugin or workflow, and the "Prism mock smoke" the API conventions described lived in a workflow file that does not exist. So `@stoplight/prism-cli` leaves `apps/api-worker`, and with it postman-collection, faker 5.5.3, and uuid, whose override existed only for that carrier. The mock server stays available on demand (`pnpm dlx @stoplight/prism-cli mock …`, documented in `docs/conventions/api.md`) without living in the audited tree. The lodash override remains as a floor. Spectral, the contract lint the gate actually runs, is untouched.
- **`lint:secrets`, `lint:containers` and `lint:native-builds` — the supply-chain family this repository had none of.**

There was **no secret scan of any kind**, on a platform that holds firm credentials, the root key that wraps every per-firm data key, and privileged client documents. A credential is compromised the moment it is pushed and stays compromised in the object database after the commit that removes it, so the only cheap moment to catch one is before it lands. Eleven rules over 7,111 tracked files, in-house for the same reason the license gate is: a hosted scanner is handed, by construction, exactly the bytes it is looking for. Findings never print the value. The tree is clean — and `apps/api-worker/.dev.vars` passes because the scan **decodes** its values and finds the placeholder inside, not because its path is allowlisted, so the file stays under the rule forever. The scan does not skip its own directory either: every pattern is written so its own source cannot satisfy it.

The container gate holds the Dockerfile properties that matter for images built here — an explicit tag, never `latest`; no `ADD` from a URL; no disabled certificate verification, in ten spellings; no credential baked into a layer. Two properties are ratchets rather than bans, with the measurement that made them so: **no** base image is digest-pinned (five distinct bases, each recorded with its reason, keyed by image so a new container reusing a known base needs no edit), and **1 of 11** runtime images drops privileges. What it leaves to review is stated rather than implied — whether a pinned hash is the right hash, and the sandbox properties that live in the Containers configuration rather than in a Dockerfile.

The native-build gate gives golden rule 14 a mechanism instead of a habit, across four surfaces: the `onlyBuiltDependencies` grants, the build scripts pnpm has blocked, the platform binaries in the lockfile, and every `-sys`/`cc`/`cmake`/`bindgen` crate in fifteen `Cargo.lock` files. It does not fail on what is already here — a gate that does gets switched off — it fails on what is **new**, and prints everything that is not memory-safe on every run with its language and its consumer. It refuses to pass when it reads nothing: a consent gate that silently scans an empty set is the one failure mode it must not have.

What that surfacing shows is worth reading: clamd is the one consented C engine, and beside it sit `onig_sys` (a C regex engine, in the OCR container's job path), `ort-sys` and `vectorscan-rs-sys` — sandboxed, but with no ruling on record the way clamd has. `openssl-sys` reaches three workspaces only through `ureq`'s `native-tls` default feature, which is a default rather than a decision. And `sharp` — libvips, the one C library the npm graph installs — is not ours: it arrives under miniflare, and so under wrangler and the Workers test pool every worker package carries.
- **Rust gets a lint floor, and `unsafe` is forbidden while the door is still shut.** `vp run rust-check` has always been `cargo fmt --check && cargo clippy -- -D warnings && cargo test`, on clippy's default lint set. There was no `[workspace.lints]` table anywhere, so nothing enforced the property the platform actually rests on: that Rust reading an opposing party's PDF, an unknown sender's `.msg` or a custodian's 7z stays memory-safe and does not abort on bytes it was handed.

`unsafe_code = "forbid"` rather than `deny`, so no crate, module or expression can take it back — the only way to reintroduce unsafe Rust is to edit the table, in a diff somebody reads. The crates workspace is unsafe-free today, which is exactly what makes it free to impose and exactly why now is the moment. `non_ascii_idents` goes the same way: a homoglyph pair reads as one word to a reviewer and is two symbols to the compiler. Two container workspaces do carry `unsafe` (the LibreOfficeKit error callback; two memory maps in the scan spool) and each omits the rule in its own manifest with the site named, so the gap is recorded rather than excused.

Panic-class clippy lints — `unwrap_used`, `panic`, `panic_in_result_fn`, `todo`, `unimplemented`, `mem_forget`, `dbg_macro` — are denied where the tree is already clean of them, and `print_stdout`/`print_stderr`/`exit` in the crates workspace, where every site was an evaluation harness. Those three are deliberately absent from the container tables: a container's binary **is** the process, so a startup diagnostic on stderr and a non-zero exit on a fatal boot failure are correct rather than a smell.

**Every level was measured first,** because the gate runs `-D warnings` and there is no level here that means "tell me later". What stayed out is recorded with its count: `clippy::indexing_slicing` at **361 sites**, clean in exactly one member so there is nothing to scope it to — the headline burn-down — and `clippy::arithmetic_side_effects` at **416**, whose real home is the byte-offset arithmetic derived from file headers. `clippy::expect_used` is four library sites away from landing.

Six source lines changed rather than watering a rule down: without them, `recovery-core` and `pdf-core` — the two crates the unwrap rule matters most for — would each have needed a crate-wide allow and lost it entirely. Test code is exempted through `clippy.toml` instead of attributes scattered through the suites.

Also fixed while in the area: the gate's cargo cache listed eight container workspaces and there are nine. `containers/discovery` rebuilt its whole dependency graph from cold on every run, silently, and that list is hand-written so nothing said so.
- **The license gate reads the Rust supply chain, and its SPDX classifier is now a parser.** `pnpm run lint:licenses` read `pnpm licenses list` and nothing else, so ten Cargo lockfiles — the crates workspace plus every container, 866 crate versions — were vulnerability-scanned by osv-scanner for a year and license-checked by nobody, against a deny-by-default policy whose whole reason is that AGPL or SSPL would force a source offer.

The policy is now one thing in `tooling/license-policy/`, read by two gates: the npm one, unchanged in behaviour, and `pnpm run lint:cargo-licenses`, which discovers every `Cargo.toml` workspace rather than listing them, so a new container joins the gate the day it is added. It runs in the gate's `rust` job, where the toolchain and a warm cargo cache make it a second or two; on the slim runner it would have paid a rustup install and a 163 MB cold fetch for an answer only a lockfile can change.

**Extracting it surfaced a real hole.** The old classifier stripped parentheses and split on the operators, so `(MIT OR GPL-3.0) AND AGPL-3.0` came out **allowed** — it found a permissive disjunct and never saw that the AGPL conjunct binds the whole work. The replacement tokenises and parses the expression at its real precedence (`OR` loosest, then `AND`, then `WITH`), which also stops it denying three forms the Rust tree genuinely carries: `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception`, the legacy `MIT/Apache-2.0` slash form, and lowercase identifiers. Anything it cannot parse is denied.

The Rust tree is clean: no AGPL, no SSPL, no GPL, no crate without a license. Six permissive identifiers the npm-era list had never met were added with their reasoning — `Unicode-3.0`, `CDLA-Permissive-2.0`, `BSL-1.0`, `MIT-0`, `NCSA`, `zlib-acknowledgement` — and they now bind both ecosystems.
- **A firm's objects are reached with a credential scoped to that firm's bucket, not one that reaches
every bucket in the account.**

A firm's bucket cannot be a binding, so the Worker signs S3 calls — and until now it signed them with
the parent R2 key, which addresses every bucket in the account for as long as it exists. That is
wider than the work: a request serving one firm's file has no business being able to address another
firm's bucket at all. `firm-bucket-credentials.ts` mints a credential derived from that parent,
scoped to one bucket, with a lifetime, and `object-read-write` rather than any admin permission — so
it cannot touch the bucket's own configuration either. A leak on the object plane now exposes one
firm for a window, where it used to expose the account.

The credential is a RESOLVER on `createS3FirmBucket`, not a value, which is what lets it be re-minted
mid-life without anything reconstructing the handle — and costs nothing, because every call there was
already awaiting a signature.

**The rule that is not obvious:** a presigned URL dies with the credential that signed it, whatever
its own `X-Amz-Expires` says, and R2's mint response carries no expiry at all — only the `ttlSeconds`
asked for. So the expiry is computed at mint time and every hand-out re-checks that the credential
outlives what is about to be signed with it, with margin. Skip that and a member gets an upload URL
good for an hour that stops working in four minutes, which reads exactly like the storage refusing
the upload and is diagnosed the same slow way.

Selection is by the presence of the provisioner's existing token — no new secret, and no code path
that only runs in production. Until it is set this behaves exactly as it did. A minting failure is
never answered with the parent key: falling back would make the narrowing decorative.

Still on the parent key: the PRESIGNER, which signs the URLs the browser follows. Same treatment,
plus `appendSessionToken` so the query-signed URL carries `X-Amz-Security-Token` — a separate change
because it is the browser-visible surface.
- **The firm's matter-visibility gate could be silently neutralized by the caller's own table names, and
the fitness functions that exist to guarantee it could never have caught that.**

The predicate every matter-scoped read composes is an `EXISTS` over `matter`, correlated to an
expression the caller supplies. Written against the bare table name, the correlation dies whenever
the CALLER's query also has an unaliased `matter` in scope: inside the subquery `matter` resolves to
the subquery's own copy, the correlation degenerates to `matter.id = matter.id` — true of every row —
and the `EXISTS` is satisfied by any visible matter in the firm rather than by the one being checked.
The gate reads exactly like a working gate and checks nothing.

**It shipped.** The call and text log's anchor check selected from `matter` and composed the
predicate over its own id, so it accepted every matter in the firm, the platform-owned custody
holding matter included. It was caught by a behavioural test asserting that holding matter is
unreachable — not by anything looking at the SQL, and not by any of the three fitness functions whose
whole purpose is this predicate. They assert the predicate's MARKER appears in the built statement,
and it did: the predicate was composed, it was composed uselessly, and a test looking for evidence of
composition cannot tell those two apart.

**Fixed at the source rather than at the call site: the subquery now aliases its own table.** A
caller's `matter` can no longer be shadowed, so an expression naming `matter.id` correlates to the
caller's row — which is what every author writing one intends. The failure becomes unwritable rather
than merely tested for. The narrowed variant gets the same treatment, and there it matters more: that
is the shape an ethical-wall overlay takes when it is built, where a dead correlation would exclude
the wrong rows rather than merely fail open.

**Swept, and this was the only instance.** All 56 call sites of the predicate were checked against
the two conditions the bug needs — the predicate composed, and an unaliased `matter` in the caller's
own FROM or JOIN. No timeline or search source is exposed: none passes `matter` as its `from`. Two
hand-written `EXISTS` clauses over `matter` exist, in the task list and the notification feed, and
both correlate against a different table, so both are sound.

Three regression tests, each verified to fail against the old predicate, including one that reads
real rows and watches the holding matter leak. The calendar's schema-name scanner now knows the
alias, with the reason attached, so nobody removes it to quiet the scan.

### Added

- Documentation foundation: reorganized white paper (Parts + stable section numbering), Decision Log with the ADR standard and stable IDs, root `CLAUDE.md` (golden rules + orientation), `docs/conventions/` standards, `docs/specs/` scaffold, and `docs/user/` end-user & admin scaffold.
- Living trackers and a documentation standard: this changelog, the living [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md), a definition-of-"done" documentation process (`docs/conventions/documentation.md`), and a shared writing language — change types, commit/changelog style, and a canonical glossary (`docs/conventions/documentation-style.md`).

### Removed

- Swept **64 stale stream notes** out of the active-work registry, leaving the streams that are genuinely
in flight. The registry exists so a starting stream can see what else is running and where it would
collide; at 64 entries — nearly all of them describing work that merged days or weeks earlier — it had
stopped answering that question, because a reader could no longer tell the live entries from the dead
ones. What remains is four notes: the orchestrator stream, this sweep, and two older streams that never
opened a pull request and still carry unmerged commits.

Merged-ness was established from the **merged-pull-request record**, matching each note's filename to
the head branch of the pull request that landed it, and corroborated against the files each note said it
would create. The obvious test — asking git whether a remote branch is an ancestor of `main` — is
misleading in this repository: pull requests are squash-merged and the git proxy refuses ref deletions,
so branches for long-landed work sit permanently ahead of `main`. Two notes whose streams left unmerged
commits and no pull request were kept on the principle that a stale note is untidy while a deleted note
for live work destroys the only record of what a stream was doing.

Each deletion is paired with its `status.d/<slice>.md` fragment flipped back to `branch: main` and an
empty `active-work:`, so nine slice fragments no longer point at notes that are gone — the pairing the
status fitness function enforces.

This also settles a **naming inconsistency** the docs-sync reports had flagged three runs running. Notes
are named after the branch they describe, slashes included, so a `claude/<name>` branch belongs at
`docs/active-work/claude/<name>.md`; a flattened `claude-<name>.md` is invisible to the registry's
branch-to-note lookup and reads as "no note at all". Exactly one flattened note remained, and it
belonged to a merged stream, so the sweep removed it and the two naming conventions became one.
- **The `/tools` area is gone — the layout, the index, the catalogue projection and the `/tools/<id>`
addresses with it.** `toolRoute()` is `/<id>`, `ToolManifest.route` is deleted (nothing needs to
declare an exception to a prefix that no longer exists), and the five tool routes moved out of
`(app)/tools/` to the top level.

What replaced the index is what was already better at its job. Its two worthwhile parts were the
descriptors and the search, and neither belonged to it: the descriptors are the presentation layer's
and the search net is `toolSearchKeywords()`, both of which the command palette has rendered all
along — over every destination at once, from one keystroke, with no navigation first.

Three registries shrank with it. `tool-catalogue.ts` is deleted; `SUBJECT_GROUP_LABELS` moved to
`navigation/clusters.ts`, where a cluster's name sits beside its glyph and the group it folds inside;
and the eight catalog subject groups became four (`records`, `internet`, `mailing`, `files`) — eight
headings over nine tools is a heading per tool. `toolsByGroup()` sorts a cluster alphabetically by
name, because catalog order is a fact about this repository rather than about the firm.

The shared catalogue framework (`$lib/catalogue`) stays, with Reports as its one consumer. One screen
using a shared shape is not a reason to un-share it.
- **The storage meter's Analytics Engine trend port is deleted, and the reason a trend is not kept
replaces it. It was not a binding away from working — as declared it wrote a raw data point indexed
by the firm id in clear, into the one dataset every other firm handle is HMAC-pseudonymized before
reaching, laying out its own blob columns beside the declared metric catalog that exists to be that
dataset's only door.**

`packages/file-manager/src/metering-statements.ts` carried a `MeterTelemetry` port and an
`emitMeterDataPoint` that nothing implemented and no caller ever passed an adapter to, under a comment
explaining that it was unfilled. Reading what it would have written is what settled it. `indexes:
[firmId]` puts a tenant identifier in the Analytics Engine index — the sampling and aggregation key,
the most durable field on the row — where `packages/telemetry/src/pseudonymize.ts` HMACs the same
handle under a pepper and drops the event entirely when the pepper is absent, because the dataset is a
cross-firm aggregate store the firm does not control and cannot have redacted afterwards. The blobs
were clean by luck rather than design: the prefix is the top-level R2 key segment and is always
`files` or `bulk`, the class and role are enum tokens. Beside that, blob one on that dataset is the
metric name by contract and every other writer goes through the metric catalog, which scrubs each
dimension and drops what it cannot place — a second writer with its own layout is the unguarded door
that catalog was built to close.

What the trend was for is real: the `storage_meter` rows are a current rollup and hold no history, so
nothing can answer how a firm's storage grew. Analytics Engine cannot answer it either — roughly
ninety days of retention, and cross-firm aggregate by policy — so the shape is named in the code
instead: a periodic snapshot row per firm in that firm's own database, read by the firm-usage surface
that already reports current totals. Nothing downstream loses anything, because nothing consumed it:
`readStorageUsage` and the `/api/v1/firm-usage` route read D1 and only D1, and the operational rate
signals that do belong in Analytics Engine (`storage.reconciliation.corrected`,
`storage.dimension.stamped`) already ride declared counters. The reconciliation pass's header, which
still claimed "the analytics trend seam consumes the corrected meter on its own path", is corrected.
- **The ten standalone file-utility rows leave the tool catalogue.** File Converter, Metadata Scrubber, File Hash & Integrity, File Decryption, File Type Verifier, AI-Text Detection, File Repair, OCR, Email Inspector and Malware Scan were each a File Workbench capability tab under another name, so the catalogue promised ten screens that do not exist and never would. The `files` subject group is now the workbench alone, and `test/catalog.test.ts` fails on a new row there.

Two things had to outlive the rows, neither enforced by a type. Their permissions: every capability module is gated on the key its sibling manifest declared, and `grantedPermissions()` built its set from `CATALOG`, so the deletion would have emptied the tab strip silently — `tool-permissions.ts` names all nine explicitly now, held to the capability registry by a test. And their search vocabulary, which moved onto the workbench's synonyms in `tool-presentation.ts`. The access-control registry entries and `role_permission` seeds are untouched and still used.
